docs.title: Python for Beginners
docs.text:
The IT industry changes and grows faster than most traditional industries. If you stop learning, you'll soon be left behind. But remember: the people left behind are always the ones who stay at beginner level – people with really solid skills are always in demand. So when it comes to learning, we need to be steady and careful.

Teaching yourself Python is the same. Don't get over-excited at the start and keep bookmarking websites, buying lots of books and downloading piles of video lessons. A few days later, your excitement fades. A few weeks later, you've finally completed the course "From Getting Started to Giving Up". So, learning Python takes one step at a time, steadily and carefully.

docs.title: About this English edition
docs.text:
This is a simple-English translation of the Chinese tutorial by walter201230 (github.com/walter201230/Python), shared under the CC BY 4.0 licence. The tutorial is written for Python 3.10+, and some chapters point out new features from 3.11/3.12/3.13.

The original author's interactive site, learn-py.org, lets you write code in the browser with automatic marking (in Chinese).

docs.title: Python is getting more and more popular
docs.text:
When Python was first created, it was not very powerful. It ran slowly, it could not use many CPU cores, and it could hardly do things at the same time. Back then, computers were not very fast, so Python did not become popular. Many people had never even heard of it.

Over time, computers got much faster, and software got much more complex. Companies started to care more about how fast people can write code. A new idea appeared: at the start of a project, speed of development matters more than speed of the program. It's not worth making the work many times bigger just to save less than 1 millisecond. In other words, the programmer's time matters more than the machine's time. So more and more developers started to love Python.

From 2012 to 2014, cloud computing became a hot topic. Lots of start-ups and big internet companies rushed into it. The most famous open-source cloud platform, OpenStack, was built with Python.

A few years later, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning became very popular – and Python was the first-choice language for them too.

By then, Python had become a focus of internet development. In the "Top 10 programming languages" trend chart, Python climbed to 3rd place, and in 2017 it became the most popular language.

Here is the trend from the TIOBE Programming Community Index, 2002 – 2018:

  • Java: in 1st place for a long time. About 25% in 2002, dropping to about 15% in 2018.
  • C: in the top 2 with Java for a long time. About 20% in 2002, about 14% in 2018.
  • Python: only about 1% in 2002, rising to about 8% in 2018, into the Top 3.
  • C++, C#, JavaScript, PHP and others: moving up and down between 5% and 10%.

Source: TIOBE Index.

docs.text:
Python developers are some of the best-paid developers, especially in data science, machine learning and web development.

In China's biggest cities (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen), Python jobs pay over 20,000 yuan a month.

docs.title: Python is easy to start and very powerful
docs.text:
If you are a beginner, Python is your best choice. It's easy to learn, it's powerful, and you can build web apps with it easily. It's a great first language.

Python has even been added to school exams and primary school textbooks in China.

"Internet-famous" AI language Python enters Shandong primary school textbooks

The Paper · Wang Xinxin · 11 Dec 2017

Besides English, some high school and even primary school students may soon need to learn another "foreign language" – Python. Shandong Province recently added Python to its new Year 6 information technology textbook.

Simply put, Python is a widely used, high-level, general-purpose programming language. It was created by Guido van Rossum from the Netherlands, and its first version came out in 1991. In ranked.com's list, Python was the most popular AI programming language in 2017, with C++ in second place.

If you already know some programming, Python is also a good choice. Python may well be the main direction for future development, and knowing one more language gives you one more useful skill. Python also has powerful libraries, so you can build tools very quickly to help with your main work.

docs.title: First, pick a small thing you want to make
docs.text:
After reading all that, you may want to start learning right away. But don't rush off to find more courses. Let's set a small goal first: learn to track how much time you spend studying each day.

Step one only needs to show one sentence on the screen. When you learn lists and dictionaries, you will put several study records together. When you learn loops, you will add up the total minutes. When you learn functions, you will turn these steps into code you can use again and again. Later, you will save it to a file and add tests. This way, after each part, you can see what problem it solved.

There are two ways to use this tutorial. If it's your first time, use the challenge pages and code along. If you want the big picture first, or want to look up an idea again, use the full reading pages. If you meet a word that isn't explained yet, write it down and where you saw it. If not knowing it stops you from understanding the example, go back to the earlier chapter. If you just want to know how it works inside, finish the exercise first and come back later.

The news and rankings above come from older sources. When you choose what to learn, also think about your own interests, what you really need, and what jobs ask for today. First finish a small task that is useful to you, then decide if you want to go deeper.

Now write down one clear note for yourself: what do you plan to finish today, and what result means you're done? When you finish studying, also write down one example you changed, one problem you met, and one thing to check next time. These help you keep learning much more than "how long I studied today".

docs.title: 4. Integrated Development Environment (IDE): PyCharm
docs.text:
While you are learning, I suggest writing Python in a plain text editor, or a tool like Sublime Text. This helps you understand the whole process.

Of course, if you already know some programming, you can use an IDE (Integrated Development Environment) to work faster. A good choice is PyCharm. PyCharm is a Python IDE made by JetBrains. It works on macOS, Windows and Linux.

Download PyCharm here: https://www.jetbrains.com/pycharm/download/

docs.title: 2. Installing Python
docs.text:
The screenshots and commands below use Python 3.6 / 3.7 as an example. The installer you see today may look different. For the exercises, download a Python 3 version that is still supported from the official Python download page, and check the minimum version each chapter asks for. After installing, run python3 --version (on Windows you can also use py --version) to check which version is really running. Use your own install location for any paths.

Python is cross-platform. It runs on Windows, Mac and all kinds of Linux/Unix systems. Python has had two main versions: 2.x and 3.x. They do not work with each other. I installed version 3.6.1.

Where should you download it? I suggest the official website, so you always get the newest version. The official website is: https://www.python.org/

docs.title: 1. Installing on Windows
docs.text:
On Windows, after downloading, just run the installer. Remember to tick Add Python 3.6 to PATH, then click Install Now to finish.

Pay attention here: make sure you tick "Add Python 3.6 to Path". If you tick it, you don't need to set up the environment variable yourself. If you don't, you will have to do it by hand.

In the "Install Python 3.6.1 (64-bit)" setup window, you will see two choices:

  • Install Now: install with the default settings. The default path is C:\Users\Administrator\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python36. It includes IDLE, pip and the documentation, and creates shortcuts and file links.
  • Customize installation: choose your own install path and features.

Whichever you choose, there are two tick boxes at the bottom: "Install launcher for all users (recommended)" and "Add Python 3.6 to PATH". Tick the second one and you won't need to set up the environment variable yourself. Don't forget this step!

If you clicked too fast and forgot to tick "Add Python 3.6 to Path", don't worry. You just need to set the environment variable by hand.

In the command prompt (cmd), type:

path=%path%;C:\Python

Very important: C:\Python is the folder where Python is installed. If you installed it somewhere else, type your own folder instead.

After installing, open a command prompt window and type python. If you see something like this, Python is installed:

C:\Users\Administrator>python
Python 3.6.1 (v3.6.1:69c0db5, Mar 21 2017, 18:41:36) [MSC v.1900 64 bit (AMD64)] on win32
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>

When you see the >>> prompt, you are in Python's interactive mode. You can type any Python code, press Enter, and see the result right away.

docs.title: 2. Installing on Mac
docs.text:
Macs often came with Python 2.x already installed, but nobody uses 2.x now. So I suggest downloading the newest version from https://www.python.org/downloads/mac-osx/ and installing it.

After installing, how do you set the environment variable?

First, check the current PATH:

echo $PATH

Then open ~/.bash_profile (create it if it doesn't exist)

vi ~/.bash_profile

I installed Python 3.7, so the Python path is /Library/Frameworks/Python. Framework/Versions/3.7/bin. So I add this line:

export PATH="/Library/Frameworks/Python. Framework/Versions/3.7/bin:$PATH"

After that, ~/.bash_profile looks roughly like this (this is from my own computer):

# Setting PATH for Python 3.6
# The original version is saved in .bash_profile.pysave
PATH="/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.7/bin:${PATH}"
export PATH

Finally, save and quit, then load the file:

source ~/.bash_profile

docs.title: 1. What is Python?
docs.text:
Python was created by Guido van Rossum (his fans call him "Uncle Turtle" in Chinese). He wrote it over Christmas 1989, just because he was bored during the holidays. Some people are simply amazing – he made a super powerful programming language just to pass the time!

Today there are about 600 programming languages in the world, but only about 20 are really popular. Have you heard of the TIOBE ranking?

Here is the TOP 20 list of programming languages from February 2017:

Feb 2017 Feb 2016 Change Programming Language Ratings Change 1 1 Java 16.676% -4.47% 2 2 C 8.445% -7.15% 3 3 C++ 5.429% -1.48% 4 4 C# 4.902% +0.50% 5 5 Python 4.043% -0.14% 6 6 PHP 3.072% +0.30% 7 9 ↑ JavaScript 2.872% +0.67% 8 7 ↓ Visual Basic .NET 2.824% +0.37% 9 10 ↑ Delphi/Object Pascal 2.479% +0.32% 10 8 ↓ Perl 2.171% -0.08% 11 11 Ruby 2.153% +0.10% 12 16 ↑↑ Swift 2.125% +0.75% 13 13 Assembly language 2.107% +0.28% 14 38 ↑↑ Go 2.105% +1.81% 15 17 ↑ R 1.922% +0.73% 16 12 ↓↓ Visual Basic 1.875% +0.02% 17 18 ↑ MATLAB 1.723% +0.63% 18 19 ↑ PL/SQL 1.549% +0.49% 19 14 ↓↓ Objective-C 1.536% +0.13% 20 23 ↑ Scratch 1.500% +0.71%

And here is how the TIOBE index changed for the Top 10 languages:

The TIOBE Programming Community Index (source: www.tiobe.com) from 2002 to 2017 shows: Java stayed high at 15% – 25% for years, taking turns in first place with C. C slowly went down overall. C++ fell from 15% to about 5%. Python, PHP, JavaScript, C# and others went up and down between 2% and 10%. Perl, Visual Basic .NET and Delphi/Object Pascal slowly faded away.

Overall, each of these languages has its own strengths. But it's easy to see that Python has grown very fast in recent years – especially because of machine learning and data analysis, which are very popular now.

Python is a high-level programming language, and one of its big strengths is that you can build things quickly. Python comes with a very complete standard library. It covers networking, files, GUIs (windows and buttons), databases, text and lots more. People say Python comes with "batteries included". With Python, you don't need to write lots of features from scratch – you can use ready-made ones. You can also build websites with Python. Many big websites were built with it, like YouTube, Instagram, and Douban in China. Many big companies, like Google and Yahoo, and even NASA, use Python a lot.

Of course, every language has good points and bad points, and Python is no different. So what are Python's weak points?

The first is that it runs slowly – very slowly compared to C. Python is an interpreted language. When your code runs, it is translated, line by line, into machine code that the CPU understands. This translation takes a lot of time, so it's slow. A C program is compiled into machine code before it runs, so it's very fast.

The second is that your code can't be hidden. If you share your Python program, you are really sharing your source code. Compiled languages like Java and C don't have this problem, but interpreted languages must share their source code.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: When you learn any programming language, your first program always says hello to the world. Python is no different. In this section, we will write our first Python program – Hello World.

docs.text:
1. What is Python?
    1. Installing Python
    1. Your First Python Program
    1. Integrated Development Environment (IDE): PyCharm

docs.title: 3. Your First Python Program
docs.text:
OK, enough talking. Now we can write our first Python program!

When you start writing Python, I don't really suggest using a special tool, because it makes it harder to get used to the syntax. So here I will use Sublime Text. Later you can switch to PyCharm.

Our first Python program will, of course, print Hello Python.

If you have never programmed before and don't understand anything yet, that's OK. For your first program, just follow along, get a feel for it, and give it a try.

Create a new file and name it HelloPython.py. Notice that the file ends with .py.

Then open the file and type print('Hello Python')

print('Hello Python')

Finally, open a command line window, go to the folder where HelloPython.py is, and you can run the program. Here is the result:

C:\Users\Administrator>cd C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\Python

C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\Python>python HelloPython.py
Hello Python

C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\Python>

If you use Sublime Text, and you set up the environment variable when you installed Python, you can just press Ctrl + B to run it. The result looks like this:

Note: in the bottom-right corner of Sublime Text, choose Python as the syntax. Otherwise Ctrl + B won't run your code correctly. After running, you will see the result in the output panel at the bottom:

Hello Python
[Finished in 0.5s]

docs.title: Once your first line works, change one small thing
docs.text:
The program above can already print text. First, write down two lines you would like to see. Then change the text below to your own version:

print('Today I start learning Python')
print('First, finish a small example that runs')

Output:

Today I start learning Python
First, finish a small example that runs

This time, only change the text inside the quotes. Run it and check that you get two lines. Next, leave out a closing bracket on purpose and run it again. Look at the error. When you read an error, first find the error type and where in the code it is. Don't delete everything and start again straight away. Put the bracket back, run it again, and check the problem is gone. This is a small but complete cycle: change, observe, fix.

The quotes and brackets here are Python syntax, so they must be normal keyboard symbols (not fancy "curly" quotes). Inside the quotes is the text we want to show, and it can be in any language. Special punctuation in the output text won't cause a syntax error.

Running code in the browser lets us focus on the code first. When you need to work with local files or the command line, set up Python by following the installation chapter. For now, just pick one editor that can run programs. You don't need to install every editor just to write your first line of code.

docs.title: 1. Python's Magic Methods
docs.text:
In Python, all methods wrapped in double underscores __ are called magic methods. The one we've used most is __init__.

What are magic methods for?

With magic methods, we can write beautiful code and wrap complicated logic into simple methods.

So what magic methods does a class have?

We can use Python's built-in dir() to list all the magic methods in a class. For example:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

class User(object):
    pass


if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(dir(User()))

Output:

['__class__', '__delattr__', '__dict__', '__dir__', '__doc__', '__eq__', '__format__', '__ge__', '__getattribute__', '__gt__', '__hash__', '__init__', '__init_subclass__', '__le__', '__lt__', '__module__', '__ne__', '__new__', '__reduce__', '__reduce_ex__', '__repr__', '__setattr__', '__sizeof__', '__str__', '__subclasshook__', '__weakref__']

You can see a class has quite a lot of magic methods. But we only need to know some of the common, useful ones.

docs.title: First, pick one thing you want your object to do
docs.text:
You don't need to memorise every magic method at once. Say we want to use len() to see how many entries a log has. Let's write the least code needed for just that:

class Logbook:
    def __init__(self):
        self.records = []

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.records)


book = Logbook()
print(len(book), bool(book))
book.records.append(15)
print(len(book), bool(book))

Output:

0 False
1 True

We only wrote __len__. If there's no separate __bool__, Python can use the length to decide if the object is true or false. So an empty log is False, and a log with one entry is True. Understanding these links between normal operations and magic methods is more important than memorising a long list of double-underscore names.

Add two more entries yourself and check that the length is 3. Then think: if all you need is to store a list of minutes, isn't a normal list already enough? A custom class should be worth it because of behaviour you really need – not just to use every magic method.

You can come back and reread the later parts on descriptors and attribute access when you need them. For now, if you can explain how a normal operation triggers a method you defined, that's enough. Go deeper step by step.

docs.title: 2. Construction (__new__) and Initialisation (__init__)
docs.text:
From what we've learned, when we define a class, we often use __init__(self) to set up attributes when an object is created.

Like this:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

class User(object):
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name;
        self.age = age;

user=User('Two Drops',23)

Actually, creating an object happens in two steps: first the object is created, then it is initialised.

__new__ creates the object and returns this new instance. __init__ only uses the arguments passed in to set up (initialise) that instance. __new__ is always called when an instance is created, but __init__ isn't always. For example, when an instance is loaded back with pickle.load, __init__ is not called.

def __new__(cls) is called before def __init__(self), and its job is to return an instance. One more thing: __new__ must always return an instance of the class, while __init__ can't return anything except None.

One more detail: __new__ can return an object of a different type. If what it returns isn't an instance of the current class, the current class's __init__ won't be called. The two-step idea above applies to the normal case of creating an instance of the current class.

Here's an example:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

class User(object):
    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        # Print some info from inside __new__
        print('def __new__ was called')
        print(args)
        # Finally, return the parent class's __new__
        return super(User, cls).__new__(cls)

    def __init__(self, name, age):
        print('def __init__ was called')
        self.name = name
        self.age = age


if __name__ == '__main__':
    usr = User('Two Drops', 23)

Look at the output:

def __new__ was called
('Two Drops', 23)
def __init__ was called

From the output, we can see how an object is created: first __new__ is called to create the object, then the arguments are passed to __init__ to set it up.

In real projects, you'll rarely use __new__, unless you want to control how objects are created. When people talk about __new__, it's usually connected to metaclasses.

And when an object's life ends, the destructor __del__ is called. But this happens when Python cleans up the object itself (garbage collection).

docs.title: 3. Controlling Attribute Access
docs.text:
We said before that Python doesn't have real private attributes. This makes it harder to "wrap up" (encapsulate) Python classes. Sometimes we want private attributes in Python, with public get and set methods to access them. Python can actually do this kind of wrapping with magic methods.

Method What it does __getattr__(self, name) Defines what happens when you try to access an attribute that doesn't exist. So by overriding it, you can catch spelling mistakes and redirect them, or warn about old attributes that shouldn't be used any more. __setattr__(self, name, value) Defines what happens when you assign or change an attribute. It lets you assign to an attribute whether it exists or not. Be careful: when you write __setattr__, avoid infinite recursion errors. __delattr__(self, name) __delattr__ is a lot like __setattr__, but it defines what happens when you delete an attribute. When writing __delattr__, also avoid infinite recursion errors. __getattribute__(self, name) __getattribute__ defines what happens every time an attribute is accessed. By comparison, __getattr__ only works when the attribute doesn't exist. So in Python versions that support __getattribute__, it is always called before __getattr__. __getattribute__ must also avoid infinite recursion errors.

From the table, you can see it's easy to make a mistake when controlling attribute access. Look at this example:

def __setattr__(self, name, value):
    self.name = value
    # Every time an attribute is assigned, __setattr__() is called, so this calls itself again (recursion).
    # It means self.__setattr__('name', value) runs, and each time the method calls itself. This will crash the program.

def __setattr__(self, name, value):
    # Store the value under the attribute name in the class's dictionary
    self.__dict__[name] = value  
    # Custom behaviour goes here

Here's an example that calls all of these methods:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

class User(object):
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        print('__getattr__ was called')
        return super(User, self).__getattr__(name)

    def __setattr__(self, name, value):
        print('__setattr__ was called')
        return super(User, self).__setattr__(name, value)

    def __delattr__(self, name):
        print('__delattr__ was called')
        return super(User, self).__delattr__(name)

    def __getattribute__(self, name):
        print('__getattribute__ was called')
        return super(User, self).__getattribute__(name)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    user = User()
    # Setting an attribute calls __setattr__
    user.attr1 = True
    # The attribute exists, so only __getattribute__ is called
    user.attr1
    try:
        # The attribute doesn't exist: first __getattribute__, then __getattr__
        user.attr2
    except AttributeError:
        pass
    # __delattr__ is called
    del user.attr1

Output:

__setattr__ was called
__getattribute__ was called
__getattribute__ was called
__getattr__ was called
__delattr__ was called

docs.title: 4. Descriptors
docs.text:
Generally speaking, a descriptor is an object attribute with "binding behaviour". Access to it is controlled by special descriptor methods.

These methods are __get__(), __set__() and __delete__().

An object that has these methods is called a descriptor.

By default, attributes are got, set and deleted using the object's dictionary (__dict__).

For example, to find a.x, Python looks in a.__dict__['x'] first, then type(a).__dict__['x'], then the parent classes of type(a) (not including metaclasses). If the value it finds is a descriptor, Python calls the descriptor's methods instead of doing the default thing.

Exactly where this happens in the search depends on which descriptor methods are defined.

Note: descriptors only work in new-style classes. We talked about new-style and old-style classes in an earlier section – have a look back if you're interested. The main feature of new-style classes is that every class inherits from type or object.

In object-oriented programming, if a class's attributes depend on each other, descriptors can help you organise the logic very neatly. In Django's ORM, fields like IntegerField in models.Model are built using descriptors.

Let's look at this example first:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

class User(object):
    def __init__(self, name='Two Drops', sex='Male'):
        self.sex = sex
        self.name = name

    def __get__(self, obj, objtype):
        print('Getting the name value')
        return self.name

    def __set__(self, obj, val):
        print('Setting the name value')
        self.name = val


class MyClass(object):
    x = User('Two Drops', 'Male')
    y = 5


if __name__ == '__main__':
    m = MyClass()
    print(m.x)

    print('\n')

    m.x = 'Three Drops'
    print(m.x)

    print('\n')

    print(m.x)

    print('\n')

    print(m.y)

Output:

Getting the name value
Two Drops


Setting the name value
Getting the name value
Three Drops


Getting the name value
Three Drops


5

This example shows clearly when __get__() and __set__() are called.

Now let's look at a classic example.

We know distance can be measured in metres or in feet. Let's define a class to represent a distance, with two attributes: metres and feet.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-


class Meter(object):
    def __init__(self, value=0.0):
        self.value = float(value)

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        return self.value

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        self.value = float(value)


class Foot(object):
    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        return instance.meter * 3.2808

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        instance.meter = float(value) / 3.2808


class Distance(object):
    meter = Meter()
    foot = Foot()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    d = Distance()
    print(d.meter, d.foot)
    d.meter = 1
    print(d.meter, d.foot)
    d.meter = 2
    print(d.meter, d.foot)

Output:

0.0 0.0
1.0 3.2808
2.0 6.5616

In this example, before we assigned anything to the Distance instance, you might expect meter and foot to be objects of their own classes. But the output shows numbers. That's because __get__ is at work.

We only changed meter, giving it an int value – but foot changed too. That's __set__ at work.

Descriptor objects (Meter, Foot) can't live on their own. They need to be held by another owner class (Distance). A descriptor can reach the attributes of the instance that owns it, like instance.meter in Foot.

docs.title: 5. Custom Containers
docs.text:
From earlier chapters, we know Python's common container types are: dict, tuple, list and string. We also talked about mutable and immutable containers. Tuples and strings are immutable containers; dicts and lists are mutable containers.

The difference is that once an immutable container is created, you can't change any of its elements. For more details, look back at the earlier articles, which have pictures.

So here's a question: are these data structures enough for everything we need?

What if they're not – what if some special need can't be met with just these basic containers?

Then we need to make our own custom container. How do we do that?

Goal What you need A custom immutable container type Define __len__ and __getitem__ A custom mutable container type On top of the immutable ones, also define __setitem__ and __delitem__ Your custom data type needs to be iterable Define __iter__ Return the length of your custom container Write __len__(self) Your container can use self[key]. If key is the wrong type, raise TypeError. If there's no value for key, raise ValueError Write __getitem__(self, key) When self[key] = value runs It calls __setitem__(self, key, value) When del self[key] runs It actually calls __delitem__(self, key) When you want your container to work with for x in container: or iter(container) Write __iter__(self), which returns an iterator

Let's use these magic methods to build a data structure from the Haskell language:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

class FunctionalList:
    ''' Works like the built-in list type, plus some extra methods: head, tail, init, last, drop, take'''

    def __init__(self, values=None):
        if values is None:
            self.values = []
        else:
            self.values = values

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.values)

    def __getitem__(self, key):
        return self.values[key]

    def __setitem__(self, key, value):
        self.values[key] = value

    def __delitem__(self, key):
        del self.values[key]

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.values)

    def __reversed__(self):
        return FunctionalList(reversed(self.values))

    def append(self, value):
        self.values.append(value)

    def head(self):
        # Get the first element
        return self.values[0]

    def tail(self):
        # Get everything after the first element
        return self.values[1:]

    def init(self):
        # Get everything before the last element
        return self.values[:-1]

    def last(self):
        # Get the last element
        return self.values[-1]

    def drop(self, n):
        # Get everything except the first n elements
        return self.values[n:]

    def take(self, n):
        # Get the first n elements
        return self.values[:n]

docs.title: 6. Magic Methods for Operators
docs.text: There are really a lot of magic methods for operators, so we'll just list two groups:

docs.title: 1. Comparison Operators
docs.text:
Magic method What it does __cmp__(self, other) If it returns a negative number, self < other; a positive number means self > other; 0 means self == other. Defining __cmp__ is strongly not recommended. Instead, define __lt__, __eq__ and so on separately. __cmp__ was removed in Python 3. __eq__(self, other) Defines how == behaves __ne__(self, other) Defines how != behaves __lt__(self, other) Defines how < behaves __gt__(self, other) Defines how > behaves __le__(self, other) Defines how <= behaves __ge__(self, other) Defines how >= behaves

A simple example makes it clear:

Look at the line labelled num1 != num2 below: inside the curly braces it actually still says num1 == num2, so the current code calls __eq__. To really test "not equal", change that expression to num1 != num2. Then __ne__ is called and you get True.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

class Number(object):
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value

    def __eq__(self, other):
        print('__eq__')
        return self.value == other.value

    def __ne__(self, other):
        print('__ne__')
        return self.value != other.value

    def __lt__(self, other):
        print('__lt__')
        return self.value < other.value

    def __gt__(self, other):
        print('__gt__')
        return self.value > other.value

    def __le__(self, other):
        print('__le__')
        return self.value <= other.value

    def __ge__(self, other):
        print('__ge__')
        return self.value >= other.value


if __name__ == '__main__':
    num1 = Number(2)
    num2 = Number(3)
    print(f'num1 == num2 ? --------> {num1 == num2} \n')
    print(f'num1 != num2 ? --------> {num1 == num2} \n')
    print(f'num1 < num2 ? --------> {num1 < num2} \n')
    print(f'num1 > num2 ? --------> {num1 > num2} \n')
    print(f'num1 <= num2 ? --------> {num1 <= num2} \n')
    print(f'num1 >= num2 ? --------> {num1 >= num2} \n')

Output:

__eq__
num1 == num2 ? --------> False

__eq__
num1 != num2 ? --------> False

__lt__
num1 < num2 ? --------> True

__gt__
num1 > num2 ? --------> False

__le__
num1 <= num2 ? --------> True

__ge__
num1 >= num2 ? --------> False

docs.title: 2. Arithmetic Operators
docs.text: Magic method What it does __add__(self, other) Addition (+) __sub__(self, other) Subtraction (-) __mul__(self, other) Multiplication (*) __floordiv__(self, other) The // operator ___div__(self, other) The / operator. Removed in Python 3, because in Python 3, division is "true division" by default __truediv__(self, other) True division. In Python 3, / is true division by default – no need for from __future__ import division __mod__(self, other) The % operator (remainder) __divmod__(self, other) The built-in divmod() function __pow__(self, other) The ** operator (power) __lshift__(self, other) The bitwise << operator __rshift__(self, other) The bitwise >> operator __and__(self, other) The bitwise & operator __or__(self, other) The bitwise | operator __xor__(self, other) The bitwise ^ operator

docs.title: 1. Using Enum Classes
docs.text:
In real projects, we always need to define constants. One way to define constants is to use capitalised variable names with integers – for example, months:

JAN = 1
FEB = 2
MAR = 3
...
NOV = 11
DEC = 12

This is quick and simple, but the type is just int, and they're still variables (they could be changed).

Is there a better way?

We can define a class, where each constant is a unique instance inside the class.

Python has an Enum class (short for enumeration) that does exactly this:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

from enum import Enum

Month = Enum('Month', ('Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct', 'Nov', 'Dec'))

# Loop through the enum
for name, member in Month.__members__.items():
    print(name, '---------', member, '----------', member.value)

# Use one constant directly
print('\n', Month.Jan)

Output:

Jan --------- Month.Jan --------- 1
Feb --------- Month.Feb --------- 2
Mar --------- Month.Mar --------- 3
Apr --------- Month.Apr --------- 4
May --------- Month.May --------- 5
Jun --------- Month.Jun --------- 6
Jul --------- Month.Jul --------- 7
Aug --------- Month.Aug --------- 8
Sep --------- Month.Sep --------- 9
Oct --------- Month.Oct --------- 10
Nov --------- Month.Nov --------- 11
Dec --------- Month.Dec --------- 12

 Month.Jan

We used Enum to define an enum class.

In the code above, we created an enum type for months called Month. Look at the arguments: the first one, Month, is the name of the enum class. The second, a tuple, gives the enum's members. And we use __members__ to loop through all its members.

Note: member.value is an int constant given to each member automatically, starting from 1 by default.

Also, every Enum member is a singleton (there's only ever one of it). Members can't be instantiated and can't be changed.

docs.title: A status's name and a status's value
docs.text:
We want to label study tasks as "To do" or "Done". Let's use an enum to list the allowed statuses clearly, and look at the member's name and value separately:

from enum import Enum


class StudyState(Enum):
    TODO = 'To do'
    DONE = 'Done'


print(StudyState.TODO.name)
print(StudyState.TODO.value)
print(StudyState('Done') is StudyState.DONE)

Output:

TODO
To do
True

TODO is the member's name, and 'To do' is the value we gave it. StudyState('Done') finds the member by its value – it doesn't create a new status with any content you like.

Try a value that was never defined and look at the ValueError. Then compare StudyState.TODO == 'To do'. The result is False, because a normal Enum member here is not the same thing as its string value. Comparison rules for other kinds of enums depend on their type – don't assume from this one example that all enums work like strings.

The source code analysis in this chapter can help you understand how it's built. But after you've finished a small task like choosing a status, coming back to it usually makes it easier to know which part of the logic you're following.

docs.title: 2. The Source Code of Enum
docs.text:
From the example above, we know __members__ lets us loop through all the members of an enum class.

But have you wondered why?

When you saw that code, did you wonder how __members__ is able to list all the members of an enum?

Let's take a rough look at how Enum is built in its source code.

Enum lives in the module enum.py. First, here's a piece of the Enum class:

class Enum(metaclass=EnumMeta):
    """Generic enumeration.
    Derive from this class to define new enumerations.
    """

You can see Enum uses the metaclass EnumMeta. Now here's the relevant piece of EnumMeta:

class EnumMeta(type):
    """Metaclass for Enum"""
    @property
    def __members__(cls):
        """Returns a mapping of member name->value.
        This mapping lists all enum members, including aliases. Note that this
        is a read-only view of the internal mapping.
        """
        return MappingProxyType(cls._member_map_)

First, the __members__ method returns a MappingProxyType that wraps a dict (a map). And @property changes how __members__(cls) is used, so it's accessed like a variable instead of a method. That's why we can just write __members__ to access it.

docs.title: 3. Enums with Custom Values
docs.text:
Sometimes we need to control the values in an enum. We can make our own class that inherits from Enum. Let's change the example above:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-
from enum import Enum, unique

Enum('Month', ('Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct', 'Nov', 'Dec'))


# The @unique decorator checks that there are no repeated values
@unique
class Month(Enum):
    Jan = 'January'
    Feb = 'February'
    Mar = 'March'
    Apr = 'April'
    May = 'May'
    Jun = 'June'
    Jul = 'July'
    Aug = 'August'
    Sep = 'September '
    Oct = 'October'
    Nov = 'November'
    Dec = 'December'


if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(Month.Jan, '----------',
          Month.Jan.name, '----------', Month.Jan.value)
    for name, member in Month.__members__.items():
        print(name, '----------', member, '----------', member.value)

Output:

Month.Jan ---------- Jan ---------- January
Jan ---------- Month.Jan ---------- January
Feb ---------- Month.Feb ---------- February
Mar ---------- Month.Mar ---------- March
Apr ---------- Month.Apr ---------- April
May ---------- Month.May ---------- May
Jun ---------- Month.Jun ---------- June
Jul ---------- Month.Jul ---------- July
Aug ---------- Month.Aug ---------- August
Sep ---------- Month.Sep ---------- September
Oct ---------- Month.Oct ---------- October
Nov ---------- Month.Nov ---------- November
Dec ---------- Month.Dec ---------- December

From this example, we can see the enum module gives us enum types that can be iterated and compared. It lets you create clearly defined names for values, instead of using bare integers or strings.

docs.title: 4. Comparing Enums
docs.text:
Enum members have no order, so they can only be compared by identity (is) and equality (==). Let's see how == and is work:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-
from enum import Enum


class User(Enum):
    Twowater = 98
    Liangdianshui = 30
    Tom = 12


Twowater = User.Twowater
Liangdianshui = User.Liangdianshui

print(Twowater == Liangdianshui, Twowater == User.Twowater)
print(Twowater is Liangdianshui, Twowater is User.Twowater)

try:
    print('\n'.join('  ' + s.name for s in sorted(User)))
except TypeError as err:
    print(f' Error : {err}')

Output:

False True
False True
 Error : '<' not supported between instances of 'User' and 'User'

Look at the last line of output: there's an error. That's because the greater-than and less-than operators raise a TypeError. In other words, members of an Enum class can't be compared with < or >.

So can we make enum members comparable by size?

Of course! Use the IntEnum class, and comparisons work.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-
import enum


class User(enum.IntEnum):
    Twowater = 98
    Liangdianshui = 30
    Tom = 12


try:
    print('\n'.join(s.name for s in sorted(User)))
except TypeError as err:
    print(f' Error : {err}')

Look at the output:

Tom
Liangdianshui
Twowater

You can see the enum members are sorted by the size of their values. So they can be compared by size.

docs.title: 1. In Python, Classes Are Objects Too
docs.text:
Before we learn about metaclasses, let's understand Python classes a bit more deeply. In most programming languages, a class is a piece of code that describes how to make an object. That's true in Python too.

We stressed this in the chapter on classes. Let's remind ourselves with an example:

class ObjectCreator(object):
    pass


mObject = ObjectCreator()
print(mObject)

Output:

<__main__.ObjectCreator object at 0x00000000023EE048>

But Python classes are different from most languages in one way: in Python, a class is also an object. Yes, that's not a typo – it's an object.

Why?

Because whenever you use the keyword class, the Python interpreter creates an object when it runs.

For example:

class ObjectCreator(object):
    pass

When the program runs this code, it creates an object in memory called ObjectCreator. This object (the class) itself has the ability to create objects (instances of the class) – and that's what makes it a class.

But underneath, it's still an object. So we can do these things with it:

class ObjectCreator(object):
    pass


def echo(ob):
    print(ob)


mObject = ObjectCreator()
print(mObject)

# You can print a class directly, because it's actually an object too
print(ObjectCreator)
# You can pass a class to a function as an argument (note: the class itself, not an instance)
echo(ObjectCreator)
# You can also assign a class to a variable
objectCreator = ObjectCreator
print(objectCreator)

Output:

<__main__.ObjectCreator object at 0x000000000240E358>
<class '__main__.ObjectCreator'>
<class '__main__.ObjectCreator'>
<class '__main__.ObjectCreator'>

docs.title: 2. Using type() to Create Classes on the Fly
docs.text:
Because classes are objects, we can create classes while the program is running.

Python is a dynamic language.

The biggest difference between dynamic and static languages is that functions and classes aren't defined when the code is compiled – they're created dynamically while the program runs.

First, let's get to know the type() function.

Create a module called hello.py, and define a class called Hello:

class Hello(object):
    def hello(self, name='Py'):
        print('Hello,', name)

Then, in another module, import the hello module and print some information.

The type() function lets you see the type of a class or a variable.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

from com.twowater.hello import Hello

h = Hello()
h.hello()

print(type(Hello))
print(type(h))

What will the output be?

Hello, Py
<class 'type'>
<class 'com.twowater.hello.Hello'>

As we said, type() shows the type of a class or variable. Hello is a class, and its type is type. h is an instance, and its type is com.twowater.hello.Hello.

The com.twowater part at the front is my package name; the hello module lives in that package.

Let's think about this a bit more. In the example above, we used type() to see the type of something.

When we looked at the type of the Hello class, it printed <class 'type'>.

In fact, type() can not only return the type of an object – it can also create new types.

Classes are created dynamically at runtime, and the way to create a class is with the type() function.

For example, we can use type() to create the Hello class from above. Look at this code:

# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

def printHello(self, name='Py'):
    # A function that prints Hello
    print('Hello,', name)


# Create a Hello class
Hello = type('Hello', (object,), dict(hello=printHello))

# Create an instance of Hello
h = Hello()
# Call the Hello class's method
h.hello()
# Look at the type of the Hello class
print(type(Hello))
# Look at the type of instance h
print(type(h))

Output:

Hello, Py
<class 'type'>
<class '__main__.Hello'>

Here's what the arguments mean when you create a class with type():

  1. The name of the class – in the example, Hello

  2. A tuple of parent classes. Python supports multiple inheritance. If there's only one parent, use the one-element tuple form. In the example, it inherits from object, so it's written (object,)

  3. A dictionary linking method names to functions. In the example, the function printHello is linked to the method name hello

The general pattern is:

type(class_name, tuple_of_parent_classes (can be empty), dict_of_attributes (names and values))

Now that we understand the arguments, look at the output: a class made with type() is exactly the same as one written with class.

This is because when the Python interpreter sees a class definition, it just reads the syntax, and then calls type() to create the class.

Normally, we define classes with class ***..., but type() can create classes too.

This means a dynamic language can create classes while running. This is very different from static languages. To create a class while a static language program is running, you'd have to build a string of source code and call the compiler, or use tools to generate bytecode. That's basically dynamic compiling, and it's very complicated.

So you can see: in Python, classes are objects too, and you can create classes dynamically.

This is actually what Python does behind the scenes when you use the class keyword – and it does it using metaclasses.

docs.title: 3. What is a Metaclass?
docs.text:
After all that, we've finally (sort of) arrived at metaclasses. But we still don't know what on earth a metaclass is.

When we create a class, it's usually so we can create instances (objects) of it.

So what's a metaclass for?

A metaclass is used to create classes. Another way to think about it: a metaclass is the class of a class.

From the type() introduction above, we know we can create a class with type():

MyClass = type('MyClass', (), {})

In fact, type is a metaclass.

type is the metaclass Python uses behind the scenes to create all classes.

Now we can guess why it's type and not Type.

Probably to match str – str is the class that creates string objects, and int is the class that creates integer objects.

type is the class that creates class objects.

You can see this by checking the __class__ attribute.

Everything in Python – yes, everything – is an object.

That includes integers, strings, functions and classes. They're all objects, and they're all created from a class.

# Integer
age = 23
print(age.__class__)
# String
name = 'Two Drops'
print(name.__class__)


# Function
def fu():
    pass


print(fu.__class__)


# Instance
class eat(object):
    pass


mEat = eat()

print(mEat.__class__)

Output:

<class 'int'>
<class 'str'>
<class 'function'>
<class '__main__.eat'>

You can see that all of these – all objects – were created by a class. So you might wonder: what's the __class__ of the __class__?

In other words, what's the class that creates these classes?

Let's add this code to the code above:

print(age.__class__.__class__)
print(name.__class__.__class__)
print(fu.__class__.__class__)
print(mEat.__class__.__class__)

Output:

<class 'type'>
<class 'type'>
<class 'type'>
<class 'type'>

Look carefully and think it through. The output above is the __class__ of the __class__ of the integer age, the string name, the function fu and the instance mEat.

You could also say it's the class of their class. And every one printed type.

As we said at the start, a metaclass is the class of a class.

So a metaclass is something that creates classes.

You can also think of it as: a metaclass is what makes classes.

And type is the built-in metaclass – the metaclass that comes with Python.

docs.title: First tell objects and classes apart, then look at the tool that makes classes
docs.text:
This chapter can get confusing, because we're not just creating instances – we're talking about classes themselves. Let's use three checks to lay out the relationships:

StudyRecord = type('StudyRecord', (), {'category': 'Study record'})
record = StudyRecord()
print(type(record) is StudyRecord)
print(type(StudyRecord) is type)
print(record.category)

Output:

True
True
Study record

The first line creates a class, and the second line uses that class to create an instance. type(record) checks what class the instance belongs to, and type(StudyRecord) goes one step further and checks the type of the class itself. In this normal example, the class was created by type.

Now write the matching version yourself using class StudyRecord:, give it the same category, and compare these three results. First understand how the two ways of creating a class line up, then come back and look at what a custom metaclass does during creation.

Metaclasses are an advanced topic. If you don't need them yet the first time through, finish the comparison above and carry on with the later lessons. Come back with the question "what else can happen when a class is created?" They are not needed for normal functions, scripts or the final project.

docs.title: 4. Writing Your Own Metaclass
docs.text:
By now, we know what on earth a metaclass is.

But we still don't know what a metaclass is actually for.

We've only got to know it a little.

Before we learn what it's for, let's learn how to write our own metaclass.

Because only once you know how to write one can you really understand what it does.

First, let's look at the __metaclass__ attribute.

"Metaclass" literally means "class beyond a class". Simply put:

Once we define a class, we can create instances from it. So: first define a class, then create instances.

But what if we want to create classes?

Then we must create the class from a metaclass. So: first define a metaclass, then create classes.

Putting it together: first define a metaclass, then you can create classes, and finally create instances.

So a metaclass lets you create classes or change classes.

In other words, you can think of a class as an "instance" created by a metaclass.

class MyObject(object):
    __metaclass__ = something…
[…]

If you write this, Python will use the metaclass to create the class MyObject.

When you write class MyObject(object), the class object MyObject hasn't been created in memory yet.

Python looks for a __metaclass__ attribute in the class definition. If it finds one, it uses it to create the class MyObject. If not, it uses the built-in type to create the class. If that's still unclear, look at this flow chart:

Another example:

class Foo(Bar):
    pass

How does Python decide here?

First, does Foo have a __metaclass__ attribute? If yes, Python uses __metaclass__ to create a class object called Foo in memory (note: a class object). If Python doesn't find __metaclass__, it looks for a __metaclass__ attribute in Bar (the parent class) and tries the same thing. If Python can't find __metaclass__ in any parent class, it looks for __metaclass__ at the module level and tries the same thing. If it still can't find __metaclass__, Python uses the built-in type to create the class object.

So __metaclass__ defines how a class behaves. Just like a class defines how an instance behaves, a metaclass defines how a class behaves. You could say a class is an instance of a metaclass.

Now we basically understand the __metaclass__ attribute. But we haven't talked about how to use it, or what you can put in it.

The answer: anything that can create a class. So what can create a class? type, or anything that uses type or subclasses type.

The main purpose of a metaclass is to automatically change a class when it's created.

You'd usually do this for an API, when you want to create classes that fit the current situation. Imagine a silly example: you decide all the attributes of all the classes in your module should be in UPPERCASE. There are several ways to do this, but one is to set __metaclass__ at the module level. That way, every class in the module is created through this metaclass, and we just need to tell the metaclass to change all attributes to uppercase.

Luckily, __metaclass__ can actually be anything you can call – it doesn't need to be a real class. So let's start with a simple function as an example.

# The metaclass automatically receives the arguments you'd normally pass to 'type'
def upper_attr(future_class_name, future_class_parents, future_class_attr):
    '''Return a class object with all attributes changed to uppercase'''
    #  Pick all attributes that don't start with '__'
    attrs = ((name, value) for name, value in future_class_attr.items() if not name.startswith('__'))

# Change them to uppercase
uppercase_attr = dict((name.upper(), value) for name, value in attrs)

# Use 'type' to create the class object
return type(future_class_name, future_class_parents, uppercase_attr)

__metaclass__ = upper_attr  
#  This affects every class in this module

class Foo(object):
    # We could also define __metaclass__ only here, so it only affects this class
    bar = 'bip'

print hasattr(Foo, 'bar')
# Output: False
print hasattr(Foo, 'BAR')
# Output: True

f = Foo()
print f.BAR
# Output: 'bip'

Using a class as the metaclass:

# Remember, 'type' is actually a class, just like 'str' and 'int'
# So you can inherit from type
class UpperAttrMetaClass(type):
    # __new__ is a special method called before __init__
    # __new__ creates the object and returns it
    # while __init__ just sets up the object with the arguments passed in
    # You rarely use __new__, unless you want to control how the object is created
    # Here, the object being created is a class, and we want to customise it, so we override __new__
    # You could also do things in __init__ if you want
    # Some advanced uses override the special __call__ method, but we won't here
    def __new__(upperattr_metaclass, future_class_name, future_class_parents, future_class_attr):
        attrs = ((name, value) for name, value in future_class_attr.items() if not name.startswith('__'))
        uppercase_attr = dict((name.upper(), value) for name, value in attrs)
        return type(future_class_name, future_class_parents, uppercase_attr)

But this isn't really OOP (object-oriented programming). We called type directly, and didn't override the parent's __new__ method. Let's do it this way instead:

class UpperAttrMetaclass(type):
    def __new__(upperattr_metaclass, future_class_name, future_class_parents, future_class_attr):
        attrs = ((name, value) for name, value in future_class_attr.items() if not name.startswith('__'))
        uppercase_attr = dict((name.upper(), value) for name, value in attrs)

        # Reuse the type.__new__ method
        # This is basic OOP – no magic
        return type.__new__(upperattr_metaclass, future_class_name, future_class_parents, uppercase_attr)

You may have noticed the extra parameter upperattr_metaclass. It's nothing special. The first parameter of a method always means the current instance, just like self in normal methods. I gave it a long name here to make it clear. But like self, all these parameters have their usual names. So in real code, a metaclass would look like this:

class UpperAttrMetaclass(type):
    def __new__(cls, name, bases, dct):
        attrs = ((name, value) for name, value in dct.items() if not name.startswith('__')
        uppercase_attr  = dict((name.upper(), value) for name, value in attrs)
        return type.__new__(cls, name, bases, uppercase_attr)

If we use super, we can make it even clearer, and it helps with inheritance (yes, you can have metaclasses that inherit from metaclasses, that inherit from type):

class UpperAttrMetaclass(type):
    def __new__(cls, name, bases, dct):
        attrs = ((name, value) for name, value in dct.items() if not name.startswith('__'))
        uppercase_attr = dict((name.upper(), value) for name, value in attrs)
        return super(UpperAttrMetaclass, cls).__new__(cls, name, bases, uppercase_attr)

People usually use metaclasses for tricky things, like introspection (code looking at itself) and controlling inheritance. It's true that metaclasses are great for "dark magic", which leads to complicated code. But metaclasses themselves are actually very simple:

  • Intercept (catch) the creation of a class
  • Change the class
  • Return the changed class

docs.title: 5. Using Metaclasses
docs.text:
We've finally reached using metaclasses. But generally speaking, we never need them. As Tim Peters, a leader in the Python world, said (roughly):

Metaclasses are deep magic that 99% of users should never worry about. If you're wondering whether you need them, you don't. The people who actually need them know for sure that they do, and don't need an explanation of why.

The main use of metaclasses is to create APIs. A typical example is the Django ORM. It lets you write something like this:

class Person(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    age = models.IntegerField()

But if you then do this:

guy  = Person(name='bob', age='35')
print guy.age

It doesn't return an IntegerField object – it returns an int, and can even get the data straight from the database.

This is possible because models.Model defines __metaclass__, and uses some magic to turn the simple Person class you just defined into a complex hook into the database.

The Django framework makes these complicated-looking things simple by giving you a simple API that uses metaclasses. Behind the scenes, it uses this API to rebuild the code and do the real work.

Everything in Python is an object. Each one is either an instance of a class or an instance of a metaclass – except type. type is actually its own metaclass. You can't do that in pure Python; it's done with some tricks at the implementation level.

Reference:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/100003/what-is-a-metaclass-in-python
