docs.title: Threads and Processes
docs.text:
Threads and processes are operating system terms. Simply put, every application has its own process.

The operating system gives each process some resources to run with, like memory space.

Inside a process, you can create threads. Threads share the process's memory space, and the operating system schedules them so they can work in parallel.

We all know modern operating systems like Mac OS X, UNIX, Linux and Windows can run many tasks at the same time.

For example, you might be browsing the web, listening to music while coding, and writing a blog post in Markdown, all at once. That's multitasking – at least 3 tasks running at the same time.

And lots of other tasks are quietly running in the background too – they just don't show on your desktop.

To the operating system, one task is one process. Opening a browser starts a browser process, opening PyCharm starts a PyCharm process, and opening a Markdown editor starts a Markdown process.

These days, multi-core CPUs are very common.

But a CPU runs code one instruction after another. So you might wonder: how does a single-core CPU run many tasks at once?

Actually, the operating system makes the tasks take turns. Task 1 runs for 0.01 seconds, then it switches to task 2, which runs for 0.01 seconds, then task 3 for 0.01 seconds… and so on, again and again.

On the surface, each task takes turns. But the CPU is so fast that we can't see or feel it – it seems like all the tasks are running at the same time.

Truly running tasks in parallel can only happen on a multi-core CPU. But because there are far more tasks than CPU cores, the operating system still automatically schedules lots of tasks to take turns on each core.

Some processes don't just do one thing. A browser, for example, can play video, play audio, show articles, let you edit text and so on. These are all sub-tasks inside the browser process. To do several things at once inside one process, you need to run several "sub-tasks" at the same time. We call these sub-tasks inside a process threads.

Every process does at least one thing, so every process has at least one thread.

Of course, a process can also have many threads, and they can run at the same time. Multiple threads work the same way as multiple processes: the operating system switches quickly between threads, letting each one run briefly in turn, so they look like they're running at the same time.

So in Python, how do we run several tasks at once?

There are two options:

One is to start several processes. Each process has only one thread, but together the processes can do several tasks.

The other is to start one process, and start several threads inside it. Then the threads can do several tasks together.

There's also a third option: start several processes, and start several threads in each one. That runs even more tasks at once, but it's much more complicated, so it's rarely used in practice.

To sum up, there are 3 ways to do multitasking:

  • Multi-process
  • Multi-thread
  • Multi-process + multi-thread

When you run several tasks at once, they usually aren't completely separate. They need to communicate and coordinate. Sometimes task 1 has to pause and wait for task 2 to finish. Sometimes task 3 and task 4 can't run at the same time. So multi-process and multi-thread programs are much more complicated than the single-process, single-thread programs we've written so far.

Because they're complicated and hard to debug, we don't want to write multitasking code unless we have to.

But very often, we really can't do without it.

Think about watching a movie on a computer. One thread must play the video, and another must play the audio. With only one thread, you'd have to play all the video first and then all the audio, or the other way round. Clearly that won't work.

docs.title: First, check which tasks can be done on their own
docs.text:
Before talking about threads and processes, let's break the task down clearly: does the calculation for each record depend on the others? Do the results need to be shown in the same order as the input, or can each one be shown as soon as it's done? These choices affect how you write the code.

The thread pool example below is for Python on your own computer. The Python that runs in a browser doesn't have the same thread and process abilities as your computer, so please run this one in a local terminal.

```python no-run from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def double_minutes(minutes): return minutes * 2

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool: results = list(pool.map(double_minutes, [15, 0, 10])) print(results) 

Output:

```text
[30, 0, 20]

The results from this map come out in the same order as the input. That doesn't mean the tasks themselves ran strictly in that order. Try changing the input to an empty list – the result should be [].

This task is too small. We're only using a thread pool here to see how it works – it can't prove that threads are always faster. To compare speed, you must keep the amount of work, the environment and the way you measure the same. When people talk about the GIL, they also need to say which interpreter and build they mean – you can't apply a conclusion about one CPython setup to every Python environment. First learn to tell apart computing, waiting and shared state, then choose your tool.

docs.title: Multithreaded Programming
docs.text:
After a thread is created, it doesn't stay in one state the whole time. Its states are roughly:

  • New – just created
  • Runnable – ready, waiting to be scheduled
  • Running – running
  • Blocked – stuck; this could be waiting, waiting for a lock, or sleeping
  • Dead – finished

Threads have different states, and also different kinds. Roughly:

  • Main thread
  • Child threads
  • Daemon threads (background threads)
  • Foreground threads

Now that we know a bit about these, let's look at some code.

docs.title: 1. Creating Threads
docs.text:
Python has two modules for working with threads: thread and threading.

The first is a low-level module for more basic operations. It's not often used in normal application development.

So let's use threading for our example:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import time
import threading


class MyThread(threading.Thread):
    def run(self):
        for i in range(5):
            print(f'thread {self.name}, @number: {i}')
            time.sleep(1)


def main():
    print("Start main threading")

    # Create three threads
    threads = [MyThread() for i in range(3)]
    # Start the three threads
    for t in threads:
        t.start()

    print("End Main threading")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Result:

Start main threading
thread Thread-1, @number: 0
thread Thread-2, @number: 0
thread Thread-3, @number: 0
End Main threading
thread Thread-2, @number: 1
thread Thread-1, @number: 1
thread Thread-3, @number: 1
thread Thread-1, @number: 2
thread Thread-3, @number: 2
thread Thread-2, @number: 2
thread Thread-2, @number: 3
thread Thread-3, @number: 3
thread Thread-1, @number: 3
thread Thread-3, @number: 4
thread Thread-2, @number: 4
thread Thread-1, @number: 4

Note: the output will definitely be different on different computers.

docs.title: 2. Joining Threads (the join method)
docs.text:
From the output above, we can see the child threads are still running after the main thread has ended. What if we want the main thread to wait for the child threads to finish before it exits?

That's when we use the join method.

Let's add some code to the example above:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import time
import threading


class MyThread(threading.Thread):
    def run(self):
        for i in range(5):
            print(f'thread {self.name}, @number: {i}')
            time.sleep(1)


def main():
    print("Start main threading")

    # Create three threads
    threads = [MyThread() for i in range(3)]
    # Start the three threads
    for t in threads:
        t.start()

    # Call join on each new thread, one after another
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    print("End Main threading")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

From the output, you can clearly see that, compared with the example above, the main thread waits until the child threads have finished before it ends.

Start main threading
thread Thread-1, @number: 0
thread Thread-2, @number: 0
thread Thread-3, @number: 0
thread Thread-1, @number: 1
thread Thread-3, @number: 1
thread Thread-2, @number: 1
thread Thread-2, @number: 2
thread Thread-1, @number: 2
thread Thread-3, @number: 2
thread Thread-2, @number: 3
thread Thread-1, @number: 3
thread Thread-3, @number: 3
thread Thread-3, @number: 4
thread Thread-2, @number: 4
thread Thread-1, @number: 4
End Main threading

docs.title: 3. Thread Synchronisation and Locks
docs.text:
When several threads load and use data, the data often gets out of sync. To fix this, we can put a lock on a resource: a thread must get the lock before it can use the resource.

The threading module gives us a Lock:

lock = threading.Lock()

Get (acquire) the lock in a thread:

lock.acquire()

When we're done, we must release the lock:

lock.release()

To let the same thread ask for the same resource several times, Python has a re-entrant lock (RLock). Inside, an RLock keeps a Lock and a counter variable. The counter records how many times acquire was called, so the resource can be acquired many times. Only after a thread has released every acquire can other threads get the resource.

How do you create a re-entrant lock? Just one line:

r_lock = threading.RLock()

docs.title: 4. Condition Variables
docs.text:
Locks can keep threads in sync, but in more complicated situations, we need to check some conditions around the lock.

Python provides the Condition object.

With a Condition object, you can wait to process data until some event happens or some condition is met. Besides the acquire and release methods of a Lock, a Condition also has wait and notify methods.

A thread first acquires the condition variable's lock. If the condition isn't met, the thread waits. If it is met, the thread runs, and can even notify other threads. Other threads that are waiting check the condition again when they get the notification.

You can think of it like this: different threads take turns acquiring the lock. If a thread's condition isn't met, it's put into a "waiting pool" (of the Lock or RLock), until another thread notifies it and it checks the condition again. Repeating this over and over solves complicated synchronisation problems.

This pattern is often used for the producer–consumer pattern. Look at this example of a buyer and seller shopping online:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import threading, time


class Consumer(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self, cond, name):
        # Set up
        super(Consumer, self).__init__()
        self.cond = cond
        self.name = name

    def run(self):
        # Make sure the Producer's code runs first
        time.sleep(1)
        self.cond.acquire()
        print(self.name + ': If I buy these two items together, can I get a discount?')
        self.cond.notify()
        self.cond.wait()
        print(self.name + ': I have placed the order. Please change the price.')
        self.cond.notify()
        self.cond.wait()
        print(self.name + ': Got it. My payment went through.')
        self.cond.notify()
        self.cond.release()
        print(self.name + ': Waiting for delivery')


class Producer(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self, cond, name):
        super(Producer, self).__init__()
        self.cond = cond
        self.name = name

    def run(self):
        self.cond.acquire()
        # Release the lock and pause the thread here, until it's notified and gets the lock back
        self.cond.wait()
        print(self.name + ': Sure, go ahead and place the order.')
        self.cond.notify()
        self.cond.wait()
        print(self.name + ': Done, I have changed it.')
        self.cond.notify()
        self.cond.wait()
        print(self.name + ': Payment received. I will ship it right away.')
        self.cond.release()
        print(self.name + ': Shipping the items')


cond = threading.Condition()
consumer = Consumer(cond, 'Buyer (Two Drops)')
producer = Producer(cond, 'Seller (Three Drops)')
consumer.start()
producer.start()

Output:

Buyer (Two Drops): If I buy these two items together, can I get a discount?
Seller (Three Drops): Sure, go ahead and place the order.
Buyer (Two Drops): I have placed the order. Please change the price.
Seller (Three Drops): Done, I have changed it.
Buyer (Two Drops): Got it. My payment went through.
Buyer (Two Drops): Waiting for delivery
Seller (Three Drops): Payment received. I will ship it right away.
Seller (Three Drops): Shipping the items

docs.title: 5. Communication Between Threads
docs.text:
If a program has several threads, they'll need to talk to each other. So how do we safely pass information or data between threads?

Probably the safest way to send data from one thread to another is to use a queue from the queue library. Create a Queue object shared by the threads, and the threads use put() and get() to add items to the queue or take them out.

# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-
from queue import Queue
from threading import Thread


def write(q):
    # The thread that writes data
    for value in ['Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops']:
        print(f'Value written to the Queue: {value}')
        q.put(value)
    q.put(None)  # Put an "end" marker when finished


def read(q):
    # The thread that reads data
    while True:
        value = q.get(True)
        if value is None:  # Stop when we read the end marker
            break
        print(f'Value read from the Queue: {value}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    q = Queue()
    t1 = Thread(target=write, args=(q,))
    t2 = Thread(target=read, args=(q,))
    t1.start()
    t2.start()

Output:

Value written to the Queue: Two Drops
Value written to the Queue: Three Drops
Value read from the Queue: Two Drops
Value written to the Queue: Four Drops
Value read from the Queue: Three Drops
Value read from the Queue: Four Drops

Python also has an Event object for communication between threads. It's a signal flag set by a thread. Other threads can wait until the signal is set.

The Event object gives a simple way for threads to communicate. It lets you set the signal, clear the signal, and wait.

  • Setting the signal

Use the Event's set() method to set its internal signal flag to true. The Event object has an isSet() method to check the flag. After you call set(), isSet() returns true.

  • Clearing the signal

Use the Event's clear() method to clear the internal signal flag (set it to false). After you call clear(), isSet() returns false.

  • Waiting

The Event's wait method returns quickly only when the internal signal is true. When the flag is false, wait keeps waiting until it becomes true.

Example:

# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import threading


class mThread(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self, threadname):
        threading.Thread.__init__(self, name=threadname)

    def run(self):
        # Use the global Event object
        global event
        # Check the Event's internal signal flag
        if event.isSet():
            event.clear()
            # Add a timeout as a safety net: checking isSet() and calling clear() is not one atomic step,
            # so two threads could both pass the check and both wait(), with only one set() to wake them
            event.wait(timeout=1)
            print(self.getName())
        else:
            print(self.getName())
            # Set the Event's internal signal flag
            event.set()

# Create an Event object
event = threading.Event()
# Set the Event's internal signal flag
event.set()
t1 = []
for i in range(10):
    t = mThread(str(i))
    # Build a list of threads
    t1.append(t)

for i in t1:
    # Run the threads
    i.start()

Output:

1
0
3
2
5
4
7
6
9
8

docs.title: 6. Background (Daemon) Threads
docs.text: By default, when the main thread exits, child threads keep running even if they weren't joined. If you want the child threads to stop when the main thread exits, you need to make them background (daemon) threads. Python provides the setDaemon method for this.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
Multithreading in Python isn't really true multithreading. If you want to make full use of a multi-core CPU, in Python you usually need to use multiple processes.

Python has a really handy package for multiple processes called multiprocessing. You just define a function, and Python does everything else.

With this package, it's easy to go from one process to running things in parallel. multiprocessing supports child processes, communication and shared data, and different kinds of synchronisation. It provides parts like Process, Queue, Pipe and Lock.

docs.title: 1. The Process Class
docs.text:
The class for creating a process: Process([group [, target [, name [, args [, kwargs]]]]])

  • target is the thing to call
  • args is a tuple of positional arguments for it
  • kwargs is a dictionary of keyword arguments for it
  • name is a nickname
  • group isn't really used

Here's an example that creates a function and runs it in several processes:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import multiprocessing
import time


def worker(interval, name):
    print(name + '[start]')
    time.sleep(interval)
    print(name + '[end]')


if __name__ == "__main__":
    p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=(2, 'Two Drops 1'))
    p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=(3, 'Two Drops 2'))
    p3 = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=(4, 'Two Drops 3'))

    p1.start()
    p2.start()
    p3.start()

    print("The number of CPU is:" + str(multiprocessing.cpu_count()))
    for p in multiprocessing.active_children():
        print("child   p.name:" + p.name + "\tp.id" + str(p.pid))
    print("END!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!")

Output:

The number of CPU is:4
child   p.name:Process-3    p.id7600
child   p.name:Process-2    p.id5560
child   p.name:Process-1    p.id7716
END!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
Two Drops 1[start]
Two Drops 2[start]
Two Drops 3[start]
Two Drops 1[end]
Two Drops 2[end]
Two Drops 3[end]

Process finished with exit code 0

docs.title: 2. Making a Process into a Class
docs.text:
We can also make a process into a class. In the example below, when process p calls start(), the run() method is called automatically.

# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import multiprocessing
import time


class ClockProcess(multiprocessing.Process):
    def __init__(self, interval):
        multiprocessing.Process.__init__(self)
        self.interval = interval

    def run(self):
        n = 5
        while n > 0:
            print(f"Current time: {time.ctime()}")
            time.sleep(self.interval)
            n -= 1


if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = ClockProcess(3)
    p.start()

Output:

Current time: Mon Oct  9 17:26:16 2017
Current time: Mon Oct  9 17:26:19 2017
Current time: Mon Oct  9 17:26:22 2017
Current time: Mon Oct  9 17:26:25 2017
Current time: Mon Oct  9 17:26:28 2017

Process finished with exit code 0

docs.title: 3. The daemon Attribute
docs.text:
To see what the daemon attribute does, look at these two examples – one with daemon and one without – and compare the output.

Without the daemon attribute:

# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-
import multiprocessing
import time


def worker(interval):
    print(f'Work start time: {time.ctime()}')
    time.sleep(interval)
    print(f'Work end time: {time.ctime()}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=(3,))
    p.start()
    print('[END]')

Output:

[END]
Work start time: Mon Oct  9 17:47:06 2017
Work end time: Mon Oct  9 17:47:09 2017

Now add the daemon attribute to process p in the same example:

# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import multiprocessing
import time


def worker(interval):
    print(f'Work start time: {time.ctime()}')
    time.sleep(interval)
    print(f'Work end time: {time.ctime()}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=(3,))
    p.daemon = True
    p.start()
    print('[END]')

Output:

[END]

From the output, you can see that if a child process has daemon set, it ends when the main process ends. That's why the child process's messages weren't printed.

docs.title: 4. The join Method
docs.text:
Carrying on from the example above: what if we want the child process to finish?

We can use the join method. Its main job is to block the current process until the process that called join has finished, and then carry on with the current process.

Here's the example with join added:

import multiprocessing
import time


def worker(interval):
    print(f'Work start time: {time.ctime()}')
    time.sleep(interval)
    print(f'Work end time: {time.ctime()}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=(3,))
    p.daemon = True
    p.start()
    p.join()
    print('[END]')

Output:

Work start time: Tue Oct 10 11:30:08 2017
Work end time: Tue Oct 10 11:30:11 2017
[END]

docs.title: 5. Pool
docs.text:
If we need lots of child processes, do we have to create them one by one?

Of course not! We can use a process pool to create child processes in bulk.

Example:

# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

from multiprocessing import Pool
import os, time, random


def long_time_task(name):
    print(f'Process name: {name}; process PID: {os.getpid()} ')
    start = time.time()
    time.sleep(random.random() * 3)
    end = time.time()
    print(f'Process {name} ran for {end - start} seconds')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(f'Main process PID: {os.getpid()}')
    p = Pool(4)
    for i in range(6):
        p.apply_async(long_time_task, args=(i,))
    p.close()
    # Wait for all child processes to finish before ending the main process
    p.join()
    print('[End]')

Output:

Main process PID: 7256
Process name: 0; process PID: 1492
Process name: 1; process PID: 12232
Process name: 2; process PID: 4332
Process name: 3; process PID: 11604
Process 2 ran for 0.6500370502471924 seconds
Process name: 4; process PID: 4332
Process 1 ran for 1.0830621719360352 seconds
Process name: 5; process PID: 12232
Process 5 ran for 0.029001712799072266 seconds
Process 4 ran for 0.9720554351806641 seconds
Process 0 ran for 2.3181326389312744 seconds
Process 3 ran for 2.5331451892852783 seconds
[End]

One thing to note: calling join() on a Pool object waits for all child processes to finish. You must call close() before join(), and after close() you can't add any new processes.

Look carefully at the output. Child processes 0, 1, 2 and 3 start straight away, but child process 4 has to wait until one of the earlier ones finishes. That's because the default size of Pool on my computer is 4, so at most 4 processes run at the same time. This is a limit Pool sets on purpose – it's not a limit of the operating system. If you change it to:

p = Pool(5)

then 5 processes can run at the same time.

docs.title: 6. Communication Between Processes
docs.text:
Processes definitely need to talk to each other. The operating system provides many ways for processes to communicate. Python's multiprocessing module wraps these low-level mechanisms and gives you several ways to exchange data, like Queue and Pipes.

Take Queue as an example. In the parent process, we create two child processes: one writes data into the Queue, and the other reads data from it:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

from multiprocessing import Process, Queue
import os, time, random


def write(q):
    # The process that writes data
    print(f'Writer process PID: {os.getpid()}')
    for value in ['Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops']:
        print(f'Value written to the Queue: {value}')
        q.put(value)
        time.sleep(random.random())


def read(q):
    # The process that reads data
    print(f'Reader process PID: {os.getpid()}')
    while True:
        value = q.get(True)
        print(f'Value read from the Queue: {value}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    # The parent process creates the Queue and passes it to each child process
    q = Queue()
    pw = Process(target=write, args=(q,))
    pr = Process(target=read, args=(q,))
    # Start child process pw
    pw.start()
    # Start child process pr
    pr.start()
    # Wait for pw to finish
    pw.join()
    # pr has an endless loop, so we can't wait for it to finish – we have to force it to stop
    pr.terminate()

Output:

Reader process PID: 13208
Writer process PID: 10864
Value written to the Queue: Two Drops
Value read from the Queue: Two Drops
Value written to the Queue: Three Drops
Value read from the Queue: Three Drops
Value written to the Queue: Four Drops
Value read from the Queue: Four Drops

docs.title: A First Look at Python Regular Expressions
docs.text:
A regular expression (regex) is a special sequence of characters used to check whether a string matches a pattern that we set.

Python added the re module in version 1.5. It provides Perl-style regular expression patterns, and gives Python the full power of regular expressions.

Let's get to know regular expressions step by step, with examples.

Say we want to check whether a string contains some character or characters. Usually we use built-in functions, like this:

# Set a constant
a = 'TwoDrops|twowater|liangdianshui|GrassRootsCoder|ReadingWithU'

# Check whether it contains the string "TwoDrops", using Python's built-in functions

print(f'Does it contain "TwoDrops"? {a.index("TwoDrops") > -1}')
print(f'Does it contain "TwoDrops"? {"TwoDrops" in a}')

Output:

Does it contain "TwoDrops"? True
Does it contain "TwoDrops"? True

So what if we use a regular expression?

As we said, Python gives us the re module for all regular expression features. Let's use one of its functions first:

re.findall(pattern, string[, flags])

This function finds all the parts of the string that match the regular expression, and returns them as a list. Like this:

import re

# Set a constant
a = 'TwoDrops|twowater|liangdianshui|GrassRootsCoder|ReadingWithU'

# Regular expression

findall = re.findall('TwoDrops', a)
print(findall)

if len(findall) > 0:
    print('a contains the string "TwoDrops"')
else:
    print('a does not contain the string "TwoDrops"')

Output:

['TwoDrops']
a contains the string "TwoDrops"

From the output, it does the same job as the built-in functions. But I must stress: this example is only to help us understand regular expressions. Writing a regex like this is pointless. Why?

Because if a problem can be solved with Python's built-in functions, there's no need for a regular expression – it's just extra work. Also, the "regular expression" in this example is just a fixed string, not a rule. The soul of a regular expression is its rules, so this doesn't mean much.

So how do you write a regex rule? Don't rush – let's go step by step. Let's start simple: find all the lowercase letters in the string. The first argument of findall is the regex rule. [a-z] matches any lowercase letter. The second argument is just the string to search. Like this:

import re

# Set a constant
a = 'TwoDrops|twowater|liangdianshui|GrassRootsCoder|ReadingWithU'

# Pick out all the lowercase English letters in a

re_findall = re.findall('[a-z]', a)

print(re_findall)

Output:

['w', 'o', 'r', 'o', 'p', 's', 't', 'w', 'o', 'w', 'a', 't', 'e', 'r', 'l', 'i', 'a', 'n', 'g', 'd', 'i', 'a', 'n', 's', 'h', 'u', 'i', 'r', 'a', 's', 's', 'o', 'o', 't', 's', 'o', 'd', 'e', 'r', 'e', 'a', 'd', 'i', 'n', 'g', 'i', 't', 'h']

Now we've got all the lowercase letters in the string.

docs.title: Prepare examples that should match AND examples that shouldn't
docs.text:
We've built up the rules step by step. Now let's make the requirement a bit narrower: a name must be made of one or more English letters. First prepare three inputs for it, then look at the results:

import re

pattern = r'[A-Za-z]+'
for name in ['Python', 'Python20', '']:
    print(bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, name)))

Output:

True
False
False

fullmatch requires the whole text to match the rule. If you used search instead, the 'Python' inside 'Python20' would be found – but that doesn't mean the whole name meets the requirement. First be clear whether you mean "contains a part that matches" or "the whole thing matches", then choose your function.

Now add 'python', 'Python!' and 'Two Drops' yourself. You should get True, False, False. The last one is False because of the space – our rule only allows English letters.

When you use index() to find a substring and it isn't there, it raises a ValueError – it does not return -1 for you to compare. If you only want to check whether some plain text is there, 'target' in text is more direct. The more complicated your rule, the more you need to keep some examples that should match, some that shouldn't, and some edge cases.

docs.title: Character Sets
docs.text:
OK, with the examples above we've had a first look at Python regular expressions. You might ask: what other rules are there? What does each letter mean?

Don't rush. Later in this chapter there's a list of regex rules, and you can easily find these on the internet too. So for now, let's go deeper into understanding regular expressions, and talk about character sets.

A character set is a group of characters inside a pair of square brackets []. With a character set, you can match one of several characters.

For example, C[ET]O matches CEO or CTO. So [ET] means one E or one T. [a-z], which we saw above, means any one lowercase letter. Here the hyphen - defines a range of characters in a row. You can put several ranges inside, like [0-9a-fA-F], which matches a single hexadecimal digit, upper or lower case. Note: the order of characters and ranges inside doesn't affect the result at all.

All of this is to show that the characters inside a character set [] have an "OR" relationship. Let's look at an example:

import re
a = 'uav,ubv,ucv,uwv,uzv,ucv,uov'

# Character sets

# Find strings where the character between u and v is a or b or c
findall = re.findall('u[abc]v', a)
print(findall)
# For letters or digits in a row, you can use -
l = re.findall('u[a-c]v', a)
print(l)

# Find strings where the character between u and v is NOT a or b or c
re_findall = re.findall('u[^abc]v', a)
print(re_findall)

Output:

['uav', 'ubv', 'ucv', 'ucv']
['uav', 'ubv', 'ucv', 'ucv']
['uwv', 'uzv', 'uov']

The example uses a negated character set: if you put a caret ^ right after the opening bracket [, the set is flipped ("not these"). Remember: a negated character set must still match one character. For example, q[^u] does not mean "match a q that isn't followed by a u". It means "match a q followed by a character that isn't u". Compare with the output of the example above to understand.

Regular expressions also have some built-in rules. For example, \d matches any digit character – it's the same as [0-9]. Here's an example that explains these special characters using character sets.

For Python string regexes, Unicode rules are used by default, so \d can also match things like full-width digits, and \w isn't limited to English letters, digits and underscores. Only when you limit it to ASCII rules can you think of them as the ASCII ranges below. When writing regex patterns, prefer raw strings like r"\d", so the backslash isn't handled by normal string rules.

import re

a = 'uav_ubv_ucv_uwv_uzv_ucv_uov&123-456-789'

# Shorthand character sets

# \d is like [0-9] – matches all digit characters
# \D is like [^0-9] – matches all non-digit characters
findall1 = re.findall('\d', a)
findall2 = re.findall('[0-9]', a)
findall3 = re.findall('\D', a)
findall4 = re.findall('[^0-9]', a)
print(findall1)
print(findall2)
print(findall3)
print(findall4)

# \w matches any "word" character, including underscore – like [A-Za-z0-9_]
findall5 = re.findall('\w', a)
findall6 = re.findall('[A-Za-z0-9_]', a)
print(findall5)
print(findall6)

Output:

['1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9']
['1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9']
['u', 'a', 'v', '_', 'u', 'b', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'w', 'v', '_', 'u', 'z', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'o', 'v', '&', '-', '-']
['u', 'a', 'v', '_', 'u', 'b', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'w', 'v', '_', 'u', 'z', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'o', 'v', '&', '-', '-']
['u', 'a', 'v', '_', 'u', 'b', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'w', 'v', '_', 'u', 'z', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'o', 'v', '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9']
['u', 'a', 'v', '_', 'u', 'b', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'w', 'v', '_', 'u', 'z', 'v', '_', 'u', 'c', 'v', '_', 'u', 'o', 'v', '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9']

docs.title: Quantifiers
docs.text:
Let's keep going deeper into regular expressions. This part is about quantifiers (how many times). Why do we need them? Think about it: if you want to match dozens or hundreds of characters, do you really want to write them one by one? That's why quantifiers exist.

The syntax of a quantifier is {min,max}. min and max are non-negative integers. If there's a comma but no max, there's no upper limit. If there's no comma and no max, it repeats exactly min times. For example, \b[1-9][0-9]{3}\b matches a number from 1000 to 9999 (\b means a word boundary), and \b[1-9][0-9]{2,4}\b matches a number from 100 to 99999.

Here's an example that matches English words of 4 to 7 letters in a string:

import re

a = 'java*&39android##@@python'

# Quantifiers

findall = re.findall('[a-z]{4,7}', a)
print(findall)

Output:

['java', 'android', 'python']

Note: there's a difference between greedy and non-greedy matching. Let's look at what they mean:

Greedy mode: it reads in the whole string at once. If it doesn't match, it spits out the rightmost character and tries again, until it finds a match or the string is empty. Its aim is to read as many characters as possible, so it returns as soon as it finds its first match.

Lazy mode: it starts from the left of the string and tries to match while reading as few characters as possible. If that fails, it reads one more character and tries again, and so on. When it finds a match, it returns it, then carries on matching until the end of the string.

The example above is greedy. How do we use non-greedy (lazy) mode instead?

To use non-greedy mode, add a ?. Let's change the example:

import re

a = 'java*&39android##@@python'

# Greedy vs non-greedy

re_findall = re.findall('[a-z]{4,7}?', a)
print(re_findall)

Output:

['java', 'andr', 'pyth']

From the output, android only gave andr, and python only gave pyth, because we're using lazy mode here.

There are also some special characters that mean "how many", like:

?: tells the engine to match the character before it 0 or 1 times

+: tells the engine to match the character before it 1 or more times

*: tells the engine to match the character before it 0 or more times

Putting it all together gives this table:

Greedy Lazy Description ? ?? Zero or one time, same as {0,1} + +? One or more times, same as {1,} * *? Zero or more times, same as {0,} {n} {n}? Exactly n times {n,m} {n,m}? At least n and at most m times {n,} {n,}? At least n times

docs.title: Boundaries and Groups
docs.text:
We've already spent a lot of space on the points above. Now let's introduce boundary matchers and groups.

The common boundary matchers are:

Syntax Description ^ Matches the start of the string (with multiple lines, the start of each line) $ Matches the end of the string (with multiple lines, the end of each line) \A Matches only the start of the string \Z Matches only the end of the string \b Matches the boundary between \w and \W \B [^\b] (not a word boundary)

Groups: an expression inside round brackets is a group. A group (...) treats those characters as one unit. You can have several groups – each new group gets the next number (1, 2, 3…). You can also put a quantifier after a group.

There should be an example here, but to save space, I've left it out.

docs.title: re.sub
docs.text:
In real work, we often need to replace characters in a string. That's when we use the function def sub(pattern, repl, string, count=0, flags=0). re.sub has five parameters: three required ones – pattern, repl, string – and two optional ones – count, flags.

Here's what each parameter means:

Parameter Description pattern The regex pattern string repl Short for "replacement" – what to replace matches with string The string to process, where replacements will happen count Of the matches found by pattern, how many to replace (from the start) flags Regex modifiers (flags)

Look at the example below – the comments explain it clearly. The main thing to notice is that the second argument can be a function. This is what makes sub so powerful. For example, the function convert in the example checks each matched character and replaces it with something different.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import re

a = 'Python*Android*Java-888'

# Replace every * in the string with &
sub1 = re.sub('\*', '&', a)
print(sub1)

# Replace only the first * in the string with &
sub2 = re.sub('\*', '&', a, 1)
print(sub2)


# Replace every * with &, and every - with |

# 1. First, define a function
def convert(value):
    group = value.group()
    if (group == '*'):
        return '&'
    elif (group == '-'):
        return '|'


# The second argument (what to replace with) can be a function
sub3 = re.sub('[\*-]', convert, a)
print(sub3)

Output:

Python&Android&Java-888
Python&Android*Java-888
Python&Android&Java|888

docs.title: re.match and re.search
docs.text:
The re.match function

Syntax:

re.match(pattern, string, flags=0)

re.match tries to match a pattern at the start of the string. If it doesn't match at the start, match() returns None.

The re.search function

Syntax:

re.search(pattern, string, flags=0)

re.search scans the whole string and returns the first match it finds.

re.match and re.search take basically the same parameters:

Parameter Description pattern The regular expression to match string The string to search flags Flags that control how matching works, e.g. whether it's case-sensitive

So what's the difference?

re.match only matches at the start of the string. If the start doesn't match the regex, matching fails and it returns None. re.search searches the whole string until it finds a match. That's the difference.

There are lots of detailed explanations of re.match and re.search online, but personally, I prefer to use re.findall.

Look at the example below to compare re.search and re.findall, and to see how multiple groups work. Read the comments and compare with the output:

Example:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

# Extract an image address

import re

a = '<img src="https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/originals/a8/c4/9e/a8c49ef606e0e1f3ee39a7b219b5c05e.jpg">'

# Using re.search
search = re.search('<img src="(.*)">', a)
# group(0) is the whole match
print(search.group(0))
print(search.group(1))

# Using re.findall
findall = re.findall('<img src="(.*)">', a)
print(findall)

# Using several groups (e.g. we want both the img tag name and the image address)
re_search = re.search('<(.*) src="(.*)">', a)
# Print img
print(re_search.group(1))
# Print the image address
print(re_search.group(2))
# Print img and the image address together, as a tuple
print(re_search.group(1, 2))
# Or use groups()
print(re_search.groups())

Output:

<img src="https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/originals/a8/c4/9e/a8c49ef606e0e1f3ee39a7b219b5c05e.jpg">
https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/originals/a8/c4/9e/a8c49ef606e0e1f3ee39a7b219b5c05e.jpg
['https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/originals/a8/c4/9e/a8c49ef606e0e1f3ee39a7b219b5c05e.jpg']
img
https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/originals/a8/c4/9e/a8c49ef606e0e1f3ee39a7b219b5c05e.jpg
('img', 'https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/originals/a8/c4/9e/a8c49ef606e0e1f3ee39a7b219b5c05e.jpg')
('img', 'https://s-media-cache-ak0.pinimg.com/originals/a8/c4/9e/a8c49ef606e0e1f3ee39a7b219b5c05e.jpg')

Finally: regular expressions are a very powerful tool. They can usually solve problems that the built-in string functions can't, and most programming languages have them. Python is used for lots of things, but web scraping and data analysis especially can't do without regular expressions. So regular expressions are really important for learning Python.

docs.title: Expressions for checking numbers
docs.text:
1.  Digits: ^[0-9]*$
2.  Exactly n digits: ^\d{n}$
3.  At least n digits: ^\d{n,}$
4.  m to n digits: ^\d{m,n}$
5.  Zero, or a number not starting with zero: ^(0|[1-9][0-9]*)$
6.  A number not starting with zero, with up to two decimal places: ^([1-9][0-9]*)+(.[0-9]{1,2})?$
7.  A positive or negative number with 1–2 decimal places: ^(\-)?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$
8.  Positive numbers, negative numbers and decimals: ^(\-|\+)?\d+(\.\d+)?$
9.  A positive real number with two decimal places: ^[0-9]+(.[0-9]{2})?$
10. A positive real number with 1–3 decimal places: ^[0-9]+(.[0-9]{1,3})?$
11. A non-zero positive integer: ^[1-9]\d*$ or ^([1-9][0-9]*){1,3}$ or ^\+?[1-9][0-9]*$
12. A non-zero negative integer: ^\-[1-9][]0-9"*$ or ^-[1-9]\d*$
13. A non-negative integer: ^\d+$ or ^[1-9]\d*|0$
14. A non-positive integer: ^-[1-9]\d*|0$ or ^((-\d+)|(0+))$
15. A non-negative float: ^\d+(\.\d+)?$ or ^[1-9]\d*\.\d*|0\.\d*[1-9]\d*|0?\.0+|0$
16. A non-positive float: ^((-\d+(\.\d+)?)|(0+(\.0+)?))$ or ^(-([1-9]\d*\.\d*|0\.\d*[1-9]\d*))|0?\.0+|0$
17. A positive float: ^[1-9]\d*\.\d*|0\.\d*[1-9]\d*$ or ^(([0-9]+\.[0-9]*[1-9][0-9]*)|([0-9]*[1-9][0-9]*\.[0-9]+)|([0-9]*[1-9][0-9]*))$
18. A negative float: ^-([1-9]\d*\.\d*|0\.\d*[1-9]\d*)$ or ^(-(([0-9]+\.[0-9]*[1-9][0-9]*)|([0-9]*[1-9][0-9]*\.[0-9]+)|([0-9]*[1-9][0-9]*)))$
19. A float: ^(-?\d+)(\.\d+)?$ or ^-?([1-9]\d*\.\d*|0\.\d*[1-9]\d*|0?\.0+|0)$

docs.title: Expressions for checking characters
docs.text:
1.  Chinese characters: ^[一-龥]{0,}$
2.  English letters and digits: ^[A-Za-z0-9]+$ or ^[A-Za-z0-9]{4,40}$
3.  Any characters, length 3–20: ^.{3,20}$
4.  A string of the 26 English letters: ^[A-Za-z]+$
5.  A string of the 26 capital English letters: ^[A-Z]+$
6.  A string of the 26 lowercase English letters: ^[a-z]+$
7.  A string of digits and the 26 English letters: ^[A-Za-z0-9]+$
8.  A string of digits, the 26 English letters or underscores: ^\w+$ or ^\w{3,20}$
9.  Chinese, English, digits and underscores: ^[一-龥A-Za-z0-9_]+$
10. Chinese, English and digits, but no underscores or other symbols: ^[一-龥A-Za-z0-9]+$ or ^[一-龥A-Za-z0-9]{2,20}$
11. Input that does not contain ^%&',;=?$\" and similar characters: [^%&',;=?$\x22]+
12. Input that does not contain ~: [^~\x22]+

docs.title: Expressions for special needs
docs.text:
1.  Email address: ^\w+([-+.]\w+)*@\w+([-.]\w+)*\.\w+([-.]\w+)*$
2.  Domain name: [a-zA-Z0-9][-a-zA-Z0-9]{0,62}(/.[a-zA-Z0-9][-a-zA-Z0-9]{0,62})+/.?
3.  Internet URL: [a-zA-z]+://[^\s]* or ^http://([\w-]+\.)+[\w-]+(/[\w-./?%&=]*)?$
4.  Mobile number (mainland China): ^(13[0-9]|14[0-9]|15[0-9]|166|17[0-9]|18[0-9]|19[8|9])\d{8}$
5.  Phone number ("XXX-XXXXXXX", "XXXX-XXXXXXXX", "XXX-XXXXXXX", "XXX-XXXXXXXX", "XXXXXXX" and "XXXXXXXX"): ^(\(\d{3,4}-)|\d{3.4}-)?\d{7,8}$
6.  Landline number in China (0511-4405222, 021-87888822): \d{3}-\d{8}|\d{4}-\d{7}
7.  18-digit Chinese ID number (digits, may end in x): ^((\d{18})|([0-9x]{18})|([0-9X]{18}))$
8.  Valid username (starts with a letter, 5–16 characters, letters, digits and underscores allowed): ^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_]{4,15}$
9.  Password (starts with a letter, 6–18 long, only letters, digits and underscores): ^[a-zA-Z]\w{5,17}$
10. Strong password (must mix capital letters, lowercase letters and digits, no special characters, 8–10 long): ^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*[A-Z]).{8,10}$  
11. Date format: ^\d{4}-\d{1,2}-\d{1,2}
12. The 12 months of a year (01–09 and 1–12): ^(0?[1-9]|1[0-2])$
13. The 31 days of a month (01–09 and 1–31): ^((0?[1-9])|((1|2)[0-9])|30|31)$
14. Money input formats:
      a. We accept four ways of writing money: "10000.00", "10,000.00", and without cents, "10000" and "10,000": ^[1-9][0-9]*$
      b. That means any number not starting with 0. But it also means the single character "0" fails, so we use this instead: ^(0|[1-9][0-9]*)$
      c. Either a 0, or a number not starting with 0. We could also allow a minus sign at the start: ^(0|-?[1-9][0-9]*)$
      d. That means a 0, or a possibly negative number not starting with 0. Let's allow users to start with 0, and remove the minus sign, since money can't be negative. Next, let's allow an optional decimal part: ^[0-9]+(.[0-9]+)?$
      e. Note that there must be at least 1 digit after the decimal point, so "10." fails, but "10" and "10.2" pass: ^[0-9]+(.[0-9]{2})?$
      f. This requires exactly two digits after the decimal point. If you think that's too strict, use this: ^[0-9]+(.[0-9]{1,2})?$
      g. This lets users write just one decimal place. Next, let's think about commas in the number: ^[0-9]{1,3}(,[0-9]{3})*(.[0-9]{1,2})?$
      h. 1 to 3 digits, followed by any number of (comma + 3 digits), with commas optional instead of required: ^([0-9]+|[0-9]{1,3}(,[0-9]{3})*)(.[0-9]{1,2})?$
15. XML file: ^([a-zA-Z]+-?)+[a-zA-Z0-9]+\\.[x|X][m|M][l|L]$
16. Regex for Chinese characters: [一-龥]
17. Double-byte characters: [^\x00-\xff]    (includes Chinese characters; can be used to work out string length, counting a double-byte character as 2 and an ASCII character as 1)
18. Regex for blank lines: \n\s*\r    (can be used to delete blank lines)
19. Regex for HTML tags: <(\S*?)[^>]*>.*?</\1>|<.*? />    (the versions shared online are terrible; this one only partly works and still can't handle complex nested tags)
20. Regex for whitespace at the start and end: ^\s*|\s*$ or (^\s*)|(\s*$)    (can be used to remove whitespace – spaces, tabs, form feeds and so on – at the start and end of a line; very useful)
21. Tencent QQ number: [1-9][0-9]{4,}    (QQ numbers start from 10000)
22. Chinese postcode: [1-9]\d{5}(?!\d)    (Chinese postcodes are 6 digits)
23. IP address: \d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+    (useful for extracting IP addresses)
24. IP address: ((?:(?:25[0-5]|2[0-4]\\d|[01]?\\d?\\d)\\.){3}(?:25[0-5]|2[0-4]\\d|[01]?\\d?\\d))  
25. docs.title: Closures
docs.text:
There are already lots of articles online about Python closures. In this one, we'll understand closures by solving a real problem.

Here's the problem: we want to keep a running record of our study time, in minutes. For example, if I study for 2 minutes, it returns 2. Later, I study for 10 more minutes, so it returns 12. It keeps adding up the study time like this.

For this problem, most people would create a global variable to store the time, and a function to add each new study time. Usually it would look like this:

time = 0

def insert_time(min):
    time = time + min
    return  time

print(insert_time(2))
print(insert_time(10))

Think carefully – is there a problem here?

In fact, this gives an error in Python:

UnboundLocalError: local variable 'time' referenced before assignment

That's because in Python, if a function uses the same name as a global variable and changes its value, that name becomes a local variable inside the function. So the function tries to use it before it's been defined inside the function, and you get this error.

If you really do want to use the global variable and change it inside a function, how?

We can use the global keyword, like this:

time = 0


def insert_time(min):
    global  time
    time = time + min
    return  time

print(insert_time(2))
print(insert_time(10))

Output:

2
12

But this uses a global variable, and in real projects we try to avoid global variables whenever we can. Because any module or function can freely access a global variable, its value can become unpredictable. For example, programmer A changes the global variable time, and at the same time programmer B changes time too. If one of them makes a mistake, it's very hard to find and fix.

Global variables make functions and modules less reusable, because different functions and modules all depend on them. Global variables also make code harder to read – the reader might not realise a variable is global.

Is there a better way?

Let's solve it with a closure. Look at the code first:

time = 0


def study_time(time):
    def insert_time(min):
        nonlocal  time
        time = time + min
        return time

    return insert_time


f = study_time(time)
print(f(2))
print(time)
print(f(10))
print(time)

Output:

2
0
12
0

The most obvious thing is that the global variable time never changes at all. This code uses the nonlocal keyword, which means "use the variable from the outer (non-global) function". So how does this code run, step by step? Look at the comments below:

time = 0


def study_time(time):
    def insert_time(min):                # Define a function inside a function. It adds the time and returns the final value
        nonlocal time
        time = time + min
        return time

    return insert_time                   # The outer function study_time returns the insert_time function. In Python, functions are objects too, so you can return a function


f = study_time(time)                     # Call study_time. It returns the insert_time function, so f is really the insert_time object
print(f(2))
print(time)
print(f(10))                             # This is like calling insert_time(10)
print(time)

When an inner function can use variables from the outer function's local scope, we call this a closure. Put more simply: when a function is returned as an object and carries outer variables with it, it forms a closure.

Closures avoid global variables. They also let you connect a function with some data (an environment) it works on. Closures can make code more elegant. And decorators, which we'll see in the next article, are built on closures too.

Now there's a question: just because I say it's a closure, does that make it one? Is there a way to check that this function really is a closure?

Yes. Every function has a __closure__ attribute. If the function is a closure, it returns a tuple of cell objects. A cell's cell_contents attribute is the variable stored in the closure.

Let's print it and see:

time = 0


def study_time(time):
    def insert_time(min):
        nonlocal  time
        time = time + min
        return time

    return insert_time


f = study_time(time)
print(f.__closure__)
print(f(2))
print(time)
print(f.__closure__[0].cell_contents)
print(f(10))
print(time)
print(f.__closure__[0].cell_contents)

Output:

(<cell at 0x0000000000410C48: int object at 0x000000001D6AB420>,)
2
0
2
12
0
12

From the output, the value is always stored in the closure's cell_contents. This is the biggest feature of closures: they bind the parent function's variables to the function defined inside it. Even after the parent function that made the closure has finished, the closure still exists.

Making a closure is a bit like a class (the parent function) making an instance (the closure). The difference: a parent function only runs when it's called, and its environment is freed when it finishes. A class is created when the file runs, and its scope usually lasts until the program ends. So for features you want to reuse, but that aren't big enough to be a class, a closure can use fewer resources than a class, and is lighter and more flexible.

docs.title: Two people recording study time – will their records get mixed up?
docs.text:
So far we've been recording one set of study time. What if one person studies Python and another reads books, and they both use the same study_time? Will their records get mixed up?

First, guess what the four prints below will show:

def study_time(time):
    def insert_time(minutes):
        nonlocal time
        time = time + minutes
        return time

    return insert_time


python_time = study_time(0)
reading_time = study_time(0)
same_record = python_time

print(python_time(2))
print(same_record(10))
print(reading_time(5))
print(python_time(0))

Output:

2
12
5
12

Let's go through them in the order they're called:

  1. study_time(0) is called twice. Each time, it creates its own time, and returns an inner function that uses that variable.
  2. same_record = python_time just makes another name point to the function we already have. It doesn't call study_time again, and doesn't create a new record.
  3. python_time(2) adds to the first record, making it 2. same_record(10) then adds to the same record, making it 12.
  4. reading_time(5) changes the second record, so it gives 5.
  5. Finally, adding 0 to the first record leaves it at 12.

The same outer function can make several separate records. The same inner function can also be pointed to by several names. Keep these two things apart, and you won't mix up "making a new closure" with "calling a closure you already have".

Here's one more detail to add to the definition above: what really matters is that the inner function uses the outer function's variables. Returning the inner function is just how this example lets the outside keep using it – it's not a required step to form a closure. You can compare with closure variable in the official glossary.

docs.title: Returning a function vs calling a function – it's all in the brackets
docs.text:
Look again at return insert_time above. There are no brackets, so it hands the function itself to the caller. Only after getting it do we write python_time(2) to record some study.

What if we wrote return insert_time(2) instead? Then the outer function would call insert_time once straight away, and return the number it calculated. The caller would get a number, and then writing python_time(2) would fail, because you can't call a number like a function.

Also, nonlocal is needed here because of the reassignment: time = time + minutes. It's not something you have to write every time an inner function uses an outer variable. You don't need it just to read an outer variable. And if you're working with an outer list, just calling the list's append() isn't reassigning the variable either. When you're not sure, ask yourself: is this line pointing the name somewhere new, or changing the existing object?

docs.title: Make your own record with a starting value
docs.text:
This time, don't start from 0. Create two records: python_time = study_time(30) and reading_time = study_time(10).

Record, in order: Python 5 minutes, reading 2 minutes, Python 3 minutes. You should get 35, 12, 38. Then create another_name = python_time and use it to add 2 minutes. The first record should become 40.

First write down on paper (or in your notes) which record each step changes, then change the code and check. If your results are different, first check whether you accidentally called study_time again and started a brand-new record.

When you print __closure__, the memory addresses change from computer to computer – they don't have to match the example. What you should look at is the variable being kept and how it changes. When comparing how many resources closures and classes use, you need to look at the actual code and actually measure it – it's not a promise that every closure uses less than every class. This problem only needs to keep one running total, so a closure expresses it clearly.

docs.title: Decorators
docs.text:
In the last article, we learned about closures by solving a real problem. This article does the same: we'll slowly change a task, step by step, to understand Python decorators.

First, here's a function that prints an employee's clock-in message:

def punch():
    print('Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work')


punch()

Output:

Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work

Then the product team says: "That's no good – the clock-in doesn't show the date! Add the date." Should be easy, done in a minute. OK, let's just add some code to print the date:

import time


def punch():
    print(time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.localtime(time.time())))
    print('Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work')


punch()

Output:

2018-01-09
Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work

This works, but it changes the structure of the function. The function was meant to print an employee's info and say they clocked in. Adding date-printing code could lead to lots of repeated code. For example, if somewhere else you only need the employee info and clock-in message without the date, do you write another function? Also, printing the current date is something you'll use often, so it could be a shared function that other modules call. Of course, this is thinking about the project as a whole.

So, let's change this code using functional programming. From what we've learned, Python functions have two features: functions are objects, and functions can be nested inside functions. Let's change the code to this:

import time


def punch():
    print('Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work')


def add_time(func):
    print(time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.localtime(time.time())))
    func()


add_time(punch)

Output:

2018-01-09
Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work

See? We didn't change the punch function at all. And any function that needs the current date printed can just be passed into add_time, like this:

import time


def punch():
    print('Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work')


def add_time(func):
    print(time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.localtime(time.time())))
    func()


def holiday():
    print('It is too cold – day off today!')


add_time(punch)
add_time(holiday)

Output:

2018-01-09
Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work
2018-01-09
It is too cold – day off today!

Functional programming is handy, isn't it? But every time we call it, we have to pass the original function in as an argument. Is there a better way? Yes – the decorator, which this article is about. Writing a decorator is a lot like writing a closure, just without the free variable. Here's the decorator version of the code above, so you can compare it with the functional version:

import time


def decorator(func):
    def punch():
        print(time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.localtime(time.time())))
        func()

    return punch


def punch():
    print('Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work')


f = decorator(punch)
f()

Output:

2018-01-09
Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work

From the code, a decorator function usually does three things:

  1. Takes a function as an argument
  2. Has a wrapper function inside it. The wrapper takes the same arguments as the original function, runs the original function, and also does something extra
  3. Returns the wrapper function

But look closely – this decorator version seems even more trouble than the functional version! It looks more complicated, and even a bit pointless.

That's because we haven't used the decorator's syntactic sugar yet. From the code above, you can see that when Python added decorators, it didn't add any new language features – it's all based on what functions can already do. This shows decorators aren't special to Python – they're a general programming idea in every language. But Python designed the @ syntactic sugar to make it simpler and easier to define a decorator, have it wrap the original function, and assign the result back to the original function's name. So you could say the heart of Python decorators is this syntactic sugar.

How do you use it? Easy. After writing the decorator function as above, just put @ and the decorator's name above the original function, like this:

import time


def decorator(func):
    def punch():
        print(time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.localtime(time.time())))
        func()

    return punch

@decorator
def punch():
    print('Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work')

punch()

Output:

2018-01-09
Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work

Now this is really convenient – especially when calling it. In the example, after adding the decorator, we just put the decorator's syntactic sugar above the original function. The function itself doesn't need to change at all, and the places that call it don't need to change either.

But there's still a problem: the clock-in message is fixed. If we want to pass it in through arguments, how do we write the decorator? The function inside the decorator can use *args for variable arguments. But *args alone doesn't cover every case – it doesn't handle keyword arguments. To handle keyword arguments too, we also add **kwargs.

So the final form of the decorator can be written like this:

import time


def decorator(func):
    def punch(*args, **kwargs):
        print(time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.localtime(time.time())))
        func(*args, **kwargs)

    return punch


@decorator
def punch(name, department):
    print(f'Nickname: {name}  Department: {department}  Clocked in for work')


@decorator
def print_args(reason, **kwargs):
    print(reason)
    print(kwargs)


punch('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept')
print_args('Two Drops', sex='Male', age=99)

Output:

2018-01-09
Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work
2018-01-09
Two Drops
{'sex': 'Male', 'age': 99}

docs.title: When you add a decorator, does the function run straight away?
docs.text:
We've gone from clocking in all the way to decorators. Now let's look clearly at the order things happen in: what happens when @decorator appears, and what happens later when we call punch()?

Let's use a list to record the steps, so we don't mix up "creating the wrapper" with "doing the clock-in":

events = []


def decorator(func):
    events.append('Wrapper created')

    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        events.append('Original function called')
        return func(*args, **kwargs)

    return wrapper


@decorator
def punch(name):
    return f'{name} clocked in'


print(events)
print(punch('Two Drops'))
print(events)

Output:

['Wrapper created']
Two Drops clocked in
['Wrapper created', 'Original function called']

The first line shows that before we reach punch('Two Drops'), the decorator has already received the original function and returned the wrapper – but the body of the original function hasn't run yet. Only when we later call punch do we go into wrapper, which then calls the original function.

This order comes from how this decorator is written: it returns wrapper and doesn't call the original function while creating the wrapper. A decorator can contain other logic too, so to know when things run, look at which level the call is written at.

You can think of @decorator as a shortcut for defining the function and then running punch = decorator(punch). Decorators are built on what functions can already do, but @ is special decorator syntax. Keep the syntax and the function-wrapping that happens behind it separate in your head.

docs.title: The original function worked out a result – did the wrapper pass it on?
docs.text:
In the clock-in example, we mostly showed the effect by printing, so the original function didn't need to return a result. But if you decorate a function that calculates something, and the wrapper only calls it without returning the result, the caller outside won't get the value it worked out.

Let's try it with a function that records study time:

def add_log(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print('Start counting')
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print('Counting done')
        return result

    return wrapper


@add_log
def total_minutes(first, second):
    return first + second


minutes = total_minutes(5, second=10)
print(minutes)

Output:

Start counting
Counting done
15

Try a small experiment: remove only the return result in wrapper, leave everything else the same, and run it again. The last line becomes None. It's not that the original function didn't work out 15 – it's that the wrapper didn't pass that result on to the caller outside.

In this example, *args collects positional arguments and **kwargs collects keyword arguments, and then they're passed on to the original function the same way. They just forward arguments – they don't make the original function accept arguments it didn't support before. If you pass the wrong arguments, the original function will still give an error.

docs.title: Check it yourself – don't stop just because you saw the log messages
docs.text:
Keep using add_log from above, and call total_minutes(0, 0) and total_minutes(first=12, second=3). Each time, you should first see two log lines, and then the print outside should show 0 and 15.

Then go back to the first example and call punch('Two Drops') once more. events should have only one 'Wrapper created', and two 'Original function called'. If you can explain why the wrapper isn't created twice, you've understood the difference between when the decorator runs and when the wrapper runs.

When you run the date examples, you'll get today's date. When checking, look at what it does and the order – the date doesn't need to match the old example.

docs.title: Type hints
docs.text:
After the earlier chapters, I'm sure you can now write pretty decent Python code. Functions, classes, closures, decorators – no problem. But here's the thing about writing code: enjoying writing it yourself is one thing. Having someone else read it, or coming back to it yourself six months later, is something else.

Come on, let's look at some code that "Brother Shui" handed over to a teammate last week:

def calc(x, y, op):
    if op == 'add':
        return x + y
    elif op == 'sub':
        return x - y

The teammate stares at calc, totally confused: are x and y numbers or strings? What else can op be? What type does it return? They have to dig through the code that calls it, or just shout: "Brother Shui, how do I use this function?!"

Sound familiar? Python is a dynamic language. Variables don't need to declare their type, which makes writing code feel great. But once a project gets big and lots of people work on it, things go wrong very easily.

Think about what problems this "unclear type" code causes:

  • Someone passes the wrong type and doesn't notice while coding. It only crashes after it's released, when a user clicks some button.
  • The IDE can't give you accurate code completion – it doesn't even know what your variable is, so how can it suggest which methods you can use?
  • Refactoring is scary – if you change this function's parameters, what else will break? You can only search the whole project, then check each line by eye.
  • Teammates keep interrupting each other – every time you want to use a function you don't know, you have to ask its author "what does this parameter mean?"

To solve this, Python 3.5 introduced type hints. They kept improving through 3.9, 3.10 and 3.12, and they're really easy to use now. Sadly, lots of older tutorials barely mention them, so many people have written Python for years and still write def f(x, y) with nothing else.

Imagine this: "Brother Shui" suddenly takes the weekend off and hands his project over to a teammate. The code has dozens of functions, and every one looks like def process(data, config, cb). The teammate opens one file and is lost – is data a dict or a list? Is config an object or a path? Is cb a function or a string? They have to ask about every single one, or trace through the whole call stack. That's their whole weekend gone.

But if the function signature had been def process(data: dict[str, int], config: Path, cb: Callable[[str], None]) from the start, the teammate would understand at a glance, without asking anyone. That's the most direct value of type hints.

So today, let's talk all about type hints, so the code you write is clearer and more professional.

docs.title: The simplest type hints
docs.text:
Let's fix the calc function above. Say it adds or subtracts two integers:

def calc(x: int, y: int, op: str) -> int:
    if op == 'add':
        return x + y
    elif op == 'sub':
        return x - y
    return 0


print(calc(3, 5, 'add'))
print(calc(10, 4, 'sub'))

Output:

8
6

See? Now the function is clear at a glance: x and y are int, op is str, and the return value is int too. Even without any comments, the signature tells you enough.

The syntax is simple. Remember two things:

  • After a parameter, add : type
  • For the return value, add -> type

Remember it like this: "parameters get a colon, the return gets an arrow". It's 100% compatible with the old way of writing. Old code without hints can run together with new code that has hints, without changing a single character.

Some of you might ask: "Can I hint only the parameters and not the return value? Or only the return value and not the parameters?"

Absolutely. You can add hints wherever you want – you don't have to hint everything. For example:

def double(x: int):
    return x * 2


def greet(name) -> str:
    return f'Hello, {name}'


print(double(3))
print(greet('Two Drops'))

Output:

6
Hello, Two Drops

But to keep the "contract" clear, I suggest you either hint everything, or hint nothing. Half-and-half looks messy, and readers will wonder: "Did they forget to hint that one, or was it on purpose?"

Here's a really important point you must remember: the Python interpreter does NOT check these types. They're just "notes" – for people, and for tools (IDEs, static checkers).

Don't believe me? Let's pass the wrong type on purpose:

def calc(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return x + y


print(calc('Two Drops', ' Coding Dept'))

Output:

Two Drops Coding Dept

See? We hinted int, but passing strings still runs, because strings support + too. Python didn't stop anything. So type hints aren't "type enforcement" – they're more like a "contract" written for your teammates.

Then someone will ask: "If it's not enforced, why bother?"

Good question. Here's why:

  • IDEs (PyCharm, VS Code) can use hints to give you accurate code completion and error warnings
  • Static checking tools (like mypy and pyright) can catch type errors before the code runs
  • Teammates (including your future self) save lots of guessing time when reading code

These three reasons alone are enough to take type hints seriously.

Another thing many people find confusing: "How do I hint a parameter that has a default value?" Easy – the hint goes first, then the equals sign and default value:

def punch(name: str, dept: str = 'Coding Dept') -> None:
    print(f'{name} ({dept}) clocked in')


punch('Two Drops')
punch('Three Drops', 'Design Dept')

Output:

Two Drops (Coding Dept) clocked in
Three Drops (Design Dept) clocked in

The format is name: type = default. Just put the three parts in that order.

What about variable arguments like *args and **kwargs? You can hint them too. You write the type of each single item, not the type of the whole tuple/dict:

def sum_all(*nums: int) -> int:
    return sum(nums)


def make_user(**fields: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    return fields


print(sum_all(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
print(make_user(name='Two Drops', dept='Coding Dept'))

Output:

15
{'name': 'Two Drops', 'dept': 'Coding Dept'}

*nums: int means "each item in the tuple nums is an int", not "nums itself is an int". **fields: str is the same – each value is a str. Beginners often get this wrong, so remember it.

docs.title: Common basic types
docs.text:
The types you can write in hints are mostly Python's built-in ones:

Type Meaning int Integer float Floating-point number str String bool Boolean list List dict Dictionary tuple Tuple set Set bytes Bytes None Nothing (used as a return type)

Here's an example that uses several of them – a function that makes an employee profile for the "Coding Dept":

def make_profile(name: str, age: int, salary: float, is_active: bool) -> str:
    return f'{name} ({age} years old, salary {salary}, active: {is_active})'


print(make_profile('Two Drops', 28, 12000.5, True))

Output:

Two Drops (28 years old, salary 12000.5, active: True)

Try pasting this code into PyCharm or VS Code. When you type make_profile(, the IDE immediately pops up parameter hints: "the first parameter name is a str, the second parameter age is an int…". Without hints, the IDE can only dully tell you "four parameters go here", and you have to remember all the types yourself.

See how adding hints instantly makes coding nicer?

And this one table covers most situations. Basic types aren't fancy – the key is to use them accurately. If it's an int, write int; if it's a str, write str. Don't be lazy and write object or Any, which swallows everything.

A few more words about bool. In Python, bool is actually a subclass of int (True == 1, False == 0). So if a parameter is hinted int and you pass True, the type checker won't complain. But the other way round – a parameter hinted bool and you pass 1 – the checker will stop you. Just be aware of this; when writing hints, follow your real intention: use bool for on/off switches, and int for numbers.

One more small trap with int: Python's int has unlimited precision. There's no int32 or int64, so there's only one int in hints. People used to C or Java sometimes look for "where's int32?" – it doesn't exist. Just use int with confidence.

Here's a mixed signature you'd often see when writing an "employee profile":

def make_employee(
    name: str,
    age: int,
    height: float,
    is_intern: bool,
    skills: list,
    address: dict,
) -> str:
    return f'{name} / {age} years old / {height}m / intern: {is_intern} / skills: {skills} / address: {address}'


print(make_employee(
    'Two Drops', 28, 1.75, False,
    ['Python', 'Django'],
    {'city': 'Shenzhen', 'street': 'Science Park'},
))

Output:

Two Drops / 28 years old / 1.75m / intern: False / skills: ['Python', 'Django'] / address: {'city': 'Shenzhen', 'street': 'Science Park'}

This signature is much clearer now. But look closely: skills: list and address: dict aren't good enough yet. What's inside the list? What types are the dictionary's keys and values? We don't know. That's what container types in the next section are for.

If a function returns nothing (that is, it returns None), write None as the return type:

def greet(name: str) -> None:
    print(f'Hello, {name}')


greet('Two Drops')

Output:

Hello, Two Drops

Note: -> None here doesn't mean "I didn't write a return type". It means "I'm clearly telling you this function has no meaningful return value". These two feel very different to a reader.

Now picture this. The "Coding Dept" clock-in function (the one from the decorators chapter), with hints added, looks like this:

import time


def punch(name: str, dept: str) -> None:
    today = time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.localtime(time.time()))
    print(f'{today}: Nickname: {name}  Department: {dept}  Clocked in for work')


punch('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept')

Output (the date changes with the current time):

2026-04-28: Nickname: Two Drops  Department: Coding Dept  Clocked in for work

Look – just adding name: str, dept: str and -> None to the signature completely explains how to use the function: pass in strings, get nothing back, and it prints something. From a reader's point of view, isn't that much easier?

docs.title: What if a function might return None?
docs.text:
Let's imagine a real situation. The "Coding Dept" employee list is a dictionary, and we write a function that looks up an employee ID by nickname:

employees = {'Two Drops': '001', 'Three Drops': '002'}


def find_id(name: str) -> str:
    return employees.get(name)


print(find_id('Two Drops'))
print(find_id('Four Drops'))

Output:

001
None

See the problem? We said the return type is str, but when the employee doesn't exist, dict.get() returns None, not a str. The hint and the real behaviour don't match.

"Either return X, or return None" is very common. The old way to write it was with Optional from the typing module:

from typing import Optional


employees = {'Two Drops': '001', 'Three Drops': '002'}


def find_id(name: str) -> Optional[str]:
    return employees.get(name)


print(find_id('Two Drops'))
print(find_id('Four Drops'))

Optional[str] means "this value is either a str or None".

But importing Optional from typing every time gets really annoying. In Python 3.10, a simpler way was introduced (PEP 604): join the types with a vertical bar |:

employees = {'Two Drops': '001', 'Three Drops': '002'}


def find_id(name: str) -> str | None:
    return employees.get(name)


print(find_id('Two Drops'))
print(find_id('Four Drops'))

Output:

001
None

Doesn't str | None read more naturally? "A string or nothing" – just like "or" in English.

I really want to stress this: a return type of str | None does not mean the caller can just use it as a str. You must check which one it is before using it. Look at this:

def find_id(name: str) -> str | None:
    db = {'Two Drops': '001'}
    return db.get(name)


emp_id = find_id('Four Drops')
print(emp_id.upper())

The IDE will immediately underline emp_id.upper() in red, because emp_id might be None, and None has no upper method. The correct way is to check first:

def find_id(name: str) -> str | None:
    db = {'Two Drops': '001'}
    return db.get(name)


emp_id = find_id('Two Drops')
if emp_id is not None:
    print(emp_id.upper())
else:
    print('Employee not found')

Output:

001

Inside this if branch, the type checker automatically narrows the type – it knows that inside if emp_id is not None:, emp_id must be a str, so .upper() is fine. This clever trick is called type narrowing, and it's one of the most useful abilities of modern type checkers.

And | isn't just for None – you can join as many types as you like:

def to_int(value: int | str | float) -> int:
    return int(value)


print(to_int(3))
print(to_int('5'))
print(to_int(7.8))

Output: 

3
5
7

int | str | float means "this parameter can be an int, a str or a float". The technical name for this is a union type.

The X | Y syntax only works in Python 3.10+. If your project still uses 3.9 or older, you have to use from typing import Union; Union[X, Y]. But honestly, it's 2026 – upgrade if you can.

To sum up:

  • Old way: Optional[str], Union[int, str] – needs from typing import ...
  • New way: str | None, int | str – no import needed, just write it

For new code, always use the new way.

One more small detail. Once a function has a return type of X | None, the caller is "reminded" to handle the None case. For example:

employees = {'Two Drops': '001', 'Three Drops': '002'}


def find_id(name: str) -> str | None:
    return employees.get(name)


emp_id = find_id('Four Drops')
if emp_id is None:
    print('Employee not found')
else:
    print(f'Employee ID: {emp_id}')

Output:

Employee not found

Without | None, the caller can easily forget to check for empty values, and go straight on to join strings or query a database with the return value – then crash halfway through. Hints + a static checker can remind you the moment you forget to check.

docs.title: How to hint container types
docs.text:
Just saying list isn't enough. Look at this function:

def total_salary(salaries: list) -> float:
    return sum(salaries)


print(total_salary([10000, 12000, 8000]))

Output:

30000

It says list, but it doesn't say what's in the list. ints? floats? strs? The reader still has to guess.

Here comes the old way again: import capitalised List, Dict, Tuple and so on from typing:

from typing import List


def total_salary(salaries: List[float]) -> float:
