Exceptions are Python's standard way of passing error information. They say much more than return None, return -1 or return False.

docs.title: Exception chaining – raise ... from e
docs.text:
Let's look at a slightly more advanced situation. Say we have this function:

def load_config(path):
    with open(path, 'r') as f:
        return f.read()

If path doesn't exist, it raises FileNotFoundError. But from the point of view of "using the config", "file not found" is too low-level. I'd like to raise a more business-like error, like ConfigError('Failed to load config'), but without losing the information about what really went wrong underneath. What do I do?

PEP 3134 gives the answer – exception chaining:

class ConfigError(Exception):
    pass


def load_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path, 'r') as f:
            return f.read()
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        raise ConfigError(f'Failed to load config: {path}') from e


try:
    load_config('not_exist.json')
except ConfigError as e:
    print(f'Business error: {e}')

Output:

Business error: Failed to load config: not_exist.json

Look at raise ConfigError(...) from e. from e attaches the original exception to the new exception's __cause__. If nothing outside catches it, the traceback prints both errors, like this:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "...", line X, in load_config
    with open(path, 'r') as f:
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'not_exist.json'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "...", line Y, in <module>
    load_config('not_exist.json')
  File "...", line Z, in load_config
    raise ConfigError(...) from e
ConfigError: Failed to load config: not_exist.json

"The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" – this sentence is the sign of an exception chain. When you see a traceback like this, know that the error at the top is the root cause, and the one below it was wrapped around it.

What if you leave out from e and just raise ConfigError(...)? Python automatically adds a __context__ for you, and the traceback says "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred". This is called an implicit chain.

An explicit from e says "I deliberately wrapped a low-level exception in a business exception". Leaving out from e says "while I was handling the last exception, something else went wrong by accident". They mean different things, so when you deliberately wrap an exception, always add from e.

docs.title: Custom exception classes
docs.text:
Did you see that ConfigError just now? A custom exception class really is just one line:

class ConfigError(Exception):
    pass

Just inherit from Exception. But why make your own? Can't you just use built-in ones like ValueError or RuntimeError?

Let's explain with a "clock-in" example. "Brother Shui" built a clock-in system for the "Coding Dept", with these business rules:

  • You can't clock in before work starts
  • You can't clock in twice in one day
  • You can't clock in if you're not on the office network

With built-in exceptions:

def punch(user, time, ip):
    if time < 9:
        raise ValueError('Work has not started yet')
    if user.already_punched_today:
        raise ValueError('You already clocked in today')
    if not ip.startswith('192.168.'):
        raise ValueError('Not on the office network')

When the caller catches a ValueError, they can't tell which situation it is. If they want to handle each one differently, they'd have to compare message strings – which is very fragile.

With a custom exception family:

class PunchError(Exception):
    """Base class for clock-in errors."""
    pass


class PunchTimeError(PunchError):
    pass


class PunchDuplicateError(PunchError):
    pass


class PunchLocationError(PunchError):
    pass


def punch(user_already_punched, hour, ip):
    if hour < 9:
        raise PunchTimeError('Work has not started yet')
    if user_already_punched:
        raise PunchDuplicateError('You already clocked in today')
    if not ip.startswith('192.168.'):
        raise PunchLocationError('Not on the office network')
    return 'Clocked in'


# The caller
try:
    punch(False, 8, '192.168.1.1')
except PunchTimeError as e:
    print(f'Time problem: {e}, please wait until 9')
except PunchDuplicateError as e:
    print(f'Already clocked in: {e}')
except PunchLocationError as e:
    print(f'Location problem: {e}, please connect to the office wifi')
except PunchError as e:
    print(f'Clock-in failed: {e}')

Output:

Time problem: Work has not started yet, please wait until 9

See?

  • Each kind of error has its own class, so the caller can catch it precisely
  • There's a shared parent class PunchError, so the caller can also catch them all at once
  • The class name itself is documentation – just from the class name, you know what happened, without reading the message

That's the value of custom exception classes – errors become part of your code's structure too.

Custom exception classes can carry data too, for example:

class PunchError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message, user_id=None, hour=None):
        super().__init__(message)
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.hour = hour


try:
    raise PunchError('Work has not started yet', user_id=123, hour=8)
except PunchError as e:
    print(f'Message: {e}')
    print(f'User: {e.user_id}')
    print(f'Hour: {e.hour}')

Output:

Message: Work has not started yet
User: 123
Hour: 8

When you need more context, put it in the exception object. For back-end logging and monitoring, structured errors like this are really valuable.

docs.title: Built-in exceptions cheat sheet
docs.text:
You've seen some already, but you might want to know "what are the common built-in exceptions?" Here's a cheat sheet that covers 90% of what you'll meet at work:

Exception class When it happens Example ValueError The type is right but the value isn't allowed int('abc') TypeError The type is wrong 'a' + 1 KeyError The key isn't in the dictionary {'a': 1}['b'] IndexError The sequence index is out of range [1, 2][5] AttributeError The object doesn't have that attribute 'abc'.foo NameError Using a variable that isn't defined print(undefined_x) FileNotFoundError The file doesn't exist open('not_exist.txt') ZeroDivisionError Dividing by zero 1 / 0 ImportError An import failed import not_exist_module ModuleNotFoundError A module can't be found (child of ImportError) import not_exist_module RuntimeError A general runtime error Not used much; avoid if you can NotImplementedError An abstract method wasn't implemented Common in interfaces/abstract classes StopIteration An iterator has run out Python usually handles this itself OSError An operating-system-level error e.g. not enough permission to read/write PermissionError Not enough permission (child of OSError) Writing to a read-only file RecursionError Recursion went too deep Recursion without a stopping condition KeyboardInterrupt The user pressed Ctrl+C Don't catch this one SystemExit Raised by sys.exit() Don't catch this one either

Let me stress those last two again: KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit are direct children of BaseException, not Exception. So a normal except Exception doesn't catch them – which is a good thing, because it avoids accidents.

docs.title: Want to report several errors at once? – Exception groups (Python 3.11+)
docs.text:
By now, you know all the normal exception handling. Next is a fairly new feature added in Python 3.11: exception groups (PEP 654).

First, the problem. Say "Brother Shui" has a batch job in the "Coding Dept": send requests to five URLs and save all the results. The code looks roughly like this:

def fetch_one(url):
    # Pretend this might fail
    if 'bad' in url:
        raise ValueError(f'Bad argument: {url}')
    if 'down' in url:
        raise ConnectionError(f'Cannot connect: {url}')
    return f'Content of {url}'


def fetch_all(urls):
    results = []
    for url in urls:
        results.append(fetch_one(url))
    return results

Think: if two of the urls raise ValueError and one raises ConnectionError, what happens with the traditional approach?

After the first URL raises an error, fetch_all exits straight away, and the rest never run. You'd never know about the other two errors. But your task needs to "see all the failing URLs at once", so the operations team can fix them all in one go, without running it again and again.

Traditional try/except can only tell you about the first error. It can't handle this. So what do you do?

The home-made way is to collect each URL's exception yourself:

def fetch_all(urls):
    results = []
    errors = []
    for url in urls:
        try:
            results.append(fetch_one(url))
        except Exception as e:
            errors.append(e)
    return results, errors

It works, but there are a few problems:

  • The caller gets a (results, errors) pair, which makes the signature ugly
  • Errors come back as a "list", so the caller has to check with if and write their own loop to report them
  • This is a home-made system, so every library does it differently – nothing's standard

PEP 654 solves this. Python 3.11 added ExceptionGroup, made specifically to "package several exceptions into one" and raise them:

def fetch_all(urls):
    results = []
    errors = []
    for url in urls:
        try:
            results.append(fetch_one(url))
        except Exception as e:
            errors.append(e)
    if errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup('Some URLs failed', errors)
    return results

Let's call it:

urls = ['ok-1', 'bad-2', 'down-3', 'ok-4', 'bad-5']
try:
    fetch_all(urls)
except ExceptionGroup as eg:
    print(f'There are {len(eg.exceptions)} errors')
    for e in eg.exceptions:
        print(f'  - {type(e).__name__}: {e}')

Output (on Python 3.11+):

There are 3 errors
  - ValueError: Bad argument: bad-2
  - ConnectionError: Cannot connect: down-3
  - ValueError: Bad argument: bad-5

That's the heart of exception groups: raise a group of exceptions at once, and the caller gets all the errors at once.

This needs Python 3.11+ – older versions can't run it. Run python3 --version to check whether yours is 3.11+.

docs.title: Splitting an exception group with except*
docs.text:
You might ask: "After catching an ExceptionGroup, can I handle it by exception type, like a normal except?"

Yes. Python 3.11 also added new syntax: except* (with a star). It's made to split an exception group by type. Look:

def fetch_all(urls):
    results = []
    errors = []
    for url in urls:
        try:
            results.append(fetch_one(url))
        except Exception as e:
            errors.append(e)
    if errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup('Some URLs failed', errors)
    return results


urls = ['ok-1', 'bad-2', 'down-3', 'ok-4', 'bad-5']
try:
    fetch_all(urls)
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(f'{len(eg.exceptions)} argument errors:')
    for e in eg.exceptions:
        print(f'  - {e}')
except* ConnectionError as eg:
    print(f'{len(eg.exceptions)} connection errors:')
    for e in eg.exceptions:
        print(f'  - {e}')

Output:

2 argument errors:
  - Bad argument: bad-2
  - Bad argument: bad-5
1 connection errors:
  - Cannot connect: down-3

See? The two except* branches automatically split the ExceptionGroup into two parts by type, and handle each one. A normal except can't do this – once a normal except matches, it runs once and that's it. But except* goes through the whole group and picks out everything of the matching type.

Key points about except*:

  • The syntax is except* ExceptionType: – note the star right after except
  • The eg you get is a new ExceptionGroup containing only the matching exceptions
  • Every except* branch is checked (not just the first). Exceptions that don't match are "re-packaged" and keep going outwards
  • You can't mix it with normal except. A try must use either all except, or all except*

Now think: if a group has both ValueError and OSError, but you only wrote except* ValueError, what happens to the OSErrors?

Answer: they're re-packaged into a new ExceptionGroup and raised again. This is the most basic difference between except* and except – except "takes one", while except* "takes the matching group, and passes the rest on".

docs.title: add_note – adding notes to exceptions (Python 3.11+)
docs.text:
Next to exception groups, there's a small feature called add_note, also added in 3.11. It's really handy for debugging.

When debugging, do you often wonder: "Which line raised this KeyError? Which user or which request caused it?" The exception itself only shows the key name, with no context. add_note is for adding that context:

def process_user(user_id, data):
    try:
        return data['name']
    except KeyError as e:
        e.add_note(f'Error while processing user {user_id}')
        e.add_note(f'Data keys: {list(data.keys())}')
        raise


process_user(123, {'age': 18})

Output (end of the traceback):

KeyError: 'name'
Error while processing user 123
Data keys: ['age']

add_note adds the string to the exception object's __notes__ list. When the traceback is printed, these notes appear automatically after the exception message.

Why not just raise a new KeyError('Error while processing user 123, data keys: [age]')? Because that would lose part of the original traceback. add_note "keeps the original exception + adds a note", which is lighter and more elegant.

You can call add_note many times, adding one note each time. It's especially useful when debugging library code or writing middleware.

docs.title: Mini project: safe_divide and batch division
docs.text:
We've covered a lot. Let's finish with a small project. The task:

  • Write a function safe_divide(a, b) that returns the result normally, returns None when dividing by zero, and also returns None for other errors
  • Write a function batch_divide(pairs) that divides a list of (a, b) pairs, and reports all the errors together using an ExceptionGroup

First, the first one:

def safe_divide(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print(f'  Division by zero: {a} / {b}')
        return None
    except TypeError as e:
        print(f'  Type error: {e}')
        return None


print(safe_divide(10, 2))
print(safe_divide(10, 0))
print(safe_divide('a', 1))

Output:

5.0
  Division by zero: 10 / 0
None
  Type error: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'str' and 'int'
None

Simple, but good enough. Now the batch version – using an exception group:

def divide_strict(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        raise ZeroDivisionError(f'{a} / 0')
    if not isinstance(a, (int, float)) or not isinstance(b, (int, float)):
        raise TypeError(f'{a!r} / {b!r} has the wrong type')
    return a / b


def batch_divide(pairs):
    results = []
    errors = []
    for a, b in pairs:
        try:
            results.append(divide_strict(a, b))
        except Exception as e:
            errors.append(e)
    if errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup(f'Batch division had {len(errors)} errors', errors)
    return results


pairs = [(10, 2), (10, 0), ('a', 1), (8, 4), (5, 0)]

try:
    print(batch_divide(pairs))
except* ZeroDivisionError as eg:
    print(f'{len(eg.exceptions)} division-by-zero errors:')
    for e in eg.exceptions:
        print(f'  - {e}')
except* TypeError as eg:
    print(f'{len(eg.exceptions)} type errors:')
    for e in eg.exceptions:
        print(f'  - {e}')

Output (Python 3.11+):

2 division-by-zero errors:
  - 10 / 0
  - 5 / 0
1 type errors:
  - 'a' / 1 has the wrong type

See how it all works:

  1. divide_strict strictly raises exceptions – if the arguments are wrong, it never quietly returns None
  2. batch_divide collects all the exceptions and raises them together in an ExceptionGroup
  3. The caller uses except* to group them by type, and reports all the errors at once

This is the partial failure pattern that exception groups bring: whatever should succeed succeeds, whatever should fail fails, and all errors are reported together. This pattern is very common in asyncio concurrency, batch RPC calls and parallel fetching. Before Python 3.11 you had to build it yourself; from 3.11, it's built into the language.

docs.title: Nested exception groups – a tree structure
docs.text:
Let's go a bit deeper. An ExceptionGroup is itself an exception. So can it go inside another ExceptionGroup?

Yes. Exception groups form a tree – a group can hold normal exceptions, and also other groups. This nesting is common in situations like "distributed tasks, where sub-tasks have their own sub-tasks".

Here's an example. Say "Brother Shui" wants to update lots of employees' information. For each employee, two parts need updating separately – "basic info" and "clock-in records" – and either part might fail:

def update_employee(emp):
    sub_errors = []
    try:
        update_basic_info(emp)
    except Exception as e:
        sub_errors.append(e)
    try:
        update_punch_record(emp)
    except Exception as e:
        sub_errors.append(e)
    if sub_errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup(f'Failed to update employee {emp}', sub_errors)


def batch_update(employees):
    errors = []
    for emp in employees:
        try:
            update_employee(emp)
        except Exception as e:
            errors.append(e)
    if errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup('Some updates in the batch failed', errors)

An exception group from this structure is nested: the outermost group holds several "Failed to update employee X" sub-groups. The clever thing about except* is that it can see through any number of nesting levels and pull out all exceptions of the given type.

try:
    batch_update(employees)
except* ConnectionError as eg:
    print(f'Network errors: {len(eg.exceptions)} groups')
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(f'Argument errors: {len(eg.exceptions)} groups')

Whether a ConnectionError is in the first level or the second, except* will find it. This is the biggest difference from a normal except.

docs.title: eg.subgroup and eg.split – working with exception groups by hand
docs.text:
except* is usually enough, but sometimes you want finer control – for example, handling only exceptions that meet a specific condition, not just grouping by type. ExceptionGroup has two useful methods for this: subgroup and split.

errors = [
    ValueError('bad value 1'),
    TypeError('bad type'),
    ValueError('bad value 2'),
    ConnectionError('network down'),
]
eg = ExceptionGroup('a pile of errors', errors)

# subgroup picks out by condition
value_eg = eg.subgroup(ValueError)
print(f'ValueError sub-group: {len(value_eg.exceptions)}')

# split splits it into two parts: "matching" and "not matching"
matched, rest = eg.split(ValueError)
print(f'Matched: {len(matched.exceptions)}; rest: {len(rest.exceptions)}')

Output (Python 3.11+):

ValueError sub-group: 2
Matched: 2; rest: 2

Both subgroup and split take either a type or a checking function as their argument. The function version is especially flexible:

matched, rest = eg.split(lambda e: 'bad' in str(e))

This picks out every error whose message contains the word "bad". When you write complicated middleware or scheduler code, these two methods are very useful.

docs.title: Don't make these mistakes (anti-patterns)
docs.text: Almost all badly-written exception handling falls into the following anti-patterns. Let's go through them one by one, each with a "wrong" and a "right" version.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 1: swallowing exceptions
docs.text:
# Wrong
try:
    do_something()
except Exception:
    pass

This is called swallowing an exception. Something went wrong, but you don't log it, don't re-raise it, and don't return a special value – you'll never be able to find the root cause of problems.

# Right
import logging

try:
    do_something()
except Exception:
    logging.exception('do_something failed')
    raise

At the very least, log it. If you decide not to re-raise it, you must have a clear business reason – and I strongly recommend adding a comment explaining "why we don't re-raise".

docs.title: Anti-pattern 2: catching too widely
docs.text:
# Wrong
try:
    age = int(input('Age: '))
    save_to_db(age)
except Exception:
    print('Something went wrong')

This try does two things: converting and saving to the database. An error in either step gets caught the same way, and the error information is lost.

# Right
try:
    age = int(input('Age: '))
except ValueError:
    print('Please enter a valid number')
    return

try:
    save_to_db(age)
except OSError as e:
    print(f'Failed to write to the database: {e}')
    return

Each try block wraps one thing only, and catches the exception types specific to it. This is the "smallest scope" rule for exception handling.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 3: using exceptions for normal flow control
docs.text:
# Wrong – checking whether a key is in a dict
try:
    val = d['key']
    use(val)
except KeyError:
    use_default()

It's not that it doesn't work – but if the logic can be written with if / else, don't use exceptions. Exceptions cost more than normal branches, and they make the code's intention less clear.

# Right
val = d.get('key')
if val is not None:
    use(val)
else:
    use_default()

So when are exceptions the right choice? When "normally, this shouldn't go wrong" – like reading files, network requests, or checking user input. These are really "error handling" situations, so exceptions fit naturally.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 4: forgetting the caller needs the original information
docs.text:
# Wrong
try:
    do_thing()
except SomeError as e:
    raise MyError('Operation failed')

This throws away the original exception completely. The caller gets MyError, but the traceback has no information about SomeError – the root cause is lost.

# Right
try:
    do_thing()
except SomeError as e:
    raise MyError('Operation failed') from e

Remember from e. It's a tiny effort, but it can save you during a real production incident.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 5: using except instead of type checking
docs.text:
# Wrong
try:
    n = int(x)
except (TypeError, ValueError):
    n = 0

If x's type should really be checked, checking it directly is clearer than relying on an exception as a safety net. Of course, a safety net for outside input is reasonable – but your internal logic shouldn't be written like this.

docs.title: assert – lightweight checks while debugging
docs.text:
Besides exception handling, Python has a cousin called assert. Its job is to put "I assume X is definitely true" checks into your code. If it's not true, it raises an AssertionError.

def calculate_average(nums):
    assert len(nums) > 0, 'Cannot average an empty list'
    return sum(nums) / len(nums)


print(calculate_average([1, 2, 3]))

Output:

2.0

The syntax is assert expression, error message. If the expression is false, it raises AssertionError.

But! assert has an important trap: when you run code with python -O (optimised mode), every assert statement is thrown away. So you must never use assert to check input in production. It should only be used for "development and debugging", "test assertions" and "protecting internal invariants" (things that should always be true inside your code).

Wrong example:

def withdraw(account, amount):
    assert amount > 0, 'Withdrawal amount must be positive'   # Wrong – the check vanishes in optimised mode
    account.balance -= amount

The right way:

def withdraw(account, amount):
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError('Withdrawal amount must be positive')
    account.balance -= amount

Remember a simple rule: assert is for programmers; raise is for the program.

docs.title: The traceback module – printing errors more nicely
docs.text:
After catching an exception, sometimes you want to control how the error is printed – for example, when writing logs, or an error page for a web back end. The standard library's traceback module does this.

import traceback


def do_work():
    return 1 / 0


try:
    do_work()
except ZeroDivisionError:
    # Turn the full traceback into a string
    s = traceback.format_exc()
    print('--- Error log ---')
    print(s)
    print('--- End ---')

Output:

--- Error log ---
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "...", line 8, in <module>
    do_work()
  File "...", line 5, in do_work
    return 1 / 0
           ~~^~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

--- End ---

traceback.format_exc() turns the full traceback of the exception currently being handled into a string. You can save that string to a log, send it in an email, or store it in a database.

Similar functions:

  • traceback.print_exc(): print it straight to stderr
  • traceback.format_exception(exc): pass in an exception object, get a list of strings
  • traceback.print_exception(exc): pass in an exception object, print it to stderr

These are really handy when writing your own middleware or logging framework.

docs.title: logging.exception – the recommended way to log
docs.text:
In production code, you'll almost always use the logging module. It has special support for exceptions:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def risky():
    return 1 / 0


try:
    risky()
except Exception:
    logger.exception('Calling risky failed')

Output (excerpt):

ERROR:__main__:Calling risky failed
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "...", line 11, in <module>
    risky()
  File "...", line 7, in risky
    return 1 / 0
           ~~^~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

logger.exception(msg) is the same as logger.error(msg, exc_info=True). It automatically adds the current exception's traceback to the log.

If you write back-end services, remember this: wherever you catch an exception, you almost always want a logger.exception. Otherwise, tracking down problems in production will make you cry.

docs.title: warnings – gentler than exceptions
docs.text:
An exception means "it blew up". But sometimes you want to say "it works, but I don't recommend it" – for example, an old API that's about to be removed, or an argument combination with performance problems. That's when you use Python's warnings module.

import warnings


def old_api(x):
    warnings.warn('old_api is deprecated, please use new_api instead', DeprecationWarning)
    return x * 2


print(old_api(3))

Output (the stderr part):

warning: DeprecationWarning: old_api is deprecated, please use new_api instead
6

warnings.warn(message, category) is a "gentle heads-up" – the program keeps running as normal, but the caller can see the message in stderr.

The key difference between warnings and exceptions: warnings don't stop the program by default. But you can use warnings.filterwarnings('error') to upgrade them to exceptions – handy in tests, to force people to clean up deprecated usage.

If you write libraries for other people, you must know this. It's much friendlier than just raising an exception.

docs.title: try/except inside an expression – not allowed
docs.text:
You might have used try expressions in other languages, like Rust's ? or Kotlin's runCatching. Python does not have this. In Python, try/except can only be a statement, not an expression:

# Wrong – the syntax doesn't allow this
result = try:
    int(x)
except ValueError:
    0

To get a one-line "use a default if conversion fails", the standard way is to wrap it in a small helper function:

def safe_int(x, default=0):
    try:
        return int(x)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return default


print(safe_int('42'))
print(safe_int('abc'))
print(safe_int(None, default=-1))

Output:

42
0
-1

"The Pythonic way is to wrap it in a small function" – remember this.

docs.title: EAFP vs LBYL – Python's philosophy
docs.text:
Finally, let's compare two styles. Understanding this really helps you organise your code.

  • LBYL (Look Before You Leap): check the condition first with if, then do the operation
  • EAFP (Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission): just do the operation, and use try/except as a safety net if it fails

For example, "open a file and read it":

# LBYL
import os

if os.path.exists('config.json'):
    with open('config.json', 'r') as f:
        data = f.read()
else:
    data = ''

# EAFP
try:
    with open('config.json', 'r') as f:
        data = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    data = ''

Many other languages (like Java) lean towards LBYL, but Python culture leans towards EAFP. There are two reasons:

  1. LBYL has a "checked, then it changed" risk when several things run at once (for example, os.path.exists says yes, but a second later someone else deletes the file, and open still blows up)
  2. EAFP reads more like natural language – "I'll just do it, and deal with it if it doesn't work"

Of course, EAFP doesn't suit every situation. For example, dict.get(key, default) is clearer than try / except KeyError for dictionary lookups. Here's how to decide:

  • Usually succeeds, occasionally fails → use EAFP (exceptions)
  • Often needs to branch in normal use → use LBYL (if/else)

docs.title: A few final words
docs.text:
Let's review today's content:

  1. try / except is Python's core structure for handling errors. Remember: "children first, parents last"
  2. Catch several exceptions with except (A, B); get the exception object with as e
  3. Exceptions form a family tree – catching a parent catches all its children. Use Exception as a catch-all, never a bare except:
  4. else runs "only if nothing went wrong"; finally runs "no matter what"
  5. raise raises an exception yourself; raise ... from e makes an explicit exception chain, so you can find the root cause when debugging
  6. Custom exception classes make errors part of your code's structure – essential when business logic gets complicated
  7. ExceptionGroup + except* (Python 3.11+) solve the problem of "reporting several errors at once"
  8. add_note (Python 3.11+) adds debugging context to an exception – more elegant than raising a new one

How well you handle exceptions is one of the biggest differences between beginners and experienced programmers. Beginners either don't handle them at all – the program blows up and that's it – or handle them badly – except Exception: pass swallows every error, and when something goes wrong, nobody can save it. Experienced programmers catch precisely, pass errors on sensibly, wrap them when needed, and never quietly swallow them.

In the next article, we'll keep moving forward and talk about generators and iterators, taking your code up another level. Keep going!

docs.title: Narrow the error down to one input
docs.text:
This time, let's change the earlier "skip negative numbers" exercise so it clearly reports the problem. First, let's agree: the input is some text, and it should contain a non-negative integer:

def parse_minutes(text):
    try:
        minutes = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        raise ValueError('Minutes must be written as a whole number') from None
    if minutes < 0:
        raise ValueError('Minutes cannot be negative')
    return minutes


for text in ['15', '0', '-3', 'abc']:
    try:
        print(parse_minutes(text))
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)

Output:

15
0
Minutes cannot be negative
Minutes must be written as a whole number

We catch ValueError here because we know exactly which failure we're dealing with. This doesn't mean it can handle every type of input. For example, passing a list as text is a different kind of problem – using the interface wrongly.

When you meet a long traceback, first look at the error type and message at the bottom, then look upwards for your own file and the line that called it. Keep the input that fails, and remove unrelated screens, loops and file operations step by step, until you have the shortest code that still shows the problem. After each removal, run it again to check it still shows the same problem.

When you need to ask for help, describe the problem in five parts: the environment you ran it in, the shortest code, the actual input, the expected result, and the actual result with the full error. Then add what you've already tried. Try describing parse_minutes('-3') in these five parts yourself, and then change the input to '15' as a working comparison.

docs.title: 1. A Quick Look at Python Syntax
docs.text:
Every language has its own grammar (syntax) – both human languages (like English and Chinese) and computer programming languages.

Python is no different. It has its own syntax rules. The interpreter takes code that follows these rules, turns it into machine code that the CPU can run, and then runs it.

Python's syntax is fairly simple. It uses indentation (spaces at the start of a line).

# Check whether a number is positive (or zero)
a = 88
if a >= 0:
    print('yes')
else:
    print('NO')

Output:

yes

In the code above, a line starting with # is a comment. Every other line is a statement. When a statement ends with a colon :, the indented lines below it form a code block.

Note that Python is case-sensitive. If you use the wrong capital or small letter, the program will give an error.

For more details, see the earlier article: Quick Overview of Python Code Style

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
I'm starting a new project soon, so work is getting busy again. But I still try to find time every day to write. I can't write a new post every day, though, because each one takes quite a long time.

Note: When I read my old, over-emotional words, I wanted to delete them straight away. But right after pressing delete, I realised I didn't know what to write instead – so I pressed undo. This chapter has many changes and lots of new examples.

docs.title: 4. String Encoding
docs.text:
We all know computers can only work with numbers. To work with text, the computer must first turn the text into numbers. Early computers used 8 bits as one byte, so the biggest number one byte can hold is 255 (binary 11111111 = decimal 255). The numbers 0 – 255 were used for capital and small English letters, digits and some symbols. This table is called ASCII encoding. For example, capital A is 65, and small z is 122.

To show Chinese, one byte is clearly not enough. You need at least two bytes, and it must not clash with ASCII. So China created the GB2312 encoding for Chinese characters.

Japanese, Korean and other languages had the same problem. To put all the world's writing into one system, Unicode was created. Unicode puts every language into one set of codes, so there are no more garbled characters.

Unicode usually uses two bytes for one character. To turn an old English (ASCII) code into Unicode, you just fill the extra byte with 0.

Python was born before the Unicode standard was published, so the earliest Python only supported ASCII. A normal string like 'ABC' was stored as ASCII inside Python.

Python added Unicode support later. Unicode strings were written as u'...'.

But in modern Python 3, strings are Unicode. This means Python strings support many languages. That's why in the examples above, I didn't need to add u'...' and everything still showed correctly.

However, Python source code is itself a text file. So when your code contains non-English text (for example Chinese), you must save the file in UTF-8 encoding. To make sure the Python interpreter reads the file as UTF-8, we usually put these two lines at the top:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

The first comment tells Linux/OS X that this is a Python program that can be run. Windows ignores it.

The second comment tells the Python interpreter to read the source code as UTF-8. Otherwise, non-English text in your code might come out as garbled characters.

Declaring UTF-8 does not mean your .py file really is UTF-8. You must also make sure your text editor is saving with UTF-8 without BOM.

docs.title: 5. Converting Between Basic Data Types
docs.text:
Here are the ways to convert between basic data types in Python.

Function What it does int(x [,base ]) Turns x into an integer float(x ) Turns x into a float complex(real [,imag ]) Makes a complex number str(x ) Turns object x into a string repr(x ) Turns object x into an expression string eval(str ) Works out a valid Python expression inside a string and returns an object tuple(s ) Turns sequence s into a tuple list(s ) Turns sequence s into a list chr(x ) Turns an integer into a character ord(x ) Turns a character into its integer value hex(x ) Turns an integer into a hexadecimal string oct(x ) Turns an integer into an octal string

Note: Python 3 has only one integer type, int, which can hold very big numbers. There is no Long type like in Python 2.

Let's try some of these functions.

For example, the int() function turns a string that looks like a whole number into an integer.

str1 = '100'
str2 = '300'

print(str1 + str2)
print(int(str1) + int(str2))

Output:

100300
400

Notice we said "a string that looks like a whole number". Strings made of words can't be turned into integers by int().

Strings with a decimal point also can't be turned into integers by int().

print(int('88.88'))

This gives an error:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(int('88.88'))
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '88.88'

But this doesn't mean floats can't become integers. It only means a string with a decimal point can't be forced into an integer by int().

A float can still be converted with int().

For example:

print(int(88.88))

Output:

88

But notice the result is 88. The 0.88 after the decimal point is gone.

This is because int() turns data into an integer. When it turns a float into an integer, it just cuts off the decimal part and keeps the whole number part. So the output is 88.

I won't go through every function one by one. Just use them and try them, and you will slowly get to know them. If you are a beginner, play with every one of them! Write anything you like, run it, and look at the result. Don't worry – your computer won't break from this.

docs.title: 1. Strings
docs.text:
A string is one of the most common data types in Python. It is easy to spot: a string is text inside quotes.

You can use single quotes ' ', double quotes " " or triple quotes ''' '''. For example: 'abc', "123" and so on.

Please note: the quotes '' or "" are only a way to show where the string starts and ends. They are not part of the string. So the string 'abc' has only 3 characters: a, b and c.

If you like to think things through, you might ask:

Why do we need single quotes ' ', double quotes " " and triple quotes ''' '''? Why not just pick one? Why have so many rules for the same thing?

Good question. Usually, one rule for one thing is best. So if strings have three ways to be written, there must be a reason.

Let's write the same string in all three ways, print them, and see what happens.

str1 = 'Sam'
str2 = "Sam"
str3 = '''Sam'''
print(str1)
print(str2)
print(str3)

The results are the same:

Sam
Sam
Sam

But what if our string is not Sam, but Sam's book – with a quote mark inside it?

Then we get an error straight away:

str1 = 'Sam's book'
print(str1)

  File "test.py", line 1
    str1 = 'Sam's book'
                  ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

Notice: single quotes ' ' don't work here, but double quotes " " do.

str2 = "Sam's book"
print(str2)

The result is just what we wanted:

Sam's book

Triple quotes work the same way. If your text has double quotes inside it, double quotes around it will give the same error. That is when you can use triple quotes:

str3 = '''Sam said: "Hello!"'''
print(str3)

Sam said: "Hello!"

So, can strings made with single or double quotes never hold text like this?

They can! You can use escape characters.

For a single quote, write \'. For a double quote, write \".

Be careful: this is a backslash \, not a forward slash /.

Now let's test it:

str1 = 'Sam\'s book'
str2 = "Sam said: \"Hello!\""
print(str1)
print(str2)

The output:

Sam's book
Sam said: "Hello!"

One last thing: triple quotes ''' ''' let a string go over several lines.

str2 = '''Sam
loves
Python'''
print(str2)

Output:

Sam
loves
Python

docs.title: 2. Integers
docs.text:
An integer in code is the same as an integer in maths: positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers and zero. Integers are numbers without a decimal point.

Python can handle integers of any size, for example 1, 100, -8080, 0 and so on.

int1 = 1
int2 = 100
int3 = -8080
int4 = 0

print(int1)
print(int2)
print(int3)
print(int4)

Output:

1
100
-8080
0

Be careful: if you put a number inside quotes, it becomes a string, not an integer. For example, '100' is a string, not an integer.

In real life we do maths with whole numbers. In code it's the same: you can add, subtract, multiply and divide integers.

For example:

int1 = 1 + 2
int2 = 1 - 2
int3 = 1 * 2
int4 = 1 / 2

print(int1)
print(int2)
print(int3)
print(int4)

Output:

3
-1
2
0.5

Now look at the example above. Do you notice anything?

Look at what int4 prints: 0.5. That is a decimal number.

And how did we define an integer earlier?

A number without a decimal point.

So int4 is definitely not an integer.

We can use the type() function to check the type:

int1 = 1 + 2
int2 = 1 - 2
int3 = 1 * 2
int4 = 1 / 2

print(int1)
print(int2)
print(int3)
print(int4)

print(type(int1))
print(type(int2))
print(type(int3))
print(type(int4))

Result:

3
-1
2
0.5
<class 'int'>
<class 'int'>
<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>

We can see that int4 is a float, while int1, int2 and int3 are all int (integer).

So what is a float?

A float is a floating-point number. We will talk about it next.

Before that, have a quick look at Python's arithmetic operators, just to get to know them.

Python Arithmetic Operators

Operator Meaning Example + Add 2 + 1 gives 3 - Subtract 1 - 2 gives -1 * Multiply 1 * 2 gives 2 / Divide 1 / 2 gives 0.5 % Modulo – gives the remainder of a division 5 % 2 gives 1 ** Power – gives x to the power of y 2 ** 3 is 2 to the power of 3 // Floor division – gives the whole-number part of the answer 11 // 2 gives 5, 11.0 // 2.0 gives 5.0

docs.title: 3. Floats
docs.text:
A float is a number with a decimal point.

Floats are like integers in many ways, but floats are the trickiest. They are the hardest to fully understand.

The famous programmer Herb Sutter once joked that there are three kinds of people: people who know they don't understand floating-point maths; people who think they understand it; and a very small number of experts who wonder if they could ever fully understand it.

Why would he say that?

Look at the example below. Just like with integers, we are only adding some floats:

print(0.55+0.41)
print(0.55+0.4)
print(0.55+0.411)

But the results might surprise a beginner:

0.96
0.9500000000000001
0.9610000000000001

The first one is fine: 0.55 + 0.41 equals 0.96, exactly right. But in the other two, where did all those zeros come from?

This is because computers cannot store floats perfectly. Computers save numbers in binary, and binary cannot show some numbers exactly. It can only get very, very close.

So be careful when you do maths with floats or compare them.

docs.title: 4. Booleans
docs.text:
Booleans work just like in Boolean algebra. A Boolean has only two values: True or False. It is always one or the other. In Python you can write True and False directly (watch the capital letters!), or you can get them from a Boolean calculation.

You can use and, or and not with Booleans.

and: the result is True only if all parts are True.

or: the result is True if at least one part is True.

not: it works on just one value. It turns True into False, and False into True.

docs.title: 5. None (the empty value)
docs.text: Almost every programming language has a special "empty" value. In Python, it is called None.

docs.title: 6. f-strings: putting variables inside strings
docs.text:
Hey everyone! What if you want to put the value of a variable inside some text? How do you do it?

The best way in Python is called an f-string (added in Python 3.6). Put an f before the opening quote, and wrap a variable name in {} inside the string. Python will replace the {} with the variable's value.

name = 'Sam'
print(f'Nickname: {name}')

Output:

Nickname: Sam

It's that simple: f at the front + {variable_name}. Single or double quotes both work, and you can use many {} in one string. This is the recommended way to build strings today.

Now that you know the basics, here are a few more advanced tricks that many people don't know about.

docs.title: (1) Self-documenting: a great debugging tool f"{x=}"
docs.text:
When you write code, do you often want to print a variable's name and value to help find bugs?

The old way looks like this:

name = 'Sam'
age = 18

print(f'name={name}, age={age}')

Output:

name=Sam, age=18

You have to type each variable name twice, and if you rename a variable, it's easy to forget one. Since Python 3.8, f-strings have an = syntax (called self-documenting expressions) that does it in one step:

name = 'Sam'
age = 18

print(f'{name=}, {age=}')

Output:

name='Sam', age=18

See? The variable name and the equals sign are added for you, and the string even gets quotes around it. This is super handy for debugging. It has been around since Python 3.8, but lots of people still don't know about it – don't miss out!

You can even put a whole expression in it:

a = 3
b = 4

print(f'{a + b = }')

Output:

a + b = 7

Notice that the spaces around = are kept exactly as you typed them. If you want neat output, just control the spaces yourself.

docs.title: (2) Format specs: alignment, decimal places, thousands separators
docs.text:
Inside the curly braces of an f-string, you can add a colon : followed by a format spec. It controls how the value looks.

Keep 2 decimal places:

pi = 3.1415926

print(f'{pi:.2f}')

Output:

3.14

Right-align in a space 10 characters wide:

name = 'Sam'

print(f'[{name:>10}]')

Output (the gap is spaces):

[       Sam]

> means right-align, < means left-align, and ^ means centre.

Add commas to big numbers:

amount = 1234567890

print(f'Order total: ${amount:,}')

Output:

Order total: $1,234,567,890

Show as a percentage:

rate = 0.875

print(f'Success rate: {rate:.1%}')

Output:

Success rate: 87.5%

See? Jobs that used to need round, format or joining strings together can all be done with one f-string.

docs.title: (3) Python 3.12+: quotes inside f-strings are no longer a problem
docs.text:
One last thing: a new feature in Python 3.12 (PEP 701). Before 3.12, f-strings had an annoying rule: if you wrote a string inside the curly braces, its quotes could not be the same as the outer quotes.

For example, the code below is wrong in Python 3.11 and earlier:

data = {'name': 'Sam', 'age': 18}

# Only allowed in Python 3.12+: single quotes inside and outside
print(f'The nickname is {data['name']}')

Output:

The nickname is Sam

In older versions, this code gives a SyntaxError. You would have to switch the outer quotes to double quotes, or use an extra variable. From 3.12, this rule is gone: you can mix the outer and inner quotes however you like. This is really helpful when you write complex templates.

Python 3.12 also removed other limits: f-strings can now have expressions over several lines, comments, and backslashes. So when you use Python 3.12+, you can write f-strings pretty much any way you want – no more strange rules.

docs.title: 1. Creating and Assigning Variables
docs.text:
In a Python program, a variable has a name, and it can hold any type of data. A variable name can only use English letters (capital or small), digits and underscores (_), and it can't start with a digit. For example:

a=88

Here, a is a variable that holds an integer. Notice that in Python you don't have to say what type of data a variable holds. In Python, = is the assignment statement, just like in other languages. Because you don't need to declare the type, you can give a variable any type of data. You can also change the same variable again and again, even to a different type.

a = 'Hello Python'
print(a)
a = 123
print(a)

Output:

Hello Python
123

A language where a variable's type isn't fixed is called a dynamic language. The opposite is a static language. In a static language, you must give each variable a type when you create it, and if you assign the wrong type, you get an error. Java is a static language, for example.

docs.title: 2. What a Variable Points To
docs.text:
Look at this code. The variable b prints Hello Python at the end.

a = 'Hello Python'
b = a
a = 123
print(b)

Output:

Hello Python

Here's why: at first, variable a points to the string Hello Python. Then b = a creates variable b, and b points to the same string that a points to, Hello Python. Finally, a = 123 makes a point to 123 instead. So when we print b, we still get Hello Python.

You can think of it like this:

  • ① Variable a points to the string 'Hello Python'
  • ② b = a: variable b also points to 'Hello Python'
  • ③ a = 123: variable a now points to the integer 123, but b still points to 'Hello Python'

docs.title: 3. Assigning Several Variables at Once
docs.text:
Python lets you assign values to several variables at the same time. For example:

a = b = c = 1

In this example, one integer object with the value 1 is created, and all three variables point to the same place in memory.

You can also give several variables different values at once. For example:

a, b, c = 1, 2, "liangdianshui"

Here, the integers 1 and 2 go to variables a and b, and the string "liangdianshui" goes to variable c.

docs.title: Guess the output first, then explain what the variables point to
docs.text:
We've covered assigning variables. Now, don't run it yet. Guess what the last two lines print:

minutes = 15
recorded = minutes
minutes = minutes + 5
print(minutes)
print(recorded)

Output:

20
15

recorded = minutes makes both names point to the same integer object at first. But it does not make them "change together forever". minutes = minutes + 5 works out a new result and points minutes to it. recorded still points to the old integer.

Now change the starting value to 0 and work it out yourself. You should get 5 and 0. If your guess was wrong, look back at "What a Variable Points To" and check, after each assignment, where each name is pointing.

One more thing that's easy to mix up: '15' is text, and 15 is an integer. When you need to do maths, convert it as needed. Just because they look the same on screen doesn't mean they work the same way. Try int('15') + 5, then try '15' + '5', and explain why you get 20 and '155'.

When you're starting out, name your variables with English letters, digits and underscores. Python actually allows some non-ASCII characters in names too, as long as they follow the rules for identifiers – it's not limited to English letters. But while learning, keep using clear English names, and remember that keywords (like if or for) can't be used as normal variable names.

docs.title: 2. The print() Function
docs.text:
Let's start with the print() function. If you are new, you may not know much about functions yet. That's fine. For now, you only need to know its parts and what it does. We will explain functions in detail later.

The print() function has two parts:

  1. The command: print
  2. What the command works on: the stuff inside the brackets after print

It looks like this:

The job of print() is to make the computer show a result on the screen (in the terminal). What it shows is whatever you put inside print().

For example, in the last chapter, our first Python program was print('Hello Python')

print('Hello Python')

Output:

Hello Python

Here is what happens step by step:

  1. You give the interpreter a command: print 'Hello Python'
  2. The interpreter turns your code into machine language the computer can understand
  3. The computer runs it and prints the result

Here is a picture of the process:

Some of you may ask: why do we need the single quotes? Can't we just write print(Hello Python)?

When you have a question like this while coding, the best thing to do is write the code and test it yourself.

print(Hello Python)

Result:

  File "test.py", line 1
    print(Hello Python)
                    ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

Clearly, without the quotes, the result turns red (an error). So this doesn't work.

This is because it breaks Python's syntax rules. Without the quotes, the Python interpreter can't understand what you wrote.

So it shows the error SyntaxError: invalid syntax, which means: syntax error. Your statement doesn't follow the rules.

docs.title: dataclass and Pydantic
docs.text:
When writing code, it's easy to get stuck in the swamp of boilerplate code. Don't argue yet – let's do a small experiment. Write an Employee class with these requirements: it stores an employee's name, department, employee ID, start date and monthly salary; it should print nicely (not something horrible like <__main__.Employee object at 0x...>); you should be able to check whether two employee objects are equal; and ideally it can be used as a dictionary key.

Doesn't sound hard, right? If you like to think things through, you've probably already written it in your head. It looks something like this:

class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, dept, emp_id, hire_date, salary):
        self.name = name
        self.dept = dept
        self.emp_id = emp_id
        self.hire_date = hire_date
        self.salary = salary

    def __repr__(self):
        return (
            f'Employee(name={self.name!r}, dept={self.dept!r}, '
            f'emp_id={self.emp_id!r}, hire_date={self.hire_date!r}, '
            f'salary={self.salary!r})'
        )

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Employee):
            return NotImplemented
        return (
            self.name == other.name
            and self.dept == other.dept
            and self.emp_id == other.emp_id
            and self.hire_date == other.hire_date
            and self.salary == other.salary
        )

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.name, self.dept, self.emp_id, self.hire_date, self.salary))


e = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 1001, '2020-03-15', 12000)
print(e)

Output:

Employee(name='Two Drops', dept='Coding Dept', emp_id=1001, hire_date='2020-03-15', salary=12000)

Count them: this ordinary little "data class" takes over twenty lines. __init__ lists the fields once, __repr__ lists them again, __eq__ lists them again, and __hash__ lists them yet again – the same field names appear five times. Now imagine your class has 15 fields. The __init__ parameter list would be as long as a train, and you'd copy and paste self.xxx = xxx again and again. By the tenth one, you'd want to scream.

This is what we call boilerplate code. It doesn't add any business value – it's only there because Python's syntax makes you write it. The person writing it hates it, and so does the person reading it, because the important information – "what fields does this class have?" – is buried in the repetitive noise of self.xxx = xxx.

Is there a way to just declare the fields, and let Python do the rest?

Yes. Python 3.7 gave us dataclass. From 3.10, it gained more modern switches like slots and kw_only. Beyond that, there's the third-party library Pydantic, which focuses on "data models with runtime validation". In this article, let's go from dataclass all the way to Pydantic, so your fingers never get tied in knots writing data structures again.

docs.title: What does your first dataclass look like?
docs.text:
Let's rewrite the Employee class above with dataclass:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Employee:
    name: str
    dept: str
    emp_id: int
    hire_date: str
    salary: int


e = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 1001, '2020-03-15', 12000)
print(e)

Output:

Employee(name='Two Drops', dept='Coding Dept', emp_id=1001, hire_date='2020-03-15', salary=12000)

Look – over twenty lines shrink to under ten. Just add the @dataclass decorator, and Python does all this for us:

  • It sees "class variables with type hints" like name: str and dept: str, and automatically treats them as fields
  • It automatically creates an __init__, with the parameters in the same order as the fields
  • It automatically creates a __repr__ that looks exactly like the hand-written "ClassName(field=value, field=value)" one
  • It automatically creates an __eq__ that compares the fields one by one

All you have to do is write the field names and their types. dataclass does all the rest.

Are the type hints required? Yes. They're how dataclass recognises fields. If you only write name = '' without name: str, dataclass won't recognise it – it treats name as a normal class attribute, and it won't go into the __init__ parameter list.

Remember this: in a dataclass, name: str is a field declaration, and name = 'default' (with no hint) is a class attribute. They do completely different things.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Demo:
    a: int        # This is a field – it goes into __init__
    b: int = 10   # This is a field with a default value – it also goes into __init__
    c = 20        # Note: no type hint here, so it's a normal class attribute – NOT in __init__


d = Demo(1)
print(d)
print(d.c)

Output:

Demo(a=1, b=10)
20

See? c doesn't appear in the repr, because it isn't a field at all – it's just a constant attached to the class.

docs.title: Comparing two dataclass objects
docs.text:
dataclass creates __eq__ by default, so two objects with exactly the same field values are considered equal:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Employee:
    name: str
    dept: str
    salary: int


a = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 12000)
b = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 12000)
c = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 15000)

print(a == b)
print(a == c)
print(a is b)

Output:

True
False
False

Look at the third line – a is b is False. == compares "are the field values equal?", while is compares "is it the very same object?". These are two completely different things – don't mix them up.

If you don't want the automatic __eq__, pass eq=False:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(eq=False)
class Employee:
    name: str


a = Employee('Two Drops')
b = Employee('Two Drops')
print(a == b)

Output:

False

Now == goes back to "comparing object identity", the same as is. I don't usually recommend turning it off – without it, the dataclass is hardly different from a normal class.

docs.title: Default values – a lazy starting value for a field
docs.text:
Just like function parameters, dataclass fields can have default values:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Employee:
    name: str
    dept: str = 'Coding Dept'
    salary: int = 8000


e1 = Employee('Two Drops')
e2 = Employee('Xiao Ming', 'R&D', 15000)
print(e1)
print(e2)

Output:

Employee(name='Two Drops', dept='Coding Dept', salary=8000)
Employee(name='Xiao Ming', dept='R&D', salary=15000)

Did you notice? It works just like function parameters – fields with default values must come after fields without them. Python will flat-out reject this:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class BadOrder:
    qty: int = 1
    name: str   # Wrong! A field without a default can't come after one with a default

Error:

TypeError: non-default argument 'name' follows default argument

What if the default value is a mutable object – like an empty list?

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Team:
    name: str
    members: list = []   # Error straight away

Error:

ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field members is not allowed: use default_factory

This time Python acts like a responsible parent and stops you at the door. Why doesn't it allow this? Because if it did, every Team instance would share the same members list. Append to one, and every instance's members would change. This is a very old Python trap – so old that when dataclass was designed, this road was simply blocked.

So how do you write it? Use field(default_factory=...).

docs.title: field() – advanced settings for fields
docs.text:
field() is another star of the dataclasses module. It's for configuring fields in more detail. The most common use is the "mutable default" mentioned above:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class Team:
    name: str
    members: list = field(default_factory=list)


t1 = Team('Team A')
t2 = Team('Team B')
t1.members.append('Two Drops')
print(t1)
print(t2)

Output:

Team(name='Team A', members=['Two Drops'])
Team(name='Team B', members=[])

default_factory=list means: "every time an instance is created, call list() to get a brand-new empty list as the default". This way, each instance has its own list, and they don't interfere with each other.

default_factory can take any callable with no arguments. For example:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class Counter:
    name: str
    counts: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    tags: set = field(default_factory=set)
    history: list = field(default_factory=lambda: ['First record'])


c = Counter('Click counter')
print(c)

Output:

Counter(name='Click counter', counts={}, tags=set(), history=['First record'])

Look at the last one, history – default_factory=lambda: ['First record']. Returning a list with a starting value each time is also a common use.

field() has a few other common arguments. Let's cover them all at once:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    price: float
    discount: float = field(default=0.0)             # Same as = 0.0, but more explicit
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)         # Mutable default
    internal_id: str = field(repr=False, default='') # Not shown in repr
    cache: dict = field(default_factory=dict, compare=False)  # Not used in == comparisons


p1 = Product('Phone', 2999.0, internal_id='SECRET-1', cache={'foo': 'bar'})
p2 = Product('Phone', 2999.0, internal_id='SECRET-2', cache={'baz': 'qux'})
print(p1)
print(p1 == p2)

Output:

Product(name='Phone', price=2999.0, discount=0.0, tags=[], cache={'foo': 'bar'})
False

Let's look at the two most useful ones:

  • repr=False: this field won't appear in the repr. Good for sensitive information (passwords, tokens), or internal state you don't want cluttering your logs
  • compare=False: this field isn't used by __eq__. Good for helper fields that don't affect the object's business identity, like caches or temporary counters

Why is p1 == p2 False? Because repr=False only hides the field when printing – it doesn't affect equality. The two internal_ids are different, so the objects aren't equal. Only compare=False stops a field being compared – that's why the different caches don't matter. To get True, you'd also need to give internal_id compare=False.

docs.title: Immutable dataclasses – frozen=True
docs.text:
By default, dataclass instances are mutable – you can reassign their fields any time:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int


p = Point(1, 2)
p.x = 100
print(p)

Output:

Point(x=100, y=2)

But sometimes you want an object to never change after it's created – things that should be read-only by nature, like "a coordinate", "an enum value" or "a config setting". That's when you use frozen=True:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int


p = Point(1, 2)
print(p)

try:
    p.x = 100
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, ':', e)

Output:

Point(x=1, y=2)
FrozenInstanceError : cannot assign to field 'x'

Assigning raises a FrozenInstanceError. This protection happens at runtime – so even if a static checker doesn't stop you, it will blow up when it runs.

frozen=True has another important side effect: Python also creates __hash__ for you, so the object can go into a set and be used as a dict key.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int


p1 = Point(1, 2)
p2 = Point(1, 2)
p3 = Point(3, 4)

s = {p1, p2, p3}
print(len(s))

mapping = {Point(0, 0): 'origin', Point(1, 0): 'one step right'}
print(mapping[Point(0, 0)])

Output:

2
origin

See? p1 and p2 have the same field values, so the set treats them as the same element – len(s) is 2, not 3. Point(0, 0) can also be used as a dict key, and a newly created Point with the same fields finds it exactly. That's "frozen + the hash that dataclass creates" working together.

Can you hash it without frozen? By default: you can use eq=True, frozen=False but you'd have to explicitly add unsafe_hash=True – and I strongly advise against it. Once a mutable object is hashed into a set, if you change its fields, it gets "lost" in the set – the hash is still the old one, but the fields have changed, so you can never find it again. Don't step in that trap. If you need hashing, use frozen.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CacheKey:
    user_id: int
    api_path: str


# A simple pretend cache
cache = {}
key = CacheKey(1001, '/api/profile')
cache[key] = {'name': 'Two Drops', 'avatar': 'xxx.png'}

# Later, any key with the same fields will hit the cache
print(cache[CacheKey(1001, '/api/profile')])

Output:

{'name': 'Two Drops', 'avatar': 'xxx.png'}

This is a very typical use of frozen dataclasses – a compound key.

docs.title: __post_init__ – work something out after construction
docs.text:
Have you needed something like this? I have an Order class with fields unit_price and qty. As soon as the object is built, I want it to automatically work out a total field (total = unit price × quantity). total shouldn't be passed in by the user – it's derived from the other fields.

dataclass gives us a hook for this: __post_init__. It's called automatically right after __init__ finishes – perfect for derived calculations.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class Order:
    unit_price: float
    qty: int
    total: float = field(init=False)   # init=False means it's not in the __init__ parameter list

    def __post_init__(self):
        self.total = self.unit_price * self.qty


o = Order(unit_price=12.5, qty=8)
print(o)

Output:

Order(unit_price=12.5, qty=8, total=100.0)

There are two details here to focus on:

  1. total: float = field(init=False) – init=False keeps total out of the __init__ parameters. When building an Order, the user doesn't need to, and shouldn't, pass total
  2. __post_init__ is called automatically by dataclass. Its name must be exactly this – even the number of underscores must be right

What if I want to validate fields during construction? That's also a job for __post_init__:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Employee:
    name: str
    salary: int

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.salary < 0:
            raise ValueError(f'Salary cannot be negative, got: {self.salary}')
        if not self.name:
            raise ValueError('Name cannot be empty')


try:
    bad = Employee('Two Drops', -100)
except ValueError as e:
    print('Blew up:', e)

ok = Employee('Two Drops', 12000)
print(ok)

Output:

Blew up: Salary cannot be negative, got: -100
Employee(name='Two Drops', salary=12000)

But note: writing validation in __post_init__ is only a stop-gap. Its real job is more about "derived calculations", and lots of validation logic in it starts to look awkward. When we get to Pydantic later, you'll see a tool that's truly built for validation.

docs.title: kw_only=True – force keyword arguments (Python 3.10+)
docs.text:
First, look at this code:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Employee:
    name: str
    dept: str
    salary: int


e = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 12000)

This way of calling is called passing by position. The three values go in, in field order, and they match up perfectly.

But once there are lots of fields, problems start:

e = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 12000)
# A month later, a field is added and the order changes:
# Employee(name, salary, dept, hire_date)
# The old code Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 12000) still runs, but the meaning is completely wrong

When the field order changes, all old code that passes by position silently passes the wrong values. Bugs like this – "the call looks right but everything's shifted" – are extremely hard to track down.

kw_only=True (Python 3.10+) cures this. Add it, and every field must be passed by keyword:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class Employee:
    name: str
    dept: str
    salary: int


# You must write name= dept= salary=
e = Employee(name='Two Drops', dept='Coding Dept', salary=12000)
print(e)

# Try to be lazy and pass by position? Error straight away
try:
    bad = Employee('Two Drops', 'Coding Dept', 12000)
except TypeError as err:
    print(err)

Output:

Employee(name='Two Drops', dept='Coding Dept', salary=12000)
Employee.__init__() takes 1 positional argument but 4 were given

The calling code instantly becomes much easier to read – when you see name='Brother Shui', you know exactly which field each value belongs to.

You can also put kw_only on a single field:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class Order:
    unit_price: float
    qty: int
    coupon: str = field(default='', kw_only=True)


o = Order(12.5, 3, coupon='VIP10')
print(o)

Output:

Order(unit_price=12.5, qty=3, coupon='VIP10')

unit_price and qty can still be passed by position, but coupon must be a keyword. This field-level kw_only is really handy for "optional extras that are easy to mix up when there are many fields".

Note: the syntax above only exists in Python 3.10+. Before that, a dataclass could only allow positional arguments for the whole class or not at all. On Python 3.9, don't bother with this.

docs.title: slots=True – make dataclasses use less memory (Python 3.10+)
docs.text:
Have you ever wondered how a normal Python object stores its attributes? Answer: in a dictionary called __dict__. Every object has its own __dict__, holding a mapping of field names to values.

Dictionaries are flexible, but they have two costs:

  • Memory – an empty dictionary alone takes up several hundred bytes
  • Speed – looking things up in a dictionary is a tiny bit slower than direct indexing

If your program creates millions of dataclass instances (for data processing, game development, financial calculations and so on), these two costs grow into real problems.

slots=True (3.10+) is the cure:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float


p = Point(1.0, 2.0)
print(p)

# Try to assign a field that doesn't exist – it blows up
try:
    p.z = 3.0
except AttributeError as e:
    print('Blew up:', e)

Output:

Point(x=1.0, y=2.0)
Blew up: 'Point' object has no attribute 'z'

slots=True does two things:

  1. It uses __slots__ = ('x', 'y') to tell Python that instances of this class may only have the attributes x and y – no __dict__
  2. Instances no longer store data in a dictionary, so memory use drops a lot, and attribute access gets slightly faster

What's the cost? Flexibility. You can't add attributes to instances "on the fly" any more. But honestly, dataclasses are meant for "fixed fields" anyway, so this cost is totally acceptable.

Remember this: dataclass + frozen=True + slots=True is the golden trio for value types.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Coord:
    x: float
    y: float
    z: float


c = Coord(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)
print(c)
print(hash(c))

Output:

Coord(x=1.0, y=2.0, z=3.0)
1234567890   # The real value will be different

Unchangeable, hashable, memory-saving and fast to access. This is the standard way to write value objects in modern Python.

docs.title: Dataclasses and inheritance
docs.text:
Dataclasses can be inherited too. But there's a long-standing problem to watch out for: a field without a default can't come after a field with a default – and this rule is especially easy to trip over with inheritance.

First, an example that works:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Animal:
    name: str
    legs: int = 4


@dataclass
class Dog(Animal):
    breed: str = 'mixed breed'


d = Dog('Goldie', 4, 'Shiba Inu')
print(d)

Output:

Dog(name='Goldie', legs=4, breed='Shiba Inu')

The child class automatically "joins on" the parent's fields. Dog.__init__'s parameters are name, legs, breed – parent fields first, child fields after.

So when does it blow up? Look at this:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Animal:
    name: str
    legs: int = 4   # Has a default


@dataclass
class Dog(Animal):
    breed: str       # No default

Error:

TypeError: non-default argument 'breed' follows default argument

Think about why. The parent's legs already has a default, and the child's breed has none. Joined together, you get name, legs=4, breed – which breaks the rule that "a field without a default can't come after a field with a default".

Think of it in the order shown: for normal positional arguments, a field with no default can't come after a field with a default, so putting breed after legs=4 gives an error. Keyword-only fields follow different rules – and the kw_only=True fix below uses exactly that difference.

How do you fix it? Choose one of three ways:

  1. Give the child's field a default too: breed: str = ''
  2. Remove the default from the parent's field (but you usually can't do this – it breaks existing calls)
  3. Use kw_only=True – the most elegant:
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class Animal:
    name: str
    legs: int = 4


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class Dog(Animal):
    breed: str


d = Dog(name='Goldie', breed='Shiba Inu')
print(d)

Output:

Dog(name='Goldie', legs=4, breed='Shiba Inu')

kw_only=True makes every field keyword-only, so the "positional order" limit disappears – and with it, the annoying "defaults can't come first" problem.

From now on, when you meet dataclass inheritance, your first thought should be kw_only.

docs.title: More than dataclass – NamedTuple and TypedDict
docs.text: dataclass is the most common "lightweight data class" tool in Python, but it's not the only one. There are two common siblings: NamedTuple and TypedDict. They do similar jobs but have different purposes. Let's look at them briefly so you know they exist.

docs.title: NamedTuple – a tuple with names
docs.text:
from typing import NamedTuple


class Point(NamedTuple):
    x: float
    y: float


p = Point(1.0, 2.0)
print(p)
print(p.x, p.y)
print(p[0], p[1])      # You can still index it like a tuple
print(tuple(p))

Output:

Point(x=1.0, y=2.0)
1.0 2.0
1.0 2.0
(1.0, 2.0)

A NamedTuple is really "a tuple with field names". It's naturally immutable (tuples are immutable), has __hash__ built in, can be unpacked and indexed. But it isn't as flexible as a dataclass – it doesn't support things like default_factory or __post_init__.

When to use NamedTuple: when what you want is "an immutable tuple with names", and it'll often be unpacked or indexed. For example: coordinates, RGB colour values, a row of database results.

When to use dataclass: when you want a class – it might have methods, derived calculations, or need to be changeable.

docs.title: TypedDict – a dictionary with type hints
docs.text:
from typing import TypedDict


class UserProfile(TypedDict):
    name: str
    age: int
    email: str


u: UserProfile = {'name': 'Two Drops', 'age': 28, 'email': 'liangdianshui@xxx.com'}
print(u)
print(u['name'])

Output:

{'name': 'Two Drops', 'age': 28, 'email': 'liangdianshui@xxx.com'}
Two Drops

Note: the object made by TypedDict is a dictionary, not a class instance. u is still a dict. You access it with u['key'], not u.key. Its job is to "tell mypy, at the static type level, which keys this dictionary must have and what type each value is". At runtime it doesn't check anything.

When to use TypedDict: when you're working with JSON or outside interfaces, already have a dictionary, and just want mypy to check that the keys and types match – without turning the dictionary into a class object.

docs.title: The limit of dataclass – it doesn't validate at runtime
docs.text:
By now, you probably think dataclass is great. It is. But it has one very important weakness: it doesn't validate anything at runtime.

Look at this code:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Employee:
    name: str
    age: int
    salary: float


# I'm passing the wrong types on purpose
e = Employee(name=123, age='twenty-eight', salary='eight thousand')
print(e)
print(type(e.name), type(e.age), type(e.salary))

Output:

Employee(name=123, age='twenty-eight', salary='eight thousand')
<class 'int'> <class 'str'> <class 'str'>

See? I passed the number 123 for name, the string 'twenty-eight' for age and the string 'eight thousand' for salary – and the dataclass quietly accepted all of them. It doesn't look at your type hints at all. Hints like name: str and age: int are only for static checkers (mypy, pyright). At runtime, dataclass doesn't enforce them at all.

For "internal code", this isn't a big deal, because you usually control the types yourself. But in situations like these, it's a big problem:

  • An HTTP endpoint receives JSON from a client
  • A YAML/TOML config file is parsed into a dictionary
  • A message from a message queue is turned back into data

All this data comes from outside, and you can't be sure its field types are right. Accepting it with a dataclass is like pouring dirty water straight into your bowl. When you later try e.salary * 12 to work out a yearly salary, and find salary is the string 'eight thousand', tracking down which step caused it is so costly you'll want to smash your keyboard.

So is there a tool that declares fields as elegantly as dataclass, AND checks types/rules at runtime?

Yes. It's Pydantic.

docs.title: Enter Pydantic – data models with runtime validation
docs.text:
Pydantic is the most popular data validation library in the Python world. It's at the heart of FastAPI, LangChain's interfaces, and the config classes of all sorts of SDKs. Its core idea is simple: when data crosses into your program, strictly check it against the declared schema, converting it when needed. After that, the code inside your program can use it with confidence.

First, note one thing: Pydantic is a third-party library, not part of the standard library, so you need to install it:

pip install pydantic

All the Pydantic code blocks below are marked with a skip-ci comment (so the example-checking script skips them). Install it yourself before running them. The current main version is Pydantic v2, and this article uses v2.

docs.title: Your first BaseModel
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Employee(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int
    salary: float


e = Employee(name='Two Drops', age=28, salary=12000.0)
print(e)

Output:

name='Two Drops' age=28 salary=12000.0

Looks almost the same as dataclass, right? That's right – inherit from BaseModel, write fields with type hints, and Pydantic does everything else. It automatically creates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__, and it also does something dataclass doesn't – type validation and conversion.

Look at this:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Employee(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int
    salary: float


# Note: I passed age as the string '28', and salary as the string '12000.5'
e = Employee(name='Two Drops', age='28', salary='12000.5')
print(e)
