print(type(e.age), type(e.salary))

Output:

name='Two Drops' age=28 salary=12000.5
<class 'int'> <class 'float'>

See? I passed age='28' as a string, but Pydantic turned it into an int. salary='12000.5' became a float too. This is Pydantic's smart conversion – if a type can sensibly be converted, it converts it for you.

What if what you pass really can't be converted?

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class Employee(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int
    salary: float


try:
    e = Employee(name='Two Drops', age='abc', salary='not a number')
except ValidationError as err:
    print(err)

Output (roughly):

2 validation errors for Employee
age
  Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer [type=int_parsing, input_value='abc', input_type=str]
salary
  Input should be a valid number, unable to parse string as a number [type=float_parsing, input_value='not a number', input_type=str]

Beautiful, right? It doesn't just raise a ValidationError – it tells you which fields, why they're wrong and what it received. Dataclass can't do any of this.

docs.title: Building a model from a dict/JSON – model_validate and model_validate_json
docs.text:
This is Pydantic's killer feature. Imagine you've written an HTTP endpoint. The front end POSTs some JSON, and you need to:

  1. Parse the JSON into a dictionary
  2. Check the field types / required fields inside it
  3. Turn it into your internal data type

With dataclass, you'd have to write lots of validation code yourself. Pydantic does it in one line:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Employee(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int
    salary: float


# Parse from a JSON string
json_str = '{"name": "Two Drops", "age": 28, "salary": 12000}'
e = Employee.model_validate_json(json_str)
print(e)

# Parse from a dictionary
data = {'name': 'Xiao Ming', 'age': 30, 'salary': 15000}
e2 = Employee.model_validate(data)
print(e2)

Output:

name='Two Drops' age=28 salary=12000.0
name='Xiao Ming' age=30 salary=15000.0

model_validate(d) builds a model from a dictionary, and model_validate_json(s) builds one from a JSON string. Both go through the full validation process. Missing fields, wrong types or broken rules all raise a ValidationError.

The other way round, turning a model back into a dictionary/JSON is easy too:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Employee(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int
    salary: float


e = Employee(name='Two Drops', age=28, salary=12000.0)
print(e.model_dump())          # To a dictionary
print(e.model_dump_json())     # To a JSON string

Output:

{'name': 'Two Drops', 'age': 28, 'salary': 12000.0}
{"name":"Two Drops","age":28,"salary":12000.0}

This "dictionary ↔ model ↔ JSON" triangle is the best part of Pydantic. Handling outside data becomes almost effortless.

docs.title: Field rules – the power of Field(...)
docs.text:
Type checking is just the start. The really powerful part is rule (constraint) checking. For example, you'll often need:

  • A number within a range: 0 <= age <= 120, salary >= 0
  • A string with a length limit: 1 <= len(name) <= 50
  • A string that matches a regular expression
  • A valid email, URL or UUID

Pydantic uses Field(...) to express these rules:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError


class Employee(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=50)
    age: int = Field(ge=18, le=65)              # ge = greater than or equal, le = less than or equal
    salary: float = Field(gt=0)                  # gt = greater than
    rating: int = Field(ge=0, le=100, default=60)


# A normal one
e = Employee(name='Two Drops', age=28, salary=12000.0)
print(e)

# Age out of range
try:
    bad = Employee(name='Xiao Ming', age=10, salary=5000.0)
except ValidationError as err:
    print(err)

Output (roughly):

name='Two Drops' age=28 salary=12000.0 rating=60
1 validation error for Employee
age
  Input should be greater than or equal to 18 [type=greater_than_equal, input_value=10, input_type=int]

Field(...) supports quite a lot of rules. The ones you'll use most are:

  • Numbers: gt, ge, lt, le, multiple_of
  • Strings: min_length, max_length, pattern (regex)
  • Lists: min_length, max_length
  • Defaults: default=..., default_factory=...
  • Aliases: alias='another_name' (for when the key in outside JSON is different from your internal field name)

alias is used a lot. Here's an example:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Employee(BaseModel):
    name: str
    employee_id: int = Field(alias='empId')   # Outside JSON uses empId; inside we use employee_id


e = Employee.model_validate({'name': 'Two Drops', 'empId': 1001})
print(e)
print(e.employee_id)

Output:

name='Two Drops' employee_id=1001
1001

The outside JSON uses camelCase empId, and the inside Python uses snake_case employee_id. Each side stays natural, and alias connects them.

docs.title: Complex types like email and URL – pydantic.types
docs.text:
Rules on numbers and strings aren't always enough. Pydantic also has some built-in meaningful types:

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, HttpUrl, ValidationError


class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    homepage: HttpUrl


u = User(name='Two Drops', email='liangdianshui@example.com', homepage='https://example.com')
print(u)

try:
    bad = User(name='X', email='not-an-email', homepage='not-a-url')
except ValidationError as err:
    print(err)

Output (roughly):

name='Two Drops' email='liangdianshui@example.com' homepage=Url('https://example.com/')
2 validation errors for User
email
  value is not a valid email address: ...
homepage
  Input should be a valid URL, ...

EmailStr needs an extra install of email-validator: pip install pydantic[email]. HttpUrl is built in and works straight away.

Dataclass can't give you meaningful types like these directly – you'd have to use str and write your own regex checks. Pydantic packs these common cases into the library, which saves a lot of effort.

docs.title: A quick look at the Pydantic ecosystem
docs.text:
Pydantic isn't just a validation library. A whole ecosystem has grown around "data modelling":

  • pydantic-settings: made for config classes. It loads settings from environment variables, .env files and command-line arguments, and validates them automatically. FastAPI apps usually use it for things like DATABASE_URL and SECRET_KEY. Install: pip install pydantic-settings
  • mypy + the Pydantic plugin: lets mypy correctly work out the field types of Pydantic models – brilliant together with IDE hints
  • FastAPI: Pydantic is at its heart. Request bodies are declared with BaseModel, validated automatically, and used to generate OpenAPI docs automatically
  • LangChain, the Anthropic SDK, the OpenAI SDK: they're full of Pydantic models inside – it has become the de facto standard for data modelling in Python

You don't need to learn all of these at once. Just know they exist, and follow the trail when you meet a real need.

docs.title: dataclass vs Pydantic vs attrs – how to choose
docs.text:
This is the part you care about most: "With all these tools, which one should I use?" Here it is in three lines:

  • dataclass: comes with the standard library, no dependencies, lightweight. Use it for data structures inside your program that you write and use yourself. Fast, but no runtime validation
  • Pydantic: third-party, needs installing. Use it at the data boundary – outside JSON, HTTP request bodies, config files and so on. Type checking, rules and smart conversion
  • attrs: the spiritual ancestor of dataclass. A third-party library that came before dataclass and has more features (like validators and converters). Since dataclass arrived, there are fewer reasons to use attrs, but it's still a good choice when you "need complex validation but don't want Pydantic's runtime cost"

A more detailed guide:

Situation Recommendation A "structured result" returned from a function dataclass Lots of small objects in memory (coordinates, cache keys) dataclass + frozen + slots Receiving HTTP request bodies / parsing outside JSON Pydantic App configuration (reading environment variables) pydantic-settings Writing FastAPI endpoints Pydantic (FastAPI requires it) You want complex validators but not Pydantic attrs

Remember: dataclass handles the "inside", Pydantic handles the "outside". Draw this line clearly, and choosing tools won't get confusing.

docs.title: Mini project – Order + OrderRequest, a pretend ordering endpoint
docs.text:
Enough theory. Let's write code close to a real situation: a pretend "place an order" endpoint.

Here's the task:

  • The client sends JSON with a product ID, quantity, delivery address and user email
  • The server checks: quantity must be over 0, the email must be valid, and the address can't be empty
  • Once it passes, turn it into an internal Order object, automatically work out the total price, and create an order number

We'll let Pydantic receive and validate the outside JSON, and let dataclass represent the internal business object. Each does its own job.

docs.title: 1. First, define the internal Order (dataclass)
docs.text:
import uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    order_id: str
    product_id: int
    qty: int
    unit_price: float
    address: str
    user_email: str
    total: float = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self):
        # A frozen class can't do self.total = ... directly, so we use object.__setattr__ to get around it
        object.__setattr__(self, 'total', self.qty * self.unit_price)


o = Order(
    order_id=str(uuid.uuid4()),
    product_id=1001,
    qty=3,
    unit_price=12.5,
    address='1 Example Road, Xihu District, Hangzhou',
    user_email='liangdianshui@example.com',
)
print(o)

Output (order_id is different every time):

Order(order_id='xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx', product_id=1001, qty=3, unit_price=12.5, address='1 Example Road, Xihu District, Hangzhou', user_email='liangdianshui@example.com', total=37.5)

Look at the line in __post_init__: object.__setattr__(self, 'total', ...). This is the standard way to write a derived field in a frozen dataclass. Once it's frozen, self.xx = yy is refused – but the derived field must be written once after construction, so we have to get around the __setattr__ block.

docs.title: 2. Then define the outside OrderRequest (Pydantic)
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr


class OrderRequest(BaseModel):
    product_id: int = Field(gt=0)
    qty: int = Field(gt=0, le=100)
    unit_price: float = Field(gt=0)
    address: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)
    user_email: EmailStr


# Pretend JSON sent from the front end
payload = '''
{
    "product_id": 1001,
    "qty": 3,
    "unit_price": 12.5,
    "address": "1 Example Road, Xihu District, Hangzhou",
    "user_email": "liangdianshui@example.com"
}
'''

req = OrderRequest.model_validate_json(payload)
print(req)

Output:

product_id=1001 qty=3 unit_price=12.5 address='1 Example Road, Xihu District, Hangzhou' user_email='liangdianshui@example.com'

If the front end sends a bad payload (for example, a negative quantity), Pydantic tells you straight away what's wrong:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr, ValidationError


class OrderRequest(BaseModel):
    product_id: int = Field(gt=0)
    qty: int = Field(gt=0, le=100)
    unit_price: float = Field(gt=0)
    address: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)
    user_email: EmailStr


bad_payload = '''
{
    "product_id": 1001,
    "qty": -1,
    "unit_price": 12.5,
    "address": "",
    "user_email": "not-an-email"
}
'''

try:
    OrderRequest.model_validate_json(bad_payload)
except ValidationError as err:
    print(err)

Output (roughly):

3 validation errors for OrderRequest
qty
  Input should be greater than 0 ...
address
  String should have at least 1 character ...
user_email
  value is not a valid email address: ...

Three fields report errors at the same time, and each error's location and reason is listed clearly. This is what Pydantic looks like as it stops dirty data at the boundary.

docs.title: 3. Turn the outside request into an internal Order
docs.text:
import uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    order_id: str
    product_id: int
    qty: int
    unit_price: float
    address: str
    user_email: str
    total: float = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self):
        object.__setattr__(self, 'total', self.qty * self.unit_price)


class OrderRequest(BaseModel):
    product_id: int = Field(gt=0)
    qty: int = Field(gt=0, le=100)
    unit_price: float = Field(gt=0)
    address: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)
    user_email: EmailStr


def create_order(payload_json: str) -> Order:
    """Boundary layer: validate the JSON with Pydantic first; if it passes, turn it into an Order business object"""
    req = OrderRequest.model_validate_json(payload_json)
    return Order(
        order_id=str(uuid.uuid4()),
        product_id=req.product_id,
        qty=req.qty,
        unit_price=req.unit_price,
        address=req.address,
        user_email=req.user_email,
    )


payload = '''
{
    "product_id": 1001,
    "qty": 3,
    "unit_price": 12.5,
    "address": "1 Example Road, Xihu District, Hangzhou",
    "user_email": "liangdianshui@example.com"
}
'''

order = create_order(payload)
print(order)
print(f'Order total: {order.total}')

Look at this structure:

  • OrderRequest (Pydantic) guards the boundary. All dirty data coming in from outside must get past it first
  • Order (dataclass, frozen) lives inside. Once built, it can't change, so business code can safely pass it around, put it in a set, or use it as a dict key

This is exactly how "dataclass handles the inside, Pydantic handles the outside" looks in practice. In real projects – FastAPI endpoints, message queue consumers or command-line tools – you can use this pattern: validate at the boundary with Pydantic, represent things inside with dataclass.

docs.title: A quick reminder – common dataclass and Pydantic traps
docs.text: We've covered theory and practice. Finally, here are a few traps that are really easy to fall into:

docs.title: Trap 1: dataclass fields must have type hints
docs.text:
Remember? name: str is recognised as a field; name = '' is not.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Bad:
    a = 1     # No hint, so not a field
    b: int = 2


print(Bad())
# You'll see a isn't in the repr, because dataclass doesn't recognise it at all

Output:

Bad(b=2)

docs.title: Trap 2: mutable defaults must use default_factory
docs.text: You can't write tags: list = []. You must write tags: list = field(default_factory=list). Python flat-out rejects the first one.

docs.title: Trap 3: once frozen, you can't write derived fields normally – use object.__setattr__
docs.text: As in the Order example above.

docs.title: Trap 4: Pydantic v1 and v2 use different API names
docs.text:
Lots of old tutorials use v1. Common equivalents:

v1 v2 obj.dict() obj.model_dump() obj.json() obj.model_dump_json() Model.parse_obj(d) Model.model_validate(d) Model.parse_raw(s) Model.model_validate_json(s) validator decorator field_validator decorator

If you see short API names like .dict() and .json(), it's probably old v1 code. Today you should use v2's model_* family.

docs.title: Trap 5: dataclass type hints are just "documentation"
docs.text: Never use dataclass as if it were Pydantic. As we said, dataclass doesn't validate at runtime. Its type hints are only for mypy/IDEs. If you need validation, either write it yourself in __post_init__, or switch to Pydantic.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Let's look back at what we covered in this article:

  • dataclass is Python's standard answer for writing "data classes" – one line of @dataclass automatically creates __init__ / __repr__ / __eq__. Goodbye, boilerplate
  • field() is the Swiss Army knife for fields – default_factory solves mutable defaults, init=False plus __post_init__ creates derived fields, and repr=False / compare=False control printing and comparison
  • frozen=True makes a dataclass immutable – as a bonus, it creates __hash__ automatically, so it can go in a set or be a dict key. Essential for "value types"
  • __post_init__ is the construction hook – used for derived calculations and validation (though validation there is only a stop-gap)
  • Python 3.10+ added kw_only=True and slots=True – the first forces keyword arguments, which is especially friendly for inheritance; the second uses __slots__ instead of __dict__, saving memory and improving speed
  • NamedTuple is "a tuple with names", TypedDict is "a dictionary with types" – two lightweight options besides dataclass, each with its own sweet spot
  • dataclass doesn't validate at runtime – that's its biggest limit. Dirty outside data gets accepted as-is
  • Pydantic fills that gap – inherit from BaseModel, and you get type checks, rule checks, smart conversion and JSON conversion
  • Pydantic uses Field(...) for rules – arguments like gt, ge, lt, le, min_length, max_length and pattern describe field rules clearly
  • Meaningful types like EmailStr and HttpUrl handle common checks in one line
  • "dataclass handles the inside, Pydantic handles the outside" – the most important sentence for choosing your architecture in future
  • The mini project showed a real pattern – validate at the boundary with OrderRequest, represent the business object inside with Order. Each one shines in its own place

This article is quite dense. You don't need to digest it all at once. Start using the dataclass part now. For the Pydantic part, come back to it when you really meet a situation where "outside data comes in and needs checking".

In the next article, we'll talk about another topic that's very common and easy to get wrong – context managers (the with statement). Starting from the most common form, with open(...) as f, we'll go through the __enter__ / __exit__ protocol, contextlib and async context managers. See you next time.

docs.title: Are the default lists in two records the same list?
docs.text:
Let's use a dataclass to save a study record, and add a list of review notes. Each record should have its own list:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class StudyRecord:
    subject: str
    minutes: int
    notes: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


first = StudyRecord('Python', 15)
second = StudyRecord('Reading', 10)
first.notes.append('Reviewed')
print(first.notes)
print(second.notes)

Output:

['Reviewed']
[]

default_factory=list means "when a default is needed, call list to make a new list". Add a note to the second record yourself, and check that it doesn't change the first one. You can compare this with the shared default argument problem from the functions chapter – but the rules for building defaults are different in the two places, so you can't just copy the syntax from one to the other.

Another thing to be clear about: having field hints and an automatically created __init__ does not mean every input automatically goes through business validation. A normal dataclass won't reject a string just because you wrote minutes: int. When you need validation, write it explicitly. If you use Pydantic, understand its actual behaviour according to its version, model settings and conversion rules.

This example only needs the standard library, so you can run it now. Do the third-party library examples after you've set up the right environment on your computer. First be clear about which boilerplate you want to get rid of and which inputs still need checking, then choose your data model.

docs.title: Context Managers: what does with really do?
docs.text:
First, look at this code and guess where the trap is:

f = open('/tmp/two_drops_of_water.txt', 'w')
f.write("Two Drops' diary: I clocked in three minutes late today.")
f.close()

"What's wrong with that? Open the file, write to it, close it – done in one go." That's what you might say if you like to think things through.

But what if the f.write line raises an exception?

Then close never runs, and the file handle is just left hanging there. Once or twice is fine. But if it's a web service running all day, and a few dozen out of thousands of requests fail to write a file, the operating system's file handles slowly get used up. Eventually you get a "Too many open files" error that seems to have nothing to do with anything. Bugs like this are really painful to track down.

So what do you do? The old way is of course try/finally:

f = open('/tmp/two_drops_of_water.txt', 'w')
try:
    f.write("Two Drops' diary: I clocked in three minutes late today.")
finally:
    f.close()

This is safe, but ugly. A simple file write gets wrapped in try/finally, adding an extra level of indentation. If you then need to open a second file, and a third, the indentation keeps stacking up, and you soon end up with "pyramid code".

You've surely seen Python's other way of writing this:

with open('/tmp/two_drops_of_water.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write("Two Drops' diary: I clocked in three minutes late today.")

Just two lines – no try, no finally, no manual close. And yet, whether or not write raises an exception, the file is always closed properly.

So what exactly is this with? How can it do something so magical? In this chapter, we'll explain it inside and out.

docs.title: The essence of with: the context manager protocol
docs.text:
What comes after with isn't a "file", a "connection" or a "lock" – it's a kind of thing. Python calls it a context manager.

What kind of object counts as a context manager? Any object with these two methods:

  • __enter__(self): called when you enter the with block. Its return value is assigned to the variable after as
  • __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb): called when you leave the with block – whether you leave normally or because of an exception

This is the context manager protocol. Those are all its rules – just these two, no third one.

Let's use our old friend, clocking in, to write the simplest context manager by hand, so you get a feel for it:

class Punch:
    def __enter__(self):
        print('Two Drops enters the clock-in area')
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        print('Two Drops leaves the clock-in area')


with Punch() as p:
    print('Two Drops is goofing off at the desk')

Output:

Two Drops enters the clock-in area
Two Drops is goofing off at the desk
Two Drops leaves the clock-in area

What do you see? The line with Punch() as p does three things:

  1. Creates a Punch() instance
  2. Calls that instance's __enter__() method
  3. Assigns the return value of __enter__() to p

Only then does it run the code inside the with block. When the with block ends (normally or because of an exception), it calls __exit__().

Does this look familiar? Yes – it's really hiding this chunk of boilerplate:

p_obj = Punch()
p = p_obj.__enter__()
try:
    print('Two Drops is goofing off at the desk')
finally:
    p_obj.__exit__(None, None, None)

behind the with syntactic sugar. That's how one line of with does the job of six.

docs.title: Let's look back at open
docs.text:
Now that we understand the protocol, let's look at open() again:

with open('/tmp/two_drops_of_water.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('One line of text.')

The file object returned by open() implements __enter__ and __exit__ itself. Its __enter__ just does return self, so f gets the file object itself. Its __exit__ calls close(). Simple – but it covers every exception path.

You can check it yourself:

f = open('/tmp/two_drops_of_water.txt', 'w')
print(hasattr(f, '__enter__'))
print(hasattr(f, '__exit__'))
f.close()

Output:

True
True

It's not just files. In the standard library, socket, threading.Lock, sqlite3.Connection, and in third-party libraries, requests.Session and so on – almost every resource that needs paired operations implements the context manager protocol. Open/close, acquire/release, connect/disconnect – whenever you "borrow something and must give it back", let with look after it.

Let's look at one more example to see how a context manager hides the details of "paired operations". threading.Lock should be familiar – you can hardly do multithreaded programming without it:

import threading


lock = threading.Lock()

# Without with, you have to acquire and release by hand
lock.acquire()
try:
    print('Two Drops is hard at work inside the critical section')
finally:
    lock.release()

# With with, Python arranges acquire and release for us
with lock:
    print('Two Drops enters the critical section again')

Output:

Two Drops is hard at work inside the critical section
Two Drops enters the critical section again

Note that with lock: has no as .... That's because the lock's __enter__ returns the lock itself, which isn't useful in most cases – what we care about is the state "it's locked", not the return value. So as can be left out. This is the usual way to write most locks, semaphores, events and similar context managers.

docs.title: A slightly more useful example: a clock-in context
docs.text:
Printing a few lines is a bit thin. Let's make Punch do something real – record when an employee enters and leaves, and write it to a "log":

import time


class PunchLog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.records = []

    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.time()
        self.records.append(f'{self.name} arrives at the desk')
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        cost = time.time() - self.start
        self.records.append(f'{self.name} leaves the desk after {cost:.4f} seconds')


log = PunchLog('Two Drops')
with log:
    time.sleep(0.05)
    print('Goofing off...')

for line in log.records:
    print(line)

The output is roughly:

Goofing off...
Two Drops arrives at the desk
Two Drops leaves the desk after 0.0507 seconds

This time it wouldn't even matter if __enter__ didn't return self, because we wrote with log: – no as to receive a return value, and the variable log is the context manager itself. But if you change it to with log as l:, l would be None if __enter__ returned nothing, because __enter__ returns None by default. This is the trap beginners fall into most: "Why is my as x None?" Nine times out of ten, __enter__ forgot to return.

docs.title: Managing several contexts at once
docs.text:
In real projects, you often need to open two or even three files at once – read one, write one, and write an error log. Early Python could only do this:

with open('/tmp/in.txt', 'w') as fin:
    pass

with open('/tmp/in.txt') as fin:
    with open('/tmp/out.txt', 'w') as fout:
        fout.write(fin.read())

Two levels of indentation. Add an err.log, and it's three.

Later, Python allowed several contexts in one with, separated by commas:

with open('/tmp/in.txt') as fin, open('/tmp/out.txt', 'w') as fout:
    fout.write(fin.read())

Much neater than nesting. But a new problem appears – with many contexts, the line gets really long, and you can't break it.

Python 3.10 added new syntax, PEP 617 "parenthesised context managers", which lets you wrap several contexts in brackets:

with (
    open('/tmp/in.txt') as fin,
    open('/tmp/out.txt', 'w') as fout,
):
    fout.write(fin.read())

Note three things:

  1. Each line inside the brackets can end with a comma, including the last one – PEP 617 allows a trailing comma
  2. This syntax only exists in Python 3.10+
  3. For code style, this is the recommended way to manage three or more contexts at once

If you're still on 3.9 or older, either use the one-line comma version, or ExitStack, which we'll cover later.

One more detail: several context managers __enter__ in order from left to right, and __exit__ in order from right to left. This is a really important guarantee – for example, code that "takes a lock, then opens a file" will always "close the file, then release the lock" when it exits. Let's test it with a small demo:

from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def stage(name):
    print(f'{name} __enter__')
    try:
        yield name
    finally:
        print(f'{name} __exit__')


with stage('A') as a, stage('B') as b, stage('C') as c:
    print(f'Inside the with block: {a} {b} {c}')

Output:

A __enter__
B __enter__
C __enter__
Inside the with block: A B C
C __exit__
B __exit__
A __exit__

See? C was the last to enter and the first to exit. It works exactly like the function call stack and nested try/finally.

docs.title: The three parameters of __exit__: handling exceptions
docs.text:
We said __exit__'s signature is __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb), but haven't explained what these three parameters are for.

Normally, if nothing in the with block raises an exception, all three are None. If there's an exception, they are:

  • exc_type: the type of the exception (e.g. ZeroDivisionError)
  • exc_val: the exception instance
  • tb: the traceback object

Even more important is the return value of __exit__:

  • Return True (or anything "truthy"): the exception is swallowed and doesn't go any further
  • Return False, None, or no return at all: the exception keeps going outwards

Let's write a context manager that swallows ZeroDivisionError:

class IgnoreZeroDivision:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        if exc_type is ZeroDivisionError:
            print(f'Swallowed a division-by-zero exception: {exc_val}')
            return True
        return False


with IgnoreZeroDivision():
    x = 1 / 0
    print('This will not print, because the line above raised an exception')

print('But this will print, because __exit__ swallowed the exception')

Output:

Swallowed a division-by-zero exception: division by zero
But this will print, because __exit__ swallowed the exception

If the with block raises anything other than ZeroDivisionError – say, ValueError – __exit__ returns False, and the exception bubbles out as normal.

I must stress this: swallowing exceptions is a very powerful ability, so please use it carefully. Generally, a context manager's job is to "clean up the resource no matter what", not to "pretend the exception never happened". Blindly writing return True can hide real bugs. Very few context managers in the standard library swallow exceptions – the most common one is contextlib.suppress, which we'll see later.

Another common question: "Can I swap the exception for a different one in __exit__?" Yes, but with care. Raising a new exception directly in __exit__ replaces the exception currently being passed along, and the original becomes the new one's __context__. Here's an example to make it clear:

class TranslateException:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        if exc_type is not None:
            raise RuntimeError(f'I translated {exc_type.__name__} into RuntimeError') from exc_val


try:
    with TranslateException():
        1 / 0
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f'What we got outside: {e}')
    print(f'The cause: {e.__cause__}')

Output:

What we got outside: I translated ZeroDivisionError into RuntimeError
The cause: division by zero

This "translate the exception" pattern is really useful when writing libraries. For example, a database driver can translate all sorts of low-level network errors into one DatabaseError, so the outer code doesn't need to care whether a socket disconnected, the SSL handshake failed, or the protocol couldn't be read. We covered raise X from Y in the exceptions chapter – this is just a quick review.

docs.title: contextlib: the standard library's good friend
docs.text:
Writing a whole class with two dunder methods just to manage a few lines of code – isn't that a bit heavy?

The standard library has a module called contextlib with lots of tools to make this easier. The most important is the @contextmanager decorator.

Remember generators? @contextmanager turns a generator function into a context manager. The rules are very simple:

  • Code before yield = __enter__
  • The value that's yielded = the return value of __enter__
  • Code after yield = __exit__

Let's rewrite PunchLog from above with @contextmanager and compare:

import time
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def punch_log(name):
    records = []
    start = time.time()
    records.append(f'{name} arrives at the desk')
    try:
        yield records
    finally:
        cost = time.time() - start
        records.append(f'{name} leaves the desk after {cost:.4f} seconds')


with punch_log('Two Drops') as records:
    time.sleep(0.05)
    print('Still goofing off...')

for line in records:
    print(line)

Output:

Still goofing off...
Two Drops arrives at the desk
Two Drops leaves the desk after 0.0506 seconds

Much cleaner, right? The class turned into a function, and the two dunder methods turned into one yield.

Notice the try/finally inside. Why do we need it?

Because the with block might raise an exception, and that exception "drills" back into the generator function at the yield line. Without try/finally, the exception would skip right past the clean-up code, and the resource would leak. Only try/finally guarantees "whether or not yield raises an exception, the clean-up code in finally always runs".

This is the most important rule when writing context managers with @contextmanager: put the clean-up code inside finally. The most common beginner bug is leaving out try/finally, so resources aren't released when there's an exception.

docs.title: @contextmanager + handling exceptions
docs.text:
What if I want to swallow an exception? How do I write that with @contextmanager?

Easy – wrap yield in try/except:

from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def ignore_zero_division():
    try:
        yield
    except ZeroDivisionError as e:
        print(f'Swallowed with @contextmanager: {e}')


with ignore_zero_division():
    x = 1 / 0
    print('This line will not run')

print('But this line will')

Output:

Swallowed with @contextmanager: division by zero
But this line will

After except catches the exception, the function returns normally – that's the same as __exit__ returning True. If the exception isn't caught and the generator raises it again unchanged, that's the same as __exit__ letting the exception carry on outwards. @contextmanager connects both paths for you, so you just write normal Python exception handling.

docs.title: Some regulars in contextlib
docs.text: contextlib doesn't just have @contextmanager. It also has a few ready-to-use tools that you'll find you can't do without once you've used them:

docs.title: closing: wrap an object that doesn't support with
docs.text:
Not every object that needs closing implements the context manager protocol. Typical examples are objects returned by urllib.request.urlopen in some old versions, and some custom resource objects. closing adds this layer for us:

from contextlib import closing


class Connection:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def close(self):
        print(f'{self.name} closed')


with closing(Connection('Database connection')) as conn:
    print(f'Using {conn.name}')

Output:

Using Database connection
Database connection closed

closing(obj) acts as a context manager: its __enter__ returns obj, and its __exit__ calls obj.close(). Simple and direct.

docs.title: suppress: ignore exceptions neatly
docs.text:
from contextlib import suppress


with suppress(FileNotFoundError):
    open('/tmp/this_file_definitely_does_not_exist_12345.txt').read()

print('Even if the file does not exist, I can carry on')

Output:

Even if the file does not exist, I can carry on

suppress is the general standard-library version of IgnoreZeroDivision above. It takes any number of exception types – if one matches, it's swallowed; if not, it's raised as normal.

suppress is shorter than try: ... except SomeError: pass, and it shows the intention "I really mean to ignore this exception" more clearly. But again, use it carefully – don't use it to hide real bugs.

docs.title: redirect_stdout / redirect_stderr: temporarily redirect standard output
docs.text:
Sometimes we want to capture the print output of some code into a string, or write it to a file, without changing its source code:

import io
from contextlib import redirect_stdout


buf = io.StringIO()
with redirect_stdout(buf):
    print('This will not appear in the terminal')
    print('Instead it gets captured in buf')

captured = buf.getvalue()
print('I captured:')
print(captured)

Output:

I captured:
This will not appear in the terminal
Instead it gets captured in buf

These two tools are really handy for test code, or for redirecting a third-party library's output to your own logger.

docs.title: nullcontext: a placeholder context that does nothing
docs.text:
Think about this: sometimes your function needs to run inside a lock, and sometimes it doesn't. How can you write that neatly?

from contextlib import nullcontext
import threading


def do_stuff(lock=None):
    cm = lock if lock is not None else nullcontext()
    with cm:
        print('Doing stuff')


lock = threading.Lock()
do_stuff(lock)
do_stuff()

Output:

Doing stuff
Doing stuff

nullcontext()'s __enter__ and __exit__ do nothing at all – it exists purely so the with line can be written the same way every time. No more long, messy branches like if lock: with lock: ... else: ....

nullcontext can also carry a value and pretend it's what __enter__ returned. This is really handy when "sometimes you already have an open object, and sometimes you need to open a new one":

from contextlib import nullcontext


def read_text(source):
    cm = nullcontext(source) if hasattr(source, 'read') else open(source)
    with cm as f:
        return f.read()


import io
text1 = read_text(io.StringIO('I am an object that is already open'))
print(text1)

with open('/tmp/two_drops_e.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('I am content written on disk')

text2 = read_text('/tmp/two_drops_e.txt')
print(text2)

Output:

I am an object that is already open
I am content written on disk

One function that can take either a string path or a file object that's already open – written in one smooth go. This little "accept two kinds of input" trick is used all the time in real projects.

docs.title: In practice: temporarily changing environment variables
docs.text:
Here's a very common need: test how some code behaves when a certain environment variable is set, without messing up the current process's environment.

How would you write it?

import os
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def set_env(**kwargs):
    old = {}
    for k, v in kwargs.items():
        old[k] = os.environ.get(k)
        os.environ[k] = v
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        for k, v in old.items():
            if v is None:
                os.environ.pop(k, None)
            else:
                os.environ[k] = v


os.environ.pop('TWO_DROPS_OF_WATER', None)
print('Before:', os.environ.get('TWO_DROPS_OF_WATER'))

with set_env(TWO_DROPS_OF_WATER='hello'):
    print('Inside with:', os.environ.get('TWO_DROPS_OF_WATER'))

print('After:', os.environ.get('TWO_DROPS_OF_WATER'))

Output:

Before: None
Inside with: hello
After: None

Look carefully: before entering with, note down the original values of the environment variables we'll change. Inside the with block, change them to the new values. When leaving – normally or not – put the original values back. This is the most classic use of a context manager: "change it temporarily, and restore it when you leave".

You can use the same pattern for "temporarily switch the working directory", "temporarily change sys.path", "temporarily raise the log level" and so on. Once you've got the hang of it, it feels very natural to write.

docs.title: Temporarily switching the working directory
docs.text:
Here's one more demo while we're at it:

import os
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def chdir(path):
    old = os.getcwd()
    os.chdir(path)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        os.chdir(old)


before = os.getcwd()
with chdir('/tmp'):
    print('Inside with:', os.getcwd())

print('Back where we started after leaving:', os.getcwd() == before)

Output (your paths may differ):

Inside with: /tmp
Back where we started after leaving: True

One more note: Python 3.11 added contextlib.chdir to the standard library. It does the same thing as the one we wrote, so you can just from contextlib import chdir. If you're on 3.11+, no need to reinvent the wheel.

docs.title: ExitStack: a variable number of contexts
docs.text:
So far, we've assumed "I have N contexts, and I know N when I write the code". But sometimes N is only known at runtime – for example, "open a list of files the user gave me, and close them all when I'm done".

You can't write it in one with line, because you don't know how many names there will be. You can't use nested withs either, because you don't know how many levels to nest. That's when ExitStack comes in.

from contextlib import ExitStack


def make_files(paths):
    with ExitStack() as stack:
        files = [stack.enter_context(open(p)) for p in paths]
        total = sum(len(f.read()) for f in files)
        print(f'Read {len(files)} files, {total} bytes in total')


with open('/tmp/two_drops_a.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('a' * 100)
with open('/tmp/two_drops_b.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('bb' * 50)
with open('/tmp/two_drops_c.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('ccc' * 30)

make_files(['/tmp/two_drops_a.txt', '/tmp/two_drops_b.txt', '/tmp/two_drops_c.txt'])

Output:

Read 3 files, 290 bytes in total

stack.enter_context(cm) "pushes" a context manager onto the stack – the same as putting it in the outermost with. When with ExitStack() exits, every context on the stack is exited one by one in "last in, first out" order – exactly the same as normal nested withs.

ExitStack also has a really handy method called callback, which registers an ordinary clean-up function – it doesn't need to be a context manager:

from contextlib import ExitStack


def cleanup(name):
    print(f'Cleaning up {name}')


with ExitStack() as stack:
    stack.callback(cleanup, 'A')
    stack.callback(cleanup, 'B')
    stack.callback(cleanup, 'C')
    print('Inside the with block')

Output:

Inside the with block
Cleaning up C
Cleaning up B
Cleaning up A

The clean-up order is C → B → A – backwards. That matches the natural feeling of "opened first, closed last".

ExitStack has some more advanced uses too, like pop_all, which moves the stack into another ExitStack to make "transaction-style clean-up". But that's an advanced topic – look it up in the docs when you actually need it.

Here's a really practical pattern: open a variable number of files, and if one of them fails partway, close all the ones already opened. ExitStack does this for us automatically:

from contextlib import ExitStack


def open_safely(paths):
    with ExitStack() as stack:
        files = []
        for p in paths:
            files.append(stack.enter_context(open(p)))
        return [f.name for f in files]


# Prepare three files that really exist
for name in ['/tmp/two_drops_x.txt', '/tmp/two_drops_y.txt', '/tmp/two_drops_z.txt']:
    with open(name, 'w') as f:
        f.write('hi')

names = open_safely(['/tmp/two_drops_x.txt', '/tmp/two_drops_y.txt', '/tmp/two_drops_z.txt'])
print(f'Safely handled {len(names)} files')

try:
    open_safely(['/tmp/two_drops_x.txt', '/tmp/this_does_not_exist_99999.txt'])
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    print(f'The second file failed, but the first one was closed automatically: {e.filename}')

Output:

Safely handled 3 files
The second file failed, but the first one was closed automatically: /tmp/this_does_not_exist_99999.txt

This is where ExitStack is worth the most in real projects: "open in bulk, and roll everything back together if anything fails". Writing that by hand with try/finally would be very wordy, and it would be easy to miss an exception path.

docs.title: async with: with in the async world
docs.text:
Finally, a quick word about the async version. Python 3.5 added the async/await syntax, and from 3.7 it gradually became mainstream. Inside an async def function, if you want to use a context manager, you write async with:

# This is just an illustration; it needs to run inside an async function
# async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
#     resp = await client.get('https://example.com')

The matching protocol methods are __aenter__ and __aexit__, and contextlib also has an @asynccontextmanager decorator. We'll go deeper in the async/await chapter. For now, just know it exists, so you're not confused when you see async with in async code.

docs.title: Mini project: writing a timer context
docs.text:
Let's tie together what we've learned in this chapter with a little tool: record the time when entering with, and print "this code took X milliseconds" when leaving.

First, the class version:

import time


class Timer:
    def __init__(self, name='Unnamed block'):
        self.name = name

    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        cost_ms = (time.perf_counter() - self.start) * 1000
        print(f'{self.name} took {cost_ms:.2f} ms')


with Timer("Two Drops' nap time"):
    time.sleep(0.05)
    s = sum(range(10000))

The output is roughly:

Two Drops' nap time took 50.46 ms

Now rewrite it with @contextmanager and compare:

import time
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def timer(name='Unnamed block'):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        cost_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        print(f'{name} took {cost_ms:.2f} ms')


with timer('Clocking in'):
    time.sleep(0.03)
    sum(range(5000))

The output is roughly:

Clocking in took 30.21 ms

Which version would you pick? I personally prefer the @contextmanager version – it's more compact. But when a context manager needs to keep complicated state, be reused, or be inherited from, the class version fits better. Both have the same abilities – choose based on the situation.

One more bonus: what if you want Timer to work both as a context manager and as a decorator? These two needs often come together. contextlib already thought of this – the base class ContextDecorator does it in one line:

import time
from contextlib import ContextDecorator


class Timer(ContextDecorator):
    def __init__(self, name='Unnamed block'):
        self.name = name

    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        cost_ms = (time.perf_counter() - self.start) * 1000
        print(f'{self.name} took {cost_ms:.2f} ms')


@Timer("Two Drops' function")
def work():
    time.sleep(0.02)


work()

The output is roughly:

Two Drops' function took 20.34 ms

And functions written with @contextmanager can be used as decorators too, with no extra work:

import time
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def timer(name='Unnamed block'):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        cost_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        print(f'{name} took {cost_ms:.2f} ms')


@timer('Clock-in function')
def punch():
    time.sleep(0.01)


punch()

The output is roughly:

Clock-in function took 10.32 ms

Notice that @contextmanager comes with ContextDecorator's abilities built in? So one function being both a decorator and a context manager feels perfectly natural. That's why lots of logging, performance-monitoring and tracing libraries like writing their core APIs with @contextmanager: one implementation, two ways to use it.

docs.title: Common anti-patterns
docs.text: Finally, a few words about the traps beginners fall into most:

docs.title: Anti-pattern 1: using a with variable outside the with
docs.text:
with open('/tmp/two_drops_d.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('hi')

print(f.closed)

Output:

True

The variable f still exists after with exits, but the file object it points to has been closed. This isn't an error, but it's very misleading – many beginners think f becomes None or gives a NameError after with, but it doesn't. You can still get the variable, but it's "dead". That's a design choice in Python's context managers.

Remember: after a with block exits, the variable after as still exists in the current scope, but its resource has been released. Touching it will probably cause an error.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 2: forgetting try/finally
docs.text:
If you leave out try/finally when writing @contextmanager, it looks fine on the normal path, but as soon as there's an exception, the resource leaks:

from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def bad():
    print('Opening the resource')
    yield
    print('Closing the resource')


try:
    with bad():
        raise ValueError('Raising an exception on purpose')
except ValueError:
    print('The outer code caught the exception')

Output:

Opening the resource
The outer code caught the exception

"Closing the resource" was never printed, because the exception skipped all the code after yield. That's why we stressed it earlier: clean-up logic must go in finally.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 3: yielding more than once in a @contextmanager function
docs.text:
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def double_yield():
    print('Getting ready')
    yield 1
    yield 2
    print('Done')


try:
    with double_yield() as v:
        print(f'Got {v}')
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f'Error: {e}')

Output:

Getting ready
Got 1
Error: generator didn't stop

A generator decorated with @contextmanager can only yield once. Before the yield is __enter__; after the yield is __exit__. If it yields twice, Python notices at the second yield that "this generator didn't end straight after the yield as expected", and raises a RuntimeError. This is an easy bug for beginners to write, because normal generator functions are allowed to yield many times – but inside @contextmanager, only once.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 4: abusing return True to swallow exceptions
docs.text:
class SwallowEverything:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, tb):
        return True


with SwallowEverything():
    1 / 0
    raise RuntimeError('what?')

print('Somehow I am still running')

Output:

Somehow I am still running

A "swallow everything" context manager like this is a huge anti-pattern. It eats real bugs too, letting the program keep running in a broken state, and making debugging impossible. return True should be a very narrow, very deliberate "I mean to ignore exactly this one exception" action – not a lazy way to "make the world a bit quieter".

docs.title: A combined example: a reusable "Brother Shui clock-in auditor"
docs.text:
To tie everything together, let's finish with a slightly more complicated example. The task: every time an employee arrives at their desk, record the start time; when they leave, record the end time; if the code raises an exception in between, record the exception type too. Finally, add a summary report.

import time
from contextlib import contextmanager


class Auditor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.events = []

    @contextmanager
    def shift(self, name):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        self.events.append({'name': name, 'phase': 'enter'})
        try:
            yield
        except Exception as e:
            self.events.append({
                'name': name,
                'phase': 'error',
                'exception': type(e).__name__,
            })
            raise
        finally:
            cost_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
            self.events.append({
                'name': name,
                'phase': 'leave',
                'cost_ms': round(cost_ms, 2),
            })

    def report(self):
        print(f'Recorded {len(self.events)} events in total:')
        for e in self.events:
            print(f'  - {e}')


auditor = Auditor()

with auditor.shift('Two Drops'):
    time.sleep(0.01)

try:
    with auditor.shift('Student A'):
        raise ValueError('The code blew up')
except ValueError:
    pass

with auditor.shift('Student B'):
    time.sleep(0.005)

auditor.report()

The output is roughly:

Recorded 7 events in total:
  - {'name': 'Two Drops', 'phase': 'enter'}
  - {'name': 'Two Drops', 'phase': 'leave', 'cost_ms': 10.42}
  - {'name': 'Student A', 'phase': 'enter'}
  - {'name': 'Student A', 'phase': 'error', 'exception': 'ValueError'}
  - {'name': 'Student A', 'phase': 'leave', 'cost_ms': 0.16}
  - {'name': 'Student B', 'phase': 'enter'}
  - {'name': 'Student B', 'phase': 'leave', 'cost_ms': 5.21}

This code gets several important things right. Check them one by one:

  1. @contextmanager decorates a method of a class – that's completely allowed, and the method's self is still available inside the generator
  2. It has the full try/except/finally trio: the exception path goes through except, and every path goes through finally
  3. except Exception as e: ...; raise: record it first, then re-raise it unchanged – no swallowing
  4. The report shows the full life cycle of an error event: enter → error → leave

This is how context managers are typically used in real projects – one object and a few lines of code wrap up "timing, recording exceptions and cleaning up resources" together. In performance monitoring, APM tools and tracing, almost every library's core API looks like this.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
with isn't an isolated bit of syntactic sugar – behind it is the context manager protocol:

  • __enter__ to go in, __exit__ to leave
  • __exit__ receives three exception-related parameters; returning True swallows the exception (use carefully)
  • Several contexts can be separated by commas; in 3.10+ you can wrap them in brackets over several lines
  • contextlib.contextmanager lets one yield replace two dunder methods – but you must use try/finally to make sure clean-up code runs
  • Little tools like closing, suppress, redirect_stdout and nullcontext save a lot of boilerplate
  • ExitStack handles "a variable number of contexts"
  • async with is the async version – same idea; we'll look closer in the async/await chapter

Anywhere you have "paired operations", "borrow and return a resource", "temporary switches" or "enter/leave", you can wrap it in a context manager. Once you build this habit, your code will not only be shorter, it'll also handle exception paths naturally – that's what makes with really valuable.

In the next chapter, we'll dive into the world of async/await, and see how Python uses one async keyword to unlock the whole async ecosystem. Get comfortable with with first, and async with will feel like the obvious next step.

docs.title: Keep the result, close the resource
docs.text:
with isn't just about saving one line of close(). Let's use some in-memory text to see what's still usable before and after leaving the block:

from io import StringIO

with StringIO('Python:15') as stream:
    content = stream.read()
print(content)
print(stream.closed)

Output:

Python:15
True

The text has already been read into content, and that string is still usable. But stream has been closed. Don't assume the resource is still readable or writable just because the variable name still exists.

Try moving stream.read() to after the with yourself, and look at the error from reading after it's closed. Then raise an exception on purpose inside the block, catch it outside, and check stream.closed. For this object, the resource is still closed on the way out.

Also remember: what with does depends on the specific context manager. It does not promise to automatically undo everything that already happened. For example, if you open a file, write some content, and then an exception happens, using with doesn't automatically restore the old file. Cleaning up resources, whether an exception is passed on, and data transactions are different problems.

docs.title: Async programming: async/await lets one thread wait for a hundred things at once
docs.text:
Have you ever written a web scraper? Here's a quick one:

import time


def fake_get(url):
    time.sleep(0.01)
    return f'GOT {url}'


def main():
    urls = [f'https://example.com/{i}' for i in range(5)]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = []
    for u in urls:
        results.append(fake_get(u))
    cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f'Got {len(results)} results in {cost:.3f} seconds')


main()

The output is roughly:

Got 5 results in 0.05 seconds

Each request pretends to take 0.01 seconds, so 5 in a row take 0.05 seconds. With real network requests of 200 milliseconds each, 100 in a row would take 20 seconds – painfully slow.

"Easy – use threads!" someone says straight away. "100 URLs, 100 threads, run them all together."

Threads can solve this, of course. But isn't 100 threads a bit extravagant? 99% of the time, those 100 threads are all doing the same thing: waiting for network packets to come back. This is really a waiting problem, not a computing problem. Starting 100 operating-system threads just to "wait" makes neither the CPU nor the memory happy.

And with lots of threads, old friends like "locks", "race conditions" and "deadlocks" start knocking on your door one by one. You just wanted to fetch some web pages – why are you suddenly studying operating systems?

Python gives us another way: asyncio. Its selling point is simple – one thread, waiting for a hundred things at once. Your first reaction to that is probably: "That can't be right – how can one thread do a hundred things at once?"

That's the question this chapter answers.

docs.title: A gut-feeling comparison: 3 seconds in a row vs 1 second together
docs.text:
Let's skip the theory and see the effect first. Below is "normal" code that runs one after another. Three tasks, each waiting 1 second:

import time


def task(name):
    time.sleep(1)
    return f'{name} done'


start = time.perf_counter()
r1 = task('Clock in')
r2 = task('Query')
r3 = task('Upload')
cost = time.perf_counter() - start
print(r1, r2, r3)
print(f'{cost:.2f} seconds in total')

Output:

Clock in done Query done Upload done
3.01 seconds in total

Each one politely waits its turn, one second at a time. Nothing special.

Now the async version:

import asyncio
import time


async def task(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return f'{name} done'


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    r1, r2, r3 = await asyncio.gather(
        task('Clock in'),
        task('Query'),
        task('Upload'),
    )
    cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(r1, r2, r3)
    print(f'{cost:.2f} seconds in total')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Clock in done Query done Upload done
1.00 seconds in total

3 seconds became 1 second – the three tasks really did finish "at the same time". Don't worry yet about what async, await and gather mean. Just remember one fact: while one coroutine is waiting in asyncio.sleep(1), another coroutine can use the CPU for its own work. The three coroutines' waits overlap, so the total time is the longest one, not all three added together.

That's the core magic of asyncio. It doesn't secretly start threads, and it doesn't make the CPU faster. What it does is simple: when a coroutine is waiting for I/O (input/output), it gives the CPU to other coroutines, and carries on when the wait is over.

By now you should have a bit of a feel for it. Let's take the syntax apart step by step.

docs.title: Your first async function: how is it different from a normal function?
docs.text:
A normal function looks like this:

def hello():
    return 'Hello, Two Drops'


print(hello())

Output:

Hello, Two Drops

Add the async keyword, and it becomes a coroutine function:

async def hello():
    return 'Hello, Two Drops'


print(hello())

Output:

<coroutine object hello at 0x...>
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'hello' was never awaited

Do you see the difference? It's the same print(hello()), but the normal function returns the string 'Hello, Two Drops', while the coroutine function returns a coroutine object – a <coroutine object>, not a string.

Even worse, Python adds a warning: "this coroutine was never awaited".

What does that mean? Here's the key idea:

  • async def does not define "a function that runs straight away"
  • When you call a function defined with async def, it doesn't run at all – it just gives you back a "to-do slip"

Think of it like this: calling a normal function hello() is like "sending someone to do a job and getting the result immediately". Calling a coroutine function hello() is like "writing a job slip and handing it to you – when and who does it is another matter".

This "job slip" is the coroutine object. It must be awaited, or handed to the event loop to run, before the code inside it actually runs.

docs.title: await: making a coroutine run
docs.text:
So how do you make the job slip actually happen? With await:

import asyncio


async def hello():
    return 'Hello, Two Drops'


async def main():
    result = await hello()
    print(result)


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Hello, Two Drops

Now we get the string. You can read await hello() as "please finish the hello() job slip for me, and give me the result".

But there's a very important limit: await can only be written inside an async def function. Try writing await in a normal function, and Python tells you SyntaxError: 'await' outside async function.

"So what if I want to call an async def function from a normal script?" That's where the next character comes in – asyncio.run().

docs.title: asyncio.run(): the door into the async world
docs.text:
asyncio.run() is the "door" between synchronous (normal) code and asynchronous code. It takes a coroutine object, starts an event loop, runs the coroutine to the end, and then closes the event loop:

import asyncio


async def main():
    print('I am in the async world')
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    print('I am in the async world again')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

I am in the async world
I am in the async world again

There's a very important design hidden here: a whole program usually has only one event loop, started by asyncio.run(). Every coroutine runs inside this loop. You can picture it like this:

  • The synchronous world → one straight road, one step after another
  • The async world → a control centre (the event loop) with lots of coroutines hanging on it; whoever can run gets to run

asyncio.run() is the entrance from the synchronous world into the async world. A program should only call it once (calling it inside itself gives an error).

So far, you've learned three basic ideas: async def defines a coroutine function, await waits for a coroutine's result, and asyncio.run() starts the event loop. With these three, you can already write the smallest working async program.

docs.title: What happens if you don't await a coroutine object?
docs.text:
How serious is that "coroutine was never awaited" warning? Here's some code where it's very easy to fall into the trap:

import asyncio


async def punch():
    print('Two Drops starts clocking in')
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    print('Two Drops finished clocking in')


async def main():
    punch()
    print('main is finished')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

main is finished
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'punch' was never awaited

Can you see what's wrong? The punch() line never printed "Two Drops starts clocking in". punch() only created a coroutine object, which was then thrown away – not a single line inside it ran.

This is one of asyncio's most classic traps: forgetting await. In the synchronous world, writing a function name with brackets means running it. In the async world, writing a function name with brackets only "gets you a job slip" – without await, you've thrown the slip in the bin.

The correct way, of course, is:

import asyncio


async def punch():
    print('Two Drops starts clocking in')
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    print('Two Drops finished clocking in')


async def main():
    await punch()
    print('main is finished')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Two Drops starts clocking in
Two Drops finished clocking in
main is finished

Remember this: a coroutine that isn't awaited might as well not exist.

docs.title: Waiting for several at once: asyncio.gather
docs.text:
Now you can write async code that runs one after another. But back to the first example – 3 tasks done in 1 second – how does "waiting for several at once" work? The answer is asyncio.gather.

First, the wrong way:

import asyncio
import time


async def task(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    return f'{name} done'


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    r1 = await task('A')
    r2 = await task('B')
    r3 = await task('C')
    cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(r1, r2, r3)
    print(f'Took {cost:.2f} seconds')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

A done B done C done
Took 1.50 seconds

"Isn't async supposed to be fast? Why is it still 1.5 seconds?"

Look carefully. await task('A') comes first, meaning "wait for A to finish, then carry on". One await after another is really just running them in a row. async/await does not make things run together automatically.

To run them together, you must clearly tell the event loop "these can all start at the same time". That's what asyncio.gather does:

import asyncio
import time


async def task(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    return f'{name} done'


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    r1, r2, r3 = await asyncio.gather(
        task('A'),
        task('B'),
        task('C'),
    )
    cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(r1, r2, r3)
    print(f'Took {cost:.2f} seconds')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

A done B done C done
Took 0.50 seconds

That's the concurrency you wanted. asyncio.gather takes any number of coroutines, gives them all to the event loop together, waits for all of them to finish, and then returns the results packed up in order.

Key points to underline:

  • gather returns a list of all the results, in the same order you passed them in
  • If any coroutine raises an exception, by default the whole gather raises it
  • You can pass in coroutines, or Task objects (covered below)

gather is one of the most-used functions in asyncio. Whenever you need "run several at once", it should be your first thought (or TaskGroup, which we'll see later).

docs.title: Task: "sending out" a coroutine
docs.text:
gather is great, but sometimes we want finer control: "send the job out first, let it run in the background, go do something else, and come back for the result when I need it".

This "send it out" action is called a Task, created with asyncio.create_task():

import asyncio
import time


async def slow_job(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f'{name} done'


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    t1 = asyncio.create_task(slow_job('A', 0.3))
    t2 = asyncio.create_task(slow_job('B', 0.5))
    print('Both tasks have been sent out; main can do other things')
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    print('Let me clock in first')
    r1 = await t1
    r2 = await t2
    cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(r1, r2)
    print(f'Took {cost:.2f} seconds')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Both tasks have been sent out; main can do other things
Let me clock in first
A done B done
Took 0.50 seconds

Look at the time – 0.5 seconds, not 0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8 seconds. Why? create_task registers the coroutine with the event loop and starts it running straight away, without waiting for await. The line await t1 only says "I want this result now – if it's not ready, I'll wait here". While it waits, t2 is also running at the same time.

So what's the difference between create_task and gather?

  • gather(coros...) sends them all out at once and collects them all at once – compact
  • create_task(coro) sends them out one by one; you can await each one separately, and cancel them – flexible

A common combination in real code: use lots of create_task calls to send tasks out, and at the end use await asyncio.gather(*tasks) to collect them all at once. That way you get Task objects for fine control, and the convenience of gather.

docs.title: A small trap: passing coroutines vs Tasks to gather
docs.text:
gather's arguments can be coroutine objects or Task objects. They look about the same, but there's a detail:

import asyncio


async def job(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return name


async def main():
    coro = job('A')
    await asyncio.gather(coro, job('B'))


asyncio.run(main())

Here job('A') and job('B') are both coroutine objects. gather automatically wraps them into Tasks and puts them in the event loop. So both ways work the same.

Just be careful: a coroutine object can only be awaited once. You can't pass the same coro to gather twice:

import asyncio


async def job():
    return 1


async def main():
    coro = job()
    await asyncio.gather(coro, coro)


asyncio.run(main())

This gives an error saying the coroutine was awaited more than once. To run the same coroutine function N times at once, write N calls, like [job() for _ in range(N)].

docs.title: asyncio.sleep vs time.sleep: the blocking trap
docs.text:
There's one trap in async programming that's the most common of all: time.sleep freezes the entire event loop.

Here's the bad example:

import asyncio
import time


async def task(name):
    time.sleep(0.5)
    return f'{name} done'


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(task('A'), task('B'), task('C'))
    cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f'Took {cost:.2f} seconds')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Took 1.50 seconds

"Isn't this gather? Why is it 1.5 seconds again?"

The reason is time.sleep. It's a synchronous blocking function – when called, it does not give the CPU back to the event loop. Writing time.sleep(0.5) is like telling the operating system "put this whole thread to sleep for 0.5 seconds". The whole event loop – meaning every coroutine – is frozen.

asyncio.sleep(0.5) is completely different. It's a coroutine, and when used with await, it tells the event loop: "I'm going to sleep for 0.5 seconds – feel free to schedule others in the meantime."

Remember this golden rule: inside an async function, every synchronous call that blocks must be swapped for an async version.

Synchronous (blocking – don't use) Async (the replacement) time.sleep(s) await asyncio.sleep(s) requests.get(url) await httpx.AsyncClient().get(url) Standard open(f).read() the aiofiles library, or hand it to a thread pool

What if you really have to call a synchronous blocking library? asyncio has an escape hatch – asyncio.to_thread – which hands the call to a thread pool:

import asyncio
import time


def blocking_call():
    time.sleep(0.5)
    return 'Sync task done'


async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    r1, r2 = await asyncio.gather(
        asyncio.to_thread(blocking_call),
        asyncio.to_thread(blocking_call),
    )
    cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(r1, r2)
    print(f'Took {cost:.2f} seconds')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Sync task done Sync task done
Took 0.50 seconds

asyncio.to_thread is a compromise: the event loop doesn't freeze, but you still pay the cost of threads. If there's a native async library you can use (like httpx, below), prefer that.

docs.title: Timeouts: wait_for and timeout
docs.text:
If you write network requests, you'll have this worry: "What if the server on the other end never replies? Will my coroutine wait forever?"

That's when you need a timeout. asyncio gives you two ways.

First: asyncio.wait_for – the old way, which "wraps" the coroutine:

import asyncio


async def slow_job():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    return 'Finally done'


async def main():
    try:
        r = await asyncio.wait_for(slow_job(), timeout=0.5)
        print(r)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        print('Timed out – not waiting any more')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Timed out – not waiting any more

wait_for(coro, timeout=0.5) means "give this coroutine 0.5 seconds; if it takes longer, cancel it and raise TimeoutError".

Second: asyncio.timeout (Python 3.11+) – the new way, using async with as a context:

import asyncio


async def slow_job():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    return 'Finally done'


async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.5):
            r = await slow_job()
            print(r)
    except TimeoutError:
        print('Timed out – not waiting any more')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Timed out – not waiting any more

Same effect, but nicer to write – if you want a timeout on "this section", just wrap it in async with. The second way is especially handy for putting one timeout on several awaits. For new code, asyncio.timeout is recommended.

Note a small change: since 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is the built-in TimeoutError, so except TimeoutError catches it too – no need to write asyncio.TimeoutError.

docs.title: Cancelling: Task.cancel()
docs.text:
A timeout is really "automatic cancelling". Cancelling by hand is easy too:

import asyncio


async def long_running():
    try:
        for i in range(10):
            print(f'Still running {i}')
            await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print('I was cancelled – cleaning up')
        raise


async def main():
    t = asyncio.create_task(long_running())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.12)
    t.cancel()
    try:
        await t
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print('The task really was cancelled')


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Still running 0
Still running 1
Still running 2
I was cancelled – cleaning up
The task really was cancelled

Task.cancel() raises a CancelledError inside the coroutine. The coroutine can catch it to clean up, but I strongly recommend raise-ing it again after cleaning up, so the outside knows the task really was cancelled. Quietly swallowing CancelledError is another very sneaky trap.

docs.title: TaskGroup: the upgraded gather from 3.11
docs.text:
gather works well, so why did Python 3.11 add TaskGroup?

Let's look at an awkward situation with gather. Three tasks; one raises an error. What should happen to the other two?

import asyncio


async def good(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f'{name} ok'


async def bad():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    raise ValueError('Broken')


async def main():
    try:
        await asyncio.gather(good('A', 0.5), bad(), good('B', 0.5))
    except ValueError as e:
        print('main caught', e)


asyncio.run(main())

The output is roughly:

main caught Broken

Looks fine. But think – what about A and B, the two 0.5-second tasks? They're actually still quietly running in the background. gather's default behaviour is "if one fails, raise the exception outwards, and let the other tasks keep running in the event loop". If A is writing a file and B is sending a request, they'll run to the end (and maybe raise errors too) before stopping. This "walk off and leave others working behind your back" behaviour isn't safe.

TaskGroup solves this:

import asyncio


async def good(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f'{name} ok'


async def bad():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    raise ValueError('Broken')


async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            t_a = tg.create_task(good('A', 0.5))
            t_bad = tg.create_task(bad())
            t_b = tg.create_task(good('B', 0.5))
    except* ValueError as eg:
        print('TaskGroup caught an exception group:', eg.exceptions)


asyncio.run(main())

The output is roughly:

TaskGroup caught an exception group: (ValueError('Broken'),)

The advantages of TaskGroup:

  • It automatically waits for everything to finish: before async with exits, every task is definitely done
  • One fails, all are cancelled: after bad raises an error, A and B are cancelled straight away – they don't keep running in the background
  • Exception groups (ExceptionGroup): when several tasks fail at once, all the exceptions are packed into one ExceptionGroup, which you catch with the except* syntax

In new code, use TaskGroup whenever you can – it's safer and more controllable than gather. gather suits simple situations with one or two tasks, where you don't care much about cancelling.

Don't panic about the strange except* syntax – it's the special syntax for "exception groups" from PEP 654, added in Python 3.11. Simply put, it means "pick out one type of exception from an exception group and catch it". If you don't need it yet, that's fine – just know it exists.

docs.title: async with and async for
docs.text:
In the asyncio.timeout(0.5) example, you saw async with. That's an asynchronous context manager – its __enter__ and __exit__ are replaced by async versions called __aenter__ and __aexit__.

When do you need async with? The most common case is network clients:

import asyncio
import httpx


async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        r = await client.get('https://httpbin.org/get')
        print(r.status_code)


asyncio.run(main())

It's async with because "closing this connection pool" might itself involve I/O, so it can't be a normal synchronous __exit__.

Similarly, there are asynchronous iterators – async for. For example, some libraries support streaming data:

import httpx
import asyncio


async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        async with client.stream('GET', 'https://httpbin.org/stream/3') as resp:
            async for line in resp.aiter_lines():
                print('line:', line)


asyncio.run(main())

async for line in resp.aiter_lines() means: each time a line is read (which may mean waiting for the network), give it to me, then keep waiting for the next line. A normal for can't do this – only async for can.

Remember the pattern:

  • Normal objects and contexts → with, for
  • Objects involving I/O and coroutines → async with, async for

docs.title: When to use async, and when not to
docs.text:
After all that, let's get back to the basic question: what situations suit async?

asyncio's strength is I/O-bound work – where the program spends most of its time waiting: for the network, the disk, a database, or user input. In these situations, the waiting can overlap, so async lets one thread wait for countless things at once, with immediate results.

asyncio's weakness is CPU-bound work – where the program spends most of its time calculating: encryption, image processing, machine-learning inference. There's no "waiting" to take advantage of – the CPU is busy all the time – so async can't help. One thread can only use one core, while the other seven cores sit idle.

A comparison table:

Situation What to use Fetching 100 URLs asyncio + httpx Reading and writing lots of files at once asyncio + aiofiles A high-traffic web service (one machine handling thousands of connections) asyncio + FastAPI / aiohttp Video conversion, big matrix calculations multiprocessing or C extensions Sorting huge amounts of data locally Multiple processes + splitting into chunks A bit of I/O and a bit of CPU at the same time An async main framework + asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor
