Remember it like this: async is for "waiting", not for "calculating".

docs.title: In practice: 100 URLs, one-by-one vs together
docs.text:
Theory's done. Time for a real comparison, to see how much faster asyncio + httpx really is than requests.

First, install httpx:

pip install httpx

The code below runs two versions: a synchronous one using httpx's synchronous client (which behaves like requests), and a concurrent one using httpx.AsyncClient with asyncio.gather. Both make 50 requests, and we compare the total time:

import asyncio
import time
import httpx

URLS = [f'https://httpbin.org/delay/1?i={i}' for i in range(50)]


def fetch_sync():
    with httpx.Client(timeout=30) as client:
        return [client.get(u).status_code for u in URLS]


async def fetch_async():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as client:
        tasks = [client.get(u) for u in URLS]
        responses = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
        return [r.status_code for r in responses]


def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    sync_codes = fetch_sync()
    sync_cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f'Synchronous, 50 requests: {sync_cost:.2f} seconds, all 200 = {all(c == 200 for c in sync_codes)}')

    start = time.perf_counter()
    async_codes = asyncio.run(fetch_async())
    async_cost = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f'Concurrent, 50 requests: {async_cost:.2f} seconds, all 200 = {all(c == 200 for c in async_codes)}')

    print(f'Speed-up: {sync_cost / async_cost:.1f} times')


main()

The httpbin.org/delay/1 endpoint deliberately waits 1 second before replying, so we can see the difference. One run looks roughly like this:

Synchronous, 50 requests: 53.21 seconds, all 200 = True
Concurrent, 50 requests: 1.62 seconds, all 200 = True
Speed-up: 32.8 times

50 requests, squeezed from 53 seconds down to under 2 – that's the power of asyncio + httpx. You can change this code to the URL list you care about – fetching blog posts, calling internal APIs, pinging services in bulk – and see results straight away.

A few things to watch out for in practice:

  1. Give httpx.AsyncClient a timeout, or it will hang forever when it meets a "zombie" service
  2. Don't blindly run thousands at once – the server on the other end might not cope, and could rate-limit you or even block your IP. Usually you use asyncio.Semaphore to limit the maximum number running at once:
import asyncio
import httpx


async def fetch_one(client, sem, url):
    async with sem:
        r = await client.get(url)
        return r.status_code


async def fetch_many(urls, max_concurrency=10):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrency)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as client:
        tasks = [fetch_one(client, sem, u) for u in urls]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)


urls = [f'https://httpbin.org/delay/1?i={i}' for i in range(100)]
codes = asyncio.run(fetch_many(urls, max_concurrency=10))
print(len(codes))

Semaphore(10) means "at most 10 tasks may come in at once" – the 11th has to queue. That way you get the benefit of running things together, without knocking the other server over.

  1. Error handling: by default, gather raises as soon as one fails, and you lose the whole batch. If you're OK with "partial failure", pass return_exceptions=True, so gather returns exceptions as results:
import asyncio
import httpx


async def fetch(client, url):
    r = await client.get(url, timeout=5)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.status_code


async def main():
    urls = ['https://httpbin.org/get', 'https://httpbin.org/status/500', 'https://httpbin.org/get']
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        results = await asyncio.gather(
            *(fetch(client, u) for u in urls),
            return_exceptions=True,
        )
    for u, r in zip(urls, results):
        if isinstance(r, Exception):
            print(f'{u} failed: {r}')
        else:
            print(f'{u} succeeded: {r}')


asyncio.run(main())

This is especially useful when scraping lots of data – it keeps going even if 99 succeed and 1 fails.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
By now, you should have a complete feel for asyncio. Let's quickly look back at the path we took:

  • The problem: 100 network requests one-by-one are painfully slow, and threads are heavy and messy
  • Gut-feeling comparison: 3 tasks in 1 second vs 3 seconds – the difference comes from overlapping the "waiting"
  • The basic trio: async def defines a coroutine function, await waits for a result, asyncio.run() enters the event loop
  • Coroutine objects: not awaiting one is like not writing it – the most common trap
  • Concurrency tools: asyncio.gather waits for several at once; asyncio.create_task sends a task out
  • The blocking trap: time.sleep freezes the whole event loop – use asyncio.sleep instead
  • Timeouts and cancelling: asyncio.wait_for (old way), asyncio.timeout (new way), Task.cancel (by hand)
  • TaskGroup: the safer upgrade from 3.11 – waits for everything automatically, cancels everything on error
  • Async contexts: async with and async for are standard for I/O situations
  • When to use it: only use async for I/O-bound work; for CPU-bound work, stick with multiple processes
  • In practice: asyncio + httpx fetching 50 URLs – a speed-up of over 30 times you can see with your own eyes

asyncio's syntax looks fancy, but really it just adds scheduling to "waiting". When you write code, ask yourself: "Is this step waiting for something?" If so, try an await – you might be pleasantly surprised.

In the next article, we'll talk about something else that's fun. First, run all the code in this chapter yourself, and get a feel for what "one thread waiting for a hundred things at once" is like.

docs.title: Look at the waiting and the results – don't compare seconds yet
docs.text:
If you only look at "how many seconds faster" in async examples, it's easy to miss what's actually being waited for. Below, each task returns a number of minutes. Focus first on how the tasks are created, waited for, and in what order the results come back:

import asyncio


async def read_minutes(value):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return value


async def main():
    tasks = [read_minutes(15), read_minutes(10)]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(results)


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

[15, 10]

read_minutes(15) creates a coroutine object. gather waits for these jobs to finish and arranges the results by the position you passed them in. It's not "whoever finishes first goes first in the results list".

Change tasks to an empty list yourself – the result should be []. Then add read_minutes(0) – you should get [15, 10, 0]. This checks whether we understand the results better than using a tiny delay to "prove" speed.

Local scripts start with asyncio.run(). If an interactive environment already has an event loop running, follow that environment's way of running things. The learning website has already adapted to this, so you can run the existing exercises here. Also, async doesn't automatically turn pure calculation into parallel calculation. Before choosing it, check whether your task is actually waiting for work it can step aside from.

docs.title: pyproject.toml + uv: putting an end to "it works on my computer but not on yours"
docs.text:
Have you ever had this nightmare? Brother Shui packs up his code and sends it to a teammate. The teammate runs it and gets a pile of ModuleNotFoundErrors. Brother Shui says: "Just pip install it." The teammate asks: "Which version?" Brother Shui searches his computer, can't find a complete requirements.txt anywhere, and finally mumbles: "Er… it works on my computer. That's weird."

This happens all the time in the Python world. It was like this three years ago, and five years ago. Go back even further to ancient times, and people used a scattered pile of files – setup.py + requirements.txt + MANIFEST.in + setup.cfg – each handling one bit of the job. Beginners wanted to cry.

"Why is it so complicated?" you might ask.

The answer is history. Python's packaging tools evolved slowly, and every generation of tools left behind some files of its own. It wasn't until PEP 518 in 2018, followed by PEP 621 in 2021, that the community finally agreed: put all project metadata, dependencies and tool settings into one single file, called pyproject.toml.

Then in 2024, a new tool called uv arrived, made by Astral (the people behind ruff). It's written in Rust, it's 10 to 100 times faster than pip, it's a single program with no dependencies, and one command installs it.

These two weapons together are what this chapter is about. After this chapter, when you start a new project, going from nothing to "a project that runs, locks its dependencies and runs tests" takes just four or five commands. When a teammate asks "which version do I install?", just send them the project folder. They run uv sync, and the exact same environment grows on their computer. That's the experience you should have in 2026.

docs.title: What was so bad about the old way?
docs.text:
First, let's remember what the old way looked like. A "proper" Python project usually had these files:

my-project/
├── setup.py
├── setup.cfg
├── requirements.txt
├── requirements-dev.txt
├── MANIFEST.in
├── pytest.ini
├── .flake8
├── tox.ini
└── my_project/
    └── __init__.py

Eight or nine config files alone, each doing something different:

  • setup.py: for packaging – tells pip the project's name, version and entry points
  • setup.cfg: part of setup.py's settings could move here, if you felt like it
  • requirements.txt: the list of production dependencies
  • requirements-dev.txt: the list of development dependencies (testing, linter, formatter)
  • MANIFEST.in: which non-code files to include when packaging
  • pytest.ini: settings for pytest
  • .flake8: settings for flake8
  • tox.ini: for testing on several Python versions

Is your head spinning yet? And that's not even the worst part. The worst part is:

requirements.txt doesn't lock versions.

Have you written a requirements.txt like this?

requests
flask
sqlalchemy

Clean and simple – three lines. Six months later, a teammate downloads it and runs it. requests automatically installs the newest version, an old API has been removed, and the code breaks. This is the famous gap between "it runs" and "it can be reproduced".

It's not that the old way couldn't solve this – but it needed a pile of patches: pip-tools to make requirements.lock, pipenv to maintain Pipfile.lock, poetry to maintain poetry.lock. Every tool had its own lock file format, and they didn't work with each other.

"Didn't Pipenv solve this?" Some of you might remember it. Pipenv was popular for a while, but it was painfully slow. Installing numpy could take 30 seconds just to work out dependencies, and big projects took minutes. Engineers' lives drained away waiting for pipenv install.

Then came poetry, much faster than pipenv, but with its own problems: it invented its own dependency syntax (using ^ and ~ for version ranges), which wasn't fully compatible with the standard PEP 508, so moving to or from it wasn't smooth.

By 2024, the community had finally cleaned things up:

  • Metadata format: unified as pyproject.toml (PEP 621)
  • Dependency format: unified as PEP 508
  • Tool: uv is recommended (the speed king)

Let's look step by step at how much easier the new way is.

docs.title: What is pyproject.toml?
docs.text:
pyproject.toml is a file name, and the file format is TOML. If you've never seen TOML, don't worry – it's a config format that's friendlier than JSON and stricter than YAML. It looks like this:

[project]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"

The square brackets [project] mark a section, and the key = value lines below it are settings. Strings use double quotes, numbers are written directly, and lists use square brackets – much like most programming languages.

The core idea of pyproject.toml is: put all of a project's information in one file. What can go in it? Look at this complete example:

[project]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A small tool by Two Drops"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
    "click>=8.0",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.0",
    "ruff>=0.5",
]

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]

Count how many jobs this one file does:

  • The [project] section: project name, version, Python version requirement, dependency list – these used to be in setup.py
  • The [project.optional-dependencies] section: development dependencies and optional dependencies – used to be requirements-dev.txt
  • The [build-system] section: how to package the project – used to be setup.py + MANIFEST.in
  • The [tool.ruff] section: ruff settings – used to be .ruff.toml or setup.cfg
  • The [tool.pytest.ini_options] section: pytest settings – used to be pytest.ini

One file does everything. When a newcomer takes over a project, they open pyproject.toml, scan it top to bottom, and have the whole project's metadata, dependencies and tool settings in their head.

"Isn't this just package.json?" you'll ask if you've written Node.js.

Yes – the idea was copied from package.json, but pyproject.toml is stricter. It says the [project] section must follow PEP 621, and tool settings go under [tool.*] sections, so nothing ends up in the wrong place.

Next, let's go through the fields one by one.

docs.title: The smallest pyproject.toml, field by field
docs.text:
Here's the minimum a project needs to run:

[project]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
]

Five fields. Let's explain each one.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
name = "my-project"

The project's name. This is the name used when publishing to PyPI, and it's unique across the whole internet. Naming rules:

  • Only letters, digits, hyphens -, underscores _ and dots .
  • Not case-sensitive – My-Project and my_project are the same name to PyPI
  • By convention, all lowercase with hyphens

When choosing a name, note that the project name (name) and the import name (what you import) aren't always the same. For example, the famous Pillow has the project name Pillow, but you import PIL. scikit-learn has a hyphen in its project name, but you import sklearn.

If your project is just for fun and won't be published to PyPI, name it however you like – but it's still good to follow the conventions.

docs.title: version
docs.text:
version = "0.1.0"

The version number. It's best to follow Semantic Versioning, in the format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:

  • MAJOR: big, incompatible changes (e.g. going from 1.x to 2.x, old code might stop working)
  • MINOR: new features that are backwards-compatible (0.1.x to 0.2.x)
  • PATCH: bug fixes that are backwards-compatible (0.1.0 to 0.1.1)

New projects start at 0.1.0, and the first stable release is 1.0.0. You can also use tools like setuptools-scm to take the version automatically from a git tag, but let's not go into that yet – get comfortable with the basics first.

docs.title: requires-python
docs.text:
requires-python = ">=3.10"

Says which version of Python the project needs. Brother Shui strongly recommends always writing this line, for three reasons:

  1. If someone installs your package with Python 3.7, they get an error straight away, instead of crashing halfway through
  2. pip uses this information to pick suitable sub-dependencies
  3. Tools (ruff, mypy) use it to decide which syntax is available

The version range syntax follows PEP 440:

  • >=3.10: 3.10 or higher
  • >=3.10,<4.0: from 3.10, but below 4.0
  • ~=3.10: the 3.10.x series, not 3.11
  • ==3.10.*: any patch version of 3.10

For a new project in 2026, Brother Shui suggests: just write >=3.10 or >=3.11. 3.9 is close to retirement, and modern features (match statements, better type hints) only start in 3.10.

docs.title: dependencies
docs.text:
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
    "click>=8.0",
]

The list of dependencies the project needs to run. Each item is a string following PEP 508 syntax. Common forms:

dependencies = [
    "httpx",                   # Any version
    "httpx>=0.27",             # From 0.27 up
    "httpx>=0.27,<1.0",        # A range
    "httpx==0.27.2",           # Pinned exactly
    "httpx[http2]",            # With extras
    "httpx ; python_version >= '3.10'",  # A conditional dependency
]

The most common form is a lower limit like >=X.Y. That's the community convention: write a lower limit, not an upper limit, unless you really know an upper version will cause problems. Why? If you write httpx<1.0 today, and httpx 1.0 comes out tomorrow, every project that depends on yours gets stuck and is forced to deal with it. This is called "upper-bound pollution", and it's poison.

The exact versions of dependencies are recorded in a lock file (uv.lock), which we'll see below.

docs.title: A complete minimal example
docs.text:
Put the five fields together, and a working minimal pyproject.toml looks like this:

[project]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
]

That's it. Five lines – much shorter than setup.py, and much shorter than setup.cfg + requirements.txt together. A newcomer understands it at a glance.

For projects that "won't be published to PyPI – just an internal script", this is enough. To publish to PyPI, you also need a [build-system] section to tell the packaging tool how to build it – uv init below creates it for you.

docs.title: What is uv, and how do you install it?
docs.text:
That's the file format. Now for the tool.

uv is a Python package manager and project manager from Astral. You might know this company – their ruff is now the standard Python linter and formatter. uv is their next product, and its goal is to replace a whole set of old tools: pip, pip-tools, pipenv, poetry, virtualenv and pyenv.

Sounds bold, right? But uv really does it. Its selling points:

  • Fast: written in Rust, it works out dependencies 10–100 times faster than pip. Installing numpy takes half a second, not ages like pipenv
  • A single program: uv itself doesn't need Python. It's one executable file you can put anywhere and use
  • All in one: project management (creating projects, adding dependencies, running scripts), Python version management (installing Python interpreters) and virtual environment management (venv) – all in one tool
  • Compatible: uv pip install is used just like pip install. pyproject.toml uses the PEP 621 standard, so there are no walls to moving in or out

Since its release in early 2024, uv has been quickly adopted by big companies and open-source projects. Now in 2026, uv is the first choice for new projects – almost no question.

docs.title: Installing uv
docs.text:
The easiest way for macOS users:

brew install uv

A general way that works on any platform:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Windows users can use PowerShell:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

If you already have pip, you can also do this:

pip install uv

But Brother Shui recommends installing it on its own – uv was designed to get away from pip, so there's no need to tie it to pip.

After installing, check the version:

uv --version

The output is something like:

uv 0.5.20

Your version number may be different – as long as it prints something, you're good.

docs.title: By the way: installing Python itself
docs.text:
Many people don't have a suitable version of Python on their computer, or only have the system's Python 3.9. uv can install Python for you too:

uv python install 3.12

After this, Python 3.12 is installed in a folder that uv manages. It's like a lightweight pyenv.

See which Pythons are installed:

uv python list

The output is roughly:

cpython-3.12.7-macos-aarch64-none           /Users/foo/.local/share/uv/python/...
cpython-3.11.10-macos-aarch64-none          /Users/foo/.local/share/uv/python/...
cpython-3.10.15-macos-aarch64-none          /Users/foo/.local/share/uv/python/...

From now on, when you start a new project, just pick the version you want – no worrying about what's installed on your computer.

docs.title: uv init: creating a project
docs.text:
Enough theory – let's get going.

uv init my-project

This one command does a lot. Look at the folder it creates:

cd my-project
ls -la

Roughly:

.git/
.gitignore
.python-version
README.md
main.py
pyproject.toml

Let's look at each file.

docs.title: .python-version
docs.text:
3.12

This one file pins the Python version the project uses. On any computer with uv installed, go into this folder, and uv automatically uses 3.12 – installing it if needed. That's where uv python install above comes in handy.

docs.title: pyproject.toml
docs.text:
[project]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

Very like the minimal example we wrote by hand, with just description and readme added. uv init assumes you'll write a README.md, so it creates an empty one for you.

dependencies = [] is empty, because we haven't added any dependencies yet.

docs.title: main.py
docs.text:
def main():
    print("Hello from my-project!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

A "Hello World" entry point you can run straight away.

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text: uv also creates a general .gitignore for Python projects, which ignores __pycache__/, .venv/, *.pyc and so on. No more copying .gitignore templates from the internet.

docs.title: Let's run it
docs.text:
uv run main.py

Output:

Hello from my-project!

uv run is one of uv's main commands. It does these things:

  1. Checks whether the project's Python version is suitable, and installs it if not
  2. Checks whether the .venv/ virtual environment exists, and creates it if not
  3. Checks whether all dependencies are installed, and installs them if not
  4. Runs the command using the project's virtual environment

So you can see: from uv init to running code takes two commands – uv init my-project and uv run main.py. No "create a virtual environment, activate it, install dependencies" steps in between. That's the uv experience.

docs.title: uv add: adding dependencies
docs.text:
The new project runs. Now let's add something. How do you usually install httpx?

The old way:

pip install httpx
# Then open requirements.txt by hand and add a line
echo "httpx" >> requirements.txt

Two steps – and it's easy to forget the second one. It works fine after installing, but you commit your code without updating requirements.txt, and your teammate's copy doesn't run.

The uv way:

uv add httpx

One command. What does it do behind the scenes?

  1. Works out the newest version of httpx (that fits the project's requires-python)
  2. Installs it in the project's .venv/
  3. Writes httpx>=0.28 into the dependencies in pyproject.toml
  4. Updates uv.lock, pinning the exact versions of httpx and all its own dependencies

Open pyproject.toml and look:

[project]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.28",
]

dependencies has a new line, added automatically. You don't need to look after this list by hand.

docs.title: Adding several dependencies
docs.text:
uv add httpx click rich

Add three at once. They're worked out together, much faster than pip install-ing them one by one.

docs.title: Adding development dependencies
docs.text:
pytest for testing and ruff as a linter aren't needed when the project runs – only while developing – so they should go in development dependencies. uv uses the --dev flag:

uv add --dev pytest ruff

This time pyproject.toml gets a new section:

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.3",
    "ruff>=0.8",
]

Note it's [dependency-groups], not [project.optional-dependencies] – this is the new PEP 735 format, which uv uses by default. Both work, but dependency-groups is the new standard from 2024, made specially for dependencies that "aren't published, only used for local development".

docs.title: Removing dependencies
docs.text:
uv remove rich

It's not only removed from pyproject.toml – it's also uninstalled from .venv/, and uv.lock is updated. Cleanly removed.

docs.title: Upgrading dependencies
docs.text:
uv add httpx --upgrade

Or:

uv lock --upgrade-package httpx

Upgrades to the newest version that fits the rules.

docs.title: Giving a version range
docs.text:
If you have special requirements for the version:

uv add "httpx>=0.27,<0.30"

This writes httpx>=0.27,<0.30 into pyproject.toml. uv picks the newest version within that range.

docs.title: uv run: running commands
docs.text:
uv run can run more than main.py – it can run any command.

Run a bit of Python:

uv run python -c "import httpx; print(httpx.__version__)"

The output is roughly:

0.28.1

Run pytest:

uv run pytest

Run your own script:

uv run python scripts/build.py

The good thing about uv run is that it makes sure the project's virtual environment is used. You don't need source .venv/bin/activate, or to activate it again every time you open a new terminal. Just go into the project folder and uv run.

"What if I want to activate it and run lots of commands?" You can do that too:

source .venv/bin/activate
python -c "import httpx; print(httpx.__version__)"
pytest

After activating, it's the same as the traditional way. But Brother Shui hardly ever activates any more – putting uv run in front of each command is enough.

docs.title: Running command-line tools
docs.text:
Many packages install a command-line tool. For example, after installing ruff you get a ruff command. In a uv project, run it like this:

uv run ruff check .

uv finds ruff in .venv/bin/ and runs it.

docs.title: Running a one-off command
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to use a tool without adding it to your project's dependencies. For example, to quickly see how httpie sends a request:

uvx httpie https://httpbin.org/get

uvx is short for uv tool run. It installs httpie in a temporary environment, runs it, and throws it away – without messing up your project. It's like pipx run, but much faster.

Similarly, run cowsay just once:

uvx cowsay "Hello Two Drops"

You can use this for lots of "install once, use once" situations.

docs.title: uv sync: syncing dependencies
docs.text:
Now for the key question: how does a teammate run it after downloading it?

The old way:

git clone <repo>
cd <repo>
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

Five commands. And they differ across platforms – the command to activate a virtual environment is different on Windows.

The uv way:

git clone <repo>
cd <repo>
uv sync

Done. uv sync will:

  1. Check the Python version set in .python-version, and install it if needed
  2. Create .venv/ (if it doesn't exist)
  3. Install every dependency (including development dependencies) at the exact versions pinned in uv.lock

"Exact versions" is the key. uv.lock doesn't record httpx>=0.28 – it records httpx==0.28.1, and pins all of httpx's own dependencies to exact versions too. So the environment uv sync creates is identical, byte for byte, to the one on Brother Shui's computer.

In the past, every time you ran pip install -r requirements.txt, the dependency resolution might pick different versions (unless you'd pinned every indirect dependency by hand in requirements.txt, which is torture). uv sync automates all of this.

docs.title: What does uv.lock look like?
docs.text:
head -30 uv.lock

Roughly:

version = 1
revision = 1
requires-python = ">=3.12"

[[package]]
name = "anyio"
version = "4.6.2.post1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "idna" },
    { name = "sniffio" },
]
sdist = { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/.../anyio-4.6.2.post1.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:..." }

Each package records:

  • Its name and version
  • Where it comes from (PyPI, git, a local path…)
  • Which other packages it depends on
  • The download address and hash of its source package (sdist)
  • The download address and hash of its binary package (wheel)

The hash is key – uv sync checks it when installing, making sure the downloaded package is exactly the same as when it was locked. This protects against supply-chain attacks like "someone tampered with a package on PyPI".

docs.title: A few common sync options
docs.text:
Install only production dependencies, not development ones (common when deploying):

uv sync --no-dev

Force everything to be reinstalled (e.g. after changing pyproject.toml):

uv sync --reinstall

Install only one dependency-group:

uv sync --only-group dev

90% of the time, plain uv sync with no options is all you need.

docs.title: Automatic virtual environment management
docs.text:
You all know the old virtual environment routine:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # macOS/Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate       # Windows
pip install ...

It has a few pain points:

  1. It's easy to forget to activate – every new terminal needs activating again
  2. It's different on different platforms – Windows and macOS use different commands
  3. Switching projects means deactivate first, then activate the new one – annoying
  4. Using the wrong virtual environment is a common bug – "I installed httpx, so why does import fail? Oh, I'm in the wrong environment"

uv's approach: you don't need to activate at all. Run every command with uv run, and uv automatically finds the .venv/ in the current folder and uses its Python. You don't even have to remember "which environment is active right now".

To see which Python is being used:

uv run which python

Output:

/Users/walter/projects/my-project/.venv/bin/python

Go into the project folder, and the project's .venv is used automatically.

docs.title: You can still activate by hand if you want
docs.text:
To work with the traditional way, uv lets you activate too:

source .venv/bin/activate
python main.py

After activating, use the python command directly – no uv run needed. Brother Shui does this occasionally, when "running lots of commands in a row and wanting to keep the environment active".

docs.title: Moving over from requirements.txt
docs.text: If you have an old project that already uses requirements.txt, how do you move it over?

docs.title: Situation 1: lock straight from requirements.txt
docs.text:
If your requirements.txt is already "input rules" (ranges like httpx>=0.27), you can do this:

uv pip compile requirements.in > requirements.txt

By convention, requirements.in is the input (with version ranges), and requirements.txt is the output (pinned exact versions). This is the pip-tools convention, and uv pip compile is fully compatible with it.

If you don't have a requirements.in, only a requirements.txt that already has exact versions, you can just use it as your lock file and skip this step.

docs.title: Situation 2: turn requirements.txt into pyproject.toml
docs.text:
This is a more complete move. Say your current requirements.txt is:

httpx>=0.27
click>=8.0
sqlalchemy>=2.0

Step 1: in the project's root folder, run:

uv init --no-package

--no-package tells uv this is just an app, not something to publish to PyPI. It creates pyproject.toml and .python-version, but no [build-system] section.

Step 2: uv add the dependencies from requirements.txt:

uv add httpx click sqlalchemy

Or all at once:

uv add -r requirements.txt

-r makes uv read requirements.txt and add all its dependencies to pyproject.toml.

Step 3: delete the old requirements.txt (or, to stay compatible, export one from pyproject.toml):

uv export --no-dev > requirements.txt

Now requirements.txt becomes "exact versions exported from the lock file", and old tools (like Docker image build scripts) can keep using it.

docs.title: Situation 3: moving over from poetry
docs.text:
poetry projects use pyproject.toml too, but the format isn't exactly PEP 621 – dependencies go in a [tool.poetry.dependencies] section.

The quickest way to move:

uvx pdm import pyproject.toml

Or rewrite the [tool.poetry.dependencies] section by hand into a dependencies list under [project]. Change poetry's ^1.0 to >=1.0,<2.0, and ~1.0 to >=1.0,<1.1 – just translate by the rules.

After moving, delete poetry.lock and run uv lock to create a new uv.lock:

uv lock

docs.title: Situation 4: moving over from pipenv
docs.text: pipenv uses Pipfile and Pipfile.lock. Convert by hand: the [packages] section in Pipfile maps to dependencies, and [dev-packages] maps to [dependency-groups].dev. Then uv lock to create the new lock file.

docs.title: uv vs pip vs poetry vs pipenv – side by side
docs.text:
You often hear people say one tool is good and another is bad. Here's Brother Shui's unemotional comparison:

Tool Speed Lock file Project management Python management Recommendation in 2026 pip Slow None (needs pip-tools) No No For maintaining old projects pipenv Very slow Pipfile.lock Yes No Not recommended poetry Medium poetry.lock Yes No Still usable uv Super fast uv.lock Yes Yes First choice

Now you know. For a new project in 2026, just choose uv. For an old project still on pip + requirements.txt, it's worth moving over soon. If an old project uses poetry, don't panic – if it works, let it run, and think about it at the next big rewrite.

docs.title: In practice: from nothing to "runs, locked, tested"
docs.text:
After all that, let's do a complete mini project. The task: write a little tool that "fetches a URL and prints the response status code". Requirements:

  1. Use httpx to send the request
  2. Write a test with pytest
  3. Lock the dependencies, so a teammate can run it straight away

The full set of commands:

# 1. Create the project
uv init url-checker
cd url-checker

# 2. Add a production dependency
uv add httpx

# 3. Add a development dependency
uv add --dev pytest

# 4. Write the code (shown below)

# 5. Run the tests
uv run pytest

# 6. Commit to git
git add .
git commit -m "init project"

Now the code. First, the main logic file url_checker.py:

import httpx


def check_url(url: str) -> int:
    """Return the response status code of the URL"""
    response = httpx.get(url, timeout=5.0)
    return response.status_code


def main():
    url = "https://httpbin.org/status/200"
    code = check_url(url)
    print(f"{url} -> {code}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Then the test file tests/test_url_checker.py:

from url_checker import check_url


def test_check_url_returns_int():
    """Just an illustration – a real test should mock httpx"""
    # In real tests you would use respx or httpx.MockTransport to mock it
    pass


def test_status_code_type():
    """Assuming 200 is 200, the type should be int"""
    assert isinstance(200, int)

Run the tests:

uv run pytest

Roughly:

========================= test session starts =========================
collected 2 items

tests/test_url_checker.py ..                                    [100%]
========================= 2 passed in 0.05s =========================

Run the main program:

uv run url_checker.py

Output:

https://httpbin.org/status/200 -> 200

Send it to a teammate:

git push origin main

The teammate downloads it:

git clone <repo>
cd url-checker
uv sync
uv run url_checker.py

Three commands, an identical environment, and it runs. That's the 2026 workflow.

docs.title: The project's final folder structure
docs.text:
url-checker/
├── .git/
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── .venv/              # Created by uv automatically – not committed to git
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
├── tests/
│   └── test_url_checker.py
├── url_checker.py
└── uv.lock

What goes into git:

  • .gitignore
  • .python-version
  • README.md
  • pyproject.toml
  • uv.lock (very important – don't forget to commit it)
  • tests/
  • url_checker.py

What doesn't go into git:

  • .venv/ (uv init adds it to .gitignore automatically)
  • __pycache__/, *.pyc

A common mistake: forgetting to commit uv.lock. Without the lock file, uv sync can't guarantee the versions match – it will work out the dependencies on the spot, and the result might be different each time. So remember: uv.lock is part of the project and must go into git.

docs.title: Trap 1: committing .venv to git
docs.text: Beginners easily forget to add .venv/ to .gitignore. uv init handles this for you, but if you moved an old project over by hand, remember to check .gitignore.

docs.title: Trap 2: forgetting uv.lock
docs.text: We just said it, but here it is again: uv.lock must go into git.

docs.title: Trap 3: installing packages globally
docs.text:
Sometimes you'll habitually type pip install something, and it gets installed into the system Python, nothing to do with your project. In a uv project:

  • To add a project dependency, use uv add
  • To install a command-line tool globally, use uv tool install (e.g. uv tool install ruff)
  • To run something just once, use uvx

Don't pip install directly in a uv project unless you really know what you're doing.

docs.title: Tip 1: a shared global cache
docs.text:
uv has a global cache, so all projects share the packages they've downloaded. You can see where it is like this:

uv cache dir

Output:

/Users/walter/.cache/uv

The first uv sync in a new project installs in seconds if the packages are already cached – no downloading again. That's another reason uv is so fast.

Clear the cache:

uv cache clean

You don't usually need to – only when you're short of disk space.

docs.title: Tip 2: use pyproject.toml as your settings centre
docs.text:
As we said, pyproject.toml isn't just for project metadata – it can hold tool settings too. A fuller example:

[project]
name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.28",
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.3",
    "ruff>=0.8",
    "mypy>=1.13",
]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
target-version = "py312"

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-v"

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.12"
strict = true

The settings for ruff, pytest and mypy are all together, so a newcomer can open one file and see everything. Settings that used to be scattered across .flake8, .pylintrc, pytest.ini, mypy.ini and so on can all be brought back into one place.

docs.title: Tip 3: install command-line tools with uv tool install
docs.text:
Want to install ruff globally so it works in any folder?

uv tool install ruff

Same as pipx install ruff, but much faster. After installing, ruff is on your PATH.

Upgrade:

uv tool upgrade ruff

Uninstall:

uv tool uninstall ruff

You can use uv tool instead of pipx, and instead of brew install for some Python command-line tools.

docs.title: Tip 4: run one-off commands with uvx
docs.text:
We mentioned uvx earlier, but it's worth saying again. When you want to try a tool without installing it globally:

uvx ruff check .
uvx pycowsay "Hello"
uvx httpie GET https://httpbin.org/get

uvx installs it in a temporary environment, runs it, and throws it away. Dozens of times faster than pipx run.

docs.title: You can use uv for single-file scripts too
docs.text:
An advanced trick: sometimes you write a one-off script – maybe just 50 lines of Python – but it needs httpx. Do you really need a whole new project for 50 lines?

uv supports inline dependencies (PEP 723). Write some metadata at the top of the script:

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = [
#     "httpx",
# ]
# ///

import httpx

response = httpx.get("https://httpbin.org/get")
print(response.status_code)

Run it:

uv run script.py

uv reads the metadata at the top of the script, creates a temporary environment, installs httpx, runs it, and throws the environment away. A single .py file is a complete project – send one file to a teammate and it runs.

Writing "one-off little tools" will never be the same again.

docs.title: About publishing to PyPI
docs.text:
This chapter is mainly about managing projects. Publishing to PyPI isn't the focus, but let's mention it briefly so you know.

Plain uv init with no options creates a pyproject.toml without a [build-system] section, meaning it's an app, not a library. If you want to publish to PyPI, start it like this:

uv init --package my-library

--package creates a pyproject.toml with a [build-system] section, and a standard package structure like src/my_library/__init__.py.

To package it, run:

uv build

This creates a .tar.gz (source package) and a .whl (wheel) in the dist/ folder.

To publish to PyPI:

uv publish

The first time, you need to register a PyPI account and set up an API token. That's beyond this chapter – read the official uv publish docs when you want to publish.

For most people, uv's core value is managing dependencies for apps – not for publishing packages, but so that "if it runs on my computer, it runs on yours". uv sync does that in one go.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This chapter has a lot of information. Here it is boiled down to a few things you can remember:

First, pyproject.toml replaces everything.

setup.py, setup.cfg, requirements.txt, requirements-dev.txt, pytest.ini, .flake8, tox.ini – in 2026, that whole scattered pile can go into one pyproject.toml file. Start new projects this way.

Second, uv is the package manager of choice in 2026.

Made by Astral, written in Rust, 10–100x faster, a single program, and it manages Python versions, virtual environments and dependencies all together.

Third, remember these five core commands.

uv init my-project       # Create a project
uv add httpx             # Add a production dependency
uv add --dev pytest      # Add a development dependency
uv sync                  # Sync the environment (what a teammate runs after downloading)
uv run python main.py    # Run a command

Fourth, uv.lock must go into git.

It's what guarantees the environment is identical, byte for byte.

Fifth, old projects can use uv pip compile to make requirements.txt; new projects use uv add + uv sync.

Next time you start a new project, free yourself from the tedious routine of "install a Python interpreter, create a virtual environment, install dependencies, write setup.py". One uv init, one uv add, and in seconds you go from nothing to running. A teammate downloads it, runs uv sync, and gets exactly the same environment.

From 2026 on, "it works on my computer but not on yours" can go in the bin of history.

docs.title: Check your setup with a small project you can hand to someone else
docs.text:
This chapter has lots of commands. Let's give them one concrete job: put the study-time tracker tool from the last chapter into its own project, and check that it runs in a clean, clear environment.

On your own computer, choose a new practice folder, and do these in order:

uv init study-tracker-practice
cd study-tracker-practice

Copy the final exercise's tracker.py and test_tracker.py into this new project, then run:

uv run tracker.py --help
uv run python -m unittest -v

The tool itself only uses the standard library. The first time you set up the environment, it may need to download Python, depending on your network. Don't take this example's lack of third-party dependencies to mean that real projects don't need to manage dependencies.

When you're done, explain to yourself: what does pyproject.toml record? Which Python is being used? Which files are source code, and which were generated locally? Once you add real dependencies, practise with the lock file and the sync command. The point of this check is getting the same result from one clear folder and one set of commands – not memorising tool names.

You can read the official uv project guide to understand what the commands mean. The terminal and environment exercises need your own computer – don't type these shell commands into the browser Python editor.

docs.title: ruff: one tool to replace black + flake8 + isort + pyupgrade
docs.text:
Do you remember back in 2022? When you started a new Python project, just "keeping the code style consistent" meant installing a pile of things:

  • black: formats code automatically – handles indentation, line breaks and quotes
  • flake8: checks for syntax errors, unused variables and bad names
  • isort: rearranges import statements in alphabetical order and in groups
  • pyupgrade: upgrades old syntax to newer versions, e.g. Dict[str, int] to dict[str, int]
  • pydocstyle: checks whether docstrings are written properly
  • bandit: scans for security problems

Six tools, six config files, six sets of rules. Install each one separately, run each one in CI, call each one before every commit. Back then, setting up the lint pipeline for a new project, Brother Shui could spend half a day just working out how to stop these tools fighting each other.

"Can't they be combined?" Lots of people asked that back then.

They couldn't. These tools were independent, and built in different ways: black was written in Python, flake8 was written in Python but built on pycodestyle, and isort was its own separate project. Combining them meant rewriting everything.

Then, at the end of 2022, Astral – the same Astral that made uv in the last chapter – released something called ruff. This company has a speciality: rewriting Python tools in Rust, and making them 10 to 100 times faster than the originals.

From the start, ruff implemented the rules of flake8, isort, pyupgrade, pydocstyle, bandit and others all at once. Later it added a format command that swallowed up black's job too. One program, one config, one set of commands.

By 2024, ruff had become the standard in the Python community. Pandas, FastAPI, Pydantic, Hugging Face Transformers and Apache Airflow all switched to it. Today in 2026, almost nobody would recommend the old flake8 + black + isort combination for a new project.

This chapter is about how to use ruff. After it, you should be able to:

  1. Set up ruff in a new project in five minutes
  2. Understand the [tool.ruff] settings in someone else's pyproject.toml
  3. Connect ruff to pre-commit, CI and your editor
  4. Smoothly move an old project over from black + flake8 + isort

docs.title: What was so annoying about the old way?
docs.text:
First, let's remember how the old way worked. A fairly "proper" project would usually have these config files in its root folder:

my-project/
├── pyproject.toml         # Settings for some tools
├── setup.cfg              # flake8 settings had to go here (or in a separate .flake8)
├── .flake8                # flake8 settings (optional)
├── .isort.cfg             # isort settings (optional)
├── .pre-commit-config.yaml
└── ...

Each tool had its own favourite place for settings:

  • black read [tool.black] in pyproject.toml
  • flake8 absolutely refused to support pyproject.toml – only .flake8 or setup.cfg
  • isort could use pyproject.toml, .isort.cfg or setup.cfg – whichever you liked
  • pyupgrade had no config file at all – only command-line options

That's the first trap – settings scattered everywhere. A newcomer taking over a project could spend ages just finding the config files.

The second trap was that the tools fought each other. The classic one is black vs flake8. black's default line length is 88 characters; flake8's default is 79 (the PEP 8 recommendation). If you didn't make them match, black would format the code and then flake8 would complain E501 line too long. What to do? Change flake8, change black, or add # noqa comments everywhere.

isort and black fought too. isort sorted imports in a certain style by default, which black didn't always accept. You had to add --profile black to isort to make them agree.

The third trap was slowness. Not "feels a bit slow" – really slow. On a medium-sized project, flake8 . took seconds to tens of seconds; black . took several to a dozen seconds; isort . took a few seconds too. Run them one after another in CI, and tens of seconds were gone. Running lint every time you saved a file was too slow to connect to your editor.

That was the reality of Python tooling before 2022. Experienced programmers reading this will know the feeling.

docs.title: What is ruff?
docs.text:
ruff is an open-source Python code checker + formatter from Astral. Two key features:

  1. It's written in Rust. Python tools written in Python hit a speed ceiling. Switch to Rust, and they get one or two orders of magnitude faster.
  2. One tool replaces a whole pile. flake8, black, isort, pyupgrade, pydocstyle, bandit, some of pylint's rules and autoflake – all built in.

Look at the speed comparison ruff published, run on the CPython project (about 250,000 lines of code):

Tool Time flake8 About 12 seconds pylint Several minutes ruff check About 0.4 seconds

You might be suspicious: "Is it really that fast? Are the numbers made up?" Brother Shui has tried it on his own computer, and yes, it really is that fast. On a project with a thousand files, ruff check . often finishes in under a second – you can't even see it "running".

ruff format is similar. On a medium-sized project, black takes a dozen seconds; ruff format takes less than one.

What's the point of that speed? Two important things:

  1. Running lint live every time you save becomes possible. Every time you press Ctrl+S in your editor, ruff runs in the background, and you hardly notice any delay.
  2. Shorter CI times. The lint step used to take 30 seconds; now it's done in 1.

"How many rules does it support?" some of you will want to know. As of 2026, ruff has implemented over 800 rules, covering mainstream flake8 + dozens of flake8-* plugins + isort + pyupgrade + pydocstyle + part of pylint + part of bandit. In other words, ruff has taken in the abilities of almost every mainstream Python lint tool.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
As usual, we recommend installing with uv:

uv add --dev ruff

"What does --dev mean?" We covered it in the last chapter – it means "install into the development dependency group", so it isn't included when you release to production. ruff is a development tool, only used while developing and in CI, so --dev is the right place.

If your project doesn't use uv yet, you can install with pip too:

pip install ruff

Or install it as a global command with pipx:

pipx install ruff

After installing, check it:

ruff --version

Output similar to:

ruff 0.8.0

The exact version number will change – in 2026, ruff is probably past 0.9 or even 1.0.

"Why hasn't the version even reached 1.0?" a sharp-eyed student might ask. ruff's authors keep improving it in small steps, and the rule set keeps growing, so the version number stayed at 0.x. But it's been stable enough for production for a long time – lots of community projects use it without any major problems.

docs.title: Running it for the first time
docs.text:
Go into your project folder and run:

ruff check .

This scans every .py file in the current folder and checks it against the default rules. The first time, you'll probably see a pile of warnings:

foo.py:3:1: F401 [*] `os` imported but unused
foo.py:8:5: E731 Do not assign a `lambda` expression, use a `def`
bar.py:12:80: E501 Line too long (95 > 79)

The format is clear: file:line:column: rule-code description. If the rule code has a [*] in front of it, that rule can be fixed automatically.

To let ruff fix things automatically, add --fix:

ruff check --fix .

After this, problems like "os imported but unused" are fixed – ruff simply deletes that import os line. Run ruff check . again, and most of the warnings are gone.

To format code, use another command:

ruff format .

This works basically the same as black . – it makes the whole project's style consistent: indentation, quotes and line breaks. If you've used black before, there's nothing new to learn.

Put these two commands together, and you have the standard routine before every commit:

ruff check --fix . && ruff format .

Lint first, then format – done.

docs.title: Settings: pyproject.toml
docs.text:
All of ruff's settings go into pyproject.toml – no other files. The settings look like this:

[tool.ruff]
# Line length – same as black's default
line-length = 88

# The target Python version – affects how some rules decide
target-version = "py312"

# Which folders to skip
exclude = [
    ".git",
    ".venv",
    "build",
    "dist",
    "__pycache__",
    "migrations",
]

[tool.ruff.lint]
# Which rule sets to turn on
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM"]

# Which specific rules to ignore
ignore = ["E501"]

[tool.ruff.format]
# Quote style: prefer double quotes (black style)
quote-style = "double"
# Indentation style: spaces
indent-style = "space"

That might look confusing, so let's take it apart piece by piece.

docs.title: line-length
docs.text:
The line length. Default 88, same as black. If you prefer 100:

line-length = 100

docs.title: target-version
docs.text:
The target Python version. This affects how some rules decide. For example, with target-version = "py312", ruff knows you can use syntax like dict[str, int], and will suggest changing old code's Dict[str, int]. If you write target-version = "py38", ruff won't suggest that (because 3.8 doesn't support it).

Valid values: py38, py39, py310, py311, py312, py313, py314.

docs.title: exclude
docs.text: Which folders not to scan. ruff skips .git, .venv, build, dist and so on by default, but folders like migrations (migration files generated automatically by Django) you need to add yourself.

docs.title: select
docs.text:
The most important field – which rule sets to turn on. ruff groups rules by letter prefixes:

  • E: pycodestyle errors (PEP 8 style rules)
  • W: pycodestyle warnings
  • F: pyflakes (unused variables, undefined names, etc.)
  • I: isort (import sorting)
  • UP: pyupgrade (suggestions to upgrade syntax)
  • B: flake8-bugbear (common bug patterns)
  • SIM: flake8-simplify (suggestions to simplify code)
  • N: pep8-naming (naming rules)
  • D: pydocstyle (docstring rules)
  • S: flake8-bandit (security checks)
  • ANN: flake8-annotations (type hints)
  • C4: flake8-comprehensions (improving comprehensions)
  • RET: flake8-return (return statement rules)
  • ARG: flake8-unused-arguments (unused arguments)

Under each prefix are specific rules. For example, E501 is "line too long", and F401 is "imported but not used".

For a new project's first setup, we recommend this set:

select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM"]

E + F are the basics (PEP 8 + pyflakes), I sorts imports, UP upgrades old syntax, B catches common bugs, and SIM gives some simplifying suggestions. These six groups cover 80% of what you need without too much noise.

If your project needs high code quality, add N (naming), C4 (comprehensions), RET (returns) and ARG (unused arguments).

If you also want docstring checks (D), be mentally prepared – pydocstyle's rules are very strict, and an old project will get hundreds of warnings straight away. Try select = ["D"] + ignore = ["D100", "D101", "D102", ...] one rule at a time – don't switch them all on at once.

docs.title: ignore
docs.text:
Ignore some specific rules. For example, some projects find 88 characters too short, so they add E501 (line too long) to ignore:

ignore = ["E501"]

Or ignore a whole group:

ignore = ["D"]

docs.title: per-file-ignores
docs.text:
Ignore rules for particular files. __init__.py often has imports that look unused (they're really there to re-export things). To stop those warnings:

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
"__init__.py" = ["F401"]
"tests/*" = ["S101", "ANN"]

In tests/*, assert is allowed (S101), and test functions don't need type hints (ANN).

docs.title: isort sub-settings
docs.text:
The I rule set (the isort replacement) has its own sub-settings, under [tool.ruff.lint.isort]:

[tool.ruff.lint.isort]
# Treat these as "first-party" packages, sorted separately from third-party ones
known-first-party = ["my_project"]

# The order of groups in an import block
section-order = [
    "future",
    "standard-library",
    "third-party",
    "first-party",
    "local-folder",
]

known-first-party is used a lot – it tells ruff "my_project is my own package", so ruff puts its imports in a separate group, not mixed in with third-party packages.

docs.title: A complete settings example
docs.text:
Here's a production-ready pyproject.toml setup you can copy and adapt:

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88
target-version = "py312"
exclude = [
    ".git",
    ".venv",
    "build",
    "dist",
    "__pycache__",
    "migrations",
    "*.ipynb",
]

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
    "E",   # pycodestyle errors
    "W",   # pycodestyle warnings
    "F",   # pyflakes
    "I",   # isort
    "UP",  # pyupgrade
    "B",   # flake8-bugbear
    "SIM", # flake8-simplify
    "C4",  # flake8-comprehensions
    "N",   # pep8-naming
    "RET", # flake8-return
]
ignore = [
    "E501",  # Line too long – let the formatter handle it
    "B008",  # Calling a function in a default argument – FastAPI's Depends uses this
]

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
"__init__.py" = ["F401"]
"tests/*" = ["S101"]

[tool.ruff.lint.isort]
known-first-party = ["my_project"]

[tool.ruff.format]
quote-style = "double"
indent-style = "space"
line-ending = "auto"

Copy this, change target-version and known-first-party, and it should basically work.

docs.title: Common rule sets at a glance
docs.text:
Here are the rule sets above in one table, for easy reference:

Prefix Original tool What it checks E pycodestyle PEP 8 style errors (indentation, spaces) W pycodestyle PEP 8 style warnings F pyflakes Unused variables, undefined names, import mistakes I isort Import sorting and grouping UP pyupgrade Upgrading old syntax to newer versions B flake8-bugbear Common bug patterns SIM flake8-simplify Suggestions to simplify code N pep8-naming Naming rules (CamelCase, underscores) D pydocstyle Docstring rules S flake8-bandit Security checks ANN flake8-annotations Type hint checks C4 flake8-comprehensions Improving comprehensions RET flake8-return Return statement style ARG flake8-unused-arguments Unused arguments PT flake8-pytest-style pytest style PL pylint Some pylint rules RUF ruff ruff's own original rules

The full list is in the official docs, on the "Rules" page, which clearly lists each rule code, its description, and whether it can be fixed automatically. If you don't understand a rule, just search for its code.

docs.title: Automatic fixes in practice
docs.text: What can ruff check --fix . fix? Let's look at some common ones.

docs.title: F401: unused import
docs.text:
import os
import sys

print(sys.version)

After ruff check --fix:

import sys

print(sys.version)

os wasn't used, so it's deleted.

docs.title: E711: compare with None using is
docs.text:
if x == None:
    print("x is None")

After fixing:

if x is None:
    print("x is None")

Why change it? Because == calls the __eq__ method, and some classes implement __eq__ in strange ways (like numpy arrays), so comparing with None can give surprising results. is None compares identity – it only asks "is this the very same object?" – so it's always safe.

docs.title: C408: unnecessary list/dict/tuple calls
docs.text:
empty = list()
d = dict()
t = tuple()

After fixing:

empty = []
d = {}
t = ()

list() and [] mean the same, but list() has to look up the name list in the global namespace and then call it, which is a little slower. Writing the literal directly is faster and shorter.

docs.title: UP006: use the new type hint style
docs.text:
from typing import List, Dict

def foo(x: List[int]) -> Dict[str, int]:
    pass

After fixing (with target-version = "py39" or higher):

def foo(x: list[int]) -> dict[str, int]:
    pass

Python 3.9+ supports list[int] directly in type hints, so you don't need to import from typing any more. ruff upgrades it for you automatically.

docs.title: UP008: use super() without arguments
docs.text:
class Foo(Bar):
    def __init__(self):
        super(Foo, self).__init__()

After fixing:

class Foo(Bar):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

In Python 3, super() with no arguments is enough. The old Python 2 style super(Foo, self) is just historical baggage.

docs.title: SIM108: use a conditional expression instead of if-else
docs.text:
if x > 0:
    y = "positive"
else:
    y = "non-positive"

ruff will suggest (this one isn't fixed automatically, because it affects readability and needs a human to decide):

y = "positive" if x > 0 else "non-positive"

docs.title: I001: import sorting
docs.text:
import sys
from my_project import utils
import os
import requests

After fixing:

import os
import sys

import requests

from my_project import utils

ruff sorts imports into three groups – "standard library → third-party → first-party" – with a blank line between groups, and alphabetical order inside each group. This is the same as running isort.

docs.title: Unsafe fixes
docs.text:
Some fixes ruff won't do by default, because they might change behaviour. For example, changing dict() to {} – in 99% of cases they're the same, but if the name dict has been overwritten in your code, the behaviour changes. These are called unsafe fixes, and you need --unsafe-fixes to apply them:

ruff check --fix --unsafe-fixes .

If you're not sure, run the safe fixes first with ruff check --fix ., then run --unsafe-fixes separately and review the changes.

docs.title: ruff format: the black replacement
docs.text:
ruff format . does almost exactly what black . does:

  • Line length 88 by default
  • Double quotes for strings by default
  • 4-space indentation
  • Automatically breaks function arguments that are too long onto new lines
  • Lays out dict, list and set literals in a consistent style

Before formatting:

def foo(a,b,c, d ):
    return  {  'name':a,'age':b,'list':[1,2,3]  }

After ruff format .:

def foo(a, b, c, d):
    return {"name": a, "age": b, "list": [1, 2, 3]}

Almost exactly the same as black's output. Astral's docs clearly say "ruff format is 99.9% compatible with black", so moving from black won't suddenly change your code style.

There are a few small differences, mainly in edge cases (extremely long lines, special magic comments and so on). Run ruff format and check git diff to see them.

ruff format also has a --check mode that checks without changing anything:

ruff format --check .

If any files need formatting, the command returns a non-zero exit code. You can use this in CI to block pull requests that "forgot to format before committing".

docs.title: Connecting to pre-commit
docs.text:
pre-commit is a git hook framework that runs checks automatically when you git commit. Install it:

uv add --dev pre-commit
pre-commit install

Then create .pre-commit-config.yaml in the project's root folder:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.8.0
    hooks:
      - id: ruff
        args: [--fix]
      - id: ruff-format

This config does two things:

  1. The ruff hook: runs ruff check --fix, fixing whatever can be fixed automatically
  2. The ruff-format hook: runs ruff format

Every time you git commit, pre-commit runs these two hooks automatically, and only lets the commit through if they pass.

"What do I put for rev: v0.8.0?" pre-commit has a command that fills in the newest version automatically:

pre-commit autoupdate

Run it, and the version number in .pre-commit-config.yaml is updated to the newest. I suggest running this every few months.

After installing pre-commit for the first time, you can run it by hand once:

pre-commit run --all-files

This goes through every file in the project and clears out all the old problems in one go.

"Why not just use ruff's own hook?" some of you will ask. ruff doesn't have its own git hook system – it relies on a general framework like pre-commit. pre-commit is the standard solution in the Python world, and besides ruff it can run other hooks too (like mypy and prettier), all managed in one place.

docs.title: Connecting to GitHub Actions CI
docs.text:
Using ruff in CI is very simple. Create .github/workflows/lint.yml:

name: Lint

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  ruff:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v3

      - name: Install ruff
        run: uv tool install ruff

      - name: Run ruff check
        run: ruff check --output-format=github .

      - name: Run ruff format check
        run: ruff format --check .

The --output-format=github option is important – it outputs warnings in a format GitHub Actions understands, so the pull request page shows a little marker right on the problem line. Hover over it to see the rule and explanation. Much better than a plain text log.

There's also an official action that's even easier:

- name: Run ruff
  uses: astral-sh/ruff-action@v3

This action installs ruff and runs ruff check automatically – one line. If you're interested, search GitHub for astral-sh/ruff-action to read its docs.

As for CI time, the ruff part usually finishes within 5 seconds (including setting up the environment) – much faster than the old flake8 + black + isort set.

"Can it fix things automatically on a pull request and commit them back?" It can, but you have to handle permissions and forked pull requests carefully. The usual approach is: CI only checks, doesn't fix; developers fix things locally and push again. Automatic fix pull requests need a special bot account + a GitHub App, which is beyond this chapter.

docs.title: Connecting to your editor
docs.text: The last mile for code style tools is your editor. Once it's set up, every time you save a file, your editor runs ruff automatically, and problems show up right on the lines they're in. This experience can't be replaced by CI or pre-commit: CI is the safety net, the editor is for every day.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Install this extension: Ruff (charliermarsh.ruff)

Then add a few lines to settings.json:

{
    "[python]": {
        "editor.defaultFormatter": "charliermarsh.ruff",
        "editor.formatOnSave": true,
        "editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
            "source.fixAll.ruff": "explicit",
            "source.organizeImports.ruff": "explicit"
        }
    }
}

The effect:

  • Runs ruff format automatically when you save a file
  • Applies every lint fix that can be done automatically
  • Tidies up imports automatically

While you write code, every Ctrl+S runs ruff in the background, and your code tidies itself up.

docs.title: PyCharm
docs.text:
PyCharm has an officially supported Ruff plugin. Go to Settings → Plugins, search for "Ruff" and install it.

After installing:

  • Settings → Tools → Ruff: tick "Use ruff format" and "Run ruff on save"
  • Settings → Editor → Code Style → Python: change the line length to 88, to match ruff

The nice thing about PyCharm is that checks show live while you edit, without waiting for a save. Problem code gets a yellow wavy line – hover over it to see the rule.

docs.title: Neovim / Vim
docs.text:
Install ruff's LSP server through nvim-lspconfig + mason.nvim:

require("lspconfig").ruff.setup({})

Or use the ruff integration in null-ls / none-ls. Which one depends on your Neovim config framework.

docs.title: Moving over from black + flake8 + isort
docs.text: How do you switch an old project? Here are the steps:

docs.title: Step 1: install ruff
docs.text: uv add --dev ruff

docs.title: Step 2: write the ruff settings
docs.text: Using the "complete settings example" above, write a [tool.ruff] section into pyproject.toml. Match key settings like line-length and target-version to your old black settings.

docs.title: Step 3: run it and look at the differences
docs.text:
ruff check .
ruff format --check .

ruff check . shows lint warnings, and ruff format --check . shows formatting differences.

ruff format is 99.9% compatible with black, but a few files will still change. Run ruff format . first, look at git diff, and commit once you're happy with the changes.

docs.title: Step 4: remove the old tools
docs.text:
uv remove --dev black flake8 isort pyupgrade

If the project still uses pip + requirements-dev.txt, remove them from there.

docs.title: Step 5: remove the old settings
docs.text: Delete .flake8, delete the [flake8] section in setup.cfg, and delete the [tool.black] and [tool.isort] sections in pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Step 6: update pre-commit and CI
docs.text: In .pre-commit-config.yaml, remove the black, flake8 and isort hooks and replace them with ruff's. Same for CI.

docs.title: Step 7: tell the team
docs.text: Send the team a message: "From [date], this project uses ruff. Please pull the latest code and run pre-commit install to reinstall the hooks." This step usually goes smoothly, because ruff format is compatible with black, so code already formatted by black won't change much.

docs.title: ruff vs black + flake8 + isort – comparison table
docs.text:
Finally, a comparison table so you've got the full picture:

Aspect The old combo ruff Number of tools At least 3 (black + flake8 + isort), more with pyupgrade and pydocstyle 1 Where settings live Scattered across pyproject.toml, .flake8, setup.cfg, etc. All in pyproject.toml Speed Seconds to tens of seconds Usually under 1 second Number of rules About 500 between them 800+ Automatic fixes Partly (black, isort, pyupgrade fix automatically; flake8 doesn't) Most rules Written in Python Rust Installation Python packages A single program (can also be pip-installed) Live lint in the editor Slow, poor experience Fast, smooth experience pyproject.toml support Partial (flake8 doesn't support it) Full

docs.title: ruff's own rules: the RUF series
docs.text: Besides copying other tools' rules, ruff has invented some rules of its own, with the prefix RUF. Let's look at a few common ones.

docs.title: RUF001/RUF002/RUF003: confusable characters
docs.text:
If your code has characters that "look like English letters but are actually Greek letters or full-width characters", it triggers RUF001. For example:

result = data["nаme"]  # The а here is the Cyrillic letter а, not the English a

You can hardly see the difference, but when the program runs it can't find the key and raises a KeyError. ruff spots characters like this and warns you, saving you from debugging until you doubt everything.

docs.title: RUF005: use unpacking instead of joining lists
docs.text:
new_list = [1, 2, 3] + list(other)

ruff suggests changing it to:

new_list = [1, 2, 3, *other]

Unpacking is faster and shorter, and it can join any iterable directly, without turning it into a list first.

docs.title: RUF013: implicit Optional types
docs.text:
def greet(name: str = None):
    print(f"Hello, {name}")

This is very common, but there's a problem – name defaults to None, but its type hint says str. They don't match. ruff suggests:

def greet(name: str | None = None):
    print(f"Hello, {name}")

The old Python way was Optional[str]; in newer Python (3.10+), str | None is cleaner.

docs.title: RUF100: unused noqa
docs.text:
x = 1  # noqa: F401

If this line actually has no lint warnings, that # noqa is just rubbish. ruff specifically marks these "out-of-date noqa" comments, reminding you to delete them.

This rule is really useful – after moving an old project to ruff, most of the # noqa comments you added for flake8 will be out of date, and RUF100 finds them all.

docs.title: A common trap: how it relates to mypy
docs.text:
Lots of people ask: "Can ruff replace mypy?"

No.

ruff is a linter + formatter. It checks "code style and common error patterns". mypy is a type checker. It works out types across the whole program, like "is the type of this variable right for that function?". They're tools for different jobs, and you use them together.

The right approach:

  • Use ruff for style, imports, obvious bugs and syntax upgrades
  • Use mypy or pyright for types

Run both in CI:

- run: ruff check .
- run: ruff format --check .
- run: mypy .

ruff does have some rules (prefix ANN) that do basic type hint checks, like "this function has no return type". But it doesn't really work out whether types are consistent. For complicated type problems, you still need mypy.

docs.title: An advanced trick: different rules for different folders
docs.text:
Big projects often want "strict rules for the core code, relaxed rules for the scripts folder". Since 0.5, ruff supports overriding settings for sub-folders, using [tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores] with glob patterns. We saw a simple use earlier; here's a more complicated one:

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
# Test files may use assert, and can be a bit longer
"tests/**/*.py" = ["S101", "ANN", "D"]

# One-off scripts – the loosest rules
"scripts/*.py" = ["ALL"]

# Documentation example code – print is allowed
"docs/examples/*.py" = ["T20"]

# Leave migration files alone
"**/migrations/*.py" = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B"]

"ALL" is a special value meaning "ignore every rule". So the scripts/*.py line means ruff doesn't check anything in the scripts folder – write it however you like.

docs.title: Nested settings
docs.text:
If your project is a monorepo with several sub-projects, and each one wants its own ruff settings, put a separate pyproject.toml or ruff.toml in the sub-folder:

mono/
├── pyproject.toml          # Root settings
├── service-a/
│   ├── pyproject.toml      # service-a's own settings (optional)
│   └── ...
└── service-b/
    ├── ruff.toml           # service-b's own settings
    └── ...

When ruff checks each file, it looks upwards for the nearest settings file. The sub-projects don't interfere with each other.

docs.title: An advanced trick: noqa comments
docs.text:
Sometimes you really do want ruff to be quiet. For example, a line uses eval() for a very good reason, but S307 (flake8-bandit) warns about it. Then you can add a # noqa comment:

result = eval(user_input)  # noqa: S307

# noqa: S307 means "ignore rule S307 on this line". Separate several rules with commas:

result = eval(user_input)  # noqa: S307, S102

A bare # noqa (without a rule code) works too, but isn't recommended – it ignores every rule on that line, like switching off all the lights. Naming the rule is the most precise.

Before writing # noqa, think: is the rule unreasonable, or should the code itself be changed? Most of the time, it's the second one.

docs.title: A few easy traps
docs.text: Finally, here are some traps that even experienced programmers fall into after moving to ruff. Knowing them in advance will save you time.

docs.title: Trap 1: the wrong prefix in select, so rules don't turn on
docs.text:
How specific the prefix is decides how many rules you get. Prefixes match like the start of a word:

  • "E": turns on every rule starting with E (E1xx, E2xx, E5xx…)
  • "E1": turns on every rule starting with E1 (E1xx)
  • "E101": turns on only rule E101

If a prefix doesn't match the rules you expected, nothing you wanted gets turned on – and you won't get an error about it. If you can't remember, start with broad groups like ["E", "F", "I"] – as long as it works.

docs.title: Trap 2: writing both select and ignore
docs.text:
select = ["E"]
ignore = ["E501"]

This means "turn on the whole E group, except E501". It's completely valid – ignore wins. You'll often see this "turn on a group + leave out one or two" pattern. It's standard.

docs.title: Trap 3: ruff format doesn't read [tool.ruff.lint] settings
docs.text:
[tool.ruff.lint] controls lint, and [tool.ruff.format] controls formatting – they're completely separate. The most common trap: you set quote-style = "double" in [tool.ruff.lint], but ruff format still uses the default style, because quote-style belongs in [tool.ruff.format].

# Wrong place
[tool.ruff.lint]
quote-style = "double"  # Writing it here does nothing

# Right place
[tool.ruff.format]
quote-style = "double"

docs.title: Trap 4: preview rules
docs.text:
ruff also has a set of preview rules still being developed, which are off by default. To turn them on:

[tool.ruff.lint]
preview = true

Or use ruff check --preview on the command line. The good thing about preview rules is getting new features early. The bad thing is that rule codes and behaviour might change between versions. For production projects, play it safe – don't turn on preview by default.

docs.title: Trap 5: forgetting to update the pre-commit hook version
docs.text:
The rev: v0.8.0 in your .pre-commit-config.yaml is fixed – when ruff releases a new version, it doesn't sync automatically. Six months later, the old ruff can't run the new rules, and different team members having different ruff versions causes problems too.

Suggestion: run pre-commit autoupdate every month or every quarter to bring all the hook versions up to date. Update CI at the same time.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  1. Install ruff: uv add --dev ruff
  2. Run ruff: ruff check --fix . and ruff format .
  3. Configure ruff: write [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM"] in pyproject.toml
  4. Connect pre-commit: write .pre-commit-config.yaml and add the ruff-pre-commit repo
  5. Connect CI: use astral-sh/ruff-action@v3 in GitHub Actions
  6. Connect your editor: install the charliermarsh.ruff extension in VS Code and set it to format on save

Once this workflow is set up, a new project goes from nothing to "automatic checks, automatic fixes, a CI safety net and live editor feedback" in ten minutes. Leave code style to ruff, and use the energy you save to write the code that really matters.

In the next chapter, we'll look at pytest – how to write good tests for Python projects. uv for dependencies, ruff for style, pytest for tests – with these three, your 2026 Python tooling is complete.

docs.title: Deal with one check result you understand at a time
docs.text:
When a code checker outputs a long list of rule codes, first pick one problem you can explain. Don't rush to turn on every rule. Do a read-only check in the final exercise's folder:

ruff check .
ruff format --check .

The first command checks the rules that are turned on; the second checks whether the formatting needs adjusting. The actual output depends on the version, settings and what's in your files – it doesn't need to match some old screenshot exactly.

If you find an unused import, first find it, make sure it really isn't used, and then fix it in your own practice file. Write down the rule code, the reason and the change, then run the check again. When you meet a rule you don't know, look it up in the Ruff rules list to see what it checks and whether there are situations where it doesn't apply.

Next, deliberately break the addition in the totals function, and check again. You'll see that a style checker doesn't decide "what the total study time should be". Running tests is still necessary. And the other way round: passing tests doesn't mean the code is clear and easy to read. Both kinds of checks are useful in their own way.

Work in your own practice folder first. Before letting a tool change things automatically, read the reason it reports. After changing, run the tests again to confirm the program's results haven't changed.

docs.title: pytest: the testing framework that runs 100 test cases in 30 seconds
docs.text:
When you write code, do questions like these often bother you?

"I just changed one line of this function – will it break something somewhere else?"

"The boss wants a new feature, but I'm scared to touch this mess of code. What if I break it and the live app crashes?"
