While debugging, you casually write logger.debug("user=%s, password=%s", user, password), forget to delete it before going live, and the password sits in plain text in app.log for years.

Fix –

  • Filter sensitive fields before logging (write a Filter that masks password, token, secret and so on)
  • With structlog, add a processor that masks them automatically
  • In code review, watch closely for any log that prints user objects

docs.title: Trap 5: mixing % placeholders and f-strings gets messy
docs.text:
logger.info(f"user={user}, count=%d", count)

This is confusing to read: the f-string has already put user in, and then logging fills %d with count. It may look like it works, but if user ever contains a % character, the formatting breaks and you get an error message instead of your log line.

Fix – pick one way: either use % throughout, or f-strings throughout. Don't mix them.

docs.title: Trap 6: logger.error(e) vs logger.exception(e)
docs.text:
try:
    ...
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(e)

This only prints the exception's "string version", with no traceback. When the live app crashes, you only see "division by zero", with no idea which line blew up.

Fix – in except, use logger.exception("xxx failed") instead, which includes the traceback automatically.

docs.title: Trap 7: logs not written to disk, so they're missing after a crash
docs.text:
Some handlers buffer – messages are kept in memory first, and only written to disk when the buffer is full or the handler is closed. If the program is killed with kill -9, the last chunk that wasn't written yet is lost.

Fix –

  • Call logging.shutdown() before the program exits to flush everything (it's called automatically by atexit)
  • Or use options that make the handler write immediately (depends on the handler)
  • For critical situations, log to syslog or straight to stdout, and let an outside system be the safety net

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Q1: Should I use print for debugging?

For short, temporary debugging, yes – it's easier than pdb, and unlike logger.debug, you see it without any setup. But build one habit: delete the prints when you've finished debugging, and use logger.debug for real logging.

Q2: Should logs go to stdout or a file?

  • A service on a single machine: write to a file with RotatingFileHandler
  • Containers / 12-factor: write to stdout/stderr, and let an outside logging system (Docker, Kubernetes, Filebeat) collect them
  • Web services: Brother Shui recommends stdout, collected by operations into ELK or Loki

Q3: Will logging slow my program down?

For almost all projects, no. logging is quite lightweight inside, and logger.debug(...) does almost nothing when its level is turned off. Unless you're madly calling logger.debug(big_object) inside a loop, don't worry.

If performance really is critical (hundreds of thousands of messages a second), switch to structlog + an async handler, or aiologger.

Q4: Should library code call basicConfig itself?

Absolutely not. Library code should only do logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) and log messages. Leave the configuration to the end user. If a library calls basicConfig itself, it messes up the user's settings.

Q5: Can logs include emoji and non-English text?

Yes. As long as file handlers have encoding='utf-8' – otherwise it can break on Windows with its default GBK/other encodings. The console is usually fine.

Q6: How do I get the traceback as a string? I don't want to log it, just save it to a database

import traceback

try:
    ...
except Exception:
    tb_str = traceback.format_exc()

format_exc() gives you a string you can save anywhere. That's a separate thing from logging.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  1. Stop debugging with print and use logging instead
  2. Tell the 5 levels apart – DEBUG / INFO / WARNING / ERROR / CRITICAL
  3. Get started with one line of logging.basicConfig
  4. Use getLogger(__name__) to give each module its own logger
  5. Attach StreamHandler + RotatingFileHandler together, for both console and file
  6. Use logger.exception() in except to include the traceback automatically
  7. Use dictConfig + yaml to manage log settings centrally in production
  8. Know when to use structured logs (python-json-logger / structlog)
  9. Avoid classic traps like several processes writing one file, or secrets ending up in logs

Once you've learned the logging system, looking back at print debugging is like going back to the Stone Age – no timestamps, no levels, no module names, and you can't see anything once it's live. When Brother Shui first added logging to an old project, it felt amazing: the day before, he'd been sticking print('111') everywhere; the next day he opened app.log, and every business process was laid out clearly in the file – which user clocked in at which second, which API timed out – all recorded. That's what it means for "the program to speak for itself".

In the next chapter, we'll see how to package and publish code – uv build + PyPI – putting your own library on PyPI so the whole world can pip install it. The last mile of Python tooling.

docs.title: Leave information in your logs that helps find problems
docs.text:
Suppose a batch of study records is being saved. Printing only "start" and "failed" makes it hard to know which batch went wrong. At the very least, write out the subject, the minutes and other information related to the problem:

import logging
import sys

logger = logging.getLogger('study-tracker-example')
logger.handlers.clear()
logger.propagate = False
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter('%(levelname)s %(message)s'))
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
logger.info('About to save: subject=%s, minutes=%s', 'Python', 15)
logger.debug('This debug message is not shown at the moment')

Output:

INFO About to save: subject=Python, minutes=15

This small experiment uses a specially named logger, and clears its own handlers when run again, so messages aren't printed twice. It doesn't change any other logger's handlers. Real modules usually use logging.getLogger(__name__), and configure logging in one place at the program's starting point.

Change the level to DEBUG yourself, and check for the extra message. Then write one useful log line each for the project's reading and saving steps, and explain what problem each one would help you track down.

Logs are records that help find problems. The lists and totals users need to see are still the program's normal output. Don't mix passwords, secret keys or the full contents of private files into your logs. And without actually checking, don't treat printing "Saved successfully" as proof the data really reached the disk correctly – still read it back and check.

docs.title: Publishing to PyPI + typer: let the whole world use your tool with one pip install
docs.text:
Have you ever had a moment like this?

Brother Shui writes a little tool on his own computer – say, "rename lots of screenshot files at once", "analyse exported chat history" or "automatically add a watermark to images". The script is a hundred or two lines, works nicely, and he uses it every day. Then one day a friend sees it and says: "That's handy – can I have a copy?"

So Brother Shui sends tool.py over in a chat message. The first thing the friend says is: "How do I use this?"

"Install pillow and httpx."

"OK, done."

"Now install pyyaml."

"Done."

"Run python tool.py."

"Error – it says it can't find requests."

"Oh right, you need requests too."

Five minutes of back and forth, and the friend gives up.

This is the "last mile" problem of Python tools – the code runs for you, but it's a struggle for anyone else to use. In the Node world it's one line, npm install -g xxx. In Rust, cargo install xxx. In Go, go install xxx. Does Python really have to be "install this, then install that"?

Of course not. Python has its own "global app store" called PyPI (the Python Package Index). Package your tool properly and upload it, and anyone can install it with one line, pip install my-tool. No more teaching people step by step.

In this chapter, we'll go through the whole process from scratch. After it, you should be able to:

  1. Know what PyPI is, and how it relates to pip
  2. Turn your own project into a standard "publishable" structure
  3. Use one uv build command to package your project as a wheel and an sdist
  4. Practise on TestPyPI first, then publish to the real PyPI
  5. Use [project.scripts] to turn a Python function into a system command
  6. Use typer to write command-line tools 10 times more elegant than argparse
  7. Connect the whole publishing process to GitHub Actions, so adding a tag publishes a release automatically

In the second half, we'll use typer to write a small command-line tool, todo-cli, and publish it to PyPI so anyone in the world can pip install todo-cli. This little project ties both halves together – run through it once and it'll all make sense.

Let's go.

docs.title: What is PyPI?
docs.text:
When you type pip install requests, where is the package downloaded from? The answer is PyPI.

PyPI (the Python Package Index) is the global public package repository maintained officially for Python, at https://pypi.org. As of 2026, it holds over 600,000 Python packages, downloaded tens of billions of times a month. All the well-known Python packages – requests, numpy, flask, django, pandas, fastapi – live on PyPI.

What pip install xxx really means is: "download the package called xxx from PyPI and install it into the current Python environment".

How does PyPI relate to GitHub? They each do their own job:

  • GitHub is where source code lives, for developers to read
  • PyPI is where packaged releases live, for users to install with pip

A project usually has both – source code hosted on GitHub, releases uploaded to PyPI. Packages you use, like requests and flask, have their source on GitHub and their packages on PyPI, with matching version numbers.

PyPI also has a "sister site" called TestPyPI, at https://test.pypi.org. It's a practice ground – before publishing a release, upload it to TestPyPI first to try it out, and only publish to the real PyPI once you're sure it's fine. The two sites are completely separate – accounts, passwords and tokens don't work across them.

"Why have TestPyPI?" Because on PyPI, a released version can never be changed or deleted. If your hand slips when publishing – you upload 0.1.0 and then find the version number was wrong, or files were missing from the package – you can't take it back. You can only publish 0.1.1, and the broken version stays on PyPI forever as part of history. So practising on TestPyPI before the real PyPI is a good habit.

Next, let's build a project that can be published to PyPI, step by step.

docs.title: First, get the project structure right
docs.text:
The most common folder layout for Python projects looks like this:

my-tool/
├── my_tool.py
└── README.md

Or, a bit more carefully:

my-tool/
├── my_tool/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── main.py
└── README.md

These work fine locally, but once you package and publish, a hidden trap appears – Python automatically adds the current folder to sys.path. So when you run tests, you're importing "the source code in the project's root folder" rather than "the package installed in the environment", and problems get hidden.

The community now recommends a layout called src layout, which looks like this:

my-tool/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── src/
│   └── my_tool/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── main.py
└── tests/
    └── test_main.py

Notice the extra src/ folder in the middle. It's not decoration. Its job is to force the source code out of the project's root folder. That way you must install the package into the environment before you can import it, which avoids the trap above.

"Is that a hassle?" Not at all. With uv and pyproject.toml, the tools recognise the src/ layout automatically – nothing to configure.

Let's start a new project with uv and look at the default structure:

uv init --package my-tool
cd my-tool
ls -R

The output is roughly:

.
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── src
    └── my_tool
        └── __init__.py

This one uv init --package line builds the src layout skeleton for you. Note the --package option – without it, uv init builds an "app" structure by default (not for packaging). With it, you get a "library/tool" structure (for packaging and publishing).

Open pyproject.toml and look at what uv created:

[project]
name = "my-tool"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = []

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project.scripts]
my-tool = "my_tool:main"

The skeleton is all there – the [project] section for metadata, the [build-system] section for the packaging back end, and the [project.scripts] section for command-line entry points. Next, let's fill in each field properly.

docs.title: The required fields in pyproject.toml
docs.text: To publish to PyPI, a few fields in the [project] section are unavoidable – name, version, description, Python version requirement and dependencies. Let's go through them one by one.

docs.title: name: the package's globally unique name
docs.text:
name is the xxx people type in pip install xxx after you publish to PyPI. It's unique across the whole of PyPI, like a domain name – first come, first served. Before choosing a name, check https://pypi.org/project/xxx/ to see whether it's taken.

Naming rules: only letters, digits, -, _ and . are allowed; it's not case-sensitive; and it can't start with a digit. The community usually uses lowercase with hyphens, like my-tool, todo-cli or http-prompt.

Note one detail: the package name (name) and the import name (the xxx in import xxx) aren't always the same. For example, you pip install scikit-learn but import sklearn. You pip install Pillow but import PIL. That's because:

  • name is the project name on PyPI, and can contain hyphens
  • The import name is a Python module name, which must be a valid Python identifier – no hyphens

Brother Shui's advice: to avoid confusing users, keep the two names as similar as possible. For example, if the package name is my-tool, call the import name my_tool (hyphens become underscores – the usual Python habit).

docs.title: version: the version number
docs.text:
version is the version number of this release, written as a string, like "0.1.0", "1.2.3" or "2.0.0a1".

The community strongly recommends Semantic Versioning (SemVer) – three numbers, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:

  • Major version: big changes that aren't backwards-compatible (removing functions, changing signatures)
  • Minor version: new features that are backwards-compatible
  • Patch version: bug fixes that are backwards-compatible

New projects start at 0.1.0. Before 1.0, everything is "unstable", and the API can change freely. After 1.0, be careful about changing the API.

PyPI also has an iron rule – each version number can only be uploaded once. If you publish 0.1.0 and want to take it back and publish again – sorry, you can't. You must change it to 0.1.1 or 0.1.0.post1 and publish again.

docs.title: description: a one-sentence description
docs.text:
description is a one-sentence summary. It's shown at the top of the PyPI page and in search results. Write something decent – don't publish with the default "Add your description here", or it'll look embarrassing once it's live.

description = "A small tool by Two Drops that adds watermarks to lots of images at once"

docs.title: readme: the long description
docs.text:
readme is the project's long description, shown as the main text on its PyPI page. Just point it to a Markdown file:

readme = "README.md"

uv init already created an empty README.md for you – fill it in. It should at least have a short introduction, the install command and a minimal usage example.

docs.title: authors / maintainers: the authors
docs.text:
authors is a list of authors. Each author is an object with at least a name; email is optional:

authors = [
    { name = "Two Drops", email = "liangdianshui@example.com" },
]

docs.title: requires-python: the Python version requirement
docs.text:
requires-python limits which Python versions this package supports:

requires-python = ">=3.10"

Don't write >=3.0 – then ancient Python versions will try to install it too, causing lots of compatibility problems. A sensible choice in 2026 is >=3.10 or >=3.11; 3.9 is at the edge of end-of-life.

docs.title: dependencies: the dependency list
docs.text:
dependencies lists the other packages this package needs to run:

dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
    "typer>=0.12",
]

Each one follows PEP 508 syntax – package name + version rule. Common version rules:

  • >=0.27: 0.27 or higher – the most common
  • ~=0.27: a compatible version, >=0.27, <0.28
  • ==0.27.1: an exact version – hardly ever used
  • >=0.27, <1.0: a range

"Should I write version numbers?" I strongly recommend writing a minimum version, like httpx>=0.27. That way, when someone installs it, at least httpx won't be so old that functions are missing. Don't casually write an upper limit – fixing it tightly makes dependency conflicts more likely for your users.

A complete minimal publishable pyproject.toml looks roughly like this:

[project]
name = "my-tool"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A small tool by Two Drops"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
authors = [
    { name = "Two Drops", email = "liangdianshui@example.com" },
]
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
]

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

The next section explains what [build-system] is.

docs.title: build-backend: who does the packaging?
docs.text:
At the end of that pyproject.toml is this section:

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

What are these two lines doing? To explain, we first need to understand the roles in Python packaging.

Python packaging has two roles – the front end and the back end:

  • The front end is the command the user types, like pip, uv or build
  • The back end is the library that does the real work – turning source code into a wheel and an sdist

The PEP 517 standard separated the two: the front end only calls the back end, and the back end can be swapped freely. The [build-system] section tells the front end "which back end I use".

The community's three main back ends today:

  • hatchling: from the Hatch project – simple to configure, very extensible, the first choice for new projects
  • setuptools: the ancient, well-established back end – used by almost every old project
  • poetry-core: the back end that comes with the Poetry project, used with the Poetry tool

You might also see flit-core, pdm-backend and maturin (for extensions written in Rust) in the wild – different choices for the same job.

Why recommend hatchling? Three reasons –

  1. Simple to configure. uv init --package uses it by default, so you don't need to change anything
  2. Modern. It natively supports src layout and PEP 621 metadata, with no historical baggage
  3. Officially backed. hatch is a project of the PyPA (Python Packaging Authority)

"Isn't setuptools more widespread?" It is, but its configuration is complicated and messy, and new projects don't need that trouble. Unless you need C extensions or compatibility with ten-year-old code, just pick hatchling.

Keep this section as the default in your pyproject.toml:

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

requires lists "packages needed to build this project". These are different from [project].dependencies – those are "packages needed to run this project", while these are "packages needed to package this project".

In the next section, let's try packaging the project.

docs.title: Building locally: one uv build command
docs.text:
Once you've written your code, how do you package it in a publishable format? One command –

uv build

Run it, and the output is roughly:

Building source distribution...
Building wheel from source distribution...
Successfully built dist/my_tool-0.1.0.tar.gz
Successfully built dist/my_tool-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

Open the dist/ folder:

dist/
├── my_tool-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
└── my_tool-0.1.0.tar.gz

What are these two files?

  • The .whl file (wheel): a ready-built package. When users pip install, this is chosen first, because it needs no building – it installs instantly
  • The .tar.gz file (sdist, source distribution): a source package. It contains the whole project's source, for users with unusual environments who need to build from source

There's a rule in the file name – package-version-PythonVersion-ABI-platform:

  • py3: works with any Python 3
  • none: doesn't depend on a specific ABI
  • any: works on any platform

If your package contains C extensions, the whl name becomes something like my_tool-0.1.0-cp311-cp311-linux_x86_64.whl, which only works on CPython 3.11 on Linux x86_64. You'd need to build a separate whl for every platform.

A pure Python project has just one py3-none-any.whl that works everywhere – the easiest.

"What if I don't have uv?" You can use the official build tool instead:

pip install build
python -m build

Same result. Use whichever you prefer – the rest of this chapter uses uv.

After building successfully, always install it locally first and try it:

uv pip install dist/my_tool-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

Or:

pip install dist/my_tool-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

After installing, run your tool and check that it works. This is the last line of defence before publishing. If you find a problem now, you can still fix it; once it's on PyPI, it's too late.

docs.title: Registering a TestPyPI account
docs.text:
The package is built. Next – upload it. First practise on TestPyPI, then publish to the real PyPI.

How to register on TestPyPI –

  1. Open https://test.pypi.org/account/register/
  2. Register an account with your email and verify the email
  3. After logging in, go to Account settings
  4. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) – TestPyPI now requires it. You can use a TOTP app like Authy, Google Authenticator or 1Password
  5. Go to the API tokens page and create a token, choosing the scope Entire account (for your first upload, you can't limit it to a specific project, because the project doesn't exist yet)
  6. Copy the token – you can only see it once; close the page and it's gone

A TestPyPI token looks like this:

pypi-AgEIcHlwaS5vcmcCJ...(a long base64 string)

Save this token in a password manager.

Registering on the real PyPI is the same – https://pypi.org/account/register/, turn on 2FA, create a token, save it. Remember, PyPI and TestPyPI are two separate websites, with separate accounts and tokens.

"How do I use the token?" You'll use it in the next section.

docs.title: Practising by uploading to TestPyPI
docs.text:
The command to publish to TestPyPI –

uv publish --publish-url https://test.pypi.org/legacy/ \
    --token pypi-AgEIcHlwaS5vcmcCJ...

Or, more safely, use an environment variable:

export UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN=pypi-AgEIcHlwaS5vcmcCJ...
uv publish --publish-url https://test.pypi.org/legacy/

If it succeeds, the output is roughly:

Uploading my_tool-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
Uploading my_tool-0.1.0.tar.gz
Published https://test.pypi.org/project/my-tool/0.1.0/

Open the link, and your little tool is sitting on TestPyPI, with its title, description, version, README and dependency list.

Next – install it from TestPyPI and check it works:

pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ \
    --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ \
    my-tool

Notice the two index options here –

  • --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/: look for the package you just uploaded on TestPyPI
  • --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/: look for dependencies on the real PyPI (because your dependencies, like httpx, are published on the real PyPI)

Without the second option, the dependencies won't install properly from TestPyPI (TestPyPI only has what you just uploaded, not httpx). This is the most common beginner trap – remember it.

After installing, run your tool. If it works – congratulations, you've mastered the publishing process.

docs.title: Uploading to the real PyPI
docs.text:
Once your TestPyPI practice succeeds, publishing to the real PyPI is one command –

export UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN=pypi-your-real-token-...
uv publish

By default, uv publish uploads to https://upload.pypi.org/legacy/ – the real PyPI.

After publishing, open https://pypi.org/project/my-tool/, and your project is on PyPI. Now anyone can:

pip install my-tool

and install your tool into their own environment. Even Brother Shui gets a little excited writing this – it means your code is on the global public repository, and anyone can use it.

"What if I want to take a release down after publishing?" PyPI has a yank feature – the version number stays, but by default new installs won't find it. Note that this only "hides" it, it doesn't "delete" it – users who already installed it can keep using it. Completely deleting a version isn't allowed, so that dependency chains don't break.

docs.title: Managing version numbers: by hand vs automatically
docs.text:
You've published 0.1.0, and after a while you want to publish 0.1.1. How do you change the version number?

By hand – open pyproject.toml, change version = "0.1.0" to version = "0.1.1", then uv build + uv publish again. Simple and direct.

But doing it by hand has a problem – pyproject.toml and your git tags can easily get out of step. For example, pyproject.toml says 0.1.1 but the git tag is v0.2.0 – which one is right? After a few versions of drifting like this, things get messy.

Automatically – use hatch-vcs to work out the version number from git tags automatically. Change pyproject.toml:

[project]
name = "my-tool"
dynamic = ["version"]
description = "A small tool by Two Drops"
# ...

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling", "hatch-vcs"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.hatch.version]
source = "vcs"

Notice three changes –

  1. version = "0.1.0" becomes dynamic = ["version"], telling hatchling "the version number isn't fixed – work it out"
  2. hatch-vcs is added to [build-system].requires, bringing in the plugin that works out the version
  3. A new [tool.hatch.version] section tells hatch-vcs "read it from git"

After that, the process becomes –

git tag v0.1.1
git push --tags
uv build
uv publish

When you uv build, hatch-vcs reads the latest git tag v0.1.1, works out the version number 0.1.1, and the package becomes my_tool-0.1.1-py3-none-any.whl.

If you change the code after adding a tag, hatch-vcs automatically adds a dev suffix, so the version becomes something like 0.1.2.dev3+gabc1234 – clearly telling you "this is a version still in development".

Brother Shui's advice: use the automatic way for new projects. Doing it by hand is fine at first, but by the third or fourth version, with more developers involved, the automatic way saves lots of checking.

docs.title: README and LICENSE: the minimum for looking "proper"
docs.text: Projects you publish to PyPI must have a README.md and a LICENSE file. That's basic good manners in the industry.

docs.title: README.md
docs.text:
README.md is shown as the main text on your PyPI project page – it's the first thing users see. It should include at least –

# my-tool

A small tool by Two Drops that adds watermarks to lots of images at once.

## Install

```bash
pip install my-tool

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: my-tool ./photos --watermark "© Two Drops"

docs.title: License
docs.text:
MIT 

Introduction, install, usage, License – four sections are enough. More careful projects also add "Features", "Examples", "FAQ" and a "Contributing guide".

### LICENSE

A licence is a legal document. It tells users "this is how I allow you to use my code". If you write an open source project without a licence, that means "all rights reserved" – which is actually the strictest option. Other people can't use your code, because they haven't been given permission.

Pick one of the three common licences –

- **MIT**: the most relaxed – "use it however you like, don't sue me, just keep the copyright notice"
- **Apache 2.0**: similar to MIT, plus a "patent grant" clause, which is friendlier for companies
- **GPL v3**: a "copyleft" licence – "if you use my code, your code must be open source too"

The community habit: tool and library projects use MIT or Apache 2.0; for app projects, decide for yourself. Brother Shui's little tools always use MIT – it's simple.

Declare it in `pyproject.toml` too:

```toml
[project]
license = { file = "LICENSE" }

Or use an SPDX identifier (PEP 639, officially adopted in 2024):

[project]
license = "MIT"

The second form is more modern, but some older tools don't understand it yet – it depends on how much you're willing to put up with.

docs.title: Publishing automatically with CI: add a tag, publish a release
docs.text:
Running uv build + uv publish by hand every time gets boring after two or three releases. The ideal is – add a git tag, and CI builds and publishes to PyPI automatically.

One GitHub Actions workflow can do this. In your project, create a file .github/workflows/release.yml:

name: Release

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v3

      - run: uv build

      - uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1

What does this configuration do –

  1. Trigger: it runs when you push a tag starting with v (like v0.1.1)
  2. permissions: id-token: write: asks for OpenID Connect permission for the workflow – the "trusted publishing" below needs it
  3. Build: packages the project with uv build
  4. Publish: uploads to PyPI with pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish

The most amazing part – this process doesn't need a PyPI token at all. It relies on a feature called Trusted Publishers, which PyPI launched in 2023 and which became the recommended approach in 2024.

How trusted publishing works – PyPI directly trusts the OIDC identity of GitHub Actions. Once you link "this workflow file in this GitHub repository" in your PyPI project settings, PyPI recognises the CI run and lets it upload without a token.

Setup steps –

  1. Log in to PyPI and go to your project page → Settings → Publishing
  2. Add a "Trusted Publisher", filling in Owner (your GitHub username/organisation), Repository name, Workflow name (release.yml) and Environment (optional)
  3. Push a tag to try it

The commands to add a tag –

git tag v0.1.1
git push origin v0.1.1

GitHub Actions starts running, and a few minutes later your package is on PyPI.

"What's better about this than a token?" Three things –

  1. No token expiry to worry about. Tokens can expire, and then you have to create a new one
  2. No fear of the token leaking. The OIDC credential only exists for the moment the workflow runs – it can't be copied out
  3. The configuration lives on the PyPI side. No need to change secrets when swapping tokens, so permissions are clearer

Brother Shui strongly recommends that new projects in 2026 use trusted publishing from day one – it's much cleaner than tokens.

That's the end of the part about publishing to PyPI. In the next section we change topic – typer, a great tool for writing CLI (command-line) tools.

docs.title: The pain of CLIs: argparse is too wordy
docs.text:
Have you ever written a command-line tool? Python's standard library comes with argparse. It works, but it's terribly wordy to write. Look at this:

import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Add a watermark to an image")
parser.add_argument("input", type=str, help="Input image path")
parser.add_argument("--watermark", type=str, default="© Two Drops", help="Watermark text")
parser.add_argument("--opacity", type=float, default=0.5, help="Opacity")
parser.add_argument("--verbose", action="store_true", help="Show details")
args = parser.parse_args()

print(f"Input: {args.input}")
print(f"Watermark: {args.watermark}")
print(f"Opacity: {args.opacity}")
print(f"Verbose: {args.verbose}")

The setup takes 7 lines, but the useful logic is just 4 variables. Why so wordy? Because argparse was written in 2009, before Python had type hints. You have to add_argument every parameter by hand, filling in the type, default and help text each time. The function signature and the parameter declarations live in two places, so it's easy to miss something when you change it.

Even worse are subcommands – a "main command + subcommand" structure like git commit and git push. In argparse you nest a pile of subparsers, and one look gives you a headache.

In 2026, is there something better?

Yes – it's called typer. It was written by Tiangolo, the author of FastAPI, and follows the same idea as FastAPI – use type hints directly as parameter declarations. The same feature written with typer looks like this:

import typer

app = typer.Typer()


@app.command()
def watermark(
    input: str,
    watermark: str = "© Two Drops",
    opacity: float = 0.5,
    verbose: bool = False,
):
    print(f"Input: {input}")
    print(f"Watermark: {watermark}")
    print(f"Opacity: {opacity}")
    print(f"Verbose: {verbose}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()

Take a look – the parameters are written right in the function signature. The type hint is the parameter type, the default value is the command-line default, and help text can be taken from the docstring automatically. The logic is the same as argparse, with half the lines and ten times the readability.

Next, let's go through typer step by step, starting from the simplest example.

docs.title: Your first typer program
docs.text:
First, install typer:

uv add typer

Or:

pip install typer

Write the simplest script, hello.py:

import typer


def hello(name: str):
    print(f"Hi {name}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    typer.run(hello)

Run it:

python hello.py TwoDrops

Output:

Hi TwoDrops

Now try it without an argument:

python hello.py

Output:

Usage: hello.py [OPTIONS] NAME
Try 'hello.py --help' for help.

Error: Missing argument 'NAME'.

typer automatically did all this for you –

  • Parsed the command-line arguments
  • Converted types (name is a str, taken straight from the command-line string)
  • Reported an error for the missing argument
  • Told you there's a --help command

Try --help:

python hello.py --help

Output:

Usage: hello.py [OPTIONS] NAME

Arguments:
  NAME  [required]

Options:
  --help  Show this message and exit.

The help text was generated by typer automatically. Did you notice? You never wrote parser.add_argument, never wrote --help, never wrote Usage – typer made all of it. That's the power of "type hints are documentation".

The line typer.run(hello) means "turn the hello function into a command-line entry point". It's good for small tools with just one command. If your tool has several commands (like add, list and done), you need the Typer app from the next section.

docs.title: An app with several commands
docs.text:
Have you used git? git commit, git push, git pull – one main command with lots of subcommands. In typer, this structure is called a multi-command app:

import typer

app = typer.Typer()


@app.command()
def add(item: str):
    """Add a task."""
    print(f"Added: {item}")


@app.command()
def list():
    """List all tasks."""
    print("Listing all tasks...")


@app.command()
def done(index: int):
    """Mark a task as done."""
    print(f"Finished task {index}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()

Look – three steps –

  1. app = typer.Typer(): create an app object
  2. Decorate the function for each command with @app.command()
  3. Start it with app()

Run it:

python todo.py add "Learn typer"
python todo.py list
python todo.py done 1

Output:

Added: Learn typer
Listing all tasks...
Finished task 1

Each function decorated with @app.command() becomes a subcommand, and the function name is the subcommand name. When the user types add, the add function runs; when they type list, the list function runs.

Try --help:

python todo.py --help

Output:

Usage: todo.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:
  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell.
  --help                Show this message and exit.

Commands:
  add   Add a task.
  done  Mark a task as done.
  list  List all tasks.

Notice the description next to each command – it comes from each function's docstring. typer reads the docstrings to make the command help. Write clear docstrings, and your CLI documentation is complete.

Subcommands have help too:

python todo.py add --help

Output:

Usage: todo.py add [OPTIONS] ITEM

  Add a task.

Arguments:
  ITEM  [required]

The description and argument list for the add subcommand are all generated automatically.

docs.title: Type hints = CLI parameters
docs.text:
The most magical thing about typer is that the type hints on your function's parameters are the types of the CLI parameters. Whatever type you write, the CLI converts to that type automatically – you don't write a single line of conversion code.

Supported types –

import typer
from pathlib import Path
from enum import Enum


class Color(str, Enum):
    red = "red"
    green = "green"
    blue = "blue"


def cmd(
    text: str,
    count: int,
    ratio: float,
    enabled: bool,
    file: Path,
    color: Color,
):
    print(f"text={text!r}")
    print(f"count={count} (type {type(count).__name__})")
    print(f"ratio={ratio} (type {type(ratio).__name__})")
    print(f"enabled={enabled}")
    print(f"file={file} (type {type(file).__name__})")
    print(f"color={color}")

Run this command –

python cmd.py "hi" 10 1.5 ./README.md red

Output:

text='hi'
count=10 (type int)
ratio=1.5 (type float)
enabled=False
file=README.md (type PosixPath)
color=Color.red

Notice a few details –

  • With the int type, "10" from the command line automatically becomes an integer
  • With the float type, "1.5" automatically becomes a float
  • With the Path type, it's automatically wrapped as a pathlib.Path object
  • With the Enum type, the value can only be red/green/blue – anything else gives an error straight away
  • A bool parameter with no default isn't a positional argument here – it becomes an --enabled/--no-enabled switch, which is why enabled=False

Try typing the wrong type:

python cmd.py "hi" abc 1.5 ./README.md red

typer refuses straight away:

Usage: cmd.py [OPTIONS] TEXT COUNT RATIO FILE COLOR
Try 'cmd.py --help' for help.

Error: Invalid value for 'COUNT': 'abc' is not a valid integer.

"Types are validation" – write int, and typer only accepts values that can become an int. Anything else never even gets into your function. Compared with argparse, where you still have to write your own try except, this is so comfortable.

docs.title: Optional parameters: the magic of default values
docs.text:
Back to the earlier example – is the parameter text: str "required" or "optional"? It's required, because it has no default value.

To make it optional, just add a default value:

def hello(name: str = "World"):
    print(f"Hi {name}")

Now typer changes it from a "positional argument" to an "option", and the command line usage becomes:

python hello.py                   # prints Hi World
python hello.py --name TwoDrops   # prints Hi TwoDrops

Notice –

  • A parameter with no default = a positional argument (Argument): required, written right after the command
  • A parameter with a default = an option (Option): optional, needs the --name prefix

This matches Python functions' "positional vs keyword arguments" logic. Whether your Python function parameter has a default decides whether the CLI gets a positional argument or an option.

Short options are easy to add too, with typer.Option:

import typer


def hello(
    name: str = typer.Option("World", "--name", "-n", help="Whose name"),
):
    print(f"Hi {name}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    typer.run(hello)

Now –

python hello.py -n TwoDrops
python hello.py --name TwoDrops

The two forms are the same. The first argument to typer.Option is the default value, then come the command-line names, and finally help is the help text.

docs.title: Required vs optional parameters: the one-sentence rule
docs.text:
If you keep going back and forth between "positional argument" and "option", here's Brother Shui's one-sentence rule –

  • "This value must be given" → positional argument. For example, cp source target – without a source or target, the command can't run
  • "This value can be left out, and there's a default behaviour" → option. For example, ls --all – it runs fine without it

In a typer function signature –

def watermark(
    input: Path,                  # positional: required
    output: Path,                 # positional: required
    text: str = "© Two Drops",    # option: optional, default watermark
    opacity: float = 0.5,         # option: optional, default 0.5
    verbose: bool = False,        # option: optional, default False
):
    ...

CLI usage:

my-tool input.jpg output.jpg
my-tool input.jpg output.jpg --text "Copyright Two Drops" --opacity 0.8 --verbose

When you write CLI tools, use 1–3 positional arguments at most – any more and users can't remember the order. If there are more than 3 parameters, make the rest options; it actually reads more clearly.

docs.title: Asking the user: prompt and confirm
docs.text:
When writing CLI tools, you often have situations like this – "the user didn't pass this value, so I want to ask them". For example, asking "Are you sure?" before deleting files, or "What's the project called?" when setting up a project.

The old way is input(). typer gives you two nicer tools – typer.prompt and typer.confirm.

First, prompt, which asks the user a question and gets the answer:

import typer


def init():
    name = typer.prompt("Project name")
    author = typer.prompt("Author", default="Two Drops")
    print(f"Creating project {name}, author {author}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    typer.run(init)

When it runs –

Project name: my-tool
Author [Two Drops]:
Creating project my-tool, author Two Drops

The default argument gives a default value – if the user just presses Enter, the default is used. Much nicer than input().

confirm asks a yes/no question:

import typer


def delete(path: str):
    sure = typer.confirm(f"Are you sure you want to delete {path}?")
    if not sure:
        print("Cancelled")
        raise typer.Abort()
    print(f"Deleted {path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    typer.run(delete)

When it runs –

$ python del.py /tmp/foo
Are you sure you want to delete /tmp/foo? [y/N]: y
Deleted /tmp/foo

By default confirm means "no" (if the user just presses Enter = no). Add default=True to make the default "yes".

typer.Abort() is another special exception – it means "the user chose to give up". The CLI exits with a standard exit code (1 by default), and the meaning is clearer than typer.Exit().

docs.title: Exiting with an error: typer.Exit and typer.Abort
docs.text:
When you write CLI tools, sometimes the command needs to exit as a "failure" – a file doesn't exist, the network is down, the user typed a wrong value. The Linux habit is "exit code 0 = success, not 0 = failure", and shell scripts use this to decide whether to carry on.

typer gives you two ways to exit –

import typer


def deploy(env: str):
    if env not in ("dev", "staging", "prod"):
        print(f"Unknown environment: {env}")
        raise typer.Exit(code=2)
    print(f"Starting deployment to {env}")

typer.Exit(code=N) makes the CLI exit straight away with exit code N. The usual conventions –

  • 0: success
  • 1: general failure
  • 2: the user typed a wrong argument

Don't just use sys.exit(N) everywhere – typer.Exit lets typer finish its own exit handling properly, so stick to typer.Exit.

The other one is typer.Abort(), meaning "the user stopped". For example, when the user answers no to the confirm above, you raise typer.Abort(). It exits with code 1 like typer.Exit(code=1), and also prints Aborted!, so the meaning is clearer.

docs.title: Coloured output: echo and secho
docs.text:
Have you noticed in the output of git status that modified files are red, staged files are green, and hint text is yellow? Adding some colour to a command-line tool makes it easier to read straight away.

typer has simple coloured output built in, called typer.echo and typer.secho:

import typer


def status():
    typer.echo("Normal text, just like print")
    typer.secho("Success!", fg=typer.colors.GREEN)
    typer.secho("Warning!", fg=typer.colors.YELLOW)
    typer.secho("Error!", fg=typer.colors.RED, bold=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    typer.run(status)

Run it in a terminal that supports colour – "Success!" is green, "Warning!" is yellow, and "Error!" is bold red. In places without colour support (like when the output is redirected to a file), typer removes the colour codes automatically, so the output stays clean.

Colours you can use – BLACK, RED, GREEN, YELLOW, BLUE, MAGENTA, CYAN, WHITE, plus styles like bold=True and underline=True.

"Why not use print?" print can't tell whether the terminal supports colour. When the output is redirected to a file, colour codes turn into messy characters like \x1b[32m and pollute the output. typer.secho handles this detail for you.

For fancier output (tables, progress bars, Markdown), typer works smoothly with rich – once rich is installed (recent versions of typer install it by default), it's used for things like nicer help and error messages.

docs.title: Nested subcommands: app.add_typer
docs.text:
When you write a big CLI tool with lots of commands, you'll want to group them – like git remote add, git remote rm, git stash push, git stash pop, "subcommands of subcommands".

typer supports nesting sub-apps:

import typer

app = typer.Typer()
remote_app = typer.Typer()
stash_app = typer.Typer()

app.add_typer(remote_app, name="remote", help="Manage remote repositories")
app.add_typer(stash_app, name="stash", help="Manage the stash")


@remote_app.command("add")
def remote_add(name: str, url: str):
    print(f"Adding remote: {name} -> {url}")


@remote_app.command("rm")
def remote_rm(name: str):
    print(f"Removing remote: {name}")


@stash_app.command("push")
def stash_push():
    print("Stashing current changes")


@stash_app.command("pop")
def stash_pop():
    print("Restoring the latest stash")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()

Run it –

python git.py remote add origin git@github.com:walter/python.git
python git.py remote rm origin
python git.py stash push
python git.py stash pop

Each sub-app can have its own sub-apps, in theory forever. But don't really nest more than three levels – users won't remember. Two levels is enough.

docs.title: Turning it into a system command: [project.scripts]
docs.text:
Right now, your typer tool runs as python todo.py add .... You have to type python every time, unlike git, which you just type directly. How do you make it a global command?

The answer is the [project.scripts] section in pyproject.toml:

[project.scripts]
todo-cli = "my_tool.cli:app"

The format is command-name = "package.path:function-name". This line means –

  • After this package is installed, the command line has a new command called todo-cli
  • Running todo-cli is the same as running app in my_tool/cli.py

A typer.Typer() object can be called like a function, so you can use app directly.

Reinstall the package:

uv pip install -e .

Then try:

todo-cli --help

The help appears straight away. Try more:

todo-cli add "Learn typer"
todo-cli list

Exactly the same as python todo.py add ... before, but the command is shorter, and it immediately feels like a real tool.

"What does uv pip install -e . mean?" -e is editable mode – it installs the package as a "link" to your source code. When you change the source, the command changes straight away, with no reinstalling. Always use -e while developing – it saves countless reinstalls.

Now all the parts for packaging + CLI are ready. In the next section, we'll tie everything together with one complete small project.

docs.title: Hands-on: todo-cli from zero to published
docs.text:
Let's follow Brother Shui and write a complete todo-cli tool, and finally publish it to PyPI (with a practice release on TestPyPI). The tool supports three commands –

  • todo-cli add "Buy vegetables": add a todo
  • todo-cli list: list all todos
  • todo-cli done 1: mark item 1 as done

The data is stored in ~/.todo-cli.json in the user's home folder – the simplest kind of local storage.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the project skeleton
docs.text:
uv init --package todo-cli
cd todo-cli
uv add typer

uv creates src/todo_cli/__init__.py automatically. We add one more file, src/todo_cli/cli.py.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the core logic
docs.text:
import json
from pathlib import Path

import typer

app = typer.Typer(help="A small todo tool by Two Drops")

DATA_FILE = Path.home() / ".todo-cli.json"


def load_todos() -> list[dict]:
    """Read the todo list. Return an empty list if the file doesn't exist."""
    if not DATA_FILE.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(DATA_FILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def save_todos(todos: list[dict]) -> None:
    """Write the todo list back to the file."""
    DATA_FILE.write_text(
        json.dumps(todos, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )


@app.command()
def add(item: str):
    """Add a todo."""
    todos = load_todos()
    todos.append({"item": item, "done": False})
    save_todos(todos)
    print(f"Added: {item}")


@app.command(name="list")
def list_todos():
    """List all todos."""
    todos = load_todos()
    if not todos:
        print("No todos yet - add one first")
        return
    for i, t in enumerate(todos, start=1):
        mark = "[x]" if t["done"] else "[ ]"
        print(f"{i}. {mark} {t['item']}")


@app.command()
def done(index: int):
    """Mark todo number index as done."""
    todos = load_todos()
    if index < 1 or index > len(todos):
        print(f"The number must be between 1 and {len(todos)}")
        raise typer.Exit(code=1)
    todos[index - 1]["done"] = True
    save_todos(todos)
    print(f"Done: {todos[index - 1]['item']}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app()

Notice a few details –

  • list is a Python built-in function, so it's better not to use it as a function name. The function is called list_todos, but @app.command(name="list") registers it as the list command
  • Path.home() / ".todo-cli.json" uses pathlib, which is much more elegant than os.path.join (see the python18 chapter)
  • typer.Exit(code=1) raises a special exception that makes the CLI exit with a non-zero exit code, so scripts can tell whether it succeeded
  • The file uses encoding="utf-8", so non-English text works on Windows too

docs.title: Step 3: Configure pyproject.toml
docs.text:
The complete pyproject.toml:

[project]
name = "todo-cli"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A tiny todo command-line tool by Two Drops"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
authors = [
    { name = "Two Drops", email = "liangdianshui@example.com" },
]
license = { file = "LICENSE" }
dependencies = [
    "typer>=0.12",
]

[project.scripts]
todo-cli = "todo_cli.cli:app"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

Notice the [project.scripts] line – after you publish, when users pip install todo-cli, they automatically get a new command called todo-cli.

docs.title: Step 4: Install it locally and try it
docs.text:
uv pip install -e .
todo-cli add "Finish python27"
todo-cli add "Go and eat"
todo-cli list
todo-cli done 1
todo-cli list

The output is roughly –

Added: Finish python27
Added: Go and eat
1. [ ] Finish python27
2. [ ] Go and eat
Done: Finish python27
1. [x] Finish python27
2. [ ] Go and eat

Open ~/.todo-cli.json and have a look:

[
  {
    "item": "Finish python27",
    "done": true
  },
  {
    "item": "Go and eat",
    "done": false
  }
]

The data is saved, so even after restarting your computer, the todos are still there.

docs.title: Step 5: Add a README and LICENSE
docs.text:
README.md:

# todo-cli

A tiny todo command-line tool by Two Drops.

## Install

```bash
pip install todo-cli

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
todo-cli add "Learn typer"
todo-cli list
todo-cli done 1

docs.title: License
docs.text:
MIT 

For the `LICENSE` file, just copy the MIT licence and change the year and name to your own.

### Step 6: Build and publish to TestPyPI

```bash
uv build
ls dist/

You get –

dist/
├── todo_cli-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
└── todo_cli-0.1.0.tar.gz

Practise on TestPyPI:

export UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN=pypi-...   # (your TestPyPI token)
uv publish --publish-url https://test.pypi.org/legacy/

After it succeeds, test it on a clean computer (or in a new virtual environment):

uv venv .test-env
source .test-env/bin/activate
pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ \
    --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ \
    todo-cli
todo-cli --help

If it works, publish to the real PyPI:

export UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN=pypi-...   # (your real PyPI token)
uv publish

Open https://pypi.org/project/todo-cli/, and your little tool is live. Brother Shui gets a bit excited again writing this – that's the feeling of "anyone in the world can use it with one line, pip install todo-cli".

"Is this name unique on PyPI?" If the name is too common, it's very likely already taken on PyPI. When you really publish, choose a more unusual name, like todo-cli-by-walter or my-todo-cli.

That's the whole process, start to finish – writing code, editing pyproject.toml, installing locally, testing locally, practising on TestPyPI, and publishing to the real PyPI.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this chapter, we've conquered two things – "packaging and publishing" and "writing CLIs". Let's review the key points –

About PyPI:

  1. PyPI is Python's global public package repository – where pip install gets things from
  2. TestPyPI is the practice ground – try a release there first, because PyPI versions can't be taken back
  3. Modern Python projects use src layout + pyproject.toml, with all the metadata in one file
  4. The minimum fields in the [project] section: name, version, description, readme, requires-python, dependencies
  5. The [build-system] section names the packaging back end – hatchling is the first choice for new projects
  6. One uv build command packages the project, producing a wheel (ready-built) and an sdist (source)
  7. One uv publish command uploads it, using a token or trusted publishing
  8. Automate version numbers – use hatch-vcs to work them out from git tags
  9. For automatic publishing in CI, use trusted publishing – cleaner than tokens: add a tag, publish a release

About typer:

  1. typer uses type hints directly as CLI parameters – 10 times simpler than argparse
  2. typer.run(func) suits single-command tools; Typer() + @app.command() suits multi-command tools
  3. Types are validation – int is checked automatically, Path is wrapped automatically, Enum limits the values automatically
  4. No default value = positional argument (required); a default value = option (optional)
  5. [project.scripts] turns a function into a system command, available everywhere once the package is installed
  6. Docstrings automatically become command help text – writing code is writing documentation

Now you have a complete chain: "write a tool → package it → publish it → let the whole world use it". Next time you want to share a little tool with a friend, don't send tool.py in a chat message – just say "pip install xxx". Very cool.

Here's some homework for you – take a Python script you use every day (renaming screenshots, counting chat messages, anything), rework it following this chapter, and practise publishing it to TestPyPI once. Even if you don't publish it to the real PyPI, going through the process once makes it muscle memory next time.

Let's go.

docs.title: First, make the rules for using your local command clear
docs.text:
When learning about packaging and publishing, let's first use the study-time tracker to check a smaller goal: when someone gets your code, can they tell how to run it, what to give as arguments, and what happens when something fails?

In the project folder, run:

python3 tracker.py --help
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json list
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json total --subject Python

For a records file that doesn't exist yet, it should show "No records yet", and the total time for the chosen subject is 0. These two queries don't create a data file just to show an empty result. Next, add a few records as in the last chapter, and check that the help, list, totals and tests all agree.

This reference tool uses the standard library's argparse, to keep the entry point separate from the core functions. You can practise typer and the packaging steps once the local features are clear – there's no need to upload a package just to check the entry point.

Write the shortest possible usage guide for your tool: which Python it needs, which folder to run it from, where records are saved, and how it reports damaged data. Once the local features work, practise packaging and installing with this chapter's TestPyPI steps, and check whether someone else can use it by following your guide.

docs.title: What to do after you finish
What to do after you finish: three paths with Python
docs.text:
Dear old friends –

If you're reading this chapter, Brother Shui wants to congratulate you first.

From python0 all the way to python27, we've talked about variables, functions, object-oriented programming, exceptions, files, modules, virtual environments, type hints, pathlib, dataclass and Pydantic, context managers, async/await + httpx, pyproject.toml, uv, pytest, working together with Git, CI/CD, publishing to PyPI… twenty-eight whole chapters, hundreds of thousands of words, hundreds of pieces of code. If you've made it here, you're no longer a beginner who "can only write print('hello')". You're a real Python engineer who can build a project from scratch, write tests, publish packages and work with a team.

But have you noticed something? After reading these twenty-eight chapters, you seem to know a lot – yet as soon as you close the book, you're not sure what to write next.

Brother Shui knows this feeling very well. Python's syntax and engineering are only the foundations. Once the foundations are built, you have to choose what kind of house to build on top. The Python world is huge – too big to learn in a lifetime. But even though it's big, there are only a few main directions. Picking one and following it is a hundred times better than aimlessly working through tutorials.

In this chapter, Brother Shui won't teach syntax or write big chunks of code. Instead, here are the three most popular paths with Python:

  1. Data / AI / machine learning – the hottest direction in 2026; Python is the native language of AI
  2. Web back-end development – fast to build, highly visible, and lots of jobs
  3. Automation / scripts / tools – turning everyday work into code; this is how Python first became popular

For each direction, Brother Shui will cover three things: why choose it, a list of must-know libraries, and three starter projects. Pick the one that suits you best and work through the projects – that's more useful than reading ten books.

Let's go.

docs.title: Why choose this direction
docs.text:
Look on job websites in 2026 and search for "Python engineer". Most of the jobs that come up include words like "data", "algorithms", "AI", "LLM", "large models" and "machine learning". That's not a coincidence – Python is the de facto native language of the AI era.

Why? Brother Shui gives three reasons –

The first is the ecosystem. From numpy/pandas in the early 2010s, to scikit-learn in 2015, to tensorflow/pytorch in 2017, to transformers/langchain and the openai/anthropic SDKs after 2022 – over twenty years, the first version of almost every important AI library was written for Python. It's not that other languages can't be used, but when you use them, you find "it doesn't connect with the main community". If everyone publishes papers using PyTorch and you rewrite things in Julia or Rust, nobody will talk to you about reproducing the paper.

The second is speed. The AI world is a place where "a paper comes out today, and someone open-sources the code tomorrow". At that speed, a Python library you can install with one pip install line is ten thousand times quicker to get going than a C++/Rust library that takes half an hour to compile. Language performance does matter, but the order "get it working first, optimise later" is pushed to the extreme in AI, and Python is the best answer for the "get it working first" step.

The third is money. In 2026, AI engineers have the highest pay of all the Python directions. Brother Shui isn't telling you to "learn AI for the money" – just that demand, earning potential and room for imagination in AI are all clearly there, so the rewards for going in this direction rise steeply.

So – if you're interested in topics like "letting machines learn by themselves", "having a model write code for me" or "making a program describe a picture", Brother Shui recommends you take a serious look at the AI path.

docs.title: Must-know libraries
docs.text:
Libraries for data/AI come in layers, from bottom to top –

Layer Example libraries What they're for Data basics numpy, pandas, matplotlib, jupyter Arrays, tables, charts and interactive notebooks – the "data starter kit" Data extras polars, seaborn, plotly A Rust-powered upgrade to pandas, prettier statistics charts, interactive charts Traditional ML scikit-learn, xgboost, lightgbm Classification, regression, clustering, decision trees, gradient boosting Deep learning pytorch, transformers, huggingface_hub Neural network frameworks; load pre-trained models in one line LLM apps anthropic, openai, langchain, llama-index Call commercial LLMs, build RAG, build agents

After seeing this table, you might feel a bit lost – "I have to learn all this?" Don't panic. This table is a map, not a checklist. A map shows you "what the scenery in this direction looks like". When you really start learning, follow this path –

  1. Master the four basics first: numpy for arrays, pandas for tables, matplotlib for charts and jupyter as your drawing board. Know these four well, and you can do 70% of data analysis tasks.
  2. scikit-learn is the way into traditional ML: decision trees, random forests, SVMs, KMeans and other classic algorithms are all inside, with a very consistent API – fit to train, predict to predict, a model in three lines of code.
  3. transformers is the shortcut to deep learning: HuggingFace packages all the main pre-trained models (BERT, GPT-2, Llama, Qwen) behind one interface. One line, pipeline('sentiment-analysis'), runs sentiment analysis. You don't need to start by chewing through PyTorch – use pre-trained models to get things done, and dig deeper when you hit a limit.
  4. LLM SDKs are the new infrastructure of 2026: anthropic calls Claude, openai calls GPT, plus langchain for orchestration and llama-index for RAG. This combination is the standard kit for the new job of "LLM application engineer".

"How can polars challenge pandas?" Brother Shui will say a little more about this – polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust. It's often 5–10 times faster than pandas, and its API is more modern (strict types, lazy evaluation, harder to get wrong). Since 2024, more and more new projects choose polars first. But pandas has a very mature ecosystem and many more tutorials, so I still recommend starting with pandas. Once you've written lots of pandas and think "this syntax is so annoying", you'll naturally go and look at polars.

docs.title: Project 1: Analyse a public dataset with pandas
docs.text:
• What to do: Download a CSV from Kaggle (try Titanic or TMDB Movies), read it into jupyter, and do 5 analyses: count missing values, draw a histogram of a distribution, draw a correlation heatmap, do a group-by summary, and make one chart that tells a story
  • Difficulty: ★☆☆☆☆
  • Amount of code: 100–200 lines
  • What you learn: the basic pandas operations read_csv/groupby/merge/pivot_table; drawing charts with matplotlib and seaborn; writing an analysis report in jupyter that "you can show other people"

Brother Shui strongly recommends making this your first project. It doesn't just teach pandas – it builds a habit every AI engineer needs: when you meet unfamiliar data, your first move is to look at the distribution, the missing values and the outliers, not to dive straight into writing a model.

docs.title: Project 2: Run a local classification model with transformers
docs.text:
• What to do: Use HuggingFace's pipeline('sentiment-analysis') to make a "good or bad movie review detector". First run a pre-trained model as it is, then download the IMDB review dataset and fine-tune it, raising the accuracy from about 85% to about 92%
  • Difficulty: ★★★☆☆
  • Amount of code: 200–400 lines
  • What you learn: how to use transformers pipeline, how to find models on the HuggingFace Hub, the Trainer API fine-tuning process, switching between GPU and CPU, saving and loading models

"What if I don't have a graphics card?" Use Google Colab. It gives you a free T4 GPU, which is enough for small models like this. Or use the MPS back end on Apple Silicon – M-series chips can train locally too.

docs.title: Project 3: Call the Claude API to make a "PDF summary" tool
docs.text:
• What to do: Write a command-line tool that takes a PDF path and outputs a 200-word summary. The process is – extract the text with pypdf → cut it into chunks of about 2000 characters → call the anthropic SDK to have Claude summarise each chunk → finally have Claude combine all the chunk summaries into one
  • Difficulty: ★★☆☆☆
  • Amount of code: 100–200 lines
  • What you learn: how to use the anthropic SDK, managing API keys (.env + python-dotenv), strategies for splitting long text, an introduction to prompt engineering, streaming output

This project is the closest to real work in 2026. Write a tool like this at a company, and it immediately solves the pain of "reading 5 industry reports every week" – your boss will want to give you a raise.

docs.title: Why choose this direction
docs.text:
"Web back end" sounds old. Do people still write it in 2026?

Yes, and lots of them. The reason is simple – every company needs APIs. Front-end frameworks keep changing (Vue, React, Svelte), and apps have gone from native to hybrid to cross-platform, but the back end is always there, steadily handling requests, reading databases, calling outside services and returning JSON.

Web back ends won't disappear – they'll only get more important, because:

  1. AI apps are really web apps. Look at ChatGPT, Claude or Cursor – the front end is a chat box, and the back end is a pile of APIs calling models. 90% of an LLM engineer's work is actually writing back ends, just with an extra "call the model" step.
  2. Microservices are still spreading. One big app per company becomes dozens of small services, and each one is a web back-end project. Python is very fast to develop with for small services like these.
  3. The widest range of jobs. Search job sites for "Python back end", and big cities post hundreds of new jobs every day – more than AI jobs, and slightly easier to get into.

So what's Python's advantage for back ends compared with Java, Go or Node? Brother Shui gives three points –

  • Fast development: A CRUD API might be about 100 lines in Python; the same feature in Java is at least 300 lines
  • Seamless connection with the AI ecosystem: If the back end needs some "call an LLM to process user input" logic, in Python it's one import
  • Since 2024, Python back-end engineering has caught up: The modern stack of fastapi + pydantic + sqlmodel + uv has type safety, automatically generated docs and decent performance – it no longer gets crushed by Go

docs.title: Must-know libraries
docs.text:
Role Example libraries What they're for Web framework fastapi, starlette Writing APIs – the main first choice Data validation pydantic Type checking for request and response bodies, deeply integrated with fastapi ASGI server uvicorn, hypercorn, granian Servers that run fastapi; in production usually uvicorn + gunicorn ORM sqlalchemy 2.x, sqlmodel Working with databases; sqlmodel is a simpler SQLAlchemy by the author of fastapi Database migrations alembic Managing table structure changes – adding a field, changing a type Caching redis-py, aiocache Redis client, in-memory cache Background tasks celery, dramatiq, arq Running emails, scrapers and scheduled jobs in the background Authentication python-jose, passlib, authlib JWT, password hashing, OAuth HTTP client httpx Calling outside APIs, sync or async Testing pytest, httpx.AsyncClient API tests

"So many – where do I start?" Go in stages, from the bottom up –

  1. Stage 1: a one-file API. Install fastapi and uvicorn, write a 50-line main.py and run it, then open http://localhost:8000/docs in a browser to see the automatically generated Swagger docs. This takes 30 minutes, and you'll be hooked straight away.
  2. Stage 2: add a database. Install sqlmodel, add a SQLite database (no separate install – Python comes with it), and write a set of CRUD endpoints (create, read, update, delete). Once this works, you can already write a decent API.
  3. Stage 3: add authentication. Install python-jose and passlib, add a /login endpoint that issues a JWT, and add Depends(get_current_user) to protect the other endpoints. After this, your API is "enterprise grade".
  4. Stage 4: add background tasks. Install celery or the lighter dramatiq, and send slow jobs like "send an email" or "generate a PDF" to the background. This step takes you to "real production" level.

"What about Django?" Django 5.x is still doing very well in 2026 – it and fastapi follow two different philosophies:

  • fastapi is "building blocks": start from nothing and install what you need – great for APIs, microservices and AI back ends
  • django is "everything included": an admin panel, ORM, templates, forms and a user system all come built in – great for "a team building a complete website from scratch"

If you later want to build content sites, online shops or company internal systems, Django is still a good choice. But if your goal is AI back ends, microservices or mobile app back ends, fastapi is the default answer in 2026.

docs.title: Project 1: A todo API (CRUD + sqlmodel)
docs.text:
• What to do: Write a to-do list API with endpoints for "create a todo", "list all todos", "get a todo by ID", "update a todo" and "delete a todo". Store the data in SQLite, use sqlmodel as the ORM, and write 5 API tests with pytest
  • Difficulty: ★☆☆☆☆
  • Amount of code: 200–300 lines
  • What you learn: fastapi routes, pydantic models, select/session.add/session.commit in the sqlmodel ORM, writing API tests with pytest, how to use the Swagger docs

Brother Shui recommends that everyone who wants to learn web back ends does this project. It's small, but it has everything – after it, you'll really feel that "writing APIs in Python is fast".

docs.title: Project 2: Add JWT authentication to the todo API
docs.text:
• What to do: Building on project 1, add a user system – a User table, a /register endpoint, a /login endpoint (returning a JWT), and protect all the other endpoints with Depends(get_current_user). Each todo is linked to a user_id, and users can only see and change their own
  • Difficulty: ★★★☆☆
  • Amount of code: 300–500 lines
  • What you learn: how JWT works, how passlib hashes passwords, fastapi's Depends dependency injection, foreign keys and joins in relational databases, "row-level isolation" for permissions

JWT is one of the most commonly asked web back-end ideas in 2026. Once you've passed this level, no back-end project will scare you.

docs.title: Project 3: Add background tasks (sending email with celery)
docs.text:
• What to do: Building on project 2, add a feature – after a user registers, send them a welcome email, but without slowing down the API response. Install celery + redis, mark the email function with @app.task, and in the register endpoint call send_welcome_email.delay(user.email) and return straight away. A worker really sends the email in the background
  • Difficulty: ★★★★☆
  • Amount of code: 400–600 lines
  • What you learn: the idea of message queues, celery's broker and backend, how to use redis as a queue, how to deploy workers, why we need background tasks (user experience, stability)

After this project, you've reached the door of "distributed back ends". Learning Kafka or microservices later all builds out from this idea.

docs.title: Why choose this direction
docs.text:
Have you heard Python's nickname – "the glue language"?

This nickname isn't praising Python for being fast, or for type safety – it's praising Python because it "can stick anything together". Python's standard library is huge, its third-party ecosystem is enormous, and it works with system calls, HTTP, databases, files, Excel, PDFs, chat apps… almost any "repetitive work" can be turned into a Python script.

This direction has a few special features –

  1. Quick results. A 50-line script might immediately save half an hour of repetitive work every day. After writing it, you use it yourself and enjoy it yourself – no need for "launches", "reviews" or "gradual rollouts".
  2. You don't need a big company. The AI and back-end directions suit working in a company (you need data, servers, a business). Automation takes off with just a laptop. You could even use it for freelance work or a side project.
  3. The easiest to start, but the ceiling isn't low. Beginners can write the simplest scripts, and more complex things like "distributed web scrapers", "company automation platforms" and "DevOps toolchains" grow from this direction too – senior jobs here are just as well paid.

If your goal is "making my daily work easier", or "doing small projects where I can see results straight away", automation is the best value choice.

docs.title: Must-know libraries
docs.text:
Purpose Example libraries What they're for HTTP requests requests, httpx Calling APIs, fetching web pages; httpx supports async Web scraping beautifulsoup4, lxml, playwright, selenium Parsing HTML, controlling a browser automatically Scheduled tasks schedule, apscheduler Run once every day at 9, or every 5 minutes Remote control paramiko, fabric SSH into a server and run commands Terminal UI rich, textual Coloured output, tables, progress bars, TUI apps CLI frameworks click, typer Writing command-line tools – argument parsing ten times more elegant than argparse Config files pyyaml, tomllib, configparser Reading YAML, TOML and INI Files pathlib, shutil, watchdog Path handling (standard library), watching files for changes Office automation openpyxl, python-docx, pypdf Excel, Word, PDF Notifications webhooks (Slack, DingTalk, Feishu, …) Send a message when something happens

"How do I learn this lot?" For automation, don't learn from the list – learn from projects. Think of "some annoying thing I do every day or every week", then use the libraries above to get rid of it, learning what you need as you go. After six months, you'll naturally know this list well.

Brother Shui has to give the rich library special praise. Written by Will McGugan, it makes Python terminal output colourful and nicely formatted, with progress bars, tables, Markdown and highlighted error tracebacks all built in. Install it, and your command-line tools immediately look "proper". textual is a TUI framework by the same author – it lets you build a responsive app inside the terminal, using components like on the web. It's loads of fun.

docs.title: Project 1: Web page change monitor + chat notifications
docs.text:
• What to do: Watch a web page (for example "the price of a product", "a blogger's latest post" or "tickets left for a train"), fetch it every 10 minutes, and when something changes, send a notification to a group chat with a webhook (Slack, DingTalk, Feishu, etc.). Schedule the script with apscheduler, use httpx for HTTP and beautifulsoup4 to parse the HTML
  • Difficulty: ★★☆☆☆
  • Amount of code: 100–200 lines
  • What you learn: HTTP GET, parsing HTML (CSS selectors), comparing states (comparing hashes, diffs), scheduled tasks, how to send webhooks

Brother Shui has written several versions of this project himself – watching blog subscriptions, concert tickets and price drops on shopping sites are all variations. Once you've made one, you can start a new monitor for anything by changing two lines – very reusable.

docs.title: Project 2: Automatically back up a folder to OSS / S3
docs.text:
• What to do: Write a script that, at 2 a.m. every day, zips a chosen folder (for example ~/Documents/Important), names it by date (backup-2026-04-28.zip), uploads it to Alibaba Cloud OSS or AWS S3, then deletes backups older than 30 days. Schedule it with apscheduler, compress with the standard library's zipfile, and upload with oss2 or boto3
  • Difficulty: ★★★☆☆
  • Amount of code: 200–300 lines
  • What you learn: walking through files (pathlib), zip compression, using an object storage SDK, managing keys (.env), lifecycle management (cleaning up by date), logging (logging)

"What's the point?" The code, notes and designs on your computer – would they all be gone if the hard drive broke one day? Write a backup script like this once, and use it for ten years. Brother Shui's Mac is still running a backup script written in 2018 that's never been changed.

docs.title: Project 3: An interactive TUI app (rich + textual)
docs.text:
• What to do: Use textual to write a terminal todo app – a list of all todos on the left, editable details on the right, a status bar at the bottom showing statistics, n to create, d to delete, e to edit. Store the data in a local JSON file
  • Difficulty: ★★★★☆
  • Amount of code: 300–500 lines
  • What you learn: textual components, layout, events, CSS styling (yes, TUIs use CSS too), keyboard shortcut bindings, managing app state

This project is a bit harder, but when you finish, you'll discover that "you can write an app like VS Code right inside the terminal". No other project gives you this sense of achievement. When Brother Shui finished his first textual app, he was so excited he posted about it on social media.

docs.title: Cross-cutting skills: things all three directions need
docs.text:
Whichever direction you choose in the end, you need to understand these cross-cutting skills – they're the "common base" of every Python engineer in 2026:

  • Git: As well as add / commit / push, learn branch / merge / rebase / cherry-pick, and be able to read git log --graph. The python25 chapter covered this – go back and look again.
  • Docker: Put your Python project into a container, write a Dockerfile, and run docker compose up to start the app + database + cache in one go. Especially important for back ends.
