  • Linux basics: ssh / cd / ls / grep / awk / tail -f / ps / top / systemctl, and be able to edit a config file with vim. A must for operations work, and the other directions should know a little too.
  • SQL basics: SELECT / JOIN / GROUP BY / WHERE / INDEX. Essential for back ends and data; automation uses it sometimes too.
  • Basic HTTP / REST ideas: GET / POST / PUT / DELETE, status codes, cookies, JWT, CORS. Useful in all three directions.

You don't need to study these separately – fill them in when you meet them while doing projects, and after six months you'll know them. The key is not to avoid unfamiliar ideas when you see them. Learn them on the spot each time, and the knowledge will naturally stick.

docs.title: How to choose a direction
docs.text:
Having read this far, you might be feeling unsure – "which one should I choose?"

Brother Shui gives a simple rule –

  • Want to ride the LLM wave, fascinated by "making machines think" → choose Data / AI
  • Want to build visible products, love seeing your results running online → choose Web back end
  • Want to lighten your workload right now, love tinkering with everyday tools → choose Automation

Or even simpler – whichever direction's "starter projects" make you want to start right away, choose that one. That "I want to get going" feeling is the most accurate inner compass.

"Can I mix them?" Of course. Brother Shui is a "automation + AI" mix himself – writing little Python tools every day, with LLM calls inside, so each tool is ten times smarter than a plain script. There are no walls between the three directions. As long as your foundations in syntax and engineering are solid, any path can take you all the way.

But at the start, Brother Shui recommends you "focus" – choose one direction for six months and finish all three projects above, then think about branching out. If you learn all three at once at the start, you'll end up half-knowing all three, with nothing to show.

docs.title: Keep learning: resources for the road ahead
docs.text:
At this point, you've graduated from "tutorial reader", and next you need to join the community yourself. Brother Shui recommends these places to follow long-term –

  • Real Python: The best Python tutorial site in the English-speaking community, from basic to advanced, with two or three in-depth articles every week
  • Talk Python To Me: A podcast hosted by Michael Kennedy – each episode invites a well-known community member to talk about one topic. Great for listening on the way to school or work
  • PyCon talks: Free to watch on YouTube – every year PyCon US / EU / China have hundreds of high-quality talks. Pick the ones that interest you
  • Python Weekly: One email a week that filters out the Python news, libraries and projects worth seeing that week
  • A new Python version comes out every October: Go to What's New in Python to see what the new version adds, and keep up with each version

The original Chinese tutorial by Brother Shui keeps being updated in the walter201230/Python repository – you're welcome to star it, watch it, and open issues and pull requests. Tutorials stay still, but communities are alive. Growing with a group of people is ten thousand times better than studying alone.

docs.title: Final words
docs.text:
Dear old friends –

Writing this, Brother Shui can't help going back to the start of the python0 chapter – "Learning Python takes one step at a time, steadily and carefully."

When Brother Shui first wrote that sentence, he never imagined it would go with you through twenty-eight chapters. "One step at a time" sounds obvious, but in daily life – writing 50 lines of code a day, reading one piece of documentation a day, making one commit a day – after six months it adds up to a real change. That's how Brother Shui learned Python too. There's no secret trick.

After python28, you have a whole Python engineer's toolbox – syntax, ecosystem, engineering and teamwork, plus a map of "where to go next". How you use this toolbox, and what kind of house you build, is up to you from now on.

Finally, Brother Shui has three things to say to every old friend who has read this far –

  1. Choose a direction, do three projects, and put them on GitHub. That's more useful than reading a hundred books.
  2. When you meet an error you don't understand, search for it first, then check Stack Overflow, and finally ask Claude. Every debugging session helps you grow.
  3. Don't stop. Python changes, AI changes, the whole industry changes every day. Stay curious and keep the habit of building things. Five years from now, when you look back at yourself in 2026, you'll thank yourself for not stopping today.

Wishing you all a bright future, and code that stays evergreen.

See you next time.

— Brother Shui April 2026

docs.title: First, finish a study-time tracker
docs.text:
The directions and resources above give you lots of choices. But first, let's use what you've already learned to make something real: a tool that records a subject and the minutes studied, lists the records, totals them by subject, and saves them to a local file.

Let's agree on the inputs and results first. Minutes are whole numbers that aren't negative, and 0 is allowed; the subject can't be empty. The same subject can appear in several records, and they're added up for the total. If the file doesn't exist, start with no records. If the file is damaged, report an error – don't treat it as an empty list and overwrite it.

Version What you do yourself How to check it Version 1 Use a list and dictionaries to store Python 15 minutes, Reading 10 minutes, Python 5 minutes It shows the three records in order Version 2 Use a loop to make the grand total and the total by subject Total 30, Python total 20 Version 3 Split it into functions, such as creating a record and totalling With no records, the total is 0; functions return results instead of only printing Version 4 Save and load with UTF-8 JSON After restarting, the text and minutes are still the same Version 5 Handle negative numbers, empty subjects and damaged files Errors are explained clearly, and an existing broken file isn't overwritten with empty data Version 6 Add a command-line entry point and tests The help explains how to use it, and all the check cases pass

After each version, first explain in your own words its inputs, its outputs and the errors it might meet, then look at the next version. Don't paste in the complete reference code at the start and then treat "it runs" as "I can write it on my own".

docs.title: Download the reference files and run them locally
docs.text:
The reference version is in the tutorial repository: tracker.py, test_tracker.py and the usage guide. Save the files into a new practice folder, open a terminal in that folder and run:

python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json add Python 15
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json add Reading 10
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json add Python 5
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json list
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json total
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json total --subject Python
python3 -m unittest -v

The last two totals are 30 and 20 minutes. Every add adds a new record, so running the whole set of commands again keeps adding up – use a fresh practice file when checking the example.

You can do the calculation practice for the first three versions in a browser first; command-line arguments, saving between runs and file tests are done on your own computer. It doesn't need an account, an API key or any online service. The records file is ordinary local JSON, with no transactions and no handling for several people writing at once – learn the process with practice data first.

docs.title: When you're done, try a new requirement
docs.text:
First add a record "Python 0 minutes", and check the total doesn't change but the record is still there. Then add a new subject, and check the subject filter isn't hard-coded. Finally, deliberately break the records file so it isn't valid JSON, and check the program reports an error and keeps the original file.

If you can explain and check all of these yourself, then think about adding dates or making a simple interface. Keep the current working version first, write down the new requirement and the result you expect, and then start changing things. You'll find that the lists, functions, exceptions and tests you learned bit by bit can now work together to finish one real job.

docs.title: 1. What is a List?
docs.text:
A List is a data type built into Python. It is an ordered collection. You can add or remove items at any time.

So why do we need lists?

Let's use an example.

A team is going on a trip, and everyone needs to sign up first. With what we have learned so far, we would store each name in its own string variable:

name1 = 'One Drop'
name2 = 'Two Drops'
name3 = 'Three Drops'
name4 = 'Four Drops'
name5 = 'Five Drops'

But this is too much work, and it doesn't look nice.

In programming, you should learn to be "lazy" and avoid repetitive work. If there were a hundred members, even copying and pasting would drive you crazy.

This is when you can use a list:

name = ['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']

Just like that, one line of code can hold lots and lots of names.

docs.title: 2. How to Create a List
docs.text:
From the example above, we can see what a list looks like:

A list is data inside square brackets []. Each piece of data inside is called an element (or item). Elements are separated by commas.

Also, the elements in a list don't have to be the same data type.

For example:

list1=['Two Drops','twowter','liangdianshui',123]

Here we have strings and an integer.

Let's print it and see what we get:

list1 = ['Two Drops', 'twowter', 'liangdianshui', 123]

print(list1)

Result:

['Two Drops', 'twowter', 'liangdianshui', 123]

docs.title: 3. How to Get Values from a List
docs.text:
Going back to our first example: sometimes we don't want to print everyone's name. Sometimes we want to know: who signed up 3rd? Who were the first two?

How do we get them out of the list?

In other words, how do we access the values in a list?

We can use the list's index (position number) to get a value. We can also use square brackets to take a slice (a part) of the list.

For example:

name = ['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']

# Get a value using its index
print(name[2])
# Take a slice of the list using square brackets
print(name[0:2])

Output:

Three Drops
['One Drop', 'Two Drops']

So, to find out who signed up third in the name list, we just use name[2].

You might ask: why 2 and not 3?

Because in the programming world, counting starts from 0, not from 1 like in everyday life.

So to find the third person,

we use name[2].

In the example, we also printed name[0:2].

Looking at the output, it only printed the first and second elements.

You might be confused here.

Why didn't it print the first three? Didn't we just say 2 means the 3rd one?

That's because a slice includes the start but excludes the end.

So name[0:2] means: start at position 0 and go up to position 2, but don't include position 2.

As always, the best way to understand is to try things and play with code.

Try all of these:

name = ['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']

print(name[0:2])
print(name[:2])
print(name[:])
print(name[1:2])
print(name[0:3])

Look at the output:

['One Drop', 'Two Drops']
['One Drop', 'Two Drops']
['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']
['Two Drops']
['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops']

With these results and what we just learned, these uses are easy to understand.

docs.title: 4. How to Update a List
docs.text:
Back to our example again. We stored the names of everyone who signed up. Later, new people might join, or we might find we spelled a name wrong and want to fix it.

What do we do then?

We can use an index to change (update) an item in the list. We can also use the append() method to add a new item.

name = ['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']


# Use an index to change or update an item
name[1]='2 Drops'
print(name)

# Use the append() method to add an item
name.append('Six Drops')
print(name)

Output:

['One Drop', '2 Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']
['One Drop', '2 Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops', 'Six Drops']

docs.title: 5. How to Delete Items from a List
docs.text:
Of course, someone might drop out halfway.

Then we need to remove their name from the list.

We use the del statement to delete an item from a list:

name = ['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']

print(name)

# Use the del statement to delete an item
del name[3]
print(name)

Output:

['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']
['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Five Drops']

Look at the output: Four Drops is no longer in the list. So it was deleted successfully.

docs.title: 6. List Operators
docs.text:
Lists work with + and * just like strings do. + joins lists together, and * repeats a list.

Python expression Result What it does len([1, 2, 3]) 3 Counts the elements [1, 2, 3] + [4, 5, 6] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] Joins ['Hi!'] * 4 ['Hi!', 'Hi!', 'Hi!', 'Hi!'] Repeats 3 in [1, 2, 3] True Checks if an element is in the list for x in [1, 2, 3]: print x, 1 2 3 Loops through it

docs.title: 7. List Functions & Methods
docs.text: Function / Method What it does len(list) Number of elements in the list max(list) Returns the biggest element min(list) Returns the smallest element list(seq) Turns a tuple into a list list.append(obj) Adds a new object to the end of the list list.count(obj) Counts how many times an element appears list.extend(seq) Adds all the values from another sequence to the end (extends the list with a new list) list.index(obj) Finds the index of the first matching value list.insert(index, obj) Inserts an object into the list list.pop(obj=list[-1]) Removes one element (the last one by default) and returns its value list.remove(obj) Removes one element (you give the element itself), and returns nothing list.reverse() Reverses the order of the elements list.sort([func]) Sorts the list

docs.title: 8. Example
docs.text:
Finally, let's use an example to get to know List operations.

Example:

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-
#-----------------------Using a list----------------------------------

# 1. A product needs to list its users. We can use a list for this
user=['liangdianshui','twowater','Two Drops']
print('1. Product users')
print(user)

# 2. To count how many users there are, len() gives the number of elements in a list
len(user)
print('\n2. Count the users')
print(len(user))

# 3. What if we need to know each user? Use an index to get the element at each position. Indexes start from 0
print('\n3. Look at each user')
print(user[0]+','+user[1]+','+user[2])

# 4. Suddenly a new user arrives. We add them to the end of the list
user.append('Yinyin')
print('\n4. Add a new user at the end')
print(user)

# 5. Another user joins, but this one is a VIP student and must go first. Use insert to put them at a chosen position
# Note: when inserting, be careful not to go out of range
user.insert(0,'VIP user')
print('\n5. Add a user at a chosen position')
print(user)

# 6. Oops, we made a mistake: "Yinyin" IS the 'VIP user', so we need to delete "Yinyin". pop() deletes the last element
user.pop()
print('\n6. Delete the last user')
print(user)

# 7. After a while, the user "liangdianshui" stopped using the product and deleted their account
# So we need to delete the element at a certain position, using pop(i), where i is the index
user.pop(1)
print('\n7. Delete the list element at a chosen position')
print(user)

# 8. The user "Two Drops" wants to change their nickname
user[2]='Three Drops'
print('\n8. Replace an element with a different one')
print(user)

# 9. Saving only nicknames isn't great. It's better to save the account number too
# The account number is an integer, not a string like the nickname, but list elements can be different types
# A list element can even be another list
newUser=[['VIP user',11111],['twowater',22222],['Three Drops',33333]]
print('\n9. A list with different types of elements')
print(newUser)

Output:

1. Product users
['liangdianshui', 'twowater', 'Two Drops']

2. Count the users
3

3. Look at each user
liangdianshui,twowater,Two Drops

4. Add a new user at the end
['liangdianshui', 'twowater', 'Two Drops', 'Yinyin']

5. Add a user at a chosen position
['VIP user', 'liangdianshui', 'twowater', 'Two Drops', 'Yinyin']

6. Delete the last user
['VIP user', 'liangdianshui', 'twowater', 'Two Drops']

7. Delete the list element at a chosen position
['VIP user', 'twowater', 'Two Drops']

8. Replace an element with a different one
['VIP user', 'twowater', 'Three Drops']

9. A list with different types of elements
[['VIP user', 11111], ['twowater', 22222], ['Three Drops', 33333]]

docs.title: You copied the list – so why do both change?
docs.text:
Let's use the sign-up list again. We want to keep a copy of the original list, then add one more person to the current list. Look carefully: do the two assignments below do the same thing?

names = ['One Drop', 'Two Drops']
another_name = names
saved_names = names.copy()
another_name.append('Three Drops')
print(names)
print(saved_names)

Output:

['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops']
['One Drop', 'Two Drops']

another_name = names just gives the same list a second name. names.copy() makes a new list. Changing the original list's items won't change this new list.

Now try it yourself: change names to an empty list, append a name, and look at both results. Then think: if the items in the list were lists themselves, would copy() make a new copy of each inner list too? No. A normal list copy is a shallow copy. When you have objects inside objects, you need to check whether the inner objects are shared.

Lists are good for storing a group of things that can change and have an order. In a tuple, you can't reassign any position. But if a tuple holds a list, the contents of that list can still change. Keep "the outer positions can't change" and "the objects inside can't change" separate in your head, and similar-looking code won't trick you.

docs.title: 1. What is a tuple?
docs.text:
In the last section we talked about an ordered list, the List. Now let's look at another kind of ordered list: the tuple.

A tuple is very similar to a List, but once a tuple is created, it can't be changed. We say a tuple is immutable. So what does "immutable" mean?

It means that once you create a tuple, it can't change. It has no methods like append() or insert(). You can still get the value at an index, but you can't assign a new value to it.

So why do we need tuples?

Because tuples can't change, your code is safer.

So if you can use a tuple instead of a list, it's a good idea to use a tuple.

docs.title: 2. How to Create a tuple
docs.text:
Creating a tuple is easy. Just put the elements inside round brackets, separated by commas.

tuple1=('Two Drops','twowter','liangdianshui',123,456)
tuple2='Two Drops','twowter','liangdianshui',123,456

Create an empty tuple:

tuple3=()

If a tuple has only one element, you must add a comma after it:

tuple4=(123,)

Without the comma, you don't get a tuple – you just get the number 123.

This is because round brackets () can mean a tuple, but they can also mean brackets in a maths formula. That's confusing.

So with only one element and no comma, the computer can't tell if you want to do maths with an integer or float, or if you mean a tuple.

So Python's rule is: in this case, treat them as maths brackets. The result is of course 123. If you want a tuple, you need to add a comma.

Look at the output of tuple4 and tuple5 below:

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-
tuple1 = ('Two Drops', 'twowter', 'liangdianshui', 123, 456)
tuple2 = 'Two Drops', 'twowter', 'liangdianshui', 123, 456
tuple3 = ()
tuple4 = (123,)
tuple5 = (123)
print(tuple1)
print(tuple2)
print(tuple3)
print(tuple4)
print(tuple5)

Output:

('Two Drops', 'twowter', 'liangdianshui', 123, 456)
('Two Drops', 'twowter', 'liangdianshui', 123, 456)
()
(123,)
123

docs.title: 3. How to Get Values from a tuple
docs.text:
Tuple indexes also start from 0. You can use an index to get a value from a tuple.

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-

tuple1=('Two Drops','twowter','liangdianshui',123,456)
tuple2='Two Drops','twowter','liangdianshui',123,456

print(tuple1[1])
print(tuple2[0])

Output:

twowter
Two Drops

docs.title: 4. "Changing" a tuple
docs.text:
When you see this heading, you might be confused. Didn't we just spend a long time saying tuples can't change?

So why are we changing a tuple now?

Because although you can't change the element values in a tuple, you can join tuples together. You can also change a list that is inside a tuple, which affects how the tuple looks.

Look at this example:

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-
list1=[123,456]
tuple1=('Two Drops','twowater','liangdianshui',list1)
print(tuple1)
list1[0]=789
list1[1]=100
print(tuple1)

Output: 

('Two Drops', 'twowater', 'liangdianshui', [123, 456])
('Two Drops', 'twowater', 'liangdianshui', [789, 100])

We can see the tuple printed differently the two times. Let's see how tuple1 is stored.

tuple1 has four elements. The last element is a List, and the List has two elements.

When we change the List's two elements from 123 and 456 to 789 and 100, the printed tuple1 looks like it really changed.

But actually, what changed was not the tuple's elements – it was the list's elements.

The tuple still points to the same list it pointed to at the start. So when we say a tuple "doesn't change", we mean that what each element points to never changes. The fourth element of tuple1 still points to the original list. We only changed the elements inside that list.

docs.title: 5. Deleting a tuple
docs.text:
You can't delete single elements from a tuple. But you can use the del statement to delete the whole tuple.

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-

tuple1=('Two Drops','twowter','liangdianshui',[123,456])
print(tuple1)
del tuple1

docs.title: 6. tuple Operators
docs.text:
Just like strings, you can use + and * with tuples. This means you can join and repeat them. The result is a new tuple.

Python expression Result What it does len((1, 2, 3)) 3 Counts the elements (1, 2, 3) + (4, 5, 6) (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) Joins ('Hi!',) * 4 ('Hi!', 'Hi!', 'Hi!', 'Hi!') Repeats 3 in (1, 2, 3) True Checks if an element is there for x in (1, 2, 3): print(x) 1 2 3 Loops through it

docs.title: 7. Built-in tuple Functions
docs.text: Function What it does len(tuple) Counts the elements in a tuple max(tuple) Returns the biggest element min(tuple) Returns the smallest element tuple(seq) Turns a list into a tuple

docs.title: 8. Example
docs.text:
Finally, just like with lists, here's an example. Try out all the different things you can do with tuples.

name1 = ('One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops')

name2 = ('1 Drop', '2 Drops', '3 Drops', '4 Drops', '5 Drops')

list1 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Count the elements
print(len(name1))
# Join: add two tuples together
print(name1 + name2)
# Repeat a tuple
print(name1 * 2)
# Is the element there? (Does name1 contain 'One Drop'?)
print('One Drop' in name1)
# The biggest element
print(max(name2))
# The smallest element
print(min(name2))
# Turn a list into a tuple
print(tuple(list1))

Output:

5
('One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops', '1 Drop', '2 Drops', '3 Drops', '4 Drops', '5 Drops')
('One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops', 'One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops')
True
5 Drops
1 Drop
(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

docs.title: 1. What is a dict?
docs.text:
In the last chapter, we learned to use lists and tuples for ordered collections.

When we talked about lists, we used a list to store people's names:

name = ['One Drop', 'Two Drops', 'Three Drops', 'Four Drops', 'Five Drops']

Now, what if we want to contact these friends easily, and we need to add their phone numbers too?

With a list, we could do this:

name = [['One Drop', '131456780001'], ['Two Drops', '131456780002'], ['Three Drops', '131456780003'], ['Four Drops', '131456780004'], ['Five Drops', '131456780005']]

But this isn't very handy. We saved the phone numbers so we can quickly contact someone when we need to.

If we store them in a list, the longer the list gets, the longer it takes to find someone.

This is when we can use a dict (dictionary). Python has dicts built in. If you know Java, a dict is like a map in Java. It stores data as key-value pairs, and it can find things extremely fast.

name = {'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780002', 'Three Drops': '131456780003', 'Four Drops': '131456780004', 'Five Drops': '131456780005'}

docs.title: 2. Creating a dict
docs.text:
A dictionary is another kind of changeable container, and it can store any type of object.

Each key: value pair is split by a colon (:). Pairs are separated by commas (,). The whole dictionary goes inside curly braces ({}), like this:

dict = {key1 : value1, key2 : value2 }

Note: keys must be unique, but values don't have to be. Values can be any data type, but keys must be immutable (unchangeable).

To be more exact, dictionary keys must be hashable. A tuple that contains a list is itself immutable, but it still can't be a dictionary key. So you can't decide only by "changeable or unchangeable".

Examples of creating dicts:

dict1={'liangdianshui':'111111' ,'twowater':'222222' ,'Two Drops':'333333'}
dict2={'abc':1234,1234:'abc'}

docs.title: 3. Getting Values from a dict
docs.text:
Now we know how to create a dict. Back to our first question: why does a dictionary help us find someone's phone number so quickly?

name = {'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780002', 'Three Drops': '131456780003', 'Four Drops': '131456780004', 'Five Drops': '131456780005'}

print(name['Two Drops'])

Output:

131456780002

As you can see, if you know someone's name (the key), you can very quickly find their phone number (the value).

One thing to note: if the key is not in the dictionary, you will get an error.

docs.title: 4. Changing a dict
docs.text:
To add new content to a dictionary, add a new key/value pair. You can also change or delete existing pairs.

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-
dict1={'liangdianshui':'111111' ,'twowater':'222222' ,'Two Drops':'333333'}
print(dict1)
# Add a new key-value pair
dict1['jack']='444444'
print(dict1)
# Change a key-value pair
dict1['liangdianshui']='555555'
print(dict1)

Output:

{'liangdianshui': '111111', 'twowater': '222222', 'Two Drops': '333333'}
{'liangdianshui': '111111', 'twowater': '222222', 'Two Drops': '333333', 'jack': '444444'}
{'liangdianshui': '555555', 'twowater': '222222', 'Two Drops': '333333', 'jack': '444444'}

docs.title: 5. Deleting from a dict
docs.text:
You can use del to delete one item from a dict, or to delete the whole dict.

You can call the clear() method to remove all items from a dict.

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-
dict1={'liangdianshui':'111111' ,'twowater':'222222' ,'Two Drops':'333333'}
print(dict1)
# Delete an item using its key
del dict1['twowater']
print(dict1)
# Remove all items from the dict
dict1.clear()
print(dict1)
# Delete the dict
del dict1

Output:

{'liangdianshui': '111111', 'twowater': '222222', 'Two Drops': '333333'}
{'liangdianshui': '111111', 'Two Drops': '333333'}
{}

docs.title: 6. Things to Watch Out For with dicts
docs.text:
(1) A dict can't have the same key twice. If you give the same key a value twice when creating a dict, the last value wins.

For example:

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-
dict1={'liangdianshui':'111111' ,'twowater':'222222' ,'Two Drops':'333333','twowater':'444444'}
print(dict1)
print(dict1['twowater'])

Output:

{'liangdianshui': '111111', 'twowater': '444444', 'Two Drops': '333333'}
444444

(2) dict keys must be immutable. Keys can be numbers, strings or tuples, but not lists.

For example:

#-*-coding:utf-8-*-
dict1={'liangdianshui':'111111' ,123:'222222' ,(123,'tom'):'333333','twowater':'444444'}
print(dict1)

Output:

{'liangdianshui': '111111', 123: '222222', (123, 'tom'): '333333', 'twowater': '444444'}

(3) The order things are stored inside a dict has nothing to do with the order you added the keys. (This changed in Python 3.7 – see section 8 below.)

Compared with a list, a dict:

  • Finds and adds items extremely fast, and doesn't get slower as you add more keys

  • Uses a lot of memory, and wastes quite a bit

A list is the opposite:

  • Finding and adding items takes longer as the list grows

  • Uses little space and wastes very little memory

docs.title: 7. dict Functions and Methods
docs.text: Method / Function What it does len(dict) Counts the items in the dict str(dict) Gives a printable string version of the dict type(variable) Returns the variable's type. If it's a dict, it returns the dict type dict.clear() Removes all items from the dict dict.copy() Returns a shallow copy of the dict dict.values() Returns all the values in the dict as a list popitem() Removes and returns a key-value pair from the dict dict.items() Returns a list of (key, value) tuples you can loop through

docs.title: 8. New in Python 3.9+: the dict merge operator
docs.text:
Hey everyone! We have covered adding, deleting, changing and finding things in a dict. Now here's a nice extra that came in Python 3.9: the dict merge operators | and |=.

Why talk about this specially?

Let's look at a task first. Say Brother Shui has two contact dictionaries, and needs to merge them into one:

old_contacts = {'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780002'}
new_contacts = {'Three Drops': '131456780003', 'Two Drops': '131456780099'}

Look carefully: the key 'Two Drops' is in both. We want the new one to win.

Before Python 3.9, people usually wrote it like this:

old_contacts = {'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780002'}
new_contacts = {'Three Drops': '131456780003', 'Two Drops': '131456780099'}

merged = {**old_contacts, **new_contacts}
print(merged)

Output:

{'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780099', 'Three Drops': '131456780003'}

This ** unpacking works fine, but it's not very easy to read. From Python 3.9, you can just use |:

old_contacts = {'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780002'}
new_contacts = {'Three Drops': '131456780003', 'Two Drops': '131456780099'}

merged = old_contacts | new_contacts
print(merged)

Output:

{'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780099', 'Three Drops': '131456780003'}

Notice anything? It looks exactly like the set union |. That's on purpose – it means "join the two dicts together".

If you don't want a new dictionary, and instead want to merge the new content into the original dictionary, use |=:

old_contacts = {'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780002'}
new_contacts = {'Three Drops': '131456780003', 'Two Drops': '131456780099'}

old_contacts |= new_contacts
print(old_contacts)

Output:

{'One Drop': '131456780001', 'Two Drops': '131456780099', 'Three Drops': '131456780003'}

Note: with |, the right side overwrites the left side, the same as {**a, **b}. Keep this in mind so you don't mix up which side is new and which is old.

Finally, one more point I didn't stress before: since Python 3.7, dicts keep insertion order. This means the earlier rule, "the order inside a dict has nothing to do with the order you added keys", is no longer true in modern Python. Look at this example:

d = {}
d['c'] = 3
d['a'] = 1
d['b'] = 2

for key in d:
    print(key)

Output:

c
a
b

See? The loop goes in the same order the keys were added. This is guaranteed by the language in Python 3.7+ (in 3.6 it already worked this way in CPython, but it wasn't an official rule). So in most cases now, you don't need import collections.OrderedDict any more – a normal dict is enough.

docs.title: Studying the same subject again: how to update the record
docs.text:
We've recorded 15 minutes of Python and 10 minutes of reading. If we study Python for another 5 minutes, do we add the same key again, or change the old value?

totals = {'Python': 15, 'Reading': 10}
totals['Python'] = totals['Python'] + 5
print(totals)
print(totals.get('Maths', 0))

Output:

{'Python': 20, 'Reading': 10}
0

In one dictionary, each key can only have one value. Before assigning, we take out the old 15, add 5, and store it back. So the Python total becomes 20. get('Maths', 0) means: if this subject isn't there, give back the default value 0 that we provided. It does not add a new key.

Try it yourself: change the right side to just 5. What's different? Then add a new subject to the dictionary and check whether the old records are still there. After we learn loops, we'll handle lots of study records.

docs.title: 2. set
docs.text:
A Python set is like sets in other languages: an unordered collection with no duplicate elements. Its main jobs are testing relationships between groups and removing duplicates.

A set is like a dict, but a set doesn't store values – only keys.

docs.title: 1. Creating a set
docs.text:
To create a set, you can give it a list:

set1=set([123,456,789])
print(set1)

Output:

{456, 123, 789}

The argument [123,456,789] is a list. The output {456, 123, 789} just tells you the set holds the 3 elements 456, 123 and 789. The order shown is different from the order in your list. This shows that a set has no order.

Also, notice the output is inside curly braces. From what we've learned: a tuple uses round brackets, a list uses square brackets, and a dict uses curly braces. A dict stores key-value pairs, while you can think of a set as storing only keys.

Note the version difference here: since Python 3.7, a normal dict keeps the order keys were added. A set still does not keep insertion order. And a dict keeping order is not the same as sorting the keys.

Remember: when creating a dict, a repeated key gets overwritten by the later key-value pair. In a set, repeated elements are automatically filtered out.

set1=set([123,456,789,123,123])
print(set1)

Output:

{456, 123, 789}

docs.title: 2. Adding Elements to a set
docs.text:
Use the add(key) method to add an element to a set. You can add the same thing again, but it has no effect.

set1=set([123,456,789])
print(set1)
set1.add(100)
print(set1)
set1.add(100)
print(set1)

Output: 

{456, 123, 789}
{456, 123, 100, 789}
{456, 123, 100, 789}

docs.title: 3. Removing Elements from a set
docs.text:
Use the remove(key) method to remove an element from a set.

set1=set([123,456,789])
print(set1)
set1.remove(456)
print(set1)

Output:

{456, 123, 789}
{123, 789}

docs.title: 4. Using sets
docs.text:
Because a set is an unordered collection with no duplicates, two sets can do maths operations like union, intersection and difference.

Think of them with a Venn diagram:

  • Union: both circles are fully coloured in – all the elements from both sets together
  • Intersection: only the middle part where the circles overlap is coloured – elements that are in both sets
  • Difference: only the first circle, minus the part that overlaps the second – elements in the first set but not in the second

Example:

set1=set('hello')
set2=set(['p','y','y','h','o','n'])
print(set1)
print(set2)

# Intersection (the elements both sets have)
set3=set1 & set2
print('\nIntersection set3:')
print(set3)
# Union (join both sets and remove duplicates)
set4=set1 | set2
print('\nUnion set4:')
print(set4)
# Difference
set5=set1 - set2
set6=set2 - set1
print('\nDifference set5:')
print(set5)
print('\nDifference set6:')
print( set6)


# To remove duplicates from a huge list, you could use hashing, but it's not very fast. A set does this nicely
list1 = [111,222,333,444,111,222,333,444,555,666]  
set7=set(list1)
print('\nRemove duplicates from a list, set7:')
print(set7)

Output:

{'h', 'l', 'e', 'o'}
{'h', 'n', 'o', 'y', 'p'}

Intersection set3:
{'h', 'o'}

Union set4:
{'h', 'p', 'n', 'e', 'o', 'y', 'l'}

Difference set5:
{'l', 'e'}

Difference set6:
{'p', 'y', 'n'}

Remove duplicates from a list, set7:
{555, 333, 111, 666, 444, 222}

docs.title: 5. A Few Extras about Modern sets
docs.text: Hey everyone! Everything above works in all versions of Python. Here are three more things that are common in modern code, to make your coding smoother.

docs.title: (1) Set comprehensions
docs.text:
When we learn about lists, we use list comprehensions like [x * x for x in range(5)]. Sets have their own set comprehensions. They look almost the same – just swap the square brackets for curly braces:

# The squares of all even numbers from 1 to 10
squares = {x * x for x in range(1, 11) if x % 2 == 0}
print(squares)

Output:

{64, 4, 36, 100, 16}

Notice the result is automatically unordered with no duplicates. You don't need to call set() yourself.

Here's a more real-world example. Say Brother Shui wants to get the unique customers from a pile of orders:

orders = [
    {'user': 'One Drop', 'amount': 100},
    {'user': 'Two Drops', 'amount': 200},
    {'user': 'One Drop', 'amount': 50},
    {'user': 'Three Drops', 'amount': 300},
]

users = {order['user'] for order in orders}
print(users)

Output (the order may be different):

{'Two Drops', 'One Drop', 'Three Drops'}

Done in one line – much cleaner than making an empty set and using add.

docs.title: (2) frozenset: a set that can't change
docs.text:
A normal set can change: you can add and remove. But sometimes we want a set that can't be changed – for example, to use it as a dict key, or to put it inside another set.

That's when you use frozenset:

fs = frozenset([1, 2, 3])
print(fs)

# You can do set operations with it
print(fs & frozenset([2, 3, 4]))

# You can use it as a dict key
config = {frozenset(['admin', 'editor']): 'Admin panel access'}
print(config[frozenset(['editor', 'admin'])])

Output:

frozenset({1, 2, 3})
frozenset({2, 3})
Admin panel access

Look at the last part: frozenset(['admin', 'editor']) and frozenset(['editor', 'admin']) are equal – because sets have no order – so both lookups find the same key.

docs.title: (3) When to use a set instead of a list
docs.text:
This last point isn't new syntax, but it's very important. When we check if something is in a group, like x in collection:

  • If collection is a list, the time is O(n). The more elements, the slower it is.
  • If collection is a set (or dict), the time is close to O(1). It hardly depends on how many elements there are.

So if your code checks "is this thing in that pile?" a lot, changing the pile from a list to a set can make it much, much faster:

# We have 100,000 usernames and want to check if a name is there
names_list = [f'user_{i}' for i in range(100000)]
names_set = set(names_list)

# Both give the same answer, but the second one is much faster
print('user_99999' in names_list)
print('user_99999' in names_set)

Output:

True
True

So a set isn't only useful for removing duplicates – even more important, it's great for fast lookups. When your code does lots of in checks, think about switching to a set.

docs.title: 1. What is a Loop?
docs.text:
Almost every programming language has loops. Why?

Ask yourself: why do we write programs?

To make our work easier and help us work more efficiently, of course!

Computers are different from humans. Computers don't get tired, don't complain, and don't need a rest. They can keep going forever.

And remember: what computers are best at is doing the same thing again and again.

That's why we need loops. A loop lets us run a statement, or a group of statements, many times.

Here's the general shape of a loop:

Python has for loops and while loops.

Now here's another question: what if I want the loop to stop after 100 times? How do I do that?

We use some loop control statements:

Loop control statement What it does break Stops the loop while it's running, and jumps out of the whole loop continue Stops the current round of the loop, skips the rest of it, and goes to the next round pass pass is an empty statement. It's there to keep the program's structure complete

These control statements let us tell the program when to stop, and when to skip this round.

docs.title: 2. The for Loop
docs.text:
Let's look at the for loop first.

Its flow chart looks like this:

The basic syntax:

for iterating_var in sequence:
   statements(s)

Using this basic syntax, let's write a quick test:

for letter in 'Hello Shui':
    print(letter)

Output:

H
e
l
l
o

S
h
u
i

From the output, we can see it prints the string Hello Shui one character at a time.

What if we use a dictionary instead of a string?

dict = {'One Drop': 'Primary student', 'Two Drops': 'Middle school student', 'Three Drops': 'High school student'}

for i in dict:
    print(i)

Output:

One Drop
Two Drops
Three Drops

You'll see it only prints each key in the dictionary.

I often tell everyone: whenever you learn something new, try it out lots of ways.

A conclusion you find yourself by trying once is better than hearing someone else say it ten times.

Don't know what to try?

Use our examples to think of new ones. For the for loop above, we tried a string and a dictionary. What other basic data types have we learned?

If you don't remember, go back and look. Try all the basic types.

For example, if you try, you'll find that integers and floats can't be put directly into a for loop:

a = 100

b = 0.01

for i in a:
    print(i)

for i in b:
    print(i)

Running it gives an error:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/twowater/dev/python/test/com/twowater/test.py", line 5, in <module>
    for i in a:
TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable

docs.title: 3. The range() Function
docs.text:
for loops are often used together with the range() function.

If you don't know range(), let's understand it with some code:

for i in range(3):
    print(i)

Output:

0
1
2

So it prints 0 up to (but not including) 3.

range(x) makes a sequence of whole numbers from 0 to x-1.

range(a,b) makes a sequence of whole numbers that includes a but not b.

In fact, range(3) in the example can be written as range(0,3) – the result is the same.

Most of the time, we use range() to run some code n times.

Here's a question: look closely at range(). Whether it has 1 argument or 2, what do they have in common?

Did you notice? They always go up by 1 each time.

range(3) is 0, 1, 2 – going up by 1 each time.

range(3,6) is 3, 4, 5 – also going up by 1 each time.

Can we go up by something other than 1?

What if I want to go up by 2?

When you write programs, you'll definitely need this. And of course Python's range can do it.

So range can also take three arguments.

For example, range(0,10,2) means: count from 0 to 10 (not including 10), going up by 2 each time.

for i in range(0, 10, 2):
    print(i)

Output:

0
2
4
6
8

docs.title: 4. The while Loop
docs.text:
A while loop does the same job as a for loop.

Let's see what a while loop looks like:

count = 1
sum1 = 0

while count <= 100:    # The condition
    sum1 = sum1 + count    # The body of the while loop
    count = count + 1

print(sum1)

Output:

5050

This example adds up all the whole numbers from 1 to 100.

docs.title: 5. The Difference Between for and while Loops
docs.text:
As we said before, if one piece of syntax can do a job, there's no need for two.

Since both are loops, for and while must be different in some way.

So when should you use a for loop, and when a while loop?

  • A for loop is mainly for going through an iterable (something you can loop over).

  • A while loop is mainly for repeating something as long as a condition is true. (For example, an endless loop that exits with break.)

  • In some cases, for and while can be swapped.

For example:

for i in range(0, 10):
    print(i)


i = 0
while i < 10:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1

The output is the same, but if you think carefully, you'll see they run in a different way and need different information.

docs.title: 6. Nested Loops
docs.text:
Like conditional statements, loops can be nested.

Here's the syntax:

Nested for loop syntax

for iterating_var in sequence:
   for iterating_var in sequence:
      statements(s)
   statements(s)

Nested while loop syntax

while expression:
   while expression:
      statement(s)
   statement(s)

You can also put a different kind of loop inside: a for loop inside a while loop, or a while loop inside a for loop.

For example:

If we want to stop adding once sum is over 1000, we can use break to exit the whole loop.

count = 1
sum = 0
while (count <= 100):
    sum = sum + count
    if ( sum > 1000):  # Exit the loop when sum is over 1000
        break
    count = count + 1
print(sum)

Output:

1035

Sometimes we only want to add up the odd numbers between 1 and 100. That means when count is even, we want to skip this round and not add it. We can use continue for this:

count = 1
sum = 0
while (count <= 100):
    if ( count % 2 == 0):  # Skip even numbers
        count = count + 1
        continue
    sum = sum + count
    count = count + 1
print(sum)

Output:

2500

And another one:

for num in range(10,20):  # Go through the numbers from 10 to 20
   for i in range(2,num): # Go through possible factors
      if num%i == 0:      # Found the first factor
         j=num/i          # Work out the second factor
         print (f'{num} is a composite number')
         break            # Jump out of the current loop
   else:                  # The else part of the loop
      print (f'{num} is a prime number')

Output:

10 is a composite number
11 is a prime number
12 is a composite number
13 is a prime number
14 is a composite number
15 is a composite number
16 is a composite number
17 is a prime number
18 is a composite number
19 is a prime number

This example also uses a for … else statement.

The statements in the for loop work as normal. The statements in else run only if the loop finishes normally – that is, if the for loop was not stopped by break.

And just like for … else, there is also while … else. They mean the same thing.

docs.title: 3. Examples Using Conditions and Loops Together
1. Print the Times Tables
docs.text:
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

# Print the 1–9 times tables
for i in range(1, 10):
        for j in range(1, i+1):
            # f-string: put f before the string, and any expression inside {} is worked out and put into the string
            print(f'{i}x{j}={i*j}\t', end='')
        print()

Output:

1x1=1   
2x1=2   2x2=4   
3x1=3   3x2=6   3x3=9   
4x1=4   4x2=8   4x3=12  4x4=16  
5x1=5   5x2=10  5x3=15  5x4=20  5x5=25  
6x1=6   6x2=12  6x3=18  6x4=24  6x5=30  6x6=36  
7x1=7   7x2=14  7x3=21  7x4=28  7x5=35  7x6=42  7x7=49  
8x1=8   8x2=16  8x3=24  8x4=32  8x5=40  8x6=48  8x7=56  8x8=64  
9x1=9   9x2=18  9x3=27  9x4=36  9x5=45  9x6=54  9x7=63  9x8=72  9x9=81

docs.title: 2. Check for a Leap Year
docs.text:
# Check whether a year is a leap year

year = int(input("Enter a year: "))
if (year % 4) == 0 and (year % 100) != 0 or (year % 400) == 0:
    print(f'{year} is a leap year')
else:
     print(f'{year} is not a leap year')

docs.title: First, write down how you'd count by hand
docs.text:
We're going to add up study time. The records might include 0, and might include negative numbers typed by mistake. Let's agree on a rule first: zero minutes is allowed and kept, but negative numbers are skipped for now. How would you do this by hand? Start from zero, look at each record one by one, and only add the ones that follow the rule.

records = [15, 0, 10, -3]
total = 0
valid_count = 0
for minutes in records:
    if minutes < 0:
        continue
    total = total + minutes
    valid_count = valid_count + 1
print(total)
print(valid_count)

Output:

25
3

Don't just look at the total. Follow the loop step by step and write down minutes, total and valid_count each time. Zero minutes doesn't add to the total, but it's still a valid record, so the count of valid records is 3.

Try two edge cases yourself: an empty list should give 0 and 0. A list of only negative numbers should too. If you change the check to minutes <= 0, the total might stay the same, but the count changes. This shows that one correct number in the output doesn't mean the whole program does what it should.

Skipping negative numbers is just the rule for this exercise. Not every program should quietly skip mistakes. When we learn about exception handling, we'll change it to tell the caller what was wrong.

docs.title: 1. What is a Conditional Statement?
docs.text:
Conditional statements in Python work basically the same as in other languages. The result of one or more checks (True or False) decides which block of code runs.

In Python, any value that is not 0 and not empty counts as True. 0 or empty (null) counts as False.

Here is the flow chart:

docs.title: 2. The Basic Form of an if Statement
docs.text:
In Python, the basic form of an if statement looks like this:

if condition:
    do something……
else:
    do something else……

As we said in earlier chapters, Python is very strict about indentation, so be careful with it here. And don't forget the colon :.

In the condition of an if statement, you can use > (greater than), < (less than), == (equal to), >= (greater than or equal to) and <= (less than or equal to) to compare things.

For example:

# -*-coding:utf-8-*-

results=59

if results>=60:
    print ('Pass')
else :
    print ('Fail')

Output:

Fail

As we said above, non-zero numbers, non-empty strings, non-empty lists and so on count as True. Everything else is False. So you can also write:

num = 6
if num :
    print('Hello Python')

Output:

Hello Python

So the message was printed.

What if we change num to an empty string?

num = ''
if num :
    print('Hello Python')

Nothing is printed (the program ends normally, without printing Hello Python).

Clearly, an empty string is False. It doesn't meet the condition, so print('Hello Python') never runs.

One more reminder: after the colon : in a condition, the next line must be indented. If it's not indented, you get an error.

num = ''
if num :
print('Hello Python')

Running it gives an error:

  File "/Users/twowater/dev/python/test/com/twowater/test.py", line 4
    print('Hello Python')
        ^
IndentationError: expected an indented block

The colon and indentation are part of the syntax. They help Python see which code belongs where, and understand the logic and order of what runs.

docs.title: 3. if with Several Conditions in Turn
docs.text:
Sometimes we need more than two choices. In the example above, 60 or more is a pass. What if we also want 90+ to be "Excellent", and 80 – 90 to be "Good"?

Then we use an if statement with several conditions.

In pseudocode (plain-language code):

if condition1:
    do thing 1……
elif condition2:
    do thing 2……
elif condition3:
    do thing 3……
else:
    do thing 4……

Example:

# -*-coding:utf-8-*-

results = 89

if results > 90:
    print('Excellent')
elif results > 80:
    print('Good')
elif results > 60:
    print ('Pass')
else :
    print ('Fail')

Output:

Good

docs.title: 4. if Checking Several Conditions at Once
docs.text:
What do we do when there are several conditions at the same time?

For example, a student is "Excellent" only if both their Java and Python test scores are over 80. How do we do that?

We can use or and and.

or means the check succeeds if at least one of the two conditions is true.

and means the check succeeds only if both conditions are true.

For example:

# -*-coding:utf-8-*-

java = 86
python = 68

if java > 80 and  python > 80:
    print('Excellent')
else :
    print('Not excellent')

if ( java >= 80  and java < 90 )  or ( python >= 80 and python < 90):
    print('Good')

Output:

Not excellent
Good

Note: when an if has several conditions, you can use brackets to show which to check first. Checks inside brackets happen first. Also, and and or have lower priority than >, < and other comparison symbols. So without brackets, greater-than and less-than are checked before and/or.

docs.title: 5. Nested if
docs.text:
What is a nested if?

It's just what it sounds like: an if statement inside another if statement.

The example above can also be written with a nested if:

java = 86
python = 68

if java > 80:
    if python > 80:
        print('Excellent')
    else:
        print('Not excellent')
else:
    print('Not excellent')

Output:

Not excellent

Of course, this is just to show that if statements can be nested. For this task, I don't really recommend nesting like this. It makes the code longer, and too much nesting makes code hard to read.

docs.title: 6. New in Python 3.10+: match / case
docs.text:
Hey everyone! If you're using Python 3.10 or newer, there's another, clearer tool besides if / elif / else: match / case. It's called structural pattern matching.

Why talk about it specially?

Let's look at a task first. Say Brother Shui wants to do different things depending on a command string from the server:

command = 'start'

if command == 'start':
    print('Starting')
elif command == 'stop':
    print('Stopping')
elif command == 'pause':
    print('Pausing')
else:
    print('Unknown command')

Output:

Starting

Nothing wrong with this. But when there are lots of choices, a long chain of elif gets wordy. Let's rewrite it with match / case:

command = 'start'

match command:
    case 'start':
        print('Starting')
    case 'stop':
        print('Stopping')
    case 'pause':
        print('Pausing')
    case _:
        print('Unknown command')

Output:

Starting

case _ is the "catch-all" branch, like else. The underscore _ is a wildcard. It matches anything that none of the earlier cases matched.

If you like to think, you might ask: isn't this just switch / case from other languages, with different syntax?

Not quite! The real power of match / case is that it can match structure, not just values.

Here's an example matching a sequence. Say the product team sends us a coordinate:

point = [10, 20]

match point:
    case [0, 0]:
        print('Origin')
    case [x, 0]:
        print(f'On the x-axis, x = {x}')
    case [0, y]:
        print(f'On the y-axis, y = {y}')
    case [x, y]:
        print(f'Normal point, x = {x}, y = {y}')
    case _:
        print('Not a 2D coordinate')

Output:

Normal point, x = 10, y = 20

See? It didn't just match "this is a list of length 2" – it also unpacked x and y for you, ready to use in that branch.

In a sequence, you can also use *rest to collect the remaining elements:

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

match nums:
    case [first, *rest]:
        print(f'First: {first}, the rest: {rest}')

Output:

First: 1, the rest: [2, 3, 4, 5]

What about dictionaries?

match / case can also match the shape of a dictionary:

response = {'status': 'ok', 'data': [1, 2, 3]}

match response:
    case {'status': 'ok', 'data': data}:
        print(f'Success, got data {data}')
    case {'status': 'error', 'message': msg}:
        print(f'Failed: {msg}')
    case _:
        print('Unknown response')

Output:

Success, got data [1, 2, 3]

Even cooler, match / case works with classes too. It's even better with dataclass:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int


p = Point(0, 5)

match p:
    case Point(x=0, y=0):
        print('Origin')
    case Point(x=0, y=y):
        print(f'On the y-axis, y = {y}')
    case Point(x=x, y=0):
        print(f'On the x-axis, x = {x}')
    case Point(x=x, y=y):
        print(f'Normal point ({x}, {y})')

Output:

On the y-axis, y = 5

Finally, one small feature called a guard: you add an if after the case:

score = 75

match score:
    case x if x >= 90:
        print('Excellent')
    case x if x >= 80:
        print('Good')
    case x if x >= 60:
        print('Pass')
    case _:
        print('Fail')

Output:

Pass

See how match / case makes code more structured and easier to read?

One more note: match / case is not meant to replace if / elif. For simple value comparisons and true/false checks, a plain if is actually clearer. match / case really shines when you choose what to do based on the structure of data – for example, reading JSON, working with syntax trees, or writing an interpreter.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
People often say computers are amazing and super smart. Actually, computers aren't smart at all. Just trying to talk to one can drive you crazy! The smart one is you, the person writing the program.

Writing a program means talking to the computer and telling it what to do.

So of course, we need some logic when we talk to it. For example, you need to tell the computer what to do in which situation, or what to do at what time.

All of this needs logical decisions. That's what this chapter is about.
