docs.title: 1. What is a Python Module?
docs.text:
As you write more and more code, a single file gets longer and longer, and harder and harder to look after.

Then we learned functions. A function is a piece of code that does one or more jobs, which makes it easier to reuse code.

After that, we learned classes. A class can wrap up methods and variables (attributes) together, which makes code even easier to look after.

We learned before that a class looks like this:

And the module we're learning now looks like this:

In a module, we can store variables directly, and also functions, and also classes.

Do you remember? We wrap up a function with def, and a class with class.

But to make a module, we don't need any statement at all.

In Python, one .py file is called a module.

Look at an example I wrote earlier in PyCharm. A test.py file like this is a module:

test ~/dev/python/test
├── com
│   └── twowater
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── iter.py
│       └── test.py        ← This is a module
│   └── __init__.py
└── venv

# What's inside test.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

A module is really an extension of what functions do. Why do we say that?

Because a module is a block of code that does one or more jobs.

From this, it's easy to see that functions and modules are both for doing jobs. A module is just bigger than a function – a module can hold many functions.

But if we already have functions, why do we need modules?

The biggest benefit is that they make code much easier to look after.

Also, you don't have to write code from scratch. Once a module is written, it can be used anywhere else. When we write programs, we often use other modules, including Python's built-in modules and modules from other people (third-party modules).

Modules also help avoid name clashes between functions and variables. Functions and variables with the same name can live in different modules without any problem. So when we write our own modules, we don't have to worry about names clashing with other modules. But be careful not to clash with the names of built-in functions.

Python comes with lots of really useful built-in modules. Once Python is installed, you can use them straight away. Let's try to find them. My Python is installed in the default folder, C:\Users\Administrator\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python36. Inside it, find the Lib folder, and you'll see it's full of modules. That's right – these .py files are modules.

Some of the files in the Lib folder look like this:

File Date modified Size _compat_pickle.py 2017/2/13 22:38 9 KB _compression.py 2017/2/13 22:38 6 KB _dummy_thread.py 2017/2/13 22:38 6 KB _markupbase.py 2017/2/13 22:38 15 KB _osx_support.py 2017/2/13 22:38 20 KB _pydecimal.py 2017/3/21 17:46 232 KB _pyio.py 2017/3/21 17:46 89 KB _sitebuiltins.py 2017/2/13 22:38 4 KB _strptime.py 2017/2/13 22:38 25 KB _threading_local.py 2017/2/13 22:38 8 KB _weakrefset.py 2017/2/13 22:38 6 KB abc.py 2017/2/13 22:38 9 KB aifc.py 2017/3/4 5:11 33 KB antigravity.py 2017/2/13 22:38 1 KB argparse.py 2017/2/13 22:38 91 KB ast.py 2017/3/21 17:46 13 KB

Modules can be split into standard library modules and custom modules (ones you write yourself). Everything we just saw in the Lib folder is a standard library module.

docs.title: 1. import
docs.text:
Using modules in Python is similar to other languages. To use a module, you must import it first. We import a module with the keyword import.

The basic syntax of import:

import module1[, module2[,... moduleN]

For example, let's use the math module from the standard library. When the interpreter sees an import statement, and the module is in the current search path, it gets imported.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import math

_author_ = 'Two Drops'

print(math.pi)

Output:

3.141592653589793

A module is only imported once, no matter how many times you run import. This stops the module from running again and again.

When we use import, how does the Python interpreter find the right file?

This involves Python's search path. The search path is a list of folders, and the Python interpreter looks for the module in each folder in turn. It's a lot like an environment variable – in fact, you can set the search path with an environment variable. The search path is decided when Python is built or installed, and installing new libraries may also change it. It's stored in the path variable of the sys module.

So we can look at the path:

#!/usr/bin/env python
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import sys

print(sys.path)

Output:

['C:\\Users\\Administrator\\Desktop\\Python\\Python8Code', 'G:\\PyCharm 2017.1.4\\helpers\\pycharm', 'C:\\Users\\Administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\Python\\Python36\\python36.zip', 'C:\\Users\\Administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\Python\\Python36\\DLLs', 'C:\\Users\\Administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\Python\\Python36\\lib', 'C:\\Users\\Administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\Python\\Python36', 'C:\\Users\\Administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\Python\\Python36\\lib\\site-packages', 'C:\\Users\\Administrator\\Desktop\\Python\\Python8Code\\com\\Learn\\module\\sys']

docs.title: 2. from···import
docs.text:
Have you wondered how to import a specific attribute or method from a module directly?

In Python, we use the import keyword to import a module. Note: this only imports the module – it doesn't import any specific attribute or method from inside it. If we want to import one specific thing from a module (an attribute or method) directly, we can use the from···import statement.

The syntax:

from modname import name1[, name2[, ... nameN]]

After reading this, you might wonder: what's the difference between from···import and import?

To find out, look at these two examples:

Use import to import the sys module, then use its version attribute:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import sys

print(sys.version)   # Use the imported sys module to get its methods or attributes
print(version)       # Error! You can't use version directly, because only the sys module was imported

Result:

3.6.1 (v3.6.1:69c0db5, Mar 21 2017, 18:41:36) [MSC v.1900 64 bit (AMD64)]
NameError: name 'version' is not defined

Use from···import to import the version attribute directly:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

from sys import version

print(version)   # Use version directly – no need for the sys. prefix

Result:

3.6.1 (v3.6.1:69c0db5, Mar 21 2017, 18:41:36) [MSC v.1900 64 bit (AMD64)]

docs.title: 3. from ··· import *
docs.text:
From the above, we know from sys import version imports the version attribute directly.

But what if we want to use other attributes too?

For example, executable from the sys module. Do we have to write another line, from sys import executable? Two is OK, but what about three, or four?

Do we just keep writing more and more lines?

That's when you use from ··· import *. This statement imports all the methods and attributes from a module. For example:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

from sys import *

print(version)
print(executable)

Output:

3.6.1 (v3.6.1:69c0db5, Mar 21 2017, 18:41:36) [MSC v.1900 64 bit (AMD64)]
C:\Users\Administrator\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python36\python.exe

Note: this gives you a simple way to import everything from a module. But you shouldn't use it too much.

docs.title: Learning to use a module you don't know
docs.text:
You don't need to memorise modules one by one. First, be clear about what you need right now: round a number up. We look in the standard library docs and find math.ceil. We check what it takes in and what it gives back, and then test it with very small inputs.

from math import ceil

print(ceil(2.1))
print(ceil(0))
print(ceil(-2.1))

Output:

3
0
-2

The negative number result is worth stopping to think about: rounding up doesn't mean making the number's size bigger. After reading a function's description, checking it with a positive number, zero and a negative number helps you spot misunderstandings much better than trying just one positive number.

Later, in the final project, we'll put functions into tracker.py, and a test file will import them. Importing a module and running a script directly have different purposes. if __name__ == '__main__' lets the command-line entry point start only when the file is run directly. That way, when a test imports the file, it won't ask for command-line input.

If an import fails, first write down which Python is actually running, the current folder, the file name and the full error. Remove the unrelated code and keep only that one import to test. Also, don't name your own files things like math.py or json.py – they might hide the module you actually wanted to import.

docs.title: 1. What Main and Non-Main Modules Are
docs.text: With Python functions, if a function calls other functions to do a job, we call it a main function. If a function doesn't call other functions, we call it a non-main function. Main and non-main modules are similar: if a module is run directly and not used by anyone else, we call it the main module. If a module is imported by another one, we call it a non-main module.

docs.title: 2. The name Attribute
docs.text:
Python has main modules and non-main modules, so of course we need a way to tell them apart. How?

We use the __name__ attribute. __name__ is a variable that Python sets for us. We can use it to check whether a module is the main module. If its value is '__main__', then this module is the main module, and if not, it isn't. But note: __name__ being '__main__' only helps us CHECK whether it's the main module. It doesn't DECIDE whether it's the main module. What decides it is only whether the module was imported by someone else.

Let's look at an example:

First we create a module called lname, and check whether it's the main module. If it is, print main; if not, print not main. When we run this module directly, it's being used directly and not imported by anyone, so it's the main module, and it prints main:

The code in com/Learn/module/nameattributes/lname.py:

#!/usr/bin/env python
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print('main')
else:
    print('not main')

Run lname.py directly. Output:

main

Then we create another module, user_lname, which simply imports the lname module. When we run it, the output is not main, because lname was imported by this module, so it's not the main module:

The code in com/Learn/module/nameattributes/user_lname.py:

#!/usr/bin/env python
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

import lname   # Import the lname module

Run user_lname.py. Output:

not main

docs.title: 4. Packages
docs.text:
We've actually already created different package names in some of the examples above – look closely and you'll see.

At the start of the modules introduction, we said modules help avoid name clashes between functions and variables.

Functions and variables with the same name can live in different modules without any problem. So when we write our own modules, we don't have to worry about names clashing with other modules. But be careful not to clash with the names of built-in functions.

But there's still a problem: what if different people write modules with the same module name?

To avoid module name clashes, Python lets you organise modules into folders. This is called a package.

The first example used packages. That way, even if two modules have the same name, they won't clash, because their package names are different – in other words, their paths are different. As shown below, with the package names added, lname.py actually becomes com.Learn.module.nameattributes.lname.

Python8Code
└── com
    └── Learn
        └── module
            └── nameattributes
                ├── __init__.py
                ├── lname.py        ← com.Learn.module.nameattributes.lname
                └── user_lname.py
            └── __init__.py
        └── __init__.py
    └── __init__.py

If you look carefully, you'll notice every package folder has an __init__.py file. Why?

Because this file is required. Without it, Python treats the folder as a normal folder, not a package. __init__.py can be an empty file, or it can have Python code in it, because __init__.py is itself a module, and its module name is the package name.

docs.title: 5. Scope
docs.text:
If you've learned Java, you know that in a Java class, methods and attributes can be public or private. This is because we want some functions and attributes to be used by others, and some to be used only inside.

Modules in Python are a bit like classes in Java. So how do we make some functions and variables in a module available to others, and keep some only for use inside the module?

In Python, we use a _ prefix. Normal function and variable names are public and can be used directly, like abc, ni12, PI and so on. Names like __xxx__ are special variables. They can be used directly, but they have special purposes. For example, __name__ above is a special variable, and so is __author__, which shows who wrote the code.

Note: don't usually use names like this for your own variables. Functions or variables like _xxx and __xxx are non-public (private) and shouldn't be used directly, like _abc, __abc and so on.

We say "shouldn't", not "can't". Python has no way to completely stop you from accessing private functions or variables. But as a good coding habit, you shouldn't use private functions or variables from outside.

For example:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-

def _diamond_vip(lv):
    print('Hello, dear Diamond member')
    vip_name = 'DiamondVIP' + str(lv)
    return vip_name


def _gold_vip(lv):
    print('Hello, dear Gold member')
    vip_name = 'GoldVIP' + str(lv)
    return vip_name


def vip_lv_name(lv):
    if lv == 1:
        print(_gold_vip(lv))
    elif lv == 2:
        print(_diamond_vip(lv))


vip_lv_name(2)

Output:

Hello, dear Diamond member
DiamondVIP2

In this module, we make the vip_lv_name function public, and the inner logic is done in the private functions _diamond_vip and _gold_vip. Since that's internal logic, the caller doesn't need to care about those functions at all – they only need to call vip_lv_name. So using private names is a really useful way to wrap up and hide details in your code.

Usually, any function that doesn't need to be used from outside should be private, and only functions that need to be used from outside should be public.

But we put it here so you can have a quick look and get a first impression. Later, as you learn, it will also be easy to come back and check.

docs.title: 1. Encoding
docs.text:
• Unless there is a special reason, always save files in UTF-8 encoding.
  • Unless there is a special reason, put #-*-coding:utf-8-*- at the top of the file.

docs.title: 2.1 Indentation
docs.text: • Always use 4 spaces for indentation.

docs.title: 2.2 Line Length
docs.text:
Try to keep each line under 80 characters. (In special cases it can be a bit longer than 80, but never more than 120.)

Why:

  • It helps when you compare two versions of code side by side.
  • It's easier to read code in a terminal window.
  • A line that is too long may mean the design has a problem.

docs.title: 2.3 Quotes
docs.text:
Simply put: use double quotes for human language, and single quotes for machine labels. So in code, you should mostly use single quotes.

  • Human language uses double quotes "..." For example, error messages. In many cases this is unicode, written as u"Hello world"
  • Machine labels use single quotes '...' For example, the keys in a dict
  • Regular expressions use raw double quotes r"..."
  • Documentation strings (docstrings) use three double quotes """......"""

docs.title: 2.4 Blank Lines
docs.text:
• Leave two blank lines between top-level functions and class definitions.
  • Leave one blank line between methods inside a class.
class A:

    def __init__(self):
        pass

    def hello(self):
        pass


def main():
    pass
  • You can use several blank lines to separate groups of related functions.
  • Inside a function, you can use blank lines to separate parts of the logic.

docs.title: 3. import Statements
docs.text:
• Write each import on its own line.
# Correct
import os
import sys

# Not recommended
import sys,os

# Correct
from subprocess import Popen, PIPE
* Use absolute imports. 
# Correct
from foo.bar import Bar

# Not recommended
from ..bar import Bar
  • Put imports at the top of the file, after the module description and docstring, and before global variables.
  • Put imports in order, with one blank line between each group.
import os
import sys

import msgpack
import zmq

import foo
  • When you import a class from another module, you can use a relative import.
from myclass import MyClass
  • If two names clash, use the namespace (the module name) to tell them apart.
import bar
import foo.bar

bar.Bar()
foo.bar.Bar()

docs.title: 4. Spaces
docs.text:
• Put one space on each side of a binary operator [=,-,+=,==,>,in,is not, and]:
# Correct
i = i + 1
submitted += 1
x = x * 2 - 1
hypot2 = x * x + y * y
c = (a + b) * (a - b)

# Not recommended
i=i+1
submitted +=1
x = x*2 - 1
hypot2 = x*x + y*y
c = (a+b) * (a-b)
  • In a function's parameter list, put a space after each ,
# Correct
def complex(real, imag):
    pass

# Not recommended
def complex(real,imag):
    pass
  • In a function's parameter list, do not put spaces around the = of a default value.
# Correct
def complex(real, imag=0.0):
    pass

# Not recommended
def complex(real, imag = 0.0):
    pass
  • Don't add extra spaces right after an opening bracket or right before a closing bracket.
# Correct
spam(ham[1], {eggs: 2})

# Not recommended
spam( ham[1], { eggs : 2 } )
  • Don't put extra spaces before the opening bracket of an index.
# Correct
dict['key'] = list[index]

# Not recommended
dict ['key'] = list [index]
  • Don't add extra spaces just to line up = signs.
# Correct
x = 1
y = 2
long_variable = 3

# Not recommended
x             = 1
y             = 2
long_variable = 3

docs.title: 5. Line Breaks
docs.text:
Python lets you break a line inside brackets. There are two ways to do it.

1) Line the second line up with the opening bracket.

foo = long_function_name(var_one, var_two,
                         var_three, var_four)

2) Indent the second line by 4 spaces. Use this when you break the line right after the opening bracket.

def long_function_name(
        var_one, var_two, var_three,
        var_four):
    print(var_one)

You can also use a backslash \ to break a line. Binary operators like + and . should go at the end of the line. Long strings can be broken this way too.

session.query(MyTable).\
        filter_by(id=1).\
        one()

print 'Hello, '\
      '%s %s!' %\
      ('Harry', 'Potter')

Don't write compound statements – that means don't put several statements on one line:

# Correct
do_first()
do_second()
do_third()

# Not recommended
do_first();do_second();do_third();

if/for/while must always start a new line for their body:

# Correct
if foo == 'blah':
    do_blah_thing()

# Not recommended
if foo == 'blah': do_blash_thing()

docs.title: 6. docstring
docs.text:
The two most basic docstring rules:

  1. Every public module, function, class and method should have a docstring. Private methods don't need one, but you should put a block comment after the def to explain them.
  2. The closing """ of a docstring should be on its own line, unless the whole docstring fits on one line.
"""Return a foobar
Optional plotz says to frobnicate the bizbaz first.
"""

"""Oneline docstring"""

docs.title: 1.1 Block Comments
docs.text:
Put one space after the #. Separate paragraphs with an empty comment line (which still needs a #).

# Block comment
# Block comment
#
# Block comment
# Block comment

docs.title: 1.2 Inline Comments
docs.text:
Leave at least two spaces between the code and the comment. Don't write comments that say nothing useful.

# Correct
x = x + 1  # Make the border one pixel thicker

# Not recommended (a useless comment)
x = x + 1 # add 1 to x

docs.title: 1.3 Tips
docs.text:
• In important parts of your code (or tricky parts), try to write comments whenever you can.

  • For really important comments, put lines of = around them so they stand out.

app = create_app(name, options)


# =====================================
# Do NOT add get/post app routes here !!!
# =====================================


if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run()

docs.title: 2. Documentation Comments (Docstrings)
docs.text:
A docstring is usually placed at the top of a module, function or class. Python can then read it through the object's __doc__ attribute. Editors and IDEs can also use docstrings to show helpful hints.

  • A docstring starts and ends with """. Don't break the line right after the opening quotes. If it has several lines, the closing quotes must be on a new line. Here is an example in Google's docstring style:
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""Example docstrings.

This module demonstrates documentation as specified by the `Google Python
Style Guide`_. Docstrings may extend over multiple lines. Sections are created
with a section header and a colon followed by a block of indented text.

Example:
    Examples can be given using either the ``Example`` or ``Examples``
    sections. Sections support any reStructuredText formatting, including
    literal blocks::

        $ python example_google.py

Section breaks are created by resuming unindented text. Section breaks
are also implicitly created anytime a new section starts.
"""
  • Don't just copy the function's signature into the docstring. Instead, describe what it does, and explain the parameters and return value.
#  Not recommended (don't just repeat the signature)
def function(a, b):
    """function(a, b) -> list"""
    ... ...


#  Correct
def function(a, b):
    """Work out and return the average of the data from a to b"""
    ... ...
  • Describe parameters and return values using the numpy style, like this:
def func(arg1, arg2):
    """Write a one-sentence summary here (e.g. Calculate the average).

    Write the detailed description here.

    Parameters
    ----------
    arg1 : int
        Description of arg1
    arg2 : int
        Description of arg2

    Returns
    -------
    int
        Description of the return value

    See Also
    --------
    otherfunc : other related functions...

    Examples
    --------
    Examples use doctest format. Code after `>>>` can be run automatically
    as test cases by doc-testing tools.

    >>> a=[1,2,3]
    >>> print [x + 3 for x in a]
    [4, 5, 6]
    """

  • Docstrings can be in any language, but don't mix two languages in one docstring.

  • Longer is not better. Usually one or two sentences are enough to explain things.

  • Modules, public classes and public methods should have docstrings whenever possible.

docs.title: 1. Modules
docs.text:
• Module names should be lowercase, starting with a lowercase letter. Try not to use underscores (unless the name has a few words).
# Good module names
import decoder
import html_parser

# Not recommended
import Decoder

docs.title: 2. Class Names
docs.text:
• Class names use CamelCase: start each word with a capital letter. Private classes can start with one underscore.
class Farm():
    pass

class AnimalFarm(Farm):
    pass

class _PrivateFarm(Farm):
    pass
  • Put related classes and top-level functions in the same module. Unlike Java, you don't need one module per class.

docs.title: 3. Functions
docs.text:
• Function names are always lowercase. If there are several words, join them with underscores.
def run():
    pass

def run_with_env():
    pass
  • Put one underscore _ in front of private function names.
class Person():

    def _private_func():
        pass

docs.title: 4. Variable Names
docs.text:
• Variable names should be lowercase. If there are several words, join them with underscores.
if __name__ == '__main__':
    count = 0
    school_name = ''
  • Constants are ALL CAPITALS. If there are several words, join them with underscores.
MAX_CLIENT = 100
MAX_CONNECTION = 1000
CONNECTION_TIMEOUT = 600

docs.title: 5. Constants
docs.text:
• Constants use capital letters, with words separated by underscores.
MAX_OVERFLOW = 100

class FooBar:

    def foo_bar(self, print_):
        print(print_)

docs.title: Study-time tracker
docs.text:
This is the complete reference version of the extra practice in "What to do after you finish". It brings together variables, containers, loops, functions, files, exceptions and tests. The input is a subject and a number of minutes (a whole number, not negative); the output is a list of records and totals. The data is saved in a local JSON file that you choose. It only uses the Python 3.10+ standard library – no account or third-party service needed.

Open a terminal in this folder, run the help first, then practise with a fresh records file:

python3 tracker.py --help
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json add Python 15
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json add Reading 10
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json add Python 5
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json list
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json total
python3 tracker.py --file practice-records.json total --subject Python
python3 -m unittest -v

The total should be 30 minutes, and the Python total should be 20 minutes. Adding more keeps adding to the existing records, so don't add the same set again and again just to compare with the example. Zero minutes is allowed; negative numbers, empty subjects, damaged JSON and content with the wrong fields all give an error. If the file doesn't exist, it starts with an empty list; if an existing file is damaged, its content is kept and not overwritten with empty data.

You can try building it yourself first without looking at tracker.py, in this order:

  1. Write three records using a list and dictionaries, and print them.
  2. Use a loop to total all the minutes, and the minutes for one subject.
  3. Write make_record(subject, minutes) and total_minutes(records, subject=None).
  4. Save and load with UTF-8 and JSON, then start the program again to check.
  5. Handle invalid input and damaged files.
  6. Read test_tracker.py and make your own version pass the tests. If you already have pytest, you can also run python3 -m pytest -q.

First explain each function's inputs, outputs and when it fails, then compare with the reference version. The test data lives in a separate system temporary folder, so the tests never read your real study records.

The browser practice page is good for running pure Python calculations. Files in the browser belong to a virtual file system inside the page – they aren't files on your computer's disk, and they might not be kept after a refresh. Do the terminal, argument and saving-between-runs practice on your own computer.

This tool is for teaching. It writes JSON directly when saving, with no transactions, no handling for several people writing at once, and no automatic backups. Use practice data to check it – don't use it as a real data store.
